3. Handoff surfaces — billing (seat overages, mid-cycle adds), permissions (who can invite, who can own a workspace), import/migration (can an SMB import 200-seat-shaped data?), human help (tier of CSM/support access).

4. Support volume + sales-assist rules — operational consequence of the above. This is where the "Q3 real" question actually answers itself, because if support load scales linearly with SMB count and the CSM tier is human, Q3 doesn't ship.

5. Refusal list — what we won't let SMB do regardless of seat count. Lives next to feature fences as a paired doc, but flagged as the hard line.

Framing for Owen (the 3-sentence version):

This isn't a product drop. It's definition drift that we already knew was coming: v3 shipped 2023-03-16, so May is fully v3-era, and the older notebook is computing v2 semantics on v3-era data. The two definitions are not interchangeable — "two logins in 14 days" and "one in-product event in 14 days" surface different signal, and v3 deliberately traded login-shell traffic for product-seen guardrails. The right move is to stop comparing them head-to-head until we've quantified the overlap; calling the gap a regression would be the manufactured emergency.

Suggested opener to Owen, if useful:

"Hey — I think this is the v2/v3 definition drift we flagged at ship, not a May regression. The notebook is still on v2 semantics. Before either of us forwards these numbers or relabels the dashboard, can we run a few sanity checks today so we know what we're actually saying?"

Pre-flight checks before forwarding May activation or editing dashboard labels:

1. Same-population check (most likely source of a "fake" mismatch)
   - Both views filtering to identical signup window
   - Both using the same segment cut — confirm mid-seg v2 reclassification (50-75 → starter on 2023-04-26) is applied consistently. May data crosses that line, so a view still using pre-4/26 segments will drift.
   - Both anchoring the 14-day window to the same start event (signup vs first integration). v2 historically anchored differently than v3 in some builds — worth confirming.

2. Definition-implementation check
   - v3's "in-product event" — confirm the PostHog event taxonomy matches what was specced at ship. Owen drove the v3 ship, so he should be able to say whether the dashboard is reading the intended events or has silently fallen back to a session-start proxy.
   - v2's "two logins" — confirm what counts: full session, SSO completion, any URL hit. If v2 is counting things v3 deliberately filters out (e.g. login-shell loads with no telemetry fired), the gap is real and intentional, not a bug.

3. Quantify the drift, don't just stare at it
   - Build a 2x2 on May signups: activated under v2 only / v3 only / both / neither. The asymmetry is the story.
   - If v3-only > v2-only, v3 is the more inclusive definition (catches product-engaged accounts v2 missed). If v2-only > v3-only, v3 is filtering out login-shell traffic that v2 was counting.
   - Memory note from earlier: v2 specifically excluded accounts that wired an integration and had data flowing but didn't click around — so expect a non-trivial v3-only bucket, not just a v2-only one.

   - v2-only: do they actually have two login events and zero product events, or is something misfiring?
   - v3-only: do they actually have a product event and <2 logins, or did we lose SSO sessions somewhere?

The framing rule: a cell is GREEN if the gate passes and the product supports it; YELLOW if either side is unclear or partially ready (default to CSM-assisted); RED if either side fails (decline/refer). FRAME (read this before the rows)

Eligibility cells = who is allowed into the SMB self-serve motion. This is a sales/CSM/onboarding decision, not an engineering one.

Product-constraint cells = what the product can safely support today. This is what Daniela's team is sizing: instrumentation, dashboards, permissions, import, migration surfaces.

If the two get merged, engineering ends up scoping the eligibility workflow (which is an ops problem, not an Eng problem). The split below prevents that.

DECISION RULE (applies to every row)

  All cells GREEN              -> self-serve
  Any cell YELLOW, no RED      -> CSM-assisted onboarding (still in motion, not self-serve)
  Any cell RED                 -> decline / refer out of motion


ROW 1 - FIRST INTEGRATION

  Eligibility gate:
    Primary integration must be one we have a stable v2 path for.
    If the integration is in the historically-troublesome set
    (the two failure patterns Ines flagged 6/9), gate = RED

  Product constraint (Eng scope):
    Integration success path is instrumented end-to-end.
    Failure path is observable in the motion dashboard.
    If telemetry doesn't exist yet, default YELLOW until it lands.


ROW 2 - ADMIN & PERMISSIONS COMPLEXITY

  Eligibility gate:
    Customer can name a single admin owner.
    Role model is standard (no nested role chains, no SCIM).
    Non-standard role model at intake = RED until a scoping call.

  Product constraint:
    Permissions engine supports the admin model without a
    CSM hand-config.
    Permission failures have an event taxonomy and a documented
    recovery path.


ROW 3 - IMPORT HELP

  Eligibility gate:
    Customer's import volume sits BELOW the self-serve volume
    threshold AND the integration type is NOT in the
    historically-troublesome set.
    Either condition fails = RED for self-serve; refer to the
    migration track.

  Product constraint:
    Self-serve import is reliable below the threshold.
    Import failures have a recoverable retry path and a

    Above-threshold imports are NOT in self-serve scope - they

Three reads of Owen's split, in the order I'd want to handle them:

WHAT IT SUPPORTS

- The nudge mechanism isn't a null. There is real expansion behavior somewhere in the cohort, and it's concentrated in accounts that have the surface area for it. That is a useful signal even if you don't ship.
- A targeting hypothesis is now on the table. "The nudge works on accounts with depth" is a falsifiable claim you didn't have a week ago. Worth keeping; not worth acting on yet.
- The low-depth slice is not catastrophically negative. "Nearly flat" rules out the worst-case read (we are burning expansion on people who don't have room to expand). That's a low bar, but it clears it.

WHAT IT DOESN'T SUPPORT

- Widening 25% to 50%. The aggregate is +$6.10 vs. the +$8 bar. The bar was set before you saw the split for a reason; the split doesn't lower the bar, it gives you a different question to ask. If Marcus wants to widen, he needs to make that case against the original aggregate, not the slice.
- Treating the high-depth number as a clean read. It's a slice of a 25% allocation that's been live for ~30 days. The N on the slice is smaller than the N on the aggregate, the variance is wider, and expansion behavior has lag — accounts nudged in week 1 may still be converting. Owen's weekly cuts presumably hold the window constant, but that doesn't give you a powered read on a sub-slice.
- Reading "low-depth nearly flat" as "low-depth is unaffected." At your current N, flat and slightly-negative are observationally identical. You have not shown the nudge is harmless on that slice; you have shown the nudge is small on that slice relative to your current sample.
- Using any of this as Helio Start gate evidence. Different cohort, different mechanism, different decision. Owen's split doesn't change the seam you drew at the readout.
- A retention read. This is expansion MRR at one window. You have nothing on whether nudged high-depth accounts retain or churn differently at month 3–6. A "ship the segment" decision made on this number is making it on one dimension.

THE TRAP

The trap is "ship the segment, not the flag." It will sound like: high-depth is materially ahead, low-depth is roughly flat, so let's narrow the rollout to high-depth at a higher percentage and call it a win. That is a targeting decision disguised as an expansion decision, and it breaks three things at once:

1. You re-define the experiment. Any post-change lift is now treatment-on-high-depth plus a targeting change. You cannot attribute the lift to the original nudge — you have confounded the nudge with the eligibility filter.
2. You move the bar. The original +$8 was the aggregate gate against which the whole 25%-vs-50% sequence was designed. Replacing it with a high-depth-only bar is letting the result choose its own threshold. Owen's weekly cuts stop being comparable to anything you've shipped before.
3. You inherit a selection effect you didn't measure. High-depth accounts that opt into being high-depth on a narrow flag are not the same population as high-depth accounts inside a broad flag. You're already doing the two most important things (brown noise, low lights). Here's a structure for the next 30 minutes and how to decide on the walk after.

30-minute anchor (8:36–9:06 PM)

- 0–5 min: Move Kibo to the most interior, sound-buffered room — back bedroom, interior bathroom, or walk-in closet beats the kitchen. Bring the water bowl, a towel/blanket that smells like you, and slide the brown noise source closer to that room. Close the door so hallway sound doesn't echo.
- 5–15 min: Sit on the floor near Kibo, not above. Don't coax out from under furniture — let them choose to come to you. Offer a long-lasting lick (peanut butter on a plate, wet food frozen in a Kong) if Kibo will take food. If you have an Adaptil diffuser or a pressure wrap, now is the time.
- 15–25 min: Quiet for you. Water, not wine yet (alcohol + fireworks + solo is a bad combo for sleep). No scrolling, no news. Just sit.
- 25–30 min: Re-check. Has the panting slowed? Is Kibo still circling, or has a spot been picked?

Walk decision

Default tonight: skip it. An adult dog can safely hold urine through one night, and the combination of hot pavement + active fireworks + a stressed dog means a walk will make things worse, not better.

Consider a walk only if all of these are true:
- It's been 10+ minutes without audible fireworks.
- You can hold your palm flat to the pavement for 5 full seconds.
- The nearest grass is within a leash-length of your door (no crossing a street).
- Kibo is moving toward the door, not freezing.

If yes: leashed, 2–3 minutes out-and-back, high-value treat to lure a quick pee, immediate return. No lingering.

If no: skip, and don't feel guilty about it. Kibo will be more stressed by being dragged out than by holding it.

When to retry

- 9:45–10:15 PM is usually the first realistic window — most neighborhood fireworks taper by then, and pavement has had real time to cool.
- After 10:30 PM: if fireworks are still going, hold the line until morning. Kibo will be fine.

One small thing: if Sam texts while you're mid-settle, a quick "fireworks loud, Kibo stressed, we're in the back room, all good" is enough. Don't manage their worry tonight.

Backfill is allowed when the source is named, locatable, and the

---------------------------------------------------

not "TBD" and not blank. UNOWNED GAP = excluded from any
readiness language entirely.

  Setup: "We're about to send the 60-day retention nudge at 25% to retained mid-segment admins. What's the non-negotiable check you run on the audience BEFORE we hit send?"

  Follow-up: "If the warehouse says 'admin' for a contact but the workspace hasn't had admin-level activity in 90 days, do they make the send?"

  Setup: "Last quarter you flagged that lifecycle email X drove a 6-point retention lift. Looking back, what would you do differently before that claim went to stakeholders?"
  Hire: Identifies the gap — didn't control for same-week changes (pricing, integration outage, CSM outreach, copy changes).   Follow-up: "Show me how you'd word the version you'd actually put your name on."

SCENARIO 4 — Thin-data handling
  Setup: "I have a cohort of 47 users split three ways and the retention deltas are 4pp, 6pp, and 2pp. The VP wants a recommendation tomorrow. What do you do?"
  Hire: Names the sample-size problem first. Asks for more data, widens the window, runs a power calc before recommending. Distinguishes "exploratory finding" from "actionable signal." Willing to ship "we don't have enough yet" rather than ship a wrong one.

TITLE: Helio Start Q4 controlled beta — operating shape
FOLDER: Growth

BODY:

Helio Start Q4 is a capped beta for learning, not a launch. This document is the operating shape staff leads reference when making day-to-day calls: who is eligible, what is not in scope, what we measure, where lifecycle ends, who owns instrumentation, and which phrases are off-limits. It is not a GA plan, a pricing-page plan, a paid-acquisition plan, or a team charter. Anything that reads like one of those belongs in a separate decision.

# 1. Eligible accounts

Helio Start beta entry is gated on three things at once: simple deployment, clear administrative ownership, and complete eligibility fields. All three must be true before an account moves into the beta cohort.

- Simple deployment. The account can complete first integration without a custom import, migration, or assisted path.
- Clear administrative ownership. A named admin is identified and reachable through the support handoff.
- Complete eligibility fields. Permissions, imports, billing expectations, and administrative complexity are field-complete with source-named evidence. Inferred or stale fields are not eligible.

Eligibility is reviewed manually per account. There is no automated promotion from discovery rows or assisted rows into the beta cohort.

The cohort is capped and named. Growth in the cohort happens by Ines's review and Riley's sign-off, not by automation or by Sales routing.

# 2. Explicit unsupported list

The following are not part of Q4 Helio Start and are not authorized by this document:

- Pricing-page exposure. No Helio Start pricing layout, plan framing, or upgrade copy is in scope.
- Paid acquisition. No paid-acq campaigns, paid-channel attribution, or acquisition-spend modeling against the beta cohort.
- GA forecasting. No GA date, Q4 forecast, or revenue projection drawn from beta activity.
- Revenue inference from activation. Activation movement in the capped beta does not imply revenue, pricing-page readiness, or wider beta expansion.
- "Before your first paid month" framing. The capped beta is for learning, not revenue generation; lifecycle copy does not position beta activity as a precursor to a paid month.
- Plan-discussion framing in billing-expectations support. Routing and expectations only; no "when you're ready" or paid-plan pitch language.
- New team charter. This document does not stand up a new team, role, or org structure. Existing owner lanes hold.

# 3. Measurement and dashboard shape

Owen maintains the Q4 beta dashboard and readout. The measurement path is the executive read beside four lenses, not a single activation number:

- Activation read, shown beside permissions, imports, billing expectations, and the fact that the pricing page is not involved. Activation on its own is not the story.
- Support-question count per active beta account, not raw support volume. Support mix is shown alongside activation, not as noise around it.
- The hard-gate trio for the administrative-complexity denominator: `entitlement_state` (downstream execution anchor), `first_integration_connected` (activation cohort anchor), `admin_invite_count` (multi-admin invite risk proxy).
- The sub-50 high-complexity cell: permissions, import help, billing exceptions, migration support.

Readouts describe what the capped beta is teaching us. They do not authorize pricing-page exposure or expansion of the cohort. That is a separate decision once the measurement path is clean.

# 4. Lifecycle boundaries

Helio Start lifecycle ends at the safe-touch boundary. Beyond that, the path is manual review, not automation.

In scope for self-serve lifecycle:

- Setup checklist touch.
- First-integration prep touch.
- Activation framing in beta communications, paired with the support-question mix being tracked.

Out of scope for self-serve lifecycle:

- Pre-integration import mapping. That belongs to the Helio Start specialist team, not the self-serve path.
- State-changing automation on beta accounts. The path is safe touches plus manual review. Beta safety is the blocker, not copy readiness.
- Proxy-CI automation that would change beta state without a human in the loop.

The conservative-fork QA rule applies: safe touches (setup checklist, first-integration prep) may move forward under the conditions cleared at the 7/26 review. Touches still blocked (billing-mismatch, import-stuck, support-handoff) require manual review per account.

# 5. Instrumentation responsibilities

Riley retains activation-definition sign-off and the gate calls across the four instrumentation properties: administrative complexity, import or migration, support handoff, and entitlement state. Until all four are clean, the beta gate stays locked.

Owner lanes for Q4:

- Owen — Q4 beta dashboard, weekly numbers freeze, support-load cut, Expansion Assist–Helio Start boundary check.
- Ines — beta copy framing (unchanged copy holds), discovery script for the seven discovery-track rows, assisted-track copy for the six routed-out rows, setup-checklist role-language review, and future-import support copy in the product/scope lane.
- Daniela — confirming annotation language for API-key retries on the live-path tile, plus the engineering sizing questions still open.
- Customer Success — tagged inherited-integration case logging.
- Data engineering — open instrumentation questions alongside Owen.
- Support — support handoff, captured at workspace creation with transitions appended when handoff starts or ends.

`support_handoff_confirmed` is the entitlement update on the core new-workspace path. `entitlement_state`, `first_integration_connected`, and `admin_invite_count` are the dashboard-anchored events.

# 6. Language that is not allowed

Phrases and framings that do not belong in Q4 Helio Start communications, internally or externally:

- "Before your first paid month" — beta is learning, not revenue.
- "When you're ready" — banned in billing-expectations support routing.
- Pricing-page, plan-options, or upgrade framing of any kind.
- GA, launch, "going wide," or expansion framing of beta activity.
- Revenue attribution or forecasting language against beta activation.
- "Wider beta" or cohort-expansion language driven by activation movement.
- Framing the capped beta as a precursor to a paid product surface.

When in doubt, write it as a learning read beside the four lenses, with the support mix alongside activation and the pricing page named as not involved. That sentence shape is the default.

Review from an Owen / Ines angle on the four-item draft:

Light enough to borrow? Mostly yes. Four items is genuinely portable. The friction isn't count — it's whether each item produces a consistent artifact across a lifecycle reader vs. an analyst reader. Three of the four are concrete; "hypothesis stack" and "decision boundary" carry ambiguity that will produce inconsistent output across the two reader types.

What would be confusing:

1. "Hypothesis stack" — the word does real work but has no definition. Lifecycle will read it as one if-then, maybe a backup. Analyst will read it as primary + null + 3 sub-mechanism hypotheses. The May readout shape runs question → hypothesis stack → evidence → effect size → conclusion, so "stack" is meant to be layered, but the checklist doesn't tell the borrower that. Needs a one-line gloss: primary + null/competing + the mechanism behind the primary, each with effect size.

2. "Effect size" — is this absolute delta (pp, %, $), standardized (Cohen's d), or relative uplift? Lifecycle and analyst pick differently and the choice changes the conversation. A one-word spec would prevent the divergence.

3. "Decision boundary" — three states named (first significance / stabilization / observation, don't ship) but no rule for the transition between them. A lifecycle reader marks "first significance" the first time p<0.05 shows up. An analyst reader requires pre-registration + one replicate. Same artifact, two readers, opposite claims. The boundary needs a stated rule, not just three labels.

4. Item 1 assumes explanation framing. "What problem are we trying to explain?" — some investigations are decision-driven (should we ship X?) or prediction-driven (will Y happen?). The verb matters. A reader filling "explain" into a "decide" slot will overclaim because they won't be looking for a threshold.

5. Item 3 is singular "metric." Most investigations have a primary + 1–2 guardrails. Calling it "metric" invites a lifecycle reader to skip the guardrail, then later claim the result is clean because no guardrail was broken. Silent omission = overclaim.

Where a lifecycle or analyst reader would accidentally overclaim:

- Lifecycle: "first significance" reads as permission to ship a message or change a flow. The checklist names the boundary but doesn't stop action — the wording is "say whether this is..." (process), not "do not act until..." (gate). A lifecycle borrower writes "first significance — yes" and treats that as a launch signal.

- Analyst: effect size reported without a business-meaning threshold. d = 0.18 on a 0.4% absolute lift in a high-volume flow is statistically detectable and operationally meaningless. The checklist asks for effect size; it doesn't require the size to clear a pre-stated threshold. Analyst reader reports "significant effect" and skips the "is this big enough to bother" check.

- Both: cohort drift. Item 3 asks the borrower to "say what population" — but doesn't ask whether the population was set before the data was looked at. A lifecycle reader will redefine cohort to "active users in the last 30 days" if the full population doesn't move. An analyst reader will refine cohort post-hoc and call the refined version the original. Pre-registration is missing from the four items.

- Both: stabilization has no operational definition. "Stabilization-cohort confirmation" is named but not defined. How many follow-up cohorts? What minimum effect-size consistency? A lifecycle reader calls it stabilized after one replicate with the same direction. An analyst reader requires 3+ cohorts with non-overlapping CIs. Same word, different bars.

- Lifecycle specifically: problem statement risk. "Users aren't engaging" is an observation, not a problem tied to a decision. Lifecycle writes observation-shaped problems, generates hypotheses, ships. The checklist doesn't require the problem to be decision-tied.

- Analyst specifically: "stack" framing can be used to manufacture rigor. Primary + 8 nested sub-mechanism hypotheses, each with effect size, looks thorough and reads as confidence. It is sometimes confidence and sometimes noise. A bound (one primary, max two sub-mechanisms; or rank by decisional impact) would prevent stack-as-rigor-theater.

If you want a one-line tightening per item, candidates not a rewrite:

- Item 1: reframe as "decision, prediction, or explanation — and the verb it implies"
- Item 2: gloss "stack" as "primary + null + mechanism, each with absolute delta on the primary metric"
- Item 3: "primary metric, 1–2 guardrails, pre-registered cohort, fixed window"
- Item 4: name the transition rule between first-significance and stabilization — e.g., stabilization = ≥2 follow-up cohorts with same direction and overlapping CI on the same pre-registered cohort definition

v0.2 — Investigation checklist (light-touch, not a mandate)

Use this when you're trying to decide whether an observation is enough to ship, nudge, or act on. Five things, in order:

1. What's the question?
   Frame it as a decision ("should we ship?"), a prediction ("what happens if we delay?"), or an explanation ("why did this segment move?"). If you find yourself writing "explain X" when the real need is a decision, rewrite it — otherwise the rest of the checklist will skip the threshold.

2. What's the hypothesis stack?
   List the explanations you'd consider, most-likely first. For each one, say what you'd expect to see and what would make you discard it. Don't just give directions — give the effect you'd expect.

3. What's the evidence?
   Cohort, window, and the slice you're reading from. One sentence each. If the cohort is small or the window is unusual, flag it here — don't paper over it later.

4. What's the effect size, in two forms?
   - Observed: what the data actually shows (absolute delta, % change, Cohen's d — pick one and stick with it).
   - Decision-changing minimum: the smallest effect that would actually change what you do.

5. Would you wait instead of ship?

6. Conclusion.
   One paragraph. What you learned, what you decided, and what would change the decision. If the only thing holding you back is more time/data, say so plainly — that's a fine outcome.

Here's a tight discussion guide that keeps the three buckets separated, fences Helio Start off, and sets a clear bar for when this would actually warrant reopening the activation definition:

CS discussion guide — starter "connected an integration, then stalled before paying"

Purpose
- Determine whether what CS is hearing reflects (1) documentation confusion, (2) teammate-invite friction, or (3) real integration-to-first-paid conversion softness — or some mix.
- Explicitly keep Helio Start out of the interpretation. Any signal that comes from a Helio Start–tagged case is not evidence for this question and should not be aggregated in.

Ground rules for the conversation
- Treat this as a triage call, not an investigation. We are looking for one of three verdicts: documentation fix, onboarding-flow fix, or genuine conversion softness that warrants a deeper cut.
- Stay on the normal starter path only. Do not borrow Helio Start copy, taxonomy, or activation logic. If a CS story turns out to be a Helio Start case, park it and tag it — do not use it to update anything here.
- Separate what the trialist did from what the trialist said. The interesting signal is the gap between action and expectation, not the verbatim quote.

Bucket 1 — Documentation confusion
What to ask CS:
- When a trialist says "I didn't know if I needed to invite a teammate before paying," do they mean (a) they didn't see any mention of teammates, (b) they saw mention but the wording was ambiguous, or (c) they read it and decided to skip it?
- Is there a single doc/email/screen that the trialist references, or is it a general "I missed it somewhere"? A specific asset points to a copy or placement fix; a vague answer points elsewhere.
- What does the trialist think "inviting a teammate" would do — unlock billing, unlock a feature, share access, satisfy a workspace requirement? The wrong mental model is itself a documentation problem.

Evidence we'd accept as a docs fix:
- Multiple trialists cite the same screen, email, or sentence.
- The wording allows more than one reasonable reading, and at least one reading leads the trialist to pause payment.
- The trialist took a "next step" that is reasonable given the doc, and that step is not the one we expected.

Bucket 2 — Teammate-invite friction
What to ask CS:
- What exactly blocked the invite — couldn't find the right email, didn't know the teammate's role, permissions looked scary, workspace felt "not theirs yet," or something else?
- Was the invite attempt made on the trialist's own initiative, or did a CS or in-product nudge drive it? Friction we caused is different from friction the trialist invented.
- If the trialist did invite successfully, what happened next — did they pay, or did they stall for a different reason?

Evidence we'd accept as a flow fix:
- Invite UI or permission prompt is the consistent blocker across multiple stories.
- Trialists who get past the invite convert at a rate comparable to the baseline, suggesting the invite itself is the gate, not payment intent.
- The friction is specific enough to point at a single screen or permission copy.

Bucket 3 — Integration-to-first-paid conversion softness
What to ask CS:
- Of trialists who connected an integration and did not pay, how many came back later, churned at trial end, or upgraded through a different path?
- Were these trialists within the activation window we expect, or were they already outside it when they "connected an integration"? A late integration does not tell us the same thing as an in-window one.
- Was the integration a real, working connection, or a partial setup that satisfied the integration event without producing usable state? The event vs. the outcome matters here.
- Did pricing, billing surface, plan selection, or seat-count surprises come up, or is the stall clearly post-integration and pre-payment?

Evidence we'd accept as a real conversion problem:
- Multiple in-window trialists with working integrations, no teammate-invite question, no documentation gap, who still do not pay.
- The same behavior shows up across customer types, not just one segment.
- The stall maps to a specific point in the post-integration journey, not a vague "they never came back."

What does NOT count toward any of the three buckets
- Helio Start cases, controlled-beta cases, or any trialist tagged as receiving HS copy. These are out of scope for this conversation and out of scope for any output that comes out of it.
- Trialists who never connected an integration. They belong in a different read.
- Anecdotes without a clear "connected an integration" event. If CS cannot place the trialist on the normal starter path with a real integration, we cannot use the story.

Decision bar for escalation
- We only treat this as an activation-definition problem worth reopening if all three of the following hold:
  1. Bucket 3 evidence appears across at least two CS-reported stories that are independently verifiable as in-window, real integrations on the normal starter path.
  2. Buckets 1 and 2 are ruled out as the primary driver for those specific stories (not just for some stories).
  3. The pattern survives a sanity check against the existing signup → first integration and first integration → first paid path numbers — a real softness shows up there before it shows up in anecdotes.
- Until those three are met, the right outputs are a docs fix, a flow fix, or both. Do not reopen the activation definition on anecdotes.

After the call
- Triage each story into one of: docs, flow, conversion, out-of-scope (HS), unplaceable.
- For docs and flow items, name the specific asset or screen and the proposed change.
- For conversion items, list the evidence and whether the three escalation conditions are met yet.
- Anything tagged out-of-scope goes back to the Helio Start support-load read, not this one.

Here's a gentle plan that respects the tin, plus a couple of short text options for Mom. No need to do everything in one sitting — even just dusting and one swatch counts as a Sunday block.

CLEANING THE PANS (preserve the paint layer)

Do:
  - Use a soft, clean, DRY brush (a soft watercolor mop, or a clean soft makeup brush) to lightly whisk dust off the pan surfaces. Brush from the center outward so dust doesn't get pushed into the edges.
  - For any pan with a light dried crust, lay a barely-damp paper towel over it for ~30 seconds, lift, and let it air dry before you swatch. Softens the surface without soaking the binder.

Don't:
  - Don't soak the tin or submerge the pans. The binder (gum arabic) swells when wet and can release pigment.
  - Don't use soap, dish detergent, vinegar, alcohol, or any solvent on the pans.
  - Don't scrub with anything abrasive — no toothbrushes, no Magic Erasers, no paper towel scrubbing on the pan faces.
  - Don't try to "rehydrate" a stubborn pan by flooding it with water. Old paint responds better to a damp brush and patience. A pan that resists after a few gentle passes can be set aside for another Sunday.

CLEANING THE CRACKED TRAY

Do:
  - Wipe with a soft cloth barely dampened with clean water, then immediately dry with a second soft cloth.
  - Treat the crack as a feature. It works fine as a mixing well.

Don't:
  - Don't use soap or any cleaner inside the tray — residue ends up in your paint mixes.
  - Don't glue it. No superglue, no epoxy, no silicone. None of those are reversible and some can leach into mixes. Only consider a conservation-grade reversible repair if a piece is actively flaking, and even then it's optional.
  - Don't flex the tray to "close" the crack — metal fatigue on a vintage tin is real.

FIRST-SWATCH PLAN (about 30–45 min, low pressure)

  1. Set up on a soft cotton dish towel. Cushions the tin and keeps the E.T. scratches from being pressed against the table.
  2. Gather: glass of clean water, two paper towels, scrap watercolor paper (140 lb cold press is friendly), one round brush size 6 or 8, and the soft dry brush for dusting.
  3. Dust the pans first, then wipe the tray, dry it, and you're set.
  4. Start with whatever color looks least dusty or caked — a yellow or earth tone usually wakes up more gently than a deep blue or green.
  5. Wet your brush, tap off the excess (damp, not dripping), then touch the pan in a small slow circle for 10–15 seconds before moving to paper.
  6. Swatch each pan you have patience for on one sheet. Tiny pencil marks beside each swatch so you can identify them later — old pans are hard to read by eye.
  7. Don't judge colors in the first five minutes. Old pigment often looks chalky until it's fully rehydrated. Make a second pass on any you actually like.
  8. When you're done, leave the tin open in a dry spot for an hour before closing it. Closing a damp tin is the fastest path to growing mold on pans that don't have it yet.

Optional keepsake move: photograph the E.T. corner of the lid and your swatch sheet. Two small artifacts of the Sunday.

TEXT OPTIONS FOR MOM

Since you already pinged her about the Sunday video swatch and she hasn't replied, the cleanest move is a separate, smaller message that doesn't double up on that ask. Two drafts — pick whichever matches your mood:

A. (with a photo of the tin lid, E.T. corner visible)
  "tin landed. E.T. still in the corner, just dustier. wiped one yellow down — it's still good. no rush on the sunday thing, just wanted you to know it made it."

B. (shorter, no photo)
  "the e.t. tin came. one yellow woke up. was gentle."

A handles the unanswered video invitation gracefully ("no rush on the sunday thing") without making it A Thing. B is the right size if Mom's having a busy day and you just want to land a small warm ping.

Here's the shape. Three blocks in the order you asked for, with the "not significant → not a ship decision" link made explicit so a reader can't quietly promote a directional result.

EXPERIMENT SUMMARY — [name] · [date range] · owner: [name]

DENOMINATOR
  Cohort: [who's in / who's out, and the cutoff rule]
  Sample size: [N]  (treatment N=t, control N=c)
  Cohort stability check: [passed/failed, verified on date, by whom]
  Assignment & exposure: [randomized / ramp / holdout; % exposed]
  Window: [start–end; any partial-period or seasonality caveat]
  Pre-registered look: [yes/no; if no, flag]

EFFECT SIZE — pinned to hypothesis
  H1 — [specific claim being tested]
    Primary metric: [name], effect [+/- X.X% / X.X pts], CI [low–high]
    Reads as: [meaningful / small / noise] against the threshold you set
  H2 — [second claim, if any]
    Primary metric: [name], effect [+/- X.X%], CI [low–high]
    Reads as: [meaningful / small / noise]
  Do not let any secondary metric float above the hypothesis it tests.
  If a number is the "biggest" one in the doc, it is still not the conclusion.

STATISTICAL READOUT
  Test: [name], p = [x], significance [NOT SIGNIFICANT at α=0.05 / significant at …]
  Power check (required when n.s.): [was the test powered to detect the observed effect at the pre-set MDE? yes/no, power = x%]

CONCLUSION
  Verdict: Directional only — NOT a ship decision.
  Why this is not ship-ready, in two lines max:
    1. Significance threshold not met (p = x).
    2. Effect size is below the threshold we pre-set for "would act on this."
  Optional: cohort stability has not yet held for [window] — re-evaluate after.
  Next step: [extend run / tighten cohort / pre-register follow-up at MDE / archive]

A few things baked in that close the holes in the draft Owen sent:

  - Denominator comes first, with a cohort-stability line. Nothing downstream is load-bearing until that line is checked.
  - Effect size sits under its hypothesis, never as a standalone headline. The biggest number in the doc can no longer be confused with the answer.

FOLLOW-UP EXERCISE — Growth Ops Analyst Panel
Time box: ~7 minutes (5 candidate, 2 panel follow-ups)

PROMPT (read to candidate)

"You are looking at an early read on a two-arm experiment in a new-user activation funnel.

  Setup
    - Arm A (control): current onboarding email cadence
    - Arm B (treatment): adds one second nudge at day 3
    - Both arms live for 6 days
    - Users randomized at signup, ~700/day per arm
    - Cumulative N: A = 4,200, B = 4,150
    - Primary metric: 14-day activation rate
    - Control activation rate: 22.0%
    - Treatment activation rate: 23.8%
    - p-value on the diff: 0.031
    - Guardrails at day 6 (unsubscribe, support tickets, refunds): all within noise
    - Context: this same nudge pattern shipped in three prior experiments — two held, one looked like a win at day 7 and reverted by day 14
    - The PM is asking whether to ship B to 100% before the November review

  Walk me through how you would evaluate this read and what you would recommend — including what you want to see before deciding ship, hold, or kill, and how you would answer the PM."


SCORING GUIDE (1–4; 4 = strong)

  What to listen for, in order:

  1. Denominator discipline
     Names the Ns (~4,200 / ~4,150) and what they support. Recognizes activation events are still accruing for the most recent cohort days, so this is a partial read on a 14-day primary metric.
     Strong: frames the read as underpowered or partial, not settled.
     Weak: treats the 0.031 p-value as the answer.

  2. Effect size
     Computes or names the absolute lift (~1.8 pp on a 22% baseline, ~+8% relative) and asks whether that effect size — even if real — is large enough to justify the product change and any support load.
     Strong: compares the lift to a noise band or a meaningful-effect threshold.
     Weak: treats significance as the only bar.

  3. First-significance vs. stabilization
     Distinguishes "p crossed 0.05 today" from "we have a stable read on activation." Asks for a run plan or a pre-registered decision rule (e.g. hold until day 14, re-test). References the prior reverting experiment as evidence for waiting.
     Strong: proposes a hold-through-end-of-primary-window rule, not a ship-now decision.
     Weak: either ships on the p-value, or holds with no defined re-read trigger.

  4. Rollout decision and PM pushback
     Names a concrete next step (extend run to day 14, segment cut, monitor guardrails). Pre-empts the PM with what would change the recommendation. Distinguishes "ship to 100%" from "ship to 100% with monitoring" — refuses a binary.
     Strong: frames the decision boundary before the recommendation.
     Weak: picks ship / hold / kill and stops.

  Bands
    4 (Strong hire): hits all four spontaneously; answer is structured around denominator, effect size, and decision boundary before the rollout call.
    3 (Hire): hits three of four; e.g. effect size + stabilization but skips denominator, or denominator + decision boundary but underweights effect size.
    2 (Mixed): names one or two of the four; default is ship-or-wait with no framing.
    1 (Weak): treats the 0.031 p-value as the answer; no denominator, no effect-size question, no stabilization distinction.

  Notes for Priya
    - The exercise is intentionally domain-light. A candidate who knows growth-ops craft should hit 3+ without any Helio context.
    - The trap is shipping on first significance. The right answer is rarely "ship now."
    - If a candidate asks for the activation event definition or the segmentation rule, that is a healthy probe, not a miss — credit it under denominator discipline or rollout decision.

Hey Priya — quick one before the panel locks the metric-judgment exercise.

The "ship/no-ship from a single p=.04" framing worries me a little: it collapses the question down to a binary call, which I think rewards decisiveness more than judgment. What I originally wanted to surface is the candidate's reasoning chain — do they interrogate the denominator, put a number on the effect size, distinguish "first significance" from "ready to ship." Those are the muscles we actually need in the role.

Want me to send this to Priya as a Slack DM now, or would you rather tighten the wording first? Two specific things you might want to adjust: the seniority of the tone in the cover note, and whether to surface the tenure sub-cut upfront vs. keep it as a "only if they ask" reveal.

Riley's read is right. The gotcha framing collapses the exercise into "do you trust p=.04?" — a calibration question — when the actual decision is "should we ship a behavior change to all users based on a one-week read?" Those are different questions. A confident "yes, ship" reads as decisive but is wrong; a confident "no, p is too close" reads as rigorous but is also wrong. Both reward bravado over judgment.

What the current prompt collapses:

1. Denominator. p without n is half-blind. The candidate should ask first.

2. Effect size. Statistical significance without business significance is a trap. +1.8pp activation at p=.04 is interesting; +0.05pp at p=.04 is noise with consequences. The candidate should ask second.

3. Cohort stability. Simpson's paradox risk — the lift may concentrate in one segment (e.g., >30-day-tenure users, where the effect is real) while being near-zero elsewhere. Shipping to all users from a segment-level lift is the textbook misread. The candidate should ask third.

4. Support risk. Onboarding nudges can move ticket volume in ways the activation metric doesn't capture. The candidate should ask fourth.

5. First significance vs stabilization. A single-week p=.04 is a peek. Whether the read holds at week-2 and week-4 is a separate question — and is the difference between "we have a result" and "we have a recommendation." The candidate should distinguish.

Concrete rewrite of the prompt:

  "An onboarding nudge experiment just hit p=.04 after one week, with
  a +1.8pp activation lift on n=12,400. The PM wants to ship. Walk me
  through what you'd want to verify about the result, what follow-up
  read you'd want before being comfortable with the call, and your
  current recommendation along with the specific evidence that would
  change your mind."

This shape does three things the gotcha version doesn't:

  - Forces the candidate to interrogate effect size, variance, and pre-registration before recommending anything
  - Forces them to name reversal conditions, which is what real ship/no-ship calls actually look like
  - Lets the panelist reveal the >30-day-tenure concentration only if the candidate asks about segments — testing whether they think past the headline number

Design choice worth a sentence in the cover note: whether to bake n and effect size into the prompt, or withhold them and force the candidate to ask. Baking them in tests reasoning given real numbers; withholding tests whether they ask for the denominator at all. Your revised exercise bakes them in, which is reasonable — but if the panelist's rewrite came from wanting exactly the "does this person ask" signal, then withholding is the cleaner test of it, and worth naming explicitly so it doesn't look like an oversight.

The five-minute framing is fine. The exercise isn't a trivia quiz; it's a reasoning test. But the gotcha version measures decisiveness, and the layered version measures judgment. Those select for different candidates.

Patch it. A clean pinhole in an undamaged casing is exactly what patch kits are for, and saving the spare tube for the M/W commute is the right call. The August rim-tape saga is worth keeping in mind, but you already covered the casing-side failure modes; the one extra thing worth eyeballing before you button it up is the rim tape, since that's where your last recurring flat actually lived.

INSPECT (before the glue sets)

  - Find the hole on the tube. Inflate just enough to feel it, listen for hiss, or dunk the tube in a sink of water and watch for bubbles. Mark the spot with a Sharpie.
  - Run a fingertip slowly around the inside of the tire casing, especially where the hole was. One shard in the tube often means another still embedded in the casing. Pull anything you find.
  - Eyeball the rim tape. It should be intact, centered, and fully covering every spoke hole — no splits, no peeling edge, no spoke nipple peeking through. If it looks questionable, that's a separate fix and a good reason to use the spare tube instead.
  - Check the bead seating. Both beads should sit evenly in the rim hook all the way around before you put any real pressure in.

PATCH (follow the kit's cure time — don't rush this)

  - Rough the marked spot with the kit sandpaper, a bit larger than the patch.
  - Thin, even glue layer; wait until tacky (usually 1-2 min, not wet).
  - Patch on, press hard for 30-60 sec, no sliding.
  - Full cure before reinstallation — most kits want 2-5 min.

REASSEMBLE & PRESSURE-TEST

  - Tube back in, valve straight, no pinch at the valve hole.
  - Inflate to about half pressure first. Walk around the wheel and look for tube peeking out anywhere — that means casing damage you missed or the bead unseated.
  - Spin the wheel off the ground. Watch for wobble, bulge, or the tire creeping on the rim.
  - Up to full pressure (sidewall max, not "feels about right"). Soap-and-water on the valve stem and over the patch — no bubbles, no hiss.
  - Wait 10 minutes, recheck pressure. Should hold rock-solid. If it drops, the leak is somewhere else — recheck the rim tape and the valve core.
  - Squeeze test: firm, not spongy.
  - One short loop around the block before the errand. If it still feels solid after that, you're good to ride.

If the rim tape looks split or the tire won't hold pressure through this checklist, swap in the spare tube and patch this one at home later — don't burn the spare tube's life on a Saturday errand without being sure the rim side is clean.

The most conservative move is to leave the rough strip alone and route your shadow wash around it. Stop the wash a few millimeters short of that border — your eye reads it as a deliberate edge, and there's zero risk of making the damage more obvious. This is the lowest-intervention option.

If you'd rather flatten the fibers before washing, here's a gentle reset for cold-press:

1. Take a clean soft brush (a mop or large round), dampen it, then blot it nearly dry. You want it barely damp — no visible bead of water when you touch the paper.
2. One slow stroke along the rough strip in the direction the fibers are laying, not against them. You're coaxing them back down, not scrubbing.
3. Press the strip flat with a clean fingertip for a few seconds while it's still slightly relaxed.
4. Lay a clean piece of tissue or plain paper towel over it, then a light flat weight (a closed paperback is plenty) for 10–15 minutes while it dries.

For the shadow wash itself, two ways to keep that edge from re-catching pigment:

  - Use a slightly drier brush with a smaller, controlled tip along that border instead of a broad wet pass.
  - Or stop the wash short of the rough strip, as in the first option.

One caution: cold-press is forgiving, but over-wetting the rough strip will lift more fibers and can buckle the card. Stay barely damp, never wet. If at any point the strip starts to pill or fuzz more rather than settle, stop — that's the paper telling you to leave it alone, and the "stop short" route becomes your best finish.

Given the loss overnight and the second shard in a different part of the tread, swapping to the spare is the right call — but given the recurring pattern in your notes (the actual cause on 8/31 was a rim-tape split, not glass), the rim side of this needs as much attention as the tire side. Here's a careful sequence.

PRE-TUBE INSPECTION ORDER

Do this completely before the spare tube goes anywhere near the rim. Each step has to come back clean.

1.  Deflate fully, unseat one bead, pull the patched tube out. While it's out, note where the (failed) patch sits on the tube vs. where the second tread shard sits on the tire — they should line up radially. If they don't, you have more than one tube injury, and a third tube isn't in your plan today.

2.  Pull the second shard. Tweezers or needle-nose, pull it out along the same angle it went in (don't lever). Set it next to the first one if you still have it — comparing sizes helps you judge whether this was a one-off or whether your commuting surface is shedding glass.

3.  Mark BOTH puncture sites on the casing with a paint pen or a small piece of tape — once on the tread, once on the matching spot inside the casing. You need to find these again after the casing flexes around.

4.  Outside of casing, at both puncture sites:
    -   Is there an actual through-hole, or only a dimple where the shard sat?
    -   Any frayed casing threads? (Especially if this is a belted tire — even one broken belt strand matters.)
    -   Any tread chunk missing, ply separation visible as a darker line, or a blister?

5.  Inside of the casing — this is the single most important step. Mount the bare tire on the rim with no tube, or hold it open with your hands. Slowly run a clean fingertip (or a thin nylon stocking over your finger — it catches slivers skin can miss) around the full inside circumference, more than once. You're feeling for:
    -   Any remaining shard or splinter
    -   A blister or soft spot (casing ply separation)
    -   Exposed threads poking inward
    -   Rough patches you didn't expect

6.  Bead inspection, both beads, full circumference. Nicks, cuts, frayed wire, deformation. Run a fingernail along the bead. It has to be continuous and undamaged. Even a small cut in the bead is a tire-replace, not a tire-reuse.

7.  Sidewalls, full circumference on both sides. Cuts, scuffs, cracks, bulges, exposed casing cords. Press each sidewall from the outside while your other hand is inside the casing — anything that gives or bulges is ply separation.

8.  RIM INSPECTION — given your history, do not skip or rush this:
    -   Rim tape: full circumference, both sides of the spoke holes. Look for splits, slippage off a spoke nipple, wrinkles that could chafe the tube, exposed spoke-hole edges. If the tape is anything other than intact and flat, replace it before installing the spare tube. Cloth tape is cheap.
    -   Spoke nipples: none should protrude through or above the rim tape. Push on each one from the rim-well side — any that moves up means the nipple has crept and is now a tube-killer.
    -   Rim bed and rim sidewalls (brake tracks / bead seats): no burrs, dents, corrosion pits that could wear the tape or cut the tube. Run a fingertip around.
    -   Valve hole: clean, no sharp edge.

TIRE UNSAFE TO REUSE — stop and replace the tire if you find any of these:

-   Bulge or blister anywhere (sidewall OR tread) when inflated — casing ply separation. Fails suddenly.
-   Sidewall cut that exposes casing cords or fabric, especially if more than roughly 3 mm or it runs along the cord direction.
-   Tread cut deep enough to expose casing, or a chunk of tread missing.
-   Bead damage of any kind — cut, exposed wire, deformation, frayed Kevlar bead. Bead failure = tire comes off rim at speed.
-   Casing ply separation felt from inside (soft spot, blister).
-   Two puncture sites clustered close together (concentrated casing damage in one area).
-   Tread worn down to the casing cords anywhere — end-of-life regardless.
-   Deep sidewall cracking that runs into the casing. (Cosmetic surface cracks are different from structural ones.)

In your current situation — no visible cut, no exposed threads, no bulge, no bead damage reported — the tire is most likely fine to reuse, provided steps 5 and 8 come back clean. Two small tread punctures from different shards, with the casing structurally intact, is normal road-debris damage.

SHORT INSTALL AND TEST SEQUENCE

-   Mount one bead, tuck the spare tube in starting at the valve, seat the second bead by hand. Avoid tire levers near the tube if you can.
-   Inflate to roughly half pressure (about 30–35 psi). Walk all the way around the wheel: bead evenly seated on both sides, no tube bulging through casing anywhere, no hissing.
-   Only then inflate to full pressure. Recheck bead seating at full pressure.

If at any point during the half-pressure check the tube bulges through the casing or you hear or feel air escaping — stop, deflate, re-inspect. Don't ride on a tire that hasn't passed the half-pressure check.

Short conservative sequence

1. Set up first, then restrain. Have someone steady Kibo (or use a calm hold with treats). Do this on a non-slip surface with good light so you can see the full length of the thorn between the pads.
2. Saline rinse before touching the thorn. Flush the interdigital skin with room-temp saline to clear debris and dampen the hair so you can see exactly what you're working with. Pat dry enough to see.
3. Grasp and pull in one motion. With clean tweezers, pinch the tip or the exposed length at the same angle the thorn is lying. Pull straight out along that angle — do not twist, lever, or dig. If it doesn't slide with light, even traction, stop.
4. Re-rinse after removal. Flush the site again with saline, then optionally a very dilute chlorhexidine or mild soap wash, then a final saline rinse. Pat dry.
5. Brief pressure only if needed. If a spot of blood appears, hold gentle pressure with a clean gauze pad for 2–3 minutes. No bandaging between pads unless your vet has told you to — moisture gets trapped there.
6. Observe for 24–48 hours. Mild short-term favoring is normal. Keep walks shorter and check the spot twice daily.

Stop and call the vet if any of these are true

- The thorn only shows as a tip, is angled downward into the skin, or you can't see both ends.
- It won't slide out with light, straight traction — don't dig.
- It breaks, splinters, or leaves a fragment behind.
- Bleeding doesn't stop with a few minutes of gentle pressure, or the paw is bleeding from more than the entry point.
- The paw swells, gets hot, feels firmer than the other one, or Kibo pulls away hard or yelps when you touch near it.
- Favoring or licking worsens instead of improving over 12–24 hours, or you see pus, a bad smell, or a red streak.
- The thorn is near a nail bed or a joint, or you can't fully visualize how deep it goes.
- Kibo seems off in general — lethargic, not eating, or feverish.

Two small things worth knowing

- A thorn that is just resting across the skin between pads (rather than puncturing it) often lifts out easily after the saline soak; if that's what you're seeing, a soaked gauze wipe may pull it off without tweezers.
- If Kibo is reliably treat-motivated, a helper feeding a continuous stream of soft treats during steps 1–4 keeps him still and makes this a one-person-feeling job.

Either way, finish with a fresh squeeze of lemon and crumbled feta. Those two finishing moves — lemon and feta held back until serving — are what make it taste just-made instead of leftover.

Same-day plan

For the next 24-48 hours, treat this as a soft-tissue injury first and worry about labeling it later. You're already doing the most important thing: you stopped.

Rest: no running, no jumping, no calf-loading gym work. Walking is fine and is actually useful as a low-load way to keep blood moving through the muscle. Avoid prolonged sitting with the calf compressed under you, which can make stiffness worse.

Ice: 15-20 minutes on, at least 40 minutes off, repeated 3-4 times today. A thin towel between skin and ice pack. Ice is most useful in the first 24-48 hours for a fresh strain. Skip it before bed if you're about to fall asleep so you don't leave it on too long.

Compression: a light calf sleeve or even an ACE wrap from ankle to just below the knee, snug but not tight enough to cause numbness or color change in the foot. Take it off for sleeping.

Elevation: when you're sitting on the couch, prop the leg on a couple of pillows so the calf is roughly at or above heart level. Helps more than it sounds.

Hydration and electrolytes: drink normally, and if your usual long-run fueling has been light, a small electrolyte source (electrolyte drink, salty snack plus water) is reasonable. Cramp-prone calves often correlate with under-fueling on easy days, not just hard ones.

Pain relief: acetaminophen is fine if it's sore. Ibuprofen is okay today but some soft-tissue protocols prefer to skip NSAIDs in the first 24 hours of an acute strain because they can blunt the inflammatory healing signal. Not a hard rule, just a consideration.

What to avoid today: deep calf stretching, foam rolling directly on the sore spot, massage guns on high, hot tub or hot bath, and any "walk it off" pace that's faster than a casual stroll.

What would make this more than ordinary muscle irritation

Watch for these over the next 24-72 hours. Any one of them moves you from "tend it at home" to "get it looked at":

- Swelling that develops, especially if it's one-sided and the sore calf looks or measures bigger than the other.
- Warmth, redness, or a firm tender cord running down the back of the calf. These plus calf pain are the classic deep-vein thrombosis pattern, and the risk is worth taking seriously even though it's unlikely for a typical runner.
- Pain that worsens over the next 24-48 hours instead of improving, or pain that's present at rest and not just with contraction.
- Bruising appearing in the calf, ankle, or arch of the foot (suggests actual fiber tear, not just irritation).
- Numbness, tingling, coldness, or color change in the foot.
- Pain that wakes you from sleep, fever, or generally feeling unwell.
- A sharp pain when the calf is passively stretched (toes pulled up toward the shin) that's noticeably worse than when you actively point the toe.
- A palpable "dent," knot, or gap in the muscle that wasn't there before.

If any of those show up, the right move is a same-day or next-day clinic visit, not "wait and see." DVT specifically is a same-day issue; the others can usually wait until tomorrow if they appear.

When another run is reasonable

The bar is boring and that is the point: pain-free at rest, pain-free on normal walking, pain-free on a calf raise, and ideally a day or two where the calf feels like a normal calf again.

- Day 0-1 (today and tomorrow): no running. Walking, gentle mobility, ice as needed.
- Day 2-3: if the calf feels fully normal, do a couple of single-leg calf raises and a few hops in place as a screen. If any of those reproduce the tightness, give it another day or two.
- First test run: short, easy, flat, same surface you usually train on. 1.5-2 miles, conversational pace, no strides, no hills. Stop the moment tightness shows up, even a hint. Don't run through it to "loosen up."
- Second test run: 2-3 days later, slight distance bump, still easy. If both test runs are clean, you can phase back into your normal mileage over a week.
- If tightness returns on either test run, rest another 5-7 days and consider a quick eval from a sports med clinician or physical therapist. Recurring calf tightness during easy running is often a load-management or biomechanics issue that's much easier to fix early than after it becomes a pattern.

Bottom line: today is rest, ice, compression, elevation, hydration, and a normal-looking walk. You're watching for swelling, worsening pain, color or sensation changes, or bruising. A short easy test run is reasonable in roughly 2-4 days if the calf behaves itself in the meantime.

Bottom line: this is almost certainly a classification problem, not customer behavior.

- Dashboard counts only monthly-recurring subscriptions and skips annual-up-front invoices.
- Annual invoices map to a different plan_type / billing_interval / SKU the dashboard filters out.
- Annual invoices arrive with no corresponding active subscription row (paid-up-front may not create a 'trialing' / 'active' sub the dashboard joins on).
- Annual rows key under a different workspace_id (parent org vs workspace) the dashboard does not bridge.

1. Pull the 7 mismatched rows in the dashboard's underlying table. Are they present at all, and if so, with what plan_type / status / interval fields? Cost: one query. Usually tells you the failure mode on its own.

2. Read the dashboard's classification filter (the dbt model or SQL that defines "paid workspace"). Look for any clause that excludes annual / invoice-paid / non-subscription payment sources. Cost: a doc or model read.

3. If 1 and 2 do not localize it, reconcile the 7 against the subscription store, not just the invoice store. The mismatch often lives there — annual-up-front invoices valid, but no active subscription row to join on.

4. If still unresolved, check whether the 7 carry a different workspace_id (org-level vs workspace-level). One bridge key.

Stop at step 2 if the cause is obvious there. Steps 3–4 are only if 1–2 leave you guessing. Step 5 always runs.

Ines finding one duplicate after a workspace merge is real and worth treating carefully, but it's a data-state artifact, not a send-system bug. The proportionate shape is: contain this recipient, audit the merge cohort (not all of day-3), reply to the customer, and add a guardrail so the next merge doesn't re-arm. Below are the four pieces.

IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT

  1. Suppress the affected workspace from any further day-N sends in this cohort. The merged record has likely re-armed the day-3 timer based on the target workspace's pre-merge state; continuing to send will compound the problem.
  2. Confirm whether the same recipient already received (or is queued for) a day-7. If day-7 is queued from the source workspace's send-log, suppress that too.
  3. Ask Ines to identify the merge that produced this — specifically whether the merge preserved the source workspace's send-log or whether the day-3 trigger re-evaluated against the target's state. The answer determines whether this is a one-off merge artifact or a recurring class.
  4. Hold the next 1-2 merges that would hit the same trigger window, but do NOT pause the day-3 send for the broader cohort. That's over-reaction for a single confirmed case.

MERGE AUDIT SCOPE (sane, bounded)

  In scope:
    - The specific merge that produced this duplicate (full trace: source state, target state, send-log at merge time, post-merge trigger re-evaluation).
    - Other workspace merges in the last 7-14 days where the source workspace was post-day-3-send and the target was pre-day-3-send — these are the merges that could re-arm the timer.
    - A cross-check on the same merge cohort for day-1 and day-7 duplicates (same root cause would produce them too).

  Out of scope (do not pull these in):
    - All historical day-3 sends.
    - The full Helio Start lifecycle.
    - Pre-merge customers who have not had a merge event.
    - Any audit of non-merge sources of duplicate sends — that's a different investigation.

  Done = the merge cohort is checked, no other duplicates are found in that window, and the merge that caused this one is traced to its root cause. That's it.

APOLOGY LANGUAGE FOR CUSTOMER SUCCESS (paste-ready)

  Subject: Re: your Helio onboarding messages

  Hi [name],

  Thanks for flagging this. We consolidated two workspace records on our end, and a duplicate day-3 onboarding message slipped through as part of that merge. You don't need to do anything — please feel free to ignore the second one.

  If anything in your workspace looks off, or you'd like us to double-check the merge on our side, just reply here and we'll take care of it.

  Apologies for the extra noise,
  [CS name]

  Notes for CS: don't promise a systemic fix we haven't made; don't frame it as "we noticed" if the customer noticed first; keep the reply under six lines.

JUDGMENT ON PAUSING THE DAY-3 PROGRAM

  No. One confirmed duplicate from a workspace merge is not enough to pause the whole day-3 program.

  Reasoning:
    - The duplicate traces to a merge-state artifact (record consolidation re-arming the day-3 timer), not a send-system double-fire. The send system worked as designed; the upstream data state produced the duplicate.
    - The shape is consistent with the 2023-12-14 release-notes overlap Ines contained by keeping the day-1 send on schedule, and with the 2023-07-27 team-invite preview issue that affected only draft test workspaces. In both cases, containment + audit + a guardrail was the right response, not a programmatic pause.
    - Capped-beta boundaries (per the Q4 closeout) mean the day-3 program is operating under tight scope already. A single duplicate inside that scope is a contained incident, not a program-level signal.

  What WOULD change the answer:
    - A second confirmed duplicate from a different merge pair in the same window — that's a pattern, not an artifact.
    - Evidence the send system is double-firing independent of merge state (vs. merge re-arming) — that's a send-system bug.
    - The duplicate carrying materially different or incorrect content from the original — that's a content/identity problem, not a duplication problem.

  In any of those three cases, pause the cohort, escalate to Ines, and revisit. Until then, contain + audit + reply is the right shape.

**Confirmed duplicate: 1 / 2,087 deliveries**

**Root-cause trace**

Two compounding causes, both necessary:

1. The alias workspace kept `eligible=true` after the merge. Whoever processed the merge (or the merge logic itself) didn't null eligible on the losing workspace. So the alias was still a live sender in its own right, not just a historical record pointing at the survivor.

Per-item call (conservative)

- Chicken thighs — KEEP, refreeze. Rock-hard with visible ice crystals means the interior never crossed 32°F, well below the 40°F safety threshold. USDA's standing rule: items that still contain ice crystals are safe to refreeze.
- Frozen vegetables — KEEP, refreeze. "Firm" reads as still frozen through. Same reasoning as above; quality impact will be negligible.
- Bread — KEEP, refreeze (or just keep using it). It felt cold, so it stayed under 40°F. Quality will take a small hit if it thawed enough to soften, but no safety concern.
- Ice cream (soft edges, frozen center) — KEEP, refreeze — but plan to use it for milkshakes/smoothies rather than scoops, because the texture will go icy/grainy. The center never thawed, so it stayed safely cold.

Bottom line: discard nothing on safety grounds. The thermometer reading of 24°F is the air near the door/wall; the deciding evidence is the physical state of the dense items — still frozen through with ice crystals — which means their internal temps never crossed 32°F. No pathogen-growth window opened.

Appliance monitoring

Close the door firmly, then recheck the thermometer at roughly 2 hours, 4 hours, and 6 hours. A healthy freezer should be trending back toward 0°F (the USDA target) and should be at or close to 0°F by hour 4–6.

Treat the appliance as a problem — i.e., stop relying on it for storage and look at the gasket, latch, and thermostat — if any of these are true:

- At ~4 hours the reading is still above ~10°F and not dropping, or
- At ~6–8 hours it hasn't returned to within a few degrees of 0°F, or
- The door doesn't seat cleanly when you close it (frost gaps, gasket looks warped, latch doesn't click).

While you're monitoring, do two quick checks: confirm the latch actually catches (not just resting shut) and listen for the compressor running. If both of those look fine and the temp is dropping on schedule, you're good — just leave the door alone for the next few hours so the freezer can recover without you letting cold air out.

Good call stopping the preflight — the numbers are telling a clear story, and shipping a 1,642-row audience that should be ~1,325 unique (and still has known suppressions bleeding through) is worse than slipping a day.

FAILURE MODE

The 1,642 rows / 1,413 unique / ~1,325 expected gap is two bugs surfacing in one query, and they share a root cause: the query is fanning out at the wrong grain.

(a) Duplicates — 1,642 rows for 1,413 unique admins (229 extra rows, ~16%)

The audience is being joined on something that produces more than one row per admin. The usual suspects are admin-to-account via a 1:many table — workspace_admins, account_members, subscriptions with multiple seats, or role assignments where one admin holds two roles on the same account. The SELECT probably has a DISTINCT or GROUP BY downstream, but the WHERE clauses are being evaluated against the inflated row set BEFORE the dedup, so a row whose duplicate sibling passes the suppression check can still survive.

(b) Suppressions not taking effect — 1,413 unique vs ~1,325 expected = ~88 admins over

Two common ways suppression conditions silently break:

  - The classic LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap. If the query LEFT JOINs admins to support_contacts (or to cs_adoption_plans) and then puts `contacted_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days'` (or `status = 'open'`) in the WHERE clause, the LEFT JOIN collapses into an INNER JOIN — only admins whose join actually matched survive. The intended semantic ("no recent support contact") gets inverted into "has a recent support contact". The fix is either to flip to NOT EXISTS / NOT IN, or to keep the LEFT JOIN and put the predicate in the JOIN ON clause.

  - Suppression evaluated at the wrong grain. If the join is admin x account and the suppression is on `cs_adoption_plans.account_id`, but the WHERE filters on a single row's account_id, an admin sitting on two accounts (one clean, one with an open adoption plan) will keep their clean-account row and slip into the audience. Suppression should be a set-membership check across ALL of the admin's accounts, not a row-level filter on whichever row happened to match.

(c) Likely status-enum drift on the adoption plan

If the WHERE clause is `status = 'open'` but the schema's actual values are `active`, `in_progress`, `paused`, etc., the filter matches zero rows and the suppression becomes a silent no-op. Worth pulling `SELECT DISTINCT status FROM cs_adoption_plans` before debugging further — a zero-row suppression set is the easiest bug to miss in a count-based review.

(d) Possible timezone / window-edge issue on the 14-day support suppression

`NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days'` computed in UTC against contact timestamps stored in local time can shift the boundary by several hours and include or drop one day at the edge. Less likely to be the dominant cause given the size of the gap, but worth a one-line check.

SAFER ACCOUNT-LEVEL QUERY PATTERN

The pattern below enforces the right grain at every step: DISTINCT in every CTE so suppression sets can't inflate, suppression evaluated as set-membership across the admin's full account portfolio, and a final GROUP BY that guarantees one row per admin.

  WITH
    -- Step 1: account-level suppression sets (DISTINCT prevents row inflation)
    suppress_adoption AS (
      SELECT DISTINCT account_id
      FROM cs_adoption_plans
      WHERE status IN ('open', 'active', 'in_progress')   -- confirm exact enum values first
    ),
    suppress_recent_support AS (
      SELECT DISTINCT account_id
      FROM support_contacts
      WHERE contacted_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days'
      -- confirm timezone: UTC vs. local, and rolling-day vs. calendar-day
    ),

    -- Step 2: canonical admin-account pairs (DISTINCT prevents fan-out)
    admin_account_pairs AS (
      SELECT DISTINCT
        a.admin_email,
        a.account_id,
        a.role
      FROM admins a
      WHERE a.is_active = TRUE
        AND a.opted_in_to_admin_comms = TRUE              -- or check global unsubscribe separately
    ),

    -- Step 3: suppressed admins = any of their accounts lands in a suppression set
    suppressed_admins AS (
      SELECT DISTINCT p.admin_email
      FROM admin_account_pairs p
      WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM suppress_adoption     s WHERE s.account_id = p.account_id)
         OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM suppress_recent_support s WHERE s.account_id = p.account_id)
    )

  -- Step 4: final audience = one row per admin, suppression set removed
  SELECT
    p.admin_email,
    MIN(p.account_id) AS primary_account_id,              -- canonical account for personalization
    ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT p.role) AS roles                   -- keep role info if the template uses it
  FROM admin_account_pairs p
  WHERE p.admin_email NOT IN (SELECT admin_email FROM suppressed_admins)
  GROUP BY p.admin_email;

Three notes on the pattern:

  - EXISTS is preferred over IN with a subquery for NULL-safety; both work here because the suppression sets are DISTINCT-account_id (no NULLs), but EXISTS is the more defensive default.
  - The status list in `suppress_adoption` is intentionally a set — once Ines confirms the actual enum values, that becomes a single hardcoded list rather than a fragile equality check.
  - MIN(account_id) for `primary_account_id` is a placeholder; if you have a real notion of "primary" (billing owner, longest-tenured, most recent login), swap that in. The point is to pick ONE deterministically rather than letting it leak through as multiple rows.

PRE-SEND QA CHECKLIST

A short checklist Ines can run before approving. Every item is a single query or a 5-minute eyeball pass — none of these should take more than a few minutes total.

  [ ] Row count equals unique-admin count
        SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT admin_email) FROM <audience>;
        The two numbers must match exactly. If they don't, the dedup is downstream of the
        suppression logic and the row count is lying about audience size.

  [ ] Total sits in the expected band
        Expected ~1,325; acceptable range 1,300–1,340 (±2%). Anything outside that band
        deserves a written explanation in the preflight note, not just an "approved".

  [ ] Suppression sets are non-empty (catches the silent-no-op bug)
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM suppress_adoption;
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM suppress_recent_support;
        If either returns 0, the WHERE clause is matching zero rows and the suppression
        isn't actually firing — most likely a status-enum or window-clock mismatch.

  [ ] Status-enum sanity check
        SELECT DISTINCT status FROM cs_adoption_plans;
        Confirm the values in the suppression WHERE clause match real schema values, not
        a synonym that doesn't exist.

  [ ] Spot-check: adoption-plan suppression actually removes the right accounts
        Pick 5 random account_ids from cs_adoption_plans WHERE status='open' (or the
        confirmed equivalent), join to admins, and verify none of those admin emails
        appear in the audience.

  [ ] Spot-check: 14-day support suppression actually removes the right accounts
        Pick 5 random account_ids from support_contacts WHERE contacted_at >= NOW() - 14
        days, join to admins, and verify those admin emails are absent.

  [ ] Multi-account edge case (catches the wrong-grain bug)
        Find 2–3 admins known to sit on multiple accounts where ONE of those accounts is
        in a suppression set. They must NOT be in the audience. This is the specific case
        a row-level filter misses and a set-membership filter catches.

  [ ] Window edge on the 14-day support filter
        Confirm NOW() - INTERVAL '14 days' is computed in the same timezone as
        support_contacts.contacted_at. A UTC vs. local mismatch can shift the boundary
        by several hours and quietly include or drop a day.

  [ ] Unsubscribe / global opt-out cross-reference
        Audience MINUS unsubscribe list MINUS global email opt-outs = final send list.
        Confirm this explicitly rather than relying on the ESP's suppression layer, which
        won't catch ESP-level delivery failures the same way.

  [ ] Internal and test accounts excluded
        Verify staging / internal account_ids are filtered. Eyeball 10 random rows for
        environment markers, internal email domains, or test data patterns.

  [ ] Sample 10 random rows
        Eyeball role distribution, account sizes, look for anomalies — test accounts,
        personal-email admins, churned-but-not-deleted records.

  [ ] Suppression overlap diagnostic (for the post-send retro)
        Run two counts: how many admins were suppressed by adoption-plan only, and how
        many by recent-support only. Non-zero on both confirms both suppression paths
        actually fired; useful evidence for the next preflight if anything looks off.
