You're right on the diagnosis — and there are actually two interlocking bugs in the same WHERE clause, not just one.

Bug 1 — row-level multiplication (the 229 duplicate rows)
When you LEFT JOIN suppression_history without aggregating, each account with N rows in suppression_history produces N output rows. The WHERE clause evaluates per row, so an account with one expired row and one active row gets BOTH rows past the filter. That's how you go from 1,413 unique admins to 1,642 output rows. Classic LEFT JOIN + WHERE-on-the-nullable-side anti-pattern; the OR-with-IS-NULL disguises it but it's still row-level filtering.

Bug 2 — inverted suppression logic (the ~88 over-included accounts)
`s.expires_at < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP OR s.account_id IS NULL` reads as "include if any joined row is expired OR there's no row at all." That's the opposite of what suppression should mean. An account is currently suppressed if it has at least one row where `expires_at >= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`. So your condition is letting through any account whose most-recent-or-only row has expired, even if there's a separate active suppression sitting in the table.

Both bugs come from the same shape: the query can't tell "this account has at least one active suppression" apart from "this account has at least one row that looks inactive." You need to flip from row-level to account-level reasoning.

The fix
NOT EXISTS with active-row semantics:

    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM suppression_history s
      WHERE s.account_id = a.account_id
        AND s.expires_at >= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    )

Kills both bugs at once: no row multiplication (EXISTS is set-level), correct semantic (exclude only when an active suppression exists).

If you must keep the LEFT JOIN shape for readability, aggregate the suppression table first:

    LEFT JOIN (
      SELECT account_id, MAX(expires_at) AS latest_expires
      FROM suppression_history
      GROUP BY account_id
    ) s ON s.account_id = a.account_id
    WHERE s.latest_expires < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP OR s.latest_expires IS NULL

NOT EXISTS is cleaner and matches the "exclude accounts with any active suppression" intent.

On the 88-account gap
1,413 - 1,325 = 88. You're showing 54 (open CS adoption) + 31 (support ≤14d) = 85. Three possibilities worth checking before locking the query:

a) Those two exclusion paths are already applied elsewhere in the query — the 88 is purely the suppression-inversion over-inclusion, and the 3-account gap is unrelated noise.

b) The 54 + 31 populations are NOT currently filtered at all — they're what you also need to exclude. In that case 85 is the over-inclusion and the remaining 3 are unaccounted for (small additional exclusion paths, or some overlap with suppression_history).

c) Mixed — some of the 54/31 are already represented in suppression_history, others need separate NOT EXISTS subqueries against cs_adoption_plans and support_contacts.

If (b) or (c), you'll need two more NOT EXISTS clauses for those populations. And while you're in there, double-check the 14-day support window is computed in the same timezone as support_contacts.contacted_at — your pre-send QA already flagged this, and rewriting the WHERE is a natural place to get it right.

Quick framing before the list: I don't have the addendum text in front of me, so what follows is the operational lens to apply when you read it — the questions a Customer.io DPA/addendum typically answers badly and the downstream consequences for Helio. Counsel will decide what's acceptable; my job is to flag what bites us in ops if it's vague or vendor-favorable.

PLAIN ENGLISH, WHAT EACH PROVISION ACTUALLY DOES

Post-termination retention
  Customer.io will hold end-user profiles, event data, segments, and suppression state for some window after we stop being a customer. Operationally, suppression state matters most: if a person unsubscribed through us, CAN-SPAM / CASL / GDPR require that opt-out survives somewhere. A short retention window is fine for marketing data; a short window for suppression state is a compliance problem. Also — what's the extraction format during that window? If it's a CSV dump and we have 6 weeks to migrate a live messaging program, that's a real operational risk, not a hypothetical one.

Deletion certification
  "We'll delete your data" is not the same as "we'll send you a signed confirmation referencing the systems and the date." For our SOC 2 and any customer-facing DPA we sign downstream, we want paper. If the addendum only promises deletion on request without certification, we can't evidence it in an audit and we can't answer a customer's "what happens to my data if you switch vendors" question with anything other than a shrug.

Deidentification standards
  Anything Customer.io retains past deletion — for product analytics, model training, abuse prevention — needs to be genuinely de-identified, not just "hashed the email." The operational question is whether their definition matches the kind of de-ID we already promise our own customers in our privacy notice. If our public commitment is HIPAA-style or strict GDPR de-ID and their standard is weaker, that's a public-statement-to-vendor-practice gap that legal will care about even if ops doesn't.

Backup handling

The minimum rerun is a CS-touch × active-admin stratification with an adjusted point estimate, a holiday-absence baseline, and a pre-registered operational threshold. Without those three, CS treating recent active-admin absence as an actionable renewal signal is not defensible.

WHY THE RAW EFFECT IS UNFIT FOR ACTION

1. CS touch is endogenous to the absence signal, not a covariate. Accounts that go quiet on admin activity are exactly the accounts CS tends to reach out to. The +7.3pp almost certainly mixes "absence predicts churn" with "CS rescued the at-risk accounts." That's not a confound you can wave at — it's the entire lift.

2. The base rate masks it. 82.4% renewal is high enough that a moderate-looking +7.3pp can be entirely produced by CS re-engaging the at-risk cohort. You cannot read the headline number as a behavioral signal about active-admin presence.

3. Holiday season compounds it. Until the holiday absence rate among healthy renewing accounts is quantified, you cannot tell whether absence in Q4 is a signal at all or just December. A trigger that fires on absence-as-signal during a high-absence holiday window will fire constantly and erode CS trust — which is the exact failure mode you wanted to avoid.

4. The readout order is wrong for action. Effect size and operational consequence have to precede the p-value in any confounded observational cohort. A statistically significant raw delta here is not a clean signal.

MINIMUM RERUN OWEN SHOULD DO BEFORE CS ACTS

A. Stratified renewal rates, not pooled. Build the 2×2:
   - active-admin present × CS-touched
   - active-admin present × CS-not-touched
   - active-admin absent × CS-touched
   - active-admin absent × CS-not-touched
   Report each cell's renewal rate and n. The treatment-vs-no-treatment comparison only means something inside the "CS-touched" and "CS-not-touched" rows separately.

B. Adjusted effect, not raw. At minimum, a CS-touch-adjusted estimate (regression with active-admin × CS-touch, or a Mantel-Haenszel-style adjustment across the strata). If Owen can't produce the adjusted lift with a confidence interval, CS does not have a number they can quote.

C. Holiday-absence baseline. The healthy-renewer absence rate during the same window, with a source. If absence is common among accounts that renewed anyway, absence alone is below the noise floor and the whole trigger premise needs to be re-asked, not re-fit.

D. Pre-registered operational threshold. Not "absence fires." A specific decline-from-baseline that would warrant CS action, named in advance of the Q1 rerun. This is what converts the analysis from a description into a rule CS can actually run.

E. Replication plan, not a launch. Q1 off-season replication with a holdout, using the same stratification. Q4 is a readout, not a firing window — Owen should not be shipping a trigger off this cohort.

WHAT CS SHOULD BE TOLD RIGHT NOW

Treat the +7.3pp as a hypothesis, not a signal. No outreach list, no "active-admin absent" playbook, no renewal-risk flag derived from this analysis. The 2023-12-21 read is: gated, joint Growth+CS, queued for Q1 with replication. Owen's job is to come back with A–D. CS's job is to wait.

GOVERNANCE

This is joint Growth + CS ownership, not CS shipping it alone. Growth owns the lifecycle instrumentation the signal is built on, so Growth has to sign off before the trigger becomes operational. That sign-off should be conditional on Owen's A–D landing, not on the current raw cut.

Safety-first sequence (assuming the single chirp ~every 45 sec with steady green light, no smoke/smell, other units quiet = classic low-battery chirp; 2020 manufacture means you're well within the 10-year life, so end-of-life is unlikely):

1. Confirm it's really a low-battery chirp and not an alarm: one brief chirp, ~30-60 sec apart, no rapid pattern, no smoke, no smell, green power light steady. If anything changes here, stop and leave.

2. Optional quick silence: press the TEST/HUSH button once briefly. Most hardwired units will silence the low-battery chirp for ~8 hours, giving you a quiet work window.

3. Prep at floor level before you climb: fresh battery out of the package, polarity confirmed (+/-), stepladder, flashlight, phone within reach. Have the replacement ready to drop in.

4. Power down safely. If the AC connector on the back of the unit unplugs (a small plastic plug/wire harness), you'll cut power by unplugging it. If it doesn't unplug (some are hardwired into the ceiling), flip that circuit at the breaker first. The green light going off tells you AC is dead.

5. Twist or slide the unit off the mounting bracket (usually a short counter-clockwise twist, sometimes a slide). Pull it down enough to reach the battery compartment. Don't yank — if it's stuck, stop.

6. Swap the battery. Note the old one's orientation. The whole swap is ~2-3 minutes; your other interconnected detectors still cover the home during that window, so the house isn't unprotected, just that one spot briefly.

7. Reconnect the AC harness, remount to the bracket (twist clockwise until it seats), confirm the green power light is steady again.

8. Reset and test: press and hold the TEST button until the unit emits a loud alarm pattern, then release. It should sound clearly and stop on release. Any interconnected units should briefly sound too. After test, the unit goes back to normal monitoring — no unprotected window.

Stop troubleshooting and leave the house if:
- You see or smell smoke/heat at any point
- The chirp turns into a full, continuous, or rapid alarm pattern
- The unit is hot to touch, discolored, melted-looking, or visibly damaged
- A chirp pattern you haven't heard before starts (some units chirp in groups of 3 or in a different cadence for non-battery faults)

Replace the unit instead of retrying if:
- Fresh battery + proper reset + green light restored doesn't silence the chirp
- The unit still chirps after a second fresh battery (rules out a bad cell)
- The manufacture date is unreadable but the unit feels older than you remember
- It's been 10 years from the manufacture date (yours is 2020, so ~2030 — flag for your calendar, not today)

Practical backup plan while you work: keep your phone nearby, leave the front door unlocked, and if anything feels off (smell, sound change, dizziness/headache), step out and call 911 from outside. A 2-3 minute battery swap is normal; a confused, escalating, or stubborn chirp is not.

That's a clean resolution — fresh battery, proper reset (power cycle + held test/reset), manufacturer test pattern, steady green, and 30 minutes of silence with no other alarm activity matches the "resolved battery chirp" outcome you treated it as. No reason to keep poking at it.

The only standalone hygiene item worth checking once, when convenient: the unit's manufacture date stamped on the back. If you can't find one or it's hitting 10 years, that swaps the unit from "fine" to "replace on the next convenient pass" — independent of today's chirp. Not urgent, just a one-time check.

Two tablespoons at one corner, with everything underneath dry, is in the small-leak range where the cause is almost always door-side (filter seating, gasket, loading, or door closure) rather than supply/drain. The supply and drain under the sink being dry rules out the usual "call a plumber" paths. Here is a safe, limited sequence you can run with the machine off and the door open. Do these in order and stop at any of the stop conditions below.

  1. Filter (highest-yield given your suspicion)

     - Pull the bottom rack.
     - Remove the filter assembly the way the manual shows (usually twist-out or lift-and-twist).
     - Look at the filter seat and the underside of the filter for: a food particle, a glass shard, a twist in the rubber seal, or grit on the seal face. Even a thin smear of grease can break the seal.
     - Wipe the seat and the seal with a damp cloth, then dry.
     - Re-seat the filter and turn until you feel it click. Try to lift it straight up without twisting — if it comes out, it isn't locked.
     - Put a dry towel flat on the tub floor under the filter area so any residual moisture from the previous leak doesn't get misread later.

  2. Door gasket (tactile, not just visual)

     - Run a finger slowly around the entire gasket perimeter, pressing gently into the channel. Feel for: twists, hardened/glossy spots, food debris, mineral scale, or sections that have popped out of the channel.
     - Pay extra attention to the bottom corner that matches where the water pooled — the lowest point of any seal failure shows up there.
     - Wipe the gasket with a damp cloth, then a dry one. Don't use harsh cleaners on it.
     - "No visible tear" is necessary but not sufficient. The most common failure is a twist or debris in the bottom corner, which you only catch by feel.

  3. Loading and spray arm

     - Confirm nothing sticks out past the rack depth. A single tall item leaning against the door will deflect water straight out the gasket.
     - Spin the spray arm by hand. It should turn freely with a full sweep — no contact with a bottle, a blade, or a rack peg. An obstructed arm can throw water sideways into the door.
     - Confirm the detergent/rinse-aid dispenser closes fully and latches. If a pod fell out and is sitting loose on the rack floor, you'll get a suds overflow out the door — that also lands at one front corner.
     - Confirm the bottom rack is fully rolled in and both rack stops are engaged. A rack sitting 1–2 cm proud of the rails can hold the door slightly off the tub at the bottom corner.

  4. Door seal test (only if 1–3 all check clean)

     - Paper test: close the door on a sheet of paper so a corner sticks out at the bottom near the pooled-water corner. Pull the paper. If it slides out with no resistance, that spot isn't sealing. Repeat at both bottom corners and at the latch side.
     - Flashlight test (better): dim the kitchen, close the door, and have someone shine a flashlight from inside the tub while you look at the gasket perimeter from outside in a dark room. Any sliver of light = same-size leak path for water.

  Decision

     - If 1–4 all pass: run one short, empty cycle on rinse/quick/eco with no detergent and no dishes. Put a dry towel at the front-right corner. Check the towel at 5 minutes in and again at cycle end. If it stays dry, the prior leak was almost certainly the filter seating or a one-off door-side issue and you're fine to resume normal use.
     - If any check fails, fix that one thing and re-test before assuming it's resolved.

  Stop conditions — call for service instead of running another cycle if any of these appear:

     - Any active dripping from the machine while it is sitting idle and off (points to an internal leak, not the door).
     - The filter housing, filter, or its seal is cracked, chipped, or missing a piece.
     - The gasket is torn, missing a section, or feels hard and non-resilient over more than a small area.
     - The door doesn't latch with a definite click, or you can see a gap between the door and tub when closed.
     - Water reappears at the front-right corner during the empty test cycle.
     - Any new water shows up under the sink, in the cabinet base, or behind the unit.
     - Standing water remains in the tub at the end of a normal cycle (points to a drain / float-switch issue, not a seal issue).
     - Any smell of burning, any water near the electrical panel, or any tripping breaker.

  One last note that isn't a failure mode but is worth ruling out: if you opened the door very soon after cycle end, steam condenses on the cooler inner door and can drip out one corner as the door opens — that is a one-time dribble, not a leak. If the prior cycle ended, you opened it within a couple of minutes, and the only sign of moisture was at the door threshold (not under the toe-kick area), that's likely what you saw. The filter check is still worth doing, but the urgency drops.

You don't need a service call for two tablespoons at one corner with everything underneath dry, but you also don't need to run a normal full load until the filter is confirmed locked and the door gasket has been felt, not just glanced at.

Diagnosis fits the front-right pattern — filter not completing its quarter-turn plus a label scrap wedging the gasket are exactly the door-side failure mode we'd expect. Empty rinse with dry supply, dry drain, and a dry cabinet is a clean closeout. Treated as resolved.

Two quick notes on the awkward ones while you grab it, so you can sanity-check my approach before I commit:

- Egg: beat one large egg (about 50g out of the shell), weigh the whole beaten amount, and use ~30g of that. The leftover ~20g keeps in the fridge for a day if you want to brush the tops or just discard it. Don't try to split yolk/white — just beat and portion by weight, it's more accurate than a "half an egg" and far less fussy than cracking a second egg and trying to eyeball half of it.
- Orange zest: I'd nudge up to roughly 80% rather than a strict 60%, so the zest of about one small orange (or 4/5 of a large one's zest, ~5–6g). Zest is mostly aromatic oil on the surface, not bulk — at 60% the cookies tend to taste flatter than the full batch, and orange is exactly the flavor that disappears first when you scale it down.

Everything else I'll just multiply by 0.6 and round to a sensible gram value (butter, sugar, flour, salt, vanilla, etc.).

Got the 30-cookie base locked as the reference. For the 60% version (about 18 cookies), here's what lands:

ORANGE BUTTER COOKIES — 60% batch (~18 cookies)

- 180 g all-purpose flour
- 102 g unsalted butter
- 90 g sugar
- 1/4 tsp salt (or ~1.5 g)
- 3/4 tsp vanilla
- 1 large egg, beaten (≈50 g out of shell) — weigh out 30 g, set the rest aside
- Zest of ~1 small orange, or about 4/5 of a large one (≈5–6 g)

Same method: cream butter and sugar, beat in the 30 g egg with zest and vanilla, fold in flour and salt, chill 30 minutes, bake at 350°F until edges are pale gold.

Three things worth flagging from prior reasoning, just so they're explicit here:
- Egg: don't split yolk and white. Beat the whole egg, weigh out 30 g, keep the leftover ~20 g covered in the fridge for a day if you want to brush tops before baking, otherwise discard.
- Zest: go heavier than a straight 60% cut. Strict 60% gives flatter cookies because the zest is mostly aromatic oil on the surface, not bulk.
- Salt and vanilla: tsp measures are awkward at 60%, so I rounded salt down to 1/4 tsp and vanilla up to 3/4 tsp — both safe directions for this dough.

If you want a different size (say half batch for ~15, or a 75% for ~22), say the word and I'll re-run the same logic.

60% batch — about 18 cookies

Practical gram amounts (assuming a standard orange butter-cookie base of 1 cup butter, 2/3 cup sugar, 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 large egg, zest of 1 large orange, 1 tsp vanilla, 1/2 tsp salt):

  Butter         ~136 g
  Sugar          ~120 g
  Flour          ~168 g
  Egg             30 g  (beaten, weighed — see below)
  Orange zest     5–6 g  (rounded — see below)
  Vanilla        3/4 tsp (rounded up from a strict 0.6 tsp)
  Salt           1/4 tsp (rounded down from a strict 0.3 tsp)

Portioning the beaten egg without over-wetting the dough

  Crack one large egg into a small bowl and beat it lightly with a fork so yolk and white are fully combined. Do not separate them — the dough wants both. A large egg yields roughly 50 g beaten.

  Weigh the beaten egg and add 30 g to the dough (about 2 level tablespoons). That is the 60% target, and it keeps hydration exactly where the base recipe is designed to be: soft and sliceable, not tacky or wet.

  You will have about 20 g left over. Three good uses, in order of preference:

    - Brush it on the tops just before baking for a soft sheen
    - Cover and refrigerate up to 1 day, then brush or discard
    - Discard

  If you go a little over — say 33–35 g — the dough is still workable; just chill a bit longer before rolling. Above ~40 g the dough turns sticky and the cookies will over-spread in the oven.

Rounding the zest

  Do not apply the same 0.6 multiplier to zest that you apply to bulk ingredients. Zest is mostly aromatic surface oil, not bulk mass, and strict scaling makes orange cookies taste flat and faintly soapy rather than bright.

  Aim for 5–6 g of zest, which is the zest of about 1 small orange or 4/5 of a large one — visually, a loosely-packed level tablespoon.

  Best technique for that amount: zest directly into the sugar, then rub the zest and sugar together between your fingertips for 10–15 seconds before creaming. This bursts the oil cells and distributes the flavor through the dough instead of leaving little flavor pockets.

Method stays the same as the base: cream butter and sugar, beat in the egg, zest, and vanilla, fold in flour and salt, chill 30 minutes, bake at 350°F until the edges are pale gold.

For a one-night 27°F snap with about six hours below freezing, the only risks at your place that actually matter are: the hose bib with a hose still attached, the second exposed bib, and the kitchen/guest-bath supply lines on the exterior walls. Everything else (no sprinkler, slab-on-grade typical for East Austin) is low concern. Here is the proportionate list.

Before the freeze (this evening, ideally before you leave for any Christmas plans — about 10 minutes of work):

1. Disconnect the garden hose from the bib. Take it off completely, drain it, and put it somewhere that won't refreeze (garage or shed). Turning the valve off is not enough — a hose left attached traps water against the valve and, if it freezes, pressure can split the bib or even the supply line inside the wall. This is the single highest-risk item on the list.

2. Cover the second exposed bib. A foam hose-bib cover ($2–3 at any hardware store, HEB often has them, many stay open late on Christmas Eve) is ideal. If you can't get one, wrap the bib with a small towel or old t-shirt and secure it with plastic wrap and a rubber band or tape. The goal is just to break the cold-air path so the metal doesn't conduct freezing temps straight into the supply line.

3. Open the cabinet doors under the kitchen sink and the guest-bath sink. Warm indoor air will reach the supply lines on the exterior wall.

4. Let both faucets drip overnight — both the hot AND cold handles, on the kitchen and guest-bath sinks. A slow trickle about the width of a pencil lead is enough; a stream wastes water without adding protection. Place a small pot or jar under each to catch it. Both lines need to drip because both can freeze, and a moving column of water plus relieved pressure is what prevents bursts, not just cold temperature alone.

5. Skip the nighttime thermostat setback tonight. If you usually drop the temp 5–7°F at night, don't. The heat you're already paying for is warming the exterior walls where the pipes run. Keep the house at normal daytime temperature.

That's it for pre-freeze. No need to wrap the water heater, no need to drain any lines, no need to leave every faucet in the house running.

After temperatures climb back above freezing (Sunday morning, after about 7 a.m.):

1. Turn off the dripping faucets. Run each one briefly at full pressure and look under the sink for any drips, bulges, or wet spots on the supply lines and shutoff valves.

2. Go outside and slowly turn on both hose bibs, the one that had the hose first. Turn the handle gently — any resistance, grinding, or a handle that doesn't move smoothly is a sign to stop and check. Then look at the wall and around the faucet base for water. A burst inside the wall often only shows up once water flows again.

3. Walk past the kitchen and guest-bath exterior walls (inside and out) and look for any new water stains, peeling paint, or moisture.

4. Recheck under both sinks about an hour after normal use resumes — a small pinhole leak can take time to show as a drip.

If everything looks dry and the faucets behave normally, you're done. If you see any dampness or a faucet acts oddly, that's worth a plumber call on Monday — not an emergency, but worth getting on the books.

One escalation only if it gets colder than forecast (longer freeze window or stronger wind): put a small space heater aimed at the open cabinet under each sink, on a timer if you have one, with nothing flammable nearby. That is the proportionate next step — not whole-house pipe warming, not running all faucets wide open.

Glad the weighted-egg approach landed cleanly — 19 even cookies with the texture you wanted is a good sign the gram-based scaling held up. Sounds like exactly the shape of afternoon you were hoping for.

Low-risk salvage sequence for the muddy lower third:

  1. Stop now and let the sheet dry bone-dry, flat, under normal indoor air.
     - This is the single most important step. Any lifting or scrubbing while the paper is damp will pill the cold-press tooth and make the mud worse.
     - Drying time on 140-lb cold-press at slightly-damp: roughly 45-90 minutes depending on room humidity. Don't judge the passage wet — a muddy wash usually looks less offensive once it dries to matte.
     - If you want to speed it, a hair dryer on COOL/LOW held 30+ cm away, moving constantly, is safer than heat. Skip the warm setting; heat can flash-dry the surface and lock in streaks.

  2. Once dry, assess the value range you actually have.
     - The mud is now a middle value. Decide what the lightest grass note and the deepest shadow pocket should be. You don't need to repaint the mud — you paint the things around it, and the mud becomes the mid-tone.

  3. Mask the figures and red boots before any further glazing.
     - Low-tack frisket, or just work with a brush short enough that it can't wander into them. Glaze passes are unforgiving when they cross a clean passage.

  4. Glaze in thin, transparent passes, drying fully between each.
     - First pass: thinned sap green + a touch of yellow ochre for the warm sun-side grass. Lay it on with a soft mop; don't scrub, don't go back into it.
     - Second pass, only after fully dry: cooler greens (sap green + a touch of phthalo or viridian) for the shadow pockets between tufts.
     - Third pass, dry: the deepest hollows in burnt sienna + a little phthalo, kept small. Define form, don't fill.
     - Keep two water jars and change them often. Muddy water makes muddy glazes.

  5. Use negative shapes for the highlights, not lifting.
     - If a grass blade or light catch should be lighter than the mud, paint the dark shape next to it and leave the mud alone to read as the light. This is the safer alternative to lifting on a sheet that's already been worked.

  6. If you must lift, lift dry and gently.
     - A damp (not wet) small round brush, pressed onto a single spot for a few seconds, then blotted with a clean paper towel. No scrubbing, no repeat passes on the same fiber. Anything that doesn't release on the first attempt is staying.

  7. Add grass texture last with a rigger or fine round.
     - A few suggestive blades and tuft shadows in the deepest mix from step 4. The eye fills in the rest; don't chase every blade.

  8. Stop when the figures, boots, and grass read as one scene.
     - Salvage is finished when the passage is coherent, not when it's perfect. A slightly muddy lower third under clean figures often reads as atmospheric rather than as a mistake.

Two habits that prevent this next time: lay large grass washes in one confident pass rather than building them, and reserve final detail work for after the wash is dry.

IMMEDIATE (next 2-4 hours)

WATER PROTOCOL OVER THE NEXT FEW HOURS

  - If he keeps ice chips / small sips down for about 30 minutes, gradually
    increase to a normal bowl.
  - If he vomits again, back off to ice chips only and hold food longer.

FOOD REINTRODUCTION (about 2-4 hours after the last vomit, assuming no
further vomiting)

  - Small, bland meal only. Two safe options:
      Plain boiled skinless chicken + plain white rice (about 1:2 ratio)
      OR just plain white rice, slightly overcooked so it's soft.
  - Portion: roughly 1/4 to 1/3 of his normal meal size.
  - If he keeps that down 2-3 hours, offer another small portion of the same.
  - Transition back to normal food gradually over the next 24 hours — mix
    increasing amounts of regular food with the bland diet.

WHAT "OK" LOOKS LIKE OVER THE NEXT 12-24 HOURS

  - Normal drinking within a few hours, normal urination, and a normal
    bowel movement (actually look at it — it shouldn't be black, tarry,
    or bloody).
  - A little more grass-eating is common and not by itself alarming.

CALL AN EMERGENCY VET RIGHT NOW IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR

    mean bloat (GDV), which is life-threatening — minutes-to-hours matter.
  - Belly becomes distended, tight, hard, or visibly swollen.
  - Gums go pale, white, bluish, or yellow.

What is wrong with the "Ship to all trial admins" conclusion

1. Denominator is hidden and conditional.
   - 1,920 randomized, 1,105 in the analysis (57%).
   - The 28% and 31% are rates among users who reached the eligible setup state. The readout never says:

   - The ship target is "all trial admins," but the measurement population is "trial admins who reached eligible setup." Those are not the same set, so the conclusion over-generalizes beyond the measured population.

2. Observation window is half complete (8 of 14 days).
   - This is an interim peek, not a verdict.
   - Novelty effect is plausible at day 8 and would inflate the lift on its own.
   - Interim peeking without a sequential-testing correction inflates the false-positive rate; p=.04 here is not a stable number.

3. Audience imbalance between arms.
   - Secondary admins: 42% treatment vs 27% control (a 15pp gap).
   - Secondary admins plausibly behave differently from primary admins (likely a lower baseline).
   - Without stratified rates per admin type, the +3pp headline could be entirely a mix artifact rather than a variant effect.

4. No confidence interval.
   - p=.04 sits roughly 1.8 SE from null; the CI almost certainly brackets zero or brushes it.
   - Point estimate + p-value alone do not show precision.

5. Support / unsubscribe view is missing.
   - Onboarding changes routinely shift support contact volume (and sometimes churn signals) before they move activation.
   - Both are absent here. Ship-readiness without them is incomplete.

6. The verb in the conclusion is wrong.
   - Honest calls from this read: hold, extend the window to the full 14 days, confirm with a stabilization cohort before broad rollout.
   - "Ship to all" over-reads the data's maturity on every dimension above.

The five blanks this readout leaves empty
  - Denominator (who counts)
  - Cohort composition (admin type, by arm)
  - Effect precision (CI)
  - Observation completeness (8/14 days)
  - Risk surface (support, unsubscribe)

A bare p-value fills none of these, which is why the conclusion does not survive contact with the data behind it.

# Critique of the current draft

The draft you and Ines have on the table is a **two-variant "bad → better" exercise** built on the live Variant B readout as the "bad" anchor and a learner-written rewrite as the "better" version. The structure is right; a few things still need work before Jan 11.

## What the draft gets right

1. **It uses a real artifact, not a synthetic one.** The Variant B readout is the canonical teachable bad example in your shared canon — p=.04 with no CI, no stratified arms, secondary admins 42% vs 27%, no support/unsubscribe pass, an over-generalized ship conclusion. Anchoring the exercise there means learners are practicing on the same shape of mistake you have actually shipped past.
2. **Five blanks, ordered by conclusion logic.** Window/effect → denominator → audience at risk → lifecycle caveat → decision. That ordering forces the *conclusion-after-evidence* discipline (Owen's readout-shape rule) instead of decision-first narrative.
3. **Ship / hold / extend, not ship / no-ship.** A binary frame on a p=.04 result is exactly the gotcha the panel fell into on 2023-11-17. Hold-plus-extend-plus-confirm lets a learner write the right call without contorting.
4. **Ownership split mirrors the session's two teaching blocks.** Owen covers 1, 2, 5 (the readout shape); Ines covers 3, 4 (the lifecycle-risk pass). Learners leave the room with both muscles named, not blurred.
5. **30-second read, 3-minute rewrite, 30-second share.** That's 4 minutes, not the 10 minutes the agenda originally allocated. The tightening is defensible because the *teaching* (Owen's 5 min + Ines's 5 min) carries the framing; the exercise just has to land the rewrite.

## What the draft still needs

1. **State the gate out loud, in the prompt.** The HS under-50 gate forbids inferred/stale evidence; an exercise prompt that says "rewrite the readout" without naming "field-complete + source-named evidence only = beta-eligible" will produce rewrites that look right but fail your own copy-boundary check. The prompt should print the gate so learners are graded against it, not just against tidiness.
2. **Name the denominator explicitly, or learners will fuzz it.** The Variant B mistake was generalizing from "users who reached eligible setup" to "all trial admins." If the rewrite prompt doesn't *label* the eligible-setup denominator, half the class will redo the same mistake with better adjectives. The exercise should require learners to name the denominator they are rewriting *for*.
3. **Don't let "effect size" become "p-value."** The draft's rubric maps question 2 to "effect-size judgment." That phrase is doing a lot of work — learners hearing it will collapse it to "is p<.05?" if the answer key doesn't model a number (e.g., "+3pp on n=… 95% CI …") and a plain-language read (small/medium/large against a meaningful delta for this surface).
4. **Stabilization is the most easily-skipped blank.** Five blanks, four minutes, decision is the loudest — stabilization cohort is the easiest to silently drop. The prompt needs the word *stabilization* visible, and the answer key needs to show that "ship to all" with no second cohort is itself a teaching failure.
5. **The 30-second share should be one learner reading the *whole* rewrite, not each learner reading one blank.** Otherwise you get five parallel micro-reads and the "hardest blank" debrief compresses into nothing. State that one learner reads theirs end-to-end; the group calls the hardest blank.
6. **The "audience at risk" blank needs Ines's lifecycle-stage vocabulary to land first.** Right now the draft assumes the 5 minutes of teaching before it has already done that work. Make the prompt read "name the lifecycle stage + the segment at risk of misreading" so the blank isn't ambiguous between "secondary admins" (a cohort inside the experiment) and "admins the new copy will hit at renewal" (the shipping audience). Those are two different audiences; the exercise should force the choice.
7. **Decision needs a reversal-evidence line, not just a label.** "Ship" / "hold" / "extend" is good. But the user's interview rubric for follow-up reads requires reversal evidence. The answer key's decision blank should include the line "and what would change my mind" — otherwise ship/hold/extend turns into a vibe vote.
8. **Tighten the "bad" anchor.** The current Variant B anchor is correct but verbose. For a 30-second read at the start of the exercise, strip it to: window, headline number, denominator as written, the ship conclusion. Save the omissions (CI, stratification, support, unsubscribe, peeking) for Owen's preceding 5 minutes. The exercise prompt is not the place to teach the omissions a second time.

# Proposed four-minute bad-to-better activity

> "Variant B onboarding checklist shipped to **all trial admins** over a **7-day window**. Treatment reached **eligible setup** at **+3 percentage points vs control**, **p=.04**. Recommend ship."

**Your job (3 minutes, individual, silent):** Rewrite this readout using the five blanks below. Use **field-complete, source-named evidence only** — no inferred denominators, no verbal recall, no cross-field leaps. You may not bring in data the readout did not contain; if a blank requires data the readout does not have, name what is missing and what you would pull before deciding.

| # | Blank | What goes here (one or two short lines max each) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Window and effect** | The actual time window, the actual effect as a number with a CI or equivalent precision read, and what the effect is *of* (e.g., "+3pp lift in eligible-setup reach, 7d, 95% CI [-1.8, +6.6], n=… per arm"). |
| 2 | **Denominator** | Name the denominator you are rewriting *for* (eligible-setup reachers, all trial admins, secondary admins, etc.). State it explicitly. |
| 3 | **Audience at risk** | Name the lifecycle stage and the segment most likely to misread or be mis-affected (e.g., "secondary admins at renewal — lifecycle stage: 60-90 day post-trial"). |

# Short answer key (for Owen + Ines only, not on the slide)

| Blank | Better answer (target shape) | What the bad readout did | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Window and effect** | "7-day window. +3pp on eligible-setup reach. **95% CI [-1.8, +6.6]** — includes zero. n per arm and effect stated as a number, not a p-value." | Reported **p=.04** with no CI, no n, no precision read. Effect buried in significance. | P=.04 with a CI that crosses zero is **first significance, not stabilization.** Shipping on it inflates false-positive rate, especially because the readout was an interim peek. |
| **2. Denominator** | "**Users who reached eligible setup**, treatment vs control. We are *not* generalizing to all trial admins in this readout." | Wrote "ship to **all trial admins**" — generalized from the eligible-setup subset to the broader population, with no composition check. | Treatment was 42% secondary admins, control was 27%. A 15pp arm-composition gap means +3pp could be composition, not variant. Without stratified results, the denominator choice **is the ship-or-hold call.** |
| **3. Audience at risk** | "**Secondary admins**, lifecycle stage 60–90 days post-trial. They compose nearly half the treatment arm, were under-represented in control, and the checklist change has not been validated for them." | Audience not named. Implicit assumption that admin = admin. | The audience most likely to be misread by the headline is also the audience most likely to churn or contact support if the change misfires. Lifecycle stage tells you *where the failure would land*, not just *who*. |
| **4. Lifecycle caveat** | "Onboarding changes can shift **support-contact volume** and **unsubscribe / churn signals** before they shift activation. Neither was measured here." | No support, no unsubscribe, no churn-by-stage. | Operational risk surface is incomplete. A readout that names only the activation effect can hide a support or churn cost that arrives 30 days later. Lifecycle caveat is the line that **delays** the ship decision, not the one that triggers it. |
| **5. Decision** | "**Hold.** Extend the window to the full 14 days. Confirm in a **stabilization cohort** (a second, separately randomized cohort at full window) before any ship decision. Evidence that would change my mind: CI excluding zero **and** stratified results showing the effect holds within primary and secondary admin segments **and** no support/unsubscribe spike in the stabilization cohort." | **Ship to all trial admins.** | A single p=.04 from an interim peek, on a 7-day window, with a 15pp arm-imbalance, no CI, no stratification, no support pass — **ship is the wrong call.** Hold-plus-extend-plus-confirm is the right call. The reversal-evidence line is what keeps a "hold" from sliding into "ship anyway next week." |

## What this answer key is *not* doing

- It is not asking learners to recompute the experiment. They don't have the data.
- It is not asking them to redesign the checklist. That is the wrong activity.
- It is not letting "ship" be a defensible answer on this artifact, even with better adjectives. On this readout, ship is wrong. The exercise is teaching that the readout shape — not the variant — forces the hold.

The right null hypothesis for a Dec 22-only cohort is holiday timing, not product failure. A single-day window that lands on the Friday before Christmas is exactly the cohort where day-7 activation should be expected to dip, because the day-5/6/7 window for almost every workspace falls across Dec 27–29 (and a non-trivial share also lands near New Year's). The Dec 5–10 cohort's day-5/6/7 windows fell on weekdays in mid-December, so it is not a like-for-like comparator — it only tells you what ordinary pre-holiday activation looks like. The diagnostic sequence below is ordered by information-per-unit-cost: the cheapest mechanical check goes first because if it lands, nothing downstream changes the conclusion.

1. Calendar placement of the day-7 window (mechanical, <1 hour)
For each of the 1,605 workspaces, mark whether day 5, 6, or 7 from signup contained Dec 25, Dec 26, Dec 31, Jan 1, or fell on a weekend. Report the share of workspaces whose activation window lost 1, 2, or 3 effective days to holiday/weekend suppression.
- Boundary: if >50% of workspaces lost ≥1 effective day to a holiday/weekend in their day-5/6/7 window, then holiday timing is a credible sufficient explanation for some share of the gap. It does not prove timing caused all of it — only that it is in scope.
- If <20% lost an effective day, timing is not the dominant story and Steps 2–5 become load-bearing.

2. Extend the activation horizon to day 14 and day 21 (cheap, sharpest causal test)
Recompute activation at day 14 and day 21 for the Dec 22 cohort and for the Dec 5–10 cohort. The activation definition should not change — only the deadline.
- Boundary: this is the single most informative check. If Dec 22 day-14 activation closes to within ~3 points of Dec 5–10 day-14 activation (and day-21 closes further), the day-7 gap is essentially a delayed-activation artifact and no product conclusion is warranted. If the gap at day 14 is still ≥5 points, there is a real activation deficit beyond timing and Steps 3–5 start to matter.
- Do not skip this. Day-7 activation on a Dec 22 cohort is structurally biased downward; day-14 and day-21 are not.

3. Cohort quality / non-genuine signup segmentation (cheap, mid-value)
The 1,605 unique workspaces are deduplicated, but the question is whether a higher share of them are non-genuine than in the Dec 5–10 cohort. Segment by: zero sessions after signup, zero teammates invited, no email opened, signup referrer fingerprints, IP clustering, signup-time-of-day pattern. Compute the activation rate on a "looks-genuine" subset for both cohorts and compare deltas.
- Boundary: if the activation gap between Dec 22 and Dec 5–10 narrows materially (>2 points) when restricted to looks-genuine workspaces, non-genuine signups are inflating the Dec 22 denominator. If the gap is unchanged, cohort quality is not driving it.

4. Event-ingestion completeness (moderate cost, important to rule out)
Check for ingest incidents or backlog between Dec 22 and Jan 5. Verify event volume vs. expected daily volume for the Dec 22 cohort's signup-day events and their day-1–7 events. Look for late-arriving events that landed in the day-1–7 window after the original window closed. Compare the cohort's activation count as-of today to what was visible on Dec 30 (day-8 boundary).
- Boundary: if late-arriving events raise activation by >1 point, ingestion was suppressing the number. If event volumes match expected and late-arrivals are negligible, ingest is clean and you stop worrying about it.
- Note: if Step 1 and Step 2 already tell the timing story, you can downgrade this step to a spot-check rather than a full audit.

5. Integration-provider error rates (moderate cost, lower priority)
Compare first-integration success/error rates for the Dec 22 cohort vs. Dec 5–10. If integration partners had reduced on-call during Dec 24–Jan 1, error rates may have spiked.
- Boundary: only relevant if Step 2 leaves a residual gap. If the gap closes at day 14, partner errors did not matter for the headline number. If the gap persists, a >X% uplift in provider-side errors on attempted integrations would indicate a partner-side contribution to the residual.

6. Prior-year Dec 22 cohort as a natural experiment (highest value if it exists)
If you have a Dec 22 signup cohort from 2022 (or any prior year), compute the same day-7, day-14, day-21 activation rates.
- Boundary: this is the cleanest test of "is Dec 22 always like this?" If prior-year Dec 22 cohorts show a similar day-7 dip that closes by day 14, you have direct evidence that Dec 22 cohorts structurally underperform at day 7 by ~5–6 points and the current cohort is behaving as expected. If prior-year Dec 22 cohorts did not dip, then something specific to this cohort (or to this holiday season's traffic mix) is in play.

What you can conclude after running Steps 1–2 alone:
- If the day-7 calendar placement shows heavy holiday overlap AND day-14/day-21 closes the gap: this is a holiday-timing artifact. Do not call a product regression. Do not change onboarding. Note the result and move on. The right comparator for any future product-decision read is either a same-day-prior-year cohort or a non-holiday-window cohort from the same quarter.
- If day-14/day-21 still shows a real gap: there is a product-or-cohort-mix issue worth investigating. Steps 3–5 then determine whether the cause is non-genuine signups, ingestion, or provider errors before you conclude it is a product change.

What you cannot conclude from the headline 25.4% number alone, even with the Dec 5–10 comparator:
- That activation is genuinely down. Dec 22 vs. Dec 5–10 is not a clean A/B.
- That onboarding regressed. No product change was made between the two windows that you have cited.
- That the metric is broken. No ingestion evidence yet.
- That the gap is small enough to ignore. 5.7 points is too large to wave off, which is precisely why Steps 1–2 need to run before any framing lands.

One sequencing note: Steps 3, 4, and 5 only change the headline number if Step 2 fails to close the gap. If Step 2 closes it, you can deprioritize the rest of the diagnostics and return to the standard weekly read. That is the "shortest useful" property — the sequence is bounded: most of the time you stop after Step 2.

1. 60-day production deletion — acceptable with one condition
We can accept 60 days, conditional on Customer.io's use of and production access to Helio data ceasing at termination. The 60 days is a deletion execution window, not a continued-use window. 120 does not work. 3. Single certification — blocker, require two separate certifications
We need (a) production-deletion certification within 30 days of completion, and (b) backup-expiry confirmation that includes the scheduled expiry date for each backup cycle that contained Helio data. Combined, we lose the ability to confirm production deletion to customers on the production timeline and backup expiry on the backup timeline — these are different operational events with different customer-facing implications. 4. Plan band + calendar month retention — acceptable with two conditions
Both are required: (a) workspace, user, message, and event identifiers stripped before the data lands in the analytical store, and (b) reidentification expressly prohibited in the agreement. 15 days is not enough diligence time on a new subprocessor handling customer event data. The objection right needs a real termination path — not one conditioned on showing the change violates applicable law. The notice trigger should be any subprocessor change, not only those Customer.io labels "material." And the protection has to survive any change-of-control or assignment at Customer.io for the full term.

The right-bracket failure mode you're describing (anchor stripped, spins freely) is the classic one — that hole will never hold a plastic anchor again, so the question is really where to put the next fastener, not how to "fix" the old hole. Here's a conservative path:

  Decide what wall material you're dealing with
    Look at an outlet cover (with breaker off if you open it) or an unfinished edge.
    - Drywall (paper-faced gypsum, hollow when you knock): standard toggle works.
    - Plaster over lath or over drywall: plastic anchors and toggles both behave
      differently here; plaster is brittle and crumbles around old holes. If it's
      plaster, lean toward "call a handyman" rather than improvising.
    If you're not sure, that's a handyman trigger.

  Find studs (knock + stud finder + a magnet for the drywall screws)
    Studs are usually 16" on center. From your failed bracket, measure left and
    right. If a stud edge falls within about 1–3" of where the right bracket
    needs to sit, remount into the stud. This is the most conservative option
    for a loaded linen shelf and is worth a small shift in shelf position.
    If the closet is narrow and the shelf can't move without hitting the door
    frame or the opposite wall, the next branch is toggles.

  No stud in range, drywall is sound?
    Use a proper toggle bolt (snap-toggle or a real metal toggle), not another
    plastic anchor. Plastic anchors are what failed here, and a heavier plastic
    anchor in the same stripped hole will just fail again.
    - Drill the hole size the toggle specifies (usually 1/2" for a 1/8" toggle).
      Go slow; if you feel the bit suddenly plunge, you may have hit the back
      side of the wall — back off and accept that location as unusable.
    - The toggle must open fully behind the wall. Pull it back gently until you
      feel it seat against the inside of the drywall before you tighten.
    - Snug, then stop. The classic mistake is over-tightening, which crushes
      the drywall from behind and turns a rated fastener into a future wobble.
    - Choose a load rating well above what the shelf actually carries. Linens
      and towels are heavier than people expect; a winter-bedding load can
      surprise you.

  Call a handyman if any of these are true
    - Wall is plaster or you can't tell.
    - The old hole is larger than ~1.5" across, or the surrounding drywall
      crushes when you press it with a fingertip.
    - The left bracket also has any movement when you test it (one failure
      often means the other has been overloaded and is about to follow).
    - There's any staining, softness, musty smell, or evidence of past leaks
      in that part of the wall.
    - You don't have a stud finder, the right drill bit, or the patience —
      honest answer is fine here, this is a small job done well or a small
      job redone.

  Conservative test before the linens go back
    1. With the bracket remounted but empty, leave it 24 hours. Check for any
       gap appearing between bracket and wall, or dust/powder falling out of
       the hole (that's the drywall starting to crush — abort and call).
    2. Apply slow, increasing downward pressure with your palm at the bracket,
       not a yank. Watch the wall surface around the fastener, not just the
       bracket itself. Any visible dimpling = stop.
    3. Load the shelf with the linens in two stages. Half load for 24 hours,
       inspect, then full load. Don't start at full.
    4. Once fully loaded, give it one firm body-weight lean against the front
       edge of the shelf for about 10 seconds, hands free, while you watch
       the bracket. This is more force than the static linens will ever apply.
    5. Recheck everything at 48 and 72 hours. If it hasn't moved in three
       days of normal use, you can stop worrying.

  Two small habits worth keeping
    - When a shelf holds folded linens, redistribute the load every few months;
      heavy stacks tend to migrate toward one bracket and that's how the right
      side ended up overloaded.
    - The day a bracket feels "almost firm but not quite" is the day to
      rehang, not the day to load more towels on it.

If you'd rather skip the diagnosing and just have it remounted right, a handyman for a single shelf bracket is a fast visit — that's a perfectly reasonable place to land on this decision tree and there's no judgment in it.

Here's a one-pass workflow. Total handling per original: twice (front + back), plus maybe one or two recaptures. Then you put them back in the album and do everything else from the digital files.

SETUP (5 min, once)
- Window light on a flat surface. White paper as backdrop. No flash (glare on glossy prints).
- Prop your phone on a stack of books ~12" above the surface, or use a flatbed scanner if you have one and don't mind the time. Phone is faster for 36.
- Two trays: "to capture" and "done — back to album."

CAPTURE PASS (40–60 min)
- For each photo: front down, snap, flip, snap back, slide into the done tray. Keep order stable in the tray so position = pair.
- Don't label or transcribe during capture. Just shoot. Use a camera app that lets you fire quickly; the iPhone Notes/Files document scanner also works and auto-crops. Either is fine.
- When you're done, originals go into a single "to return to mom" pile. Don't touch them again.

TRANSCRIBE THE BACKS (15–20 min, digital only)
- This is the highest-value step. The handwritten text is the part most at risk of being lost.
- Two options, pick one:
  (a) Sidecar text file per pair (universal, works everywhere):
        001_front.jpg
        001_back.jpg
        001_back.txt   <- type what's written on the back
  (b) Type the back's text into the photo's Description / IPTC caption field in your viewer of choice. Cleaner, but tied to that app.
- Don't skip this. A scanned back image of cursive you can't read in 10 years is almost useless; a typed transcription is forever.

FOLDER STRUCTURE
Cleanest, zero risk of separation — folder per pair:

  shoebox_2024-01-06/
    001/front.jpg
    001/back.jpg
    001/notes.txt
    002/front.jpg
    002/back.jpg
    002/notes.txt
    ...

Easier browsing, slight separation risk — flat folder with paired names:

  shoebox_2024-01-06/
    front_001.jpg   back_001.jpg   notes_001.txt
    front_002.jpg   back_002.jpg   notes_002.txt
    ...

If you might ever move files between devices or rename in bulk, go folder-per-pair.

QUICK QA (10 min, digital only — don't re-handle originals yet)
- Confirm counts: 36 fronts, 36 backs, ~18 notes files (for the half with backs).
- Flag any capture that's obviously blurry, has your thumb in it, or caught the wrong side. Pull just those few from the "return to mom" pile, reshoot, then return the rest.
- Sanity-check a few pairings: does the back's name/date roughly match what's on the front? (E.g., back says "Mom and Dad, 1985" — does the front look like two people, not a kid?) Catches mis-pairs before originals leave your hands.
- After QA passes, originals go back to mom for the albums. You're done with the physical pile.

ONE BACKUP (last step)
- Copy the whole `shoebox_2024-01-06` folder to a second medium.
- Easiest: external USB stick or SD card in a drawer.
- Or a cloud upload to a dedicated folder (Backblaze, Google Drive, an iCloud folder shared with mom). Per your usual setup — don't toggle iCloud Photos on/off, don't sign out of Apple ID, don't dump these into the main Photos library where sync would complicate cleanup. Just upload to a folder.
- After the copy finishes, spot-check that file counts match. Don't trust "copy complete" alone.

TOTAL: roughly 90 minutes, originals handled twice each, one backup. If anything is worth over-protecting it's the typed transcriptions — those are what make the scans useful in 20 years.

Ground truth: USPS, UPS, FedEx, DHL, and Amazon never collect delivery fees via SMS link. A real address-correction fee is paid by the sender, not the recipient. The text is almost certainly smishing — the small $0.30 amount is the trick. She did the right thing by not tapping.

VERIFICATION SEQUENCE — start from official, never from the text:

  1. Identify the expected package out-of-band: which retailer, which carrier, what tracking number is on her order confirmation email (or visible in the retailer's app/site)?
  2. Go directly to the retailer's site or app — type the URL or use the bookmark, do not follow any link from the text. Check the order status page. Real address issues will show there with specifics (item, ETA, reason for hold).
  3. If a carrier is named or implied, take the tracking number from the order confirmation (not the text) and enter it on that carrier's own tracking page — tools.usps.com, ups.com/track, fedex.com/track, or Amazon's "Track Package" in the app.
  4. Sanity-check with mom out loud: who is the package from, what address is on file, and is anything actually being held? If the carrier and retailer both show nothing held, the text is fraudulent.
  5. If she wants a second opinion from the carrier, call the number printed on the carrier's website (not any number from the text) and ask if any package is being held for her.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TEXT — no-click case (her situation):

  - Do not reply. Replying confirms the number is live and invites more smishing.
  - Do not tap or long-press the link.
  - Screenshot it first, in case she wants to file a complaint.
  - On iPhone: long-press the message thread → Report Junk → Delete. That sends the message to Apple and her carrier.
  - Forward a copy to 7726 (SPAM) — that shortcode is the US carrier reporting channel used by AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and works regardless of carrier.
  - Optional but useful: report at reportfraud.ftc.gov, and forward to the retailer being impersonated if it can be identified (most have a security@ or phishing@ address on their site).
  - Delete the message after reporting.
  - No device action is needed. She did not tap, did not enter, did not download — there is nothing to clean up on the phone.

ONLY IF SHE HAD ENTERED INFORMATION — separate set, ignore unless true:

  1. Stop interacting with the page and close it. Do not submit anything more.
  2. If a card or bank login was entered: call the bank or card issuer using the number on the back of the card (not a number from the text). Freeze or replace the card and watch the account for 30 to 90 days.
  3. If a password was entered: change that password on the affected account and on every other account that shares it. Use a unique password per site. Turn on two-factor authentication.
  4. If an app was installed or a file downloaded: on iPhone, delete the app and update iOS; iOS sandboxing limits the blast radius but not to zero, so also change the Apple ID password. On Android, run a security scan and consider a factory reset if the app came from outside the Play Store.
  5. If SSN, date of birth, or similar PII was entered: place a free fraud alert with one of the three credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) — that bureau notifies the other two — and file a report at IdentityTheft.gov for a guided recovery plan. A credit freeze is the stronger option if SSN was exposed.
  6. Turn on transaction alerts on bank and credit card accounts, and pull a free credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com to check for new accounts she did not open.

Bottom line for her actual situation: verify the package through the retailer and carrier directly, then report and delete the text. Nothing else to do.

This pattern — one soft scrape per revolution plus a pulse through the lever — is almost always the rotor's high spot pushing a pad/piston back as it passes. Two common causes: a slightly bent rotor (most likely), or a contamination spot (oil/chain lube) on the rotor that makes one pad grab harder there. Both are fixable, but the way you distinguish "ride carefully to the shop" from "walk it" is the inspection below.

QUICK INSPECTION (do this before deciding anything):

1. Wheel off the ground, spin slowly. Look through the caliper window at the rotor's gap to the pads. It should look roughly even as the rotor passes. Visible side-to-side wobble, especially with an obvious high spot, means a bent rotor. Note how much.

2. Eyeball the rotor edge, especially the arc that lines up with the rub point. Any visible bend, nick, crack, or blue/purple heat discoloration = walk it.

3. Pull the lever firmly while stationary. It should firm up with normal travel. Spongy, mushy, or pulls to the bar = walk it.

4. Confirm the wheel is truly seated. QR halfway-closed should leave an imprint in your palm at full close. Thru-axle should be properly torqued. (You said it looks seated — just verify.)

5. Look at the rotor surface at the rub point. A glistening/wet-looking spot = contamination. That's the most benign cause — wipe with isopropyl and a clean rag, re-spin. If the rub is gone, ride normally.

WALK IT — any one of these:
  - Rotor visibly wobbling side-to-side, or you can see a clear high spot
  - Any visible bend, gouge, crack, or heat-blueing on the rotor
  - Lever feels soft, spongy, or has more travel than normal
  - Harsh metallic grinding (different from the soft scrape you describe)
  - Brake doesn't bite effectively when you test-pull at walking speed
  - Wheel not fully secured in the dropouts

RIDE GENTLY TO THE SHOP — only if ALL of these hold:
  - Rotor looks visually true, or wobble is so slight you have to look hard to see it
  - No damage anywhere on the rotor
  - Lever feel and brake power are normal
  - Wheel is properly secured
  - The rub is a soft scrape, not a thump

If you ride: short trip, avoid descents, favor the rear brake, no hard front braking. Heavy braking on a slightly bent rotor heats the high spot unevenly and can turn a "ride it" situation into a "walk it" one mid-ride.

My read on what you described — soft pulse, single contact point, no rim damage, wheel still seated, brakes still working — sits at the "ride gently to the shop" end of the spectrum IF your inspection confirms no visible rotor damage and the lever feels normal. If anything in the WALK list shows up, walk it. There's no upside to guessing wrong on the front brake.

What the $38 is actually buying

You're paying $38/year (~$3.17/month) to keep a $5,000 water-backup endorsement that the competing quote excludes. As a stand-alone endorsement, water backup at that limit usually runs $30–$60/year on the open market, so the price itself is reasonable — you're not being overcharged for it. The real question is whether the endorsement is worth it for your specific situation.

Water backup covers water that enters the unit through sewers, drains, or a failing sump pump — typically during heavy rain, municipal sewer surges, or sump-pump failure. It's distinct from flood insurance (natural flooding from outside, excluded by both quotes) and from burst-pipe coverage (usually included in modern renters policies now). The realistic exposure depends on floor level (ground-floor and basement units carry most of the risk), building age and plumbing, the landlord's maintenance of the main lines, and any local history of backups. For a higher-floor unit with no basement exposure, $38 is mostly peace of mind. For a ground-floor or basement unit with anything stored on the floor, one backup event commonly runs $3,000–$10,000 in damaged belongings — the endorsement pays for itself many times over.

Short list of questions for the current carrier, in priority order

  1. Is water backup built into the base policy or a separate endorsement? If separate, does it carry its own deductible? Water-backup deductibles are often $2,500, not your $1,000 base — that changes the math.
  2. Exact scope: sewer backup only, sump pump overflow only, or both? Does it cover water entering through floor drains during a municipal overflow?
  3. Is "replacement cost" actually replacement cost across all categories, or does ACV apply to electronics, jewelry, or anything above a sub-limit?
  4. What are the sub-limits on the categories that probably matter to you — bikes, music/photography gear, jewelry, computers? A $30K aggregate with $1K on jewelry is a real gap that the headline number hides.
  5. Is $286 a clean annual price, or does it assume bundling you don't have? And are there discounts you haven't applied — claims-free, paperless, autopay?

Once you have those answers, the competitor's quote either still looks like real savings, or it looks like a coverage downgrade dressed as savings. If it turns out the only real difference is the water-backup endorsement and you can add it to the competitor's policy for something close to $38, the decision is simple; if the competitor won't add it at all, the decision comes down to whether your floor level and plumbing make the $38 a real hedge or just an insurance tax.

Yes — proposing a bounded invite-reminder experiment is supported by this readout, and it's the natural next step under the Q1 readout framework, not a leap. But the language has to stay on the mechanism-test side. Here's the read against the framework.

Why it lands:

1. Denom is complete. 312/312, no UNOWNED GAP, no discovery-only inferences. Under the field-completeness rule, this is beta-eligible evidence, not inferred or stale.

2. Owen's readout shape (denom, effect, conclusion order) is fully satisfied. Full denom, 11.1pt observed effect visible, and the conclusion can sit cleanly on the descriptive side.

3. Ines's lifecycle-risk framing is met by the 2x2 risk parity. Support-contact 11.4% vs 12.0% and lifecycle-unsubscribe 2.5% vs 3.0% — both within rounding. That is the precondition for putting anything into her 1/15–2/23 lifecycle QA+ops environment: the test would not push lifecycle burden materially above the high-invite group's actuals.

4. The 12/22 EA precedent is the comparison case to keep clean, and it's a different situation. There, an experiment ran and failed significance (p=.26, CI -1.8/+6.6), so the right move was demotion to descriptive-only. Here, you haven't attempted significance yet. A bounded test is how you GET first significance — it's the supported path, not a shortcut around the framework.

5. "First significance → stabilization cohort before rollout" means no broad rollout without first significance. It does not mean no bounded test. The bounded test is what feeds that gate.

Framing requirements to keep the proposal on the descriptive side:

- Mechanism language, not metric language: "test whether an invite reminder closes the descriptive renewal gap," not "drive renewal via invites." The 11.1pt is a prior, not a target — and it's selection-biased observational, so the true causal effect is almost certainly smaller and could be zero.

- Pre-register the decision rule: holdout design, pre-defined stopping criteria, pre-defined effect size you'd consider informative. Decision language lives in the pre-registration, not in the readout.

- Risk parity is the lifecycle ceiling, not an opt-out. Support-contact and lifecycle-unsubscribe should not materially exceed the high-invite group's actuals during the test.

- Explicit non-claims. No launch, pipeline, broad-retained, forecast, alerts, revenue-credit, or day-60-nudge language. This is a mechanism test.

- Rollout language stays gated on first significance + a stabilization cohort after that, per the framework. The proposal is not a stabilization cohort, and it doesn't pre-approve one.

What would push it from "supported proposal" to "too far":

- "We'll see how it looks and decide after" — ship language in disguise, and exactly what the pre-registration rule is meant to prevent.

- Treating the 11.1pt as a causal estimate to size the expected effect against.

- Any framing that puts the proposal on the launch/pipeline/broad-retained list before first significance.

- Treating risk parity as license to skip lifecycle monitoring during the test.

Bottom line: the readout supports proposing a bounded invite-reminder experiment as a mechanism test, sized and decisioned in advance, bounded by the high-invite group's risk actuals, with explicit non-rollout language until first significance. That stays within the Q1 framework. What would not stay within the framework is treating the proposal as a decision to ship, or letting the 11.1pt drift from "descriptive prior" into "expected causal effect."

What you're describing — rapid clicking, dimming interior lights, no smoke, no swelling, no smell — is almost always a discharged or end-of-life 12V battery. The clicking is the starter solenoid engaging without enough current to spin the motor; the dimming is the same thing happening to the cabin lights. A battery dated March 2019 is ~4 years 10 months old, which is at the upper end of normal service life for a flooded or AGM battery, so "old battery that finally gave up" is the leading hypothesis. Charging-system failure is less likely but worth ruling out.

Below is a conservative sequence with explicit stop conditions, then the minimum set of post-start checks that distinguishes the two.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. BEFORE YOU CONNECT ANYTHING
────────────────────────────────────────
- Confirm the jump pack is actually charged (LED/full indicator on the pack, not just "I charged it last week").
- Vehicle in Park (automatic) or Neutral (manual), parking brake set, ignition OFF, key out of pocket.
- Turn everything off: headlights (auto or manual), climate, blower, radio, heated seats, defrost, phone chargers. Close doors so dome/courtesy lights don't stay on.
- Quick visual on the battery: heavy white/blue corrosion on the terminals → clean with a wire brush or a baking-soda paste before clamping. Don't delay clamping to clean if corrosion is light.
- Locate a chassis ground point: an unpainted metal bracket, engine lift hook, or alternator bracket, away from the battery and any moving belts. You'll use this instead of the battery's negative post.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. CONNECTION ORDER
────────────────────────────────────────
Follow your jump pack's manual for its specific clamp behavior (many are spark-proof and won't energize until both clamps are correctly placed). The universal correct order is:

  1. RED clamp to battery POSITIVE (+) terminal. Wiggle to confirm metal-on-metal bite.
  2. BLACK clamp to the chassis ground point, NOT the battery's negative post. This keeps any spark away from the battery, where hydrogen can off-gas even from a sealed unit.
  3. Power the jump pack on (if it has a manual switch).

Reverse polarity protection should reject a swapped connection. If the pack alarms, stop and re-check the clamps before touching them.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. CRANK — THE "DON'T HAMMER" RULE
────────────────────────────────────────
This is the part you specifically asked about. The cap is hard:

  - ONE attempt: turn the key and hold for 3 to 5 seconds maximum. No more.
  - Release the key to the RUN position. Wait 60 seconds.
  - If it didn't start, attempt #2: another 3–5 second crank, then another 60-second rest.
  - If it didn't start, attempt #3: same.
  - Total: three cranking attempts, no more.

  STOP IMMEDIATELY (don't try a 4th crank) if:
    - Any of the three attempts produces smoke, a burning smell, a hissing sound, or visible heat from the battery or jump pack.
    - The battery case swells, bulges, or feels warm to the touch.
    - The jump pack shuts itself off or its temperature warning trips — respect its protection circuit.
    - You hear a single loud CLUNK with no further clicking — the starter is getting voltage but is mechanically stuck or shorted; further cranking can weld contacts or burn the starter.
    - The engine cranks strongly but won't fire — that's not a battery problem anymore; stop cranking to avoid flooding a gas engine and to avoid loading a no-start fuel/ignition issue onto the starter.

Three failed attempts with clicking/dimming means the jump pack can't deliver enough current — the battery is likely internally dead (shorted cell) or so deeply discharged that even a healthy jump pack can't push through it. Continued cranking at that point only kills the jump pack and overheats the cables.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. AFTER IT STARTS — DON'T DISCONNECT YET
────────────────────────────────────────
  - Leave the engine idling. Keep the jump pack connected for 2–5 minutes.
  - With the engine running, turn on as many loads as the car can handle and watch the dashboard for the alternator/battery warning light. If it stays on, that's already a charging-system signal — drive straight to a shop, don't disconnect yet, the jump pack is keeping it alive.
  - If no warning light: turn the engine OFF, then disconnect the jump pack — BLACK clamp off first, then RED. (Red-off-first is fine too; the order matters less than not letting the clamps touch each other.)
  - Now do the diagnostic checks below BEFORE driving normally.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. THE SMALLEST SET OF POST-START CHECKS
────────────────────────────────────────
The question you're actually asking is: "Is this just an old battery, or is the alternator not charging it?" You only need two or three data points to answer it.

IF YOU HAVE A MULTIMETER (cheap ones are fine, DC volts, 20V range):

  Reading A — Resting voltage, engine OFF, all loads off, sit ~10 minutes:
    12.6 V or higher  = fully charged battery
    12.4 V            = ~75% (usable)
    12.2 V or lower   = discharged / failing — battery is the problem
    Below 11.9 V      = failed cell — replace battery regardless

  Reading B — Running voltage at the battery terminals, engine idling, accessories off:
    13.7–14.7 V       = alternator is charging normally
    Below 13.5 V      = alternator undercharging — charging-system problem, replace alternator before it kills the next battery
    Above 15.0 V      = voltage regulator stuck open — overcharging, will destroy the new battery quickly, fix immediately

  Reading C — optional but quick: rev to ~2000 RPM and re-check. Should stay in the 13.7–14.7 band. Climbing above 15 V at RPM confirms a failed regulator.

  Interpretation for a March 2019 battery:
    - A healthy and B healthy → battery was simply discharged (left a light on, sat unused, short-trip pattern). Charge it fully with a real charger or by driving 30+ minutes; no replacement needed yet, but it's old.
    - A low (≤12.2 V) and B healthy → battery is end-of-life, won't hold charge. Replace it. Alternator is fine.
    - A healthy after a full charge BUT the next morning it reads A-low again → either parasitic drain (a light or accessory staying on) OR alternator never actually topped it up. Re-check B carefully; if B is good, hunt the parasitic drain by pulling fuses one at a time and watching resting voltage.
    - A anything and B outside 13.7–14.7 → charging-system problem, not just a battery. Don't just put a new battery in; it will die again.

IF YOU DON'T HAVE A MULTIMETER, this two-step test is the minimum:

  1. After driving 30+ minutes (high-way or steady RPM, minimal electrical loads), shut the engine off and immediately try to restart. If it starts, the alternator put some charge back in — that's a weak positive signal but doesn't rule out a borderline alternator.
  2. Let it sit overnight (8+ hours, cold). Try to start it cold the next morning.
       - Starts fine → most likely an old battery that experienced one discharge event, or a one-time drain (left a light on, door ajar, etc.). Drive normally and watch for a repeat.
       - Won't start again → either the battery won't hold charge (replace battery) or the alternator never recharged it (replace alternator, then battery, because a deeply discharged battery is often damaged). At that point, get a multimeter or take it to a shop — guessing between the two wastes parts.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. WHEN TO STOP DIY AND CALL FOR SERVICE
────────────────────────────────────────
- Three crank attempts and no start.
- Any of the stop conditions in section 3 fire (smell, smoke, swelling, heat, single loud clunk).
- Dashboard battery/alternator warning light stays on with the engine running.
- Multimeter shows B outside 13.7–14.7 V.
- The car won't restart the morning after a successful jump-and-drive.

A reasonable plan for your situation, given the battery's age: plan on replacing the battery within the next week or two even if the jump works, and do the multimeter readings at the first idle so you know whether to budget for an alternator too. A March 2019 battery is at end-of-life regardless of what the alternator says today — the question is just whether to also replace a failing alternator before it kills the new battery in a month.

The manual you already have should cover any model-specific quirks for Sam's car (battery location if it's under a seat or in the trunk, jump-post locations if there's no direct battery access). If the battery isn't easily accessible, use the remote jump posts — they're labeled + and − in the engine bay and exist exactly so you don't have to fish the jump pack into a battery tray.
