The duplicate touched a confirmation message, not an outcome. The subject ("Next step: confirm your Helio Start setup") carries the eligible-but-pending frame, not approval; the body presumably does the same. None of the six have an admitted, assisted, or ineligible determination yet, so the second send did not contradict or overwrite anything they will receive later. They are mildly annoyed, not misled. A clarification email:
- would itself be exposed to the same retry semantics you are about to fix,
- would teach these six (and anyone they tell) that Helio Start messaging is fragile,
- adds another lifecycle send the funnel does not need.

What I'd do instead is internal-only: log the incident, exclude the six from the confirmation send on resume (their `confirmation_sent` is already true), and let the normal outcome email close the loop when eligibility completes.

**Safest idempotency fix.**

Root cause is the retry key being scoped to message attempt rather than the eligibility-submission ID, so each retry counted as a fresh send. Anchor idempotency to the business-meaningful entity, not the transport attempt. For the confirmation touch specifically:

- Add a `confirmation_sent` flag (or `confirmation_sent_at` timestamp) on the submission record.
- Gate the send on `confirmation_sent IS NULL` at both enqueue time (so a re-enqueued job short-circuits before it ever hits Customer.io) and at send time (defense in depth).
- Set the flag in the same DB write that records the send, so two concurrent retries cannot both pass the gate.
- Treat the new idempotency key as `(submission_id, "confirmation")`. Keep it scoped to this touch — do not generalize the same gate to outcome emails.

Two things this fix must NOT do:
- It must not suppress a legitimate re-send if a user writes support asking for the confirmation again. That should be an explicit operator action, not a side effect of the retry machinery.
- It must not couple to outcome sends. Admitted / assisted / ineligible are keyed on `(submission_id, outcome)` and remain independent.

This is a one-record, one-gate change — smallest-possible-correction shape, which fits the standing runbook preference.

**Compact validation checklist for Ines before resuming the confirmation message.**

Pre-resume — all must pass before unpausing retries:
- Idempotency gate in place: confirmation send short-circuits if `confirmation_sent` is set, at both enqueue and send.
- Staging retry test: simulate a queue retry on a submission whose `confirmation_sent` is already true; verify exactly one historical send and zero new sends.
- Six affected submissions: `confirmation_sent = true` for all six, so resume does not deliver a third copy.
- Outcome-email integrity: each of admitted / assisted / ineligible still triggers exactly once per submission, gated on its own outcome key, independent of the confirmation gate.
- Downstream coupling check: no later email in the sequence depends on `confirmation_sent` being false. The flag should only block re-sends of itself, not gate downstream sends.

Resume protocol:
- Run a small batch first (a handful of pending, non-affected submissions), watch the queue for 15–30 minutes.
- Go/no-go: zero new duplicates in the first hour, then resume normal cadence.

Post-resume — incident log, not customer-facing:
- One paragraph in the runbook: scope (six submissions, confirmation touch only, no outcome sent yet), cause (retry key on attempt), fix (gate on `confirmation_sent`), validation passed, support volume zero.
- No executive-note language change needed unless support contacts start — at that point the line is "briefly received the same setup-confirmation email twice during a queue retry; no impact on eligibility outcome."

Stop conditions: if the staging retry test fails, or if any downstream email behaves differently on the small batch, do not resume.

Denominator statement first.
The 34 admitted launch-day workspaces all completed the full seven-day observation window, so the activation split is not a survival-biased reading — the 23/11 split is the matured outcome of the cohort, not a partial-window estimate. 23 + 11 reconciles cleanly to 34, and 7 + 3 + 2 reconciles to 12 contacts, so the inputs are internally consistent.

What this single cohort does justify:
1. A point estimate of seven-day activation (67.6%) and nonactivation (32.4%) for this launch-day admitted population, with no missing-window caveat attached.
2. A point estimate of support volume (35.3 contacts per 100 admitted) and reach (26.5% of admitted had at least one contact).
3. A characterization of the support mix on this cohort: ordinary setup is the majority at 7/12 = 58.3%; permissions/ownership reviews and supported billing together are 5/12 = 41.7%.
4. A note that contact volume is somewhat concentrated — 12 contacts across 9 workspaces means 3 of the 9 contacting workspaces had a follow-up (1.33 contacts per contacting workspace on average).
5. A directional read against prior controlled-beta readings on comparable populations (the 2/7 mature-cohort reading of 64.3% sits in the same neighborhood on the activation point estimate), without overstating what one cohort says about another.

What this single cohort does not justify:
1. Generalization beyond this cohort. n = 34 with no confidence interval given — the 67.6% activation and 32.4% nonactivation are point estimates, not ranges, and this cohort alone does not establish that the seven-day definition is right, wrong, or stable.
2. A causal claim about why the 11 did not activate. Support contacts do not automatically map onto the nonactivation outcome, and the cross-tab (contacts per non-activator, contacts per activator) was not provided.
3. A lifecycle-stage read. A single matured seven-day cohort cannot speak to early-stage vs late-stage dynamics on its own.
4. A forecast, pipeline implication, or rollout recommendation. A single cohort is not a base rate.
5. Any recharacterization of the seven-day activation definition (v3) or of the "field-completeness" gate language — this cohort sits inside that frame, it does not revise it.

TONIGHT

Kibo is showing a textbook acute stress response to a sudden, large, unfamiliar object set in his space. The good news: he's still taking treats, drinking, going out normally, and has zero physical illness signs. That's the "ordinary environmental stress" profile, not a medical one.

Low-pressure moves for the next few hours:

1. Pick one zone in Holly that stays empty of boxes and packing materials — ideally where his bed already is. The plan already on the books (don't box in his bed) basically defines this zone for you. Don't move his bed to "save" it; relocating the bed adds a second stressor on top of the first.

2. Park the flattened stack against a wall in a low-traffic spot (a closet, behind the couch, in the office). Out of his main paths means he's not stepping over them to reach water, the door, or his bed.

3. Run the rest of the evening as normal — dinner, walk if it's a walk night, treats, calm voices. Don't make a fuss over the boxes, and don't make a fuss over Kibo. Fussing teaches him that boxes = something to monitor.

4. If he settles on his bed within the next hour or two, that's a strong signal the "one clear zone" strategy worked. If he's still mildly restless at bedtime, that's still inside the normal range for a first night with new objects.

5. Don't start packing tonight. The boxes just exist as background.

NEXT FEW DAYS (gradual introduction)

Days 1–2: Boxes just exist. Keep treats and meals in their normal spots — don't move his bowl next to the boxes "to desensitize." That often backfires. Kibo learns boxes = neutral only if you don't shove them in his face.

Day 3: First small interaction. If he's stopped actively avoiding the stack, drop a single treat ON one flattened box, once during the day. Not on every box, not a pile. If he takes it, good. If he sniffs and walks away, also good — don't push it.

Day 4 onward: When actual packing starts, run short sessions — 15 to 20 minutes. Pack, then put the boxes away or cover them, then resume normal life. The helpful pattern is "packing is a discrete activity with a clear end," not a permanent state. Long unbroken packing days are the thing that pushes dogs over the edge.

Throughout: keep the one quiet zone box-free and packing-free for the full pre-move stretch. His bed stays where it is. Walks, dinner, treats, the routine — those are the load-bearing parts of his week, and they don't change because cardboard showed up.

WHERE THIS STOPS BEING ENVIRONMENTAL STRESS

The line is symptom-based, not duration-based. A dog being weird about boxes for a week is still environmental. A dog being weird in specific ways is a vet call.

Call the vet if any of these show up, even one:

  - Refuses food for more than 24 hours, or water for more than 12
  - Vomiting or diarrhea (one episode = call and describe; repeated = urgent)
  - Panting or trembling that doesn't stop when the room is quiet and he's not being handled
  - Hiding that becomes constant — under furniture, in a closet, won't come out for meals
  - New reactivity: growl, snap, lip curl, guarding — at people, other pets, or objects he never guarded before
  - Self-soothing that causes harm: licking one spot raw, scratching until bleeding, chewing paws
  - Restlessness severe enough that he can't sleep for more than one or two nights running
  - Lethargy that looks different from "tired" — won't get up for dinner, won't engage, doesn't react to his name
  - Bathroom accidents in the house after being reliably trained, especially sudden and unexplained
  - Any physical symptom at all: limping, breathing changes, coughing, glazed eyes

Tonight's behavior — pacing, hallway-checking, won't settle, but eating and drinking and walking normally with no other symptoms — is on the "monitor, don't escalate" side of that line. The plan above is what moves the needle over the next few days.

If it'd help, I can drop a short recurring calendar block for the next couple of weeks titled something like "Kibo — quiet zone check" so the box-free area stays a conscious habit through the heavier packing stretch. Up to you whether that's useful or feels like one more thing on the list.

Cherrywood renter's-insurance quote comparison

Note: you mentioned "cheaper" and "higher" but didn't share the dollar amounts. The structural differences below hold regardless of the price gap; whether Quote B is worth the upgrade depends on that gap. If you can drop the two annual premiums in, I can give a more concrete cost-vs-coverage read.

  Quote A (cheaper)
    ACV coverage, $100K liability, $1,000 deductible, no water backup

  Quote B (higher)
    RC coverage, $300K liability, $500 deductible, water-backup endorsement

1. Annual cost

  Get the actual annual premium for each. Dividing by 12 confirms your earlier ~$20/month budget; if Quote B is more than ~$60–80/year higher than Quote A, the trade-offs need a closer look. Renter's insurance in Austin typically runs $150–300/year, so a meaningful coverage upgrade is usually a small premium step.

2. Practical coverage tradeoffs for what you actually own

  Work equipment (laptop, monitors, etc.)
    ACV: a 2–3 year old laptop that cost $1,800 new might pay out $700–900. Older items may be near zero.
    RC: pays current replacement cost — typically $1,500–2,000+ for a comparable current laptop.
    Real difference: $800–$1,500+ per item at claim time.

  Bikes (commuter, possibly a second)
    Most renter's policies have a bike sublimit (often $1,000–2,500 total) unless you schedule separately. Worth confirming before deciding.
    ACV on a 3-year-old hybrid commuter might value at $300–500. RC: $800–1,500+ for a current equivalent.
    Stolen from the unit or damaged in a covered peril — RC pays materially more.

  Art supplies (watercolor kit, brushes, paper, palette)
    Mixed bag. Sealed tubes and unopened pads hold value; used paint in your palette and worn brushes depreciate fast.
    ACV for a kit bought two years ago might pay 30–50% of original. RC for what you can rebuy at retail is the win; for used consumables, adjusters typically apply a heavy haircut.
    Dollar exposure here is smaller than bikes and gear; the bigger water-related loss is finished pieces, paper, frames, and supplies ruined by a leak.

  Liability ($100K vs $300K)
    $100K is the lease-portal floor. Covers a guest injury or pet incident involving Kibo — relevant given he's reactive to wind on walks.
    $300K adds real protection if someone is seriously hurt in the unit and sues. A personal umbrella is $200–300/year for $1M, so jumping from $100K to $300K is often disproportionately cheap relative to the protection.

  Water backup
    Austin has flash-flood and sewer-backup risk. Whether the Cherrywood unit is ground-floor or has any below-grade plumbing matters.
    Endorsement typically covers $5,000–$25,000 of damage from drain or sump-pump backup, separate from the personal-property limit. Inexpensive to add, expensive to skip if it ever triggers.

  Deductible ($500 vs $1,000)
    Saves $500 out of pocket per claim. The bigger effect: with RC coverage, the higher payout often clears a $1,000 deductible that ACV wouldn't, so you'd actually file the claim instead of eating the loss.

3. ACV vs RC in real terms

  Actual cash value (ACV) reimburses what the item is worth today after depreciation.
    A 3-year-old laptop bought for $1,800: insurer calculates useful life (often 5 years for electronics), subtracts depreciation, pays ~$720. You use that to buy a current equivalent that costs $1,500–2,000 — the gap is yours.
    A watercolor tube: claims adjusters usually treat consumables as fully depreciated at use; ACV may be a few dollars at most.
    Bikes depreciate slower than electronics but still lose roughly a third in three years.

  Replacement cost (RC) reimburses what it costs to buy a comparable new item today, no depreciation applied.
    Same laptop: RC pays the current equivalent price — $1,500–2,000.
    Trade-off: most RC policies pay ACV up front and refund the depreciation only after you submit a receipt proving replacement. Confirm that mechanic.
    Trade-off 2: premiums typically run 10–25% higher than ACV. Often pays for itself in a single mid-size claim.

  Real-world difference for your situation: highest-exposure categories are bikes and work equipment — both mid-life items where RC pays materially more. Art supplies are smaller dollar exposure but skewed toward RC advantage for items you can rebuy.

4. Three focused questions to ask the insurer

  a) "What are the sublimits on bikes, art supplies/collectibles, and electronics/computer equipment? Do any items need to be scheduled separately, and what does scheduling cost?"
    Most renter's policies have per-category caps well below the headline personal-property limit. If bikes are capped at $1,500 and you own a $2,500 commuter, you need to schedule it or you're underinsured regardless of ACV vs RC.

  b) "What exactly does 'listing Cherrywood as an interested party' mean on this policy — interested party, loss payee, or additional insured — and which does the lease require? Does any of those give Cherrywood claim-payment rights or notification duties that change how the policy works?"
    The three terms are legally distinct. Interested party is generally just a notification address; loss payee has claim-payment rights; additional insured extends liability coverage. You want the lease wording matched exactly so move-in isn't delayed and your claim authority isn't diluted.

  c) "For the replacement-cost policy, is RC paid up front, or is ACV paid first with the depreciation refunded after I submit a receipt? Does RC apply to partial-use items like half-used watercolor paints and worn brushes, or only to items I can prove I bought new?"
    RC that requires proof of new-purchase receipt often excludes most of what makes RC valuable. Confirm in writing that RC applies to your full kit, including consumables, and confirm the timing of the depreciation refund so you're not waiting months out of pocket.

Bottom line: both quotes meet Cherrywood's portal requirements, but Option B is materially stronger on every dimension that matters for your situation, and the $81.60/year premium gap is small.

Cherrywood portal compliance (both options)
  - Effective date 5/1/24: matches lease start and the keys-release trigger
  - Personal liability ≥ $100K: A is exactly at the floor ($100K); B is 3x ($300K)
  - Proof before keys: both can issue cert with effective 5/1/24
  - Property listed as interested party: both allow (no extra fee noted)
  - No separate pet exclusion: Kibo covered on both

Material differences (in favor of B)
  1. Water backup — $5K included on B, none on A. This is the most decision-relevant gap given that watercolor paper, finished paintings, frames, and art supplies are water-vulnerable even though the dollar exposure is below bikes/electronics. A unit or neighbor-unit leak on A would come out of personal property limits.
  2. Replacement cost vs actual cash value — B is RC ($30K); A is ACV ($20K). RC matters most for rebuyable supplies (paper, new brushes, frames, palette items); it pays less for heavily used paint tubes and worn brushes. A would depreciate everything.
  3. Personal liability — $300K vs $100K. A is at the stated minimum, fine for portal compliance but thin if a claim escalates (dog incident, kitchen fire reaching a neighbor). The 3x liability is part of the $6.80/mo gap.
  4. Deductible — $500 vs $1,000. Saves $500 out-of-pocket per claim. A single mid-sized claim more than offsets the annual premium gap on its own.
  5. Loss of use — $10K vs $5K. ~3-4 weeks of temporary housing at typical Austin rates on B; ~1.5-2 weeks on A.

Cost math
  - A: $17.80 x 12 = $213.60/yr
  - B: $24.60 x 12 = $295.20/yr
  - Gap: $81.60/yr ($6.80/mo)

Still to confirm with the insurer/agent before binding (apply to both, more sharply to B):
  - Water backup endorsement: confirm the $5K figure is the sublimit, not the out-of-pocket floor; ask if it has its own deductible
  - Replacement-cost terms for partially used paint tubes and worn brushes — does B pay ACV initially and refund depreciation only after you submit a replacement receipt, and what's the window?
  - Whether RC covers equivalent-grade replacements or requires provably new purchases
  - In writing, exactly what claim-payment or notification rights Cherrywood receives under the "interested party" listing (typically notice of cancellation/nonrenewal, not claim-handling, but confirm)

Recommendation: B, primarily on the strength of the water-backup endorsement plus replacement-cost valuation. The liability, deductible, and loss-of-use upgrades reinforce that, and the price gap is small.

1.  Personal-property classification. Your laptop (used for ordinary remote work), bicycle, and watercolor supplies are personal property — not business inventory — so they sit under the personal-property limits on both quotes. No business-property inventory needed.

2.  Off-premises theft. Bike theft away from home is covered on both quotes, but the deductible applies. On Option A ($1,000 deductible) a stolen bike worth under $1,000 isn't worth claiming; on Option B ($500 deductible) the same logic applies at a lower threshold. Either way, your commute bike is protected — just above the deductible.

3.  RC payout mechanic — this is the substantive clarification. The replacement-cost quote does not pay replacement cost up front. The flow is:
       a.  Insurer pays actual cash value (depreciated) at claim time.
       b.  You buy a replacement.
       c.  You submit receipts.
       d.  Insurer pays the recoverable depreciation.

    Practical implications:
       -  You have to actually replace the item to collect the full RC.

       -  If you choose not to replace (e.g., an item you were already planning to retire), you only get ACV.

4.  $2,500 scheduling. Standard policy requirement. You said neither of you has a single item over $2,500, so nothing needs to be scheduled. Standard category sublimits (jewelry, electronics, furs, etc.) still apply, but no itemized endorsement is required.

5.  $84/year gap. Confirms Option B (RC) is $84/year more than Option A (ACV). Small note: the original packet implied $81.60 ($6.80/month × 12). The insurer's $84 is authoritative for this decision; the $2.40/year difference is rounding or a slight revision.

       -  The items most likely to be claimed (laptop, bike, art supplies, paintings) are items you'd actually replace — so the RC mechanic pays out in full for you, not just in theory.

RECOMMENDATION

Hold the 23. Release the 15,217 now, on the April 2 schedule. The 23 go into a second wave, not back into the April 2 send log.

Why hold the 23:
- Send-time integrity. Once a record goes out it cannot be unsent, and the collision creates two failure modes that cannot be cleanly reversed post-send:
  1. Duplicate delivery if two of the 23 aliases canonicalize to a recipient already covered by the 15,217.
  2. Silent suppression bypass if a canonical on active suppression is reachable through a non-suppressed alias.
- Operational cost of a second wave is low. This is an integration-stalled nudge, not a time-critical promo. Reaching the affected records a day or two later does not change the read.
- Holding the 23 does not protect the 15,217. The clean audience has already cleared suppression and merge independently. Their send window should not be hostage to an unrelated data-quality issue on 23 records.

VALIDATION INES WORKS BEFORE ANY CANONICAL IS ADDED BACK

Work these gates in order per record. None is optional. None of them is bypassable by re-routing to a different channel.

1. Merge resolution
   - How many distinct canonicals actually emerge from the 23? The collision count is a record count, not a person count — Ines should confirm before any send decision.
   - What is the identity-match confidence? Verified email change, login history, or explicit user action only. Reject low-confidence (fuzzy / heuristic) merges from driving send decisions — those records stay out.

2. Cross-check against the 15,217 already-sent audience
   - For each emergent canonical, is it already represented in the 15,217 (under a different alias, or as itself)?
   - If yes: that canonical has already received this email. Do not re-send any alias that maps to it. This is the duplicate-send gate.

3. Suppression, applied at the right granularity
   - Check the canonical, not just the alias we'd send to.
   - If suppression is attached at the person/canonical level: any alias resolving to a suppressed canonical stays out, regardless of that alias's own address-level status.
   - If suppression is address-level only: treat conservatively. A user who unsubscribed at one address has expressed intent at the person level — Ines makes an explicit call before any other alias of theirs is sent to.

4. Deliverability on the actual sending address
   - MX valid. Not a role address (info@, no-reply@, support@, etc.). No spam-trap signal.

5. Bounce and complaint history on the address you'd send to
   - Hard bounce → out.
   - Complaint in the last 90 days → out unless manually overridden and documented.

6. Recency of suppression events
   - Any unsubscribe or hard bounce in the last 24-48h may not be in the snapshot used for the 15,217 pass. Re-check against current suppression state at the moment of re-preflight, not at the moment the original preflight ran.

7. Documentation
   - For each of the 23: record the merge confidence, the canonical it resolved to, the suppression source checked, and the send decision. This is the artifact that lets the next preflight catch the same shape instead of rediscovering it.

8. Wave shape
   - Cleared records go out as a separate, later wave with a fresh preflight at send time. They are not retroactively logged into the April 2 send.

ONE THING TO FLATLY NOT DO

Do not reach for a workaround. If a merge is low-confidence, or suppression granularity is ambiguous, or any cross-check fails, the record stays out of this campaign. The cost of an "integration stalled" email landing on someone who unsubscribed — or going out twice to the same person — is materially worse than the cost of reaching a small number of additional records this week. Workarounds are how the suppression system gets quietly compromised, and once compromised the next campaign inherits the loss of trust.

Here's a concrete plan and a clean rule.

INTERIM LIGHTING PLAN (Mon evening through Thu)

The cracked bracket can't hold aim over bumps, so the primary light isn't trustworthy on its own. Treat it as a backup and run a clip-on as your main visibility for the next few rides.

1. Tonight — stabilize the primary so it's at least usable if needed
   - Zip-tie the bracket body to the seatpost or to a sturdy bag strap
   - Or wrap a heavy rubber band / a strip of electrical tape around the bracket
   - Goal: keep the lens horizontal, not pointing at the ground
   - This is a stopgap, not the plan. Don't rely on it as your sole rear marker.

2. Run a clip-on as your actual primary
   - Use a small USB-rechargeable red rear light (matches your standing preference) clipped to a backpack shoulder strap or sternum strap. If you don't already own one, a basic USB-rechargeable seatpost-style light with a rubberized clip works fine on a strap.
   - Best mount: backpack strap — most visible to drivers and unaffected by seatpost vibration. Next best: jersey pocket or belt loop. Avoid helmet-only mounting alone; height makes it harder for cars to gauge distance.
   - Mode: steady-on in daylight for max conspicuity. Switch to flashing if the ride runs long and battery gets tight.

3. Pre-ride checklist (about 30 seconds, every ride)
   - Both lights: charged, turning on, no flicker
   - Primary: aiming straight back, not down
   - Clip-on: clipped securely, visible from directly behind the bike
   - Rule of thumb: if the primary slips during the ride, stop and re-seat it. Don't finish a ride with a downward-pointing light as your only rear marker.

4. What not to treat as sufficient on its own
   - A reflective vest alone — you already know this isn't a substitute for a working rear light in dusk/dark
   - The cracked primary alone, even after zip-tying — vibration can re-fail it mid-ride
   - One light doing both jobs (primary + backup) — redundancy is the whole point this week

If you don't have a clip-on at home, grab one before Tuesday's commute. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons are both still in daylight (sunset ~7:45pm), so you won't be riding in true dark, but the bracket situation is the reason to have redundancy anyway.

REPAIR vs. REPLACE — RULE FOR THURSDAY'S INSPECTION

After the shop looks at it, ask them two questions and let the answers decide.

Question 1: Is the light body itself healthy?
   - Battery holds a full charge and isn't swollen
   - LED is consistent across modes (no flicker, no dead modes)
   - No moisture or fogging inside the lens/housing
   - Charging port and cable work cleanly
   - Unit is fairly recent and has been trouble-free

Question 2: Is the bracket available as a separately-replaceable part?
   - Most reputable lights (Cygolite, Lezyne, Knog, Garmin, Blackburn) sell bracket/mount kits for roughly $5–15
   - Some cheaper or fully-integrated units don't — the mount is molded into the housing and isn't a standalone SKU

Decision:
   - Both healthy body AND bracket is a separate part → REPAIR (just swap the bracket). Cheaper, faster, and the electronics you've already vetted stay in service. The failure mode was isolated and mechanical.
   - Either is "no" → REPLACE the whole light with a USB-rechargeable red rear light matching your standing criteria (steady-on mode, seatpost mount, water-resistant).

Sanity check: if the replacement bracket plus labor runs more than about 60% of a comparable new light, just replace — the math stops favoring repair at that point.

Why this rule: bracket failure alone is a localized mechanical problem, so a $10 bracket into a healthy light is the right call. Replacement becomes the right call when the bracket failure is part of broader wear (aging battery, intermittent LED, moisture entry) or when the bracket can't be sourced separately — because bolting a new mount onto a degrading light just sets up the next failure, and a fresh unit gives you a clean clock on the new component.

Quick note on the math tool: this session doesn't have a code-execution or shell terminal loaded (I searched the catalog and confirmed). The crossover math below is hand-computed and cross-checked at the boundary — but flagging that explicitly per the "no fabricated output" rule.

**Crossover multiplier (Option B overtakes A).**

Total pay at payout multiplier m (0 = no bonus, 1 = full target):

    A(m) = 128,000 + 0.10 · 128,000 · m = 128,000 + 12,800m
    B(m) = 121,000 + 0.18 · 121,000 · m = 121,000 + 21,780m

Set B(m) = A(m):

    21,780m + 121,000 = 12,800m + 128,000
    (21,780 − 12,800) · m = 7,000
    8,980m = 7,000
    m = 7,000 / 8,980 = 350 / 449 ≈ 0.7795 ≈ 77.95%

**At m = 77.95%**, both options pay ≈ $137,977.73. Below that, A pays more; above it, B pays more. (Sanity points: at m = 0 A leads by $7,000; at m = 0.5 A leads by $2,510; at m = 0.75 A leads by ~$265; at m = 0.80 B leads by ~$184; at m = 1.0 B leads by $1,980.)

So the question for Marcus's planning isn't "which pays more on average" — it's "how often does the team actually pay above ~78% of target." That's where payout history matters.

**Payout history Marcus should pull before deciding.**

For this comparison to be informative, the history needs to be specific enough to estimate the realized distribution of m at his level/team, not the company-wide average. Ask for:

1. Multi-year realized m for his role/level/team (at least 3 years, ideally 5). Mean alone isn't enough — he needs the spread. Does m ever sit near or above 0.78 regularly, or is it clustered low?
2. The dispersion: how often does m hit 0, 0.5, 1.0, or exceed 1.0? A single point estimate ("average is 0.9") hides whether most years are 0.7 and one was 1.1.
3. The base-vs-bonus trade-off in the history. If his team has historically averaged ~0.85, B has clearly been winning; if it averages ~0.6, A has been winning by roughly $1,500–2,000/year.
4. Forward-looking signal. Is the team's payout trending up or down? Any guidance from leadership about the upcoming cycle's target (e.g., "we'll be at 1.1 this year") shifts the expected m materially.
5. Cliff/gating structure on the bonus. Some plans pay 0 below a threshold (e.g., company must hit 95% of plan) — if B's 18% target has a higher effective hurdle than A's 10%, the realized m distributions aren't comparable even at the same headline number.
6. Risk preference context. A has higher floor ($7,000 cushion), lower upside. B has lower floor, higher upside. The "right" answer depends on whether Marcus wants the larger guaranteed base or is optimizing for upside in good years — that should be his call once he sees the history.

You said you don't want a recommendation yet, so I'll stop there. Once Marcus has the historical m distribution (and ideally the dispersion, not just the mean), the crossover math plus that distribution will usually make the choice fairly obvious to him.

Practical check against your commute (3 rides × 70 min = 210 min/week of light, weekly charging):

Option 1 — $28 bracket only, corroded connector retained
  * Cheaper by $17, but it leaves the connector problem in place. The crack exposed the connector in the first place, so the corrosion will keep progressing regardless of how new the bracket is.
  * Your standing rule is bracket-only is acceptable only when the charging port/cable are clean. A corroded wired connector fails that test, so the rule says replace.
  * Your price threshold is: replace the whole light if bracket-plus-labor exceeds ~60% of a comparable new light. $28 is ~62% of $45 — already past the cutoff before you even factor in the corrosion.
  * Net: you'd be paying $28 to inherit a known electrical failure that's likely to worsen.

Option 2 — $45 rechargeable (new bracket + new light, 4 hr stated runtime)
  * Fixes both problems at once: clean bracket AND clean connector AND fresh battery.
  * Runtime check: 210 min of weekly use against 240 min stated capacity = 30 min buffer (about 12%). Workable, but tight if you take it literally.
  * The "tight" part is the only real concern. Two ways to make it comfortable:
      - Charge mid-week instead of only weekly (e.g., after 2 rides = 140 min used, ~100 min left). Your light supports this since it's rechargeable.
      - Treat 4 hr as the ceiling, not the average. Cold weather, battery age, or a single longer ride (detour, flat, rain reroute) can eat that buffer fast.
  * If you'd rather not babysit the charge schedule, look for a model with longer stated runtime — but for your stated 3×/week pattern, this one is workable if you top it up after ride 2.

Final call: yes, the $45 rechargeable is the sounder option. The $17 premium buys you a clean connector (the actual reason the bracket failed in the first place), a fresh battery, and peace of mind that nothing is degrading behind the new bracket. The only caveat worth acting on is the runtime margin — plan to charge after every two rides, not strictly weekly, so you don't ride into the last 30 minutes of capacity.

Three of the five applicants (A, B, C) treated the under-50 threshold as the only eligibility check that mattered — A and C assumed size alone qualified, B read the remaining fields as onboarding noise rather than gates. The other two (D, E) clear size cleanly but each hits a single prerequisite that routes them out: a CSV import (D) and a one-time migration (E). FAQ 1 — Company size
Q: Our team is under 50 people. Doesn't that qualify us for Helio Start self-serve?
A: No. To use Helio Start self-serve, an account has to be under 50 people AND clear all five additional required checks: direct admin (the named customer admin can prove they administer the account), simple deployment, week-one integration fit, entitlement, and supported billing. Being under 50 is necessary but not sufficient on its own. If any of those five checks fall short, the account is routed to the assisted path regardless of team size.

FAQ 2 — Direct admin
Q: Our consultant or implementation partner handles setup. Does that count as direct admin?
A: No. Direct admin requires the named customer-side account administrator to be able to prove they administer the account — that's an admin-proof check on you, not on a partner. A consultant owning configuration, training, or go-live doesn't substitute, even if they'll be hands-on after launch. If you can demonstrate admin access but a different check routes you out (for example, a CSV import or migration), the assisted path is still the outcome.

FAQ 3 — Import or migration routing
Q: Our integration is supported and we'll move our data over. Why does that put us on the assisted path?
A: Supported integration and supported billing describe the steady-state setup, but the routing decision is made on the prerequisite, not the destination. If getting to that steady state requires a one-time step that Helio Start doesn't cover self-serve — a CSV import, a data migration, or another prerequisite — that prerequisite itself routes the account to the assisted path, even if every other check would otherwise pass.

Here's the comparison, built around Marcus's own numbers and stated preference.

The two options (from prior context):
  Option A: $128,000 base + 10% target bonus ($12,800 at 100%)
  Option B: $121,000 base + 18% target bonus ($21,780 at 100%)

Break-even multiplier
  $128,000 + $12,800m = $121,000 + $21,780m
  $7,000 = $8,980m  →  m ≈ 0.7795 (77.95%)
  Below 77.95% → Option A pays more. Above → Option B pays more.

Simple three-year average of Marcus's stated history (100%, 60%, 0%)
  Average = (100 + 60 + 0) / 3 = 160/3 ≈ 53.33%

At 53.33%:
  Option A: $128,000 + $12,800 × 0.5333 = $134,826.67
  Option B: $121,000 + $21,780 × 0.5333 = $132,616.00
  Option A leads by ≈ $2,211

So on the arithmetic of the three past observations, Option A comes out ahead by about $2.2K. That's because 53.33% sits well below the 77.95% break-even — there's a roughly 25-point cushion before Option B's larger bonus target catches up.

How to recommend without overclaiming
  The 53.33% figure is a description of three past payouts, not a forecast. Two things make it weak as a predictor:
    - n = 3, with one observation at 0%. The "average" is doing very little work; removing or changing any one year moves it noticeably.
    - Marcus himself said he doesn't have better information for next year. That admission rules out treating the mean as a base rate.

What you can defend without pretending:
    1. Below 77.95%, Option A pays more; above, Option B does. That's structural, not statistical.
    2. Marcus said he values dependable cash over maximum upside. Option A's $128K base is $7K heavier than Option B's $121K — a real, contractual difference that doesn't depend on next year's payout decision.
    3. Option A's downside (a 0% year, like the most recent one in his history) pays $128,000. Option B's same year pays $121,000. The base gap is the floor protection.

Recommendation
  Option A. The reason you can give Marcus without faking a forecast is that the argument isn't "the average predicts next year will be 53%." It's: "You told me dependable cash matters more than upside, and Option A puts $7,000 more of your pay in the part that doesn't depend on the multiplier. The historical average happens to land below break-even, but the case for A rests on the base gap, not on predicting the next payout."

If you want to soften it for Marcus: Option B is only the better choice if you expect next year's multiplier to clear 77.95% — and you said you have no information suggesting that. Picking A is consistent with both the preference and the uncertainty.

Why this breakdown cannot establish that integration type caused the
activation gap:

  1. Assignment to category is non-random. The category is the FIRST
     integration the account attempted, which is a customer choice /
     product behavior, not a controlled treatment. There is no random
     allocation, no counterfactual, and no pre-registration.

  2. Account complexity and customer choice jointly determine the path.
     Accounts with engineering capacity and a clean API surface tend to
     start there; accounts that don't yet have API plumbing (or aren't
     ready to wire it up in week 1) reach for CSV; warehouse sits
     between those. So the rate differences track WHO is in each
     category as much as WHAT the category is. The category is acting
     as a proxy for underlying account characteristics — technical
     readiness, data maturity, team size, time-to-first-action — that
     also drive whether day-7 activation happens at all.

  3. Reverse reading is equally possible. An account that is going to
     activate regardless may simply start with the path it finds
     first; an account that won't activate in week 1 may also stall
     on whichever path it picked. The first-attempted integration is
     downstream of the same factors that drive activation, not
     upstream of them in any causal sense here.

  4. No baseline / no within-account comparison. We don't know what
     would happen to the API accounts had they attempted CSV first,
     nor the CSV accounts had they attempted API first.

  complexity rather than a randomized assignment, these rates describe
  who attempted what and how each group fared; they do not support a
  claim that the integration type itself moved activation.

The quick read: 18 months is past most manufacturers' 12-month post-opening window, and visible phase separation that won't recombine means the latex has at least partially coagulated. That alone meets a reasonable discard threshold, but a 2 cm corner test on the same paper you'll use Sunday takes about 20 minutes and gives real signal, so it's worth running as confirmation rather than as the question.

Test gate (in order, stop and discard if any step fails):
  1. Shake/roll for 5–10 minutes. If it doesn't return to a uniform milky liquid, it's done — discard.
  2. Brush a 2 cm dab onto scrap of the actual paper stock. Let dry fully (should be flexible and matte, not tacky).
  3. Remove with your rubber pickup, pulling parallel to or slightly under the surface.

Discard criteria — any one of these means the bottle is unsafe for the painting:
  - Won't recombine after thorough mixing (you're already here).
  - Goes on lumpy or streaky, with visible rubber flecks on brush or paper.
  - Dries soft, sticky, or noticeably slower than fresh fluid.
  - Lifts fibers or roughens the paper on removal — same failure mode as your 2024-03-10 sky wash.
  - Leaves a yellow or brown tint on the paper (oxidized latex).
  - Leaves a residue ghost that won't lift with a damp brush.

If it passes all six, you can use it Sunday, but keep the use conservative: confine it to a non-critical area or short mask runs, stop washes 2–3 mm short of the mask edge, and only remove after the wash is bone-dry. Even a clean pass is a judgment call — a fresh bottle is roughly $8–12 and cheaper insurance than risking the painting.

The two options aren't quite parallel — Mom's is 6 hours with a familiar person, vet boarding is 11 hours supervised in a facility. The trial's purpose is to convert boarding from a hypothetical backup into a known option, so the worth-it question is really: would you actually use boarding if Mom's plan fell through?

Quick comparison

  Mom's option (7:30am-1:30pm at her place):
    - Familiar person + likely familiar environment, lower stress for Kibo
    - Free or near-free
    - Covers movers (8am-noon) plus a small buffer
    - Single point of failure — if Mom can't do it day-of, scramble
    - Handoff at 1:30pm may not line up with where you'll actually be (likely at or heading to Cherrywood by then)

  Vet day boarding (7am-6pm):
    - Supervised, much longer coverage (absorbs mover overruns, full-day chaos)
    - Late pickup fits your likely afternoon at Cherrywood
    - Unknown stress load for Kibo — new facility, new dogs, new smells
    - Typical cost $30-50/day plus trial fee
    - Handoff is a single stop on your way home from move day

Decision factors for whether the trial is worthwhile

  1. Failure modes for Mom's option
     - Mom's standing rule with you is small ~25-min drop-ins, not 6-hour sits. A full morning + early afternoon of Kibo is meaningfully outside her usual pattern — confirm she's comfortable with the full window, not just the principle of helping.
     - Her own schedule, energy, or Kibo's behavior at her place could shift the picture.

  2. Kibo's stress profile
     - 3/27/2024: Kibo reacted to moving boxes appearing in Holly by pacing, checking the hallway, refusing to settle on his usual bed. That's evidence of environmental sensitivity.
     - Mom's house is familiar — likely the lower-stress choice.
     - A boarding facility is a much bigger change than mom's living room. The trial is the only way to learn how he handles it without gambling on move day.

  3. The coverage gap
     - Movers are scheduled to noon. Clean-up, last items, key handoff, and a drive to Cherrywood can easily push you past 1:30pm.
     - Mom's window ends 1:30pm — that's the tight spot.
     - Vet boarding covers to 6pm and removes the gap.

  4. Handoff logistics on move day
     - At 1:30pm you'll most plausibly be at Cherrywood receiving the truck or doing first-pass placement.
     - Picking Kibo up from Mom = either an extra drive back to her side of town, or asking her to bring him to Cherrywood mid-afternoon.
     - Vet pickup at 6pm = one stop, on your normal evening route.

  5. Trial cost vs. insurance value
     - Trial fee is typically modest and is sunk whether or not you board on 5/1.
     - The booking deadline is 4/16 — only 3 days out from today. That's a firm commitment regardless of whether the trial has happened yet.

  6. Sequencing question worth asking the vet
     - Confirm whether booking on 4/16 requires the trial to be completed by 4/24, or whether booking can happen with the trial still pending. This affects whether you can lock in the backup now and test it later.

The deciding question

  Do you have a Plan C if Mom can't do it on 5/1? If the honest answer is "no, I'd be scrambling," the trial is worth booking — it's cheap insurance against a known single point of failure, and the only way to know whether boarding will actually work for Kibo. If you have a real Plan C (Sam, a friend, a sitter service), the trial's incremental value drops and you can skip it.

  If you do book, do the trial before 4/24 even if you're leaning toward Mom's option — a positive trial result means you have a 6pm coverage fallback that costs nothing to keep on the books, and a negative trial result means you find out now rather than on move morning.

VERDICT
Yes for narrow rollout, conditional on three test gaps being either filled or explicitly accepted as out-of-scope for v1. The patch addresses the root cause (empty-blob submission after camera-chooser cancel or background), preserves form state (the right call given applicant re-do cost), and clears the stalled spinner (the UX failure behind the support tickets). "Passes on iOS 16 and 17" is the floor, not the ceiling, for a rollout that will sit in a real funnel. Hold the rollout if gaps (a)–(d) below aren't dispositioned.

TEST COVERAGE GAPS
- Covered: camera-chooser cancel (iOS 16, 17), photo-library cancel (iOS 16, 17), empty-blob rejection, form-state preservation, clean retry UI.
- Not covered in the report — decide explicitly:
  (a) iOS 15 Safari. Small residual iOS share. For a narrow rollout, acceptable to exclude behind a UA gate; say so if you do.
  (b) iPadOS Safari. Same WebKit, distinct viewport. Can ship in the same rollout if you trust WebKit parity, or hold.
  (c) Background-mid-capture vs. chooser-cancel. The report says "cancels or backgrounds." Confirm the patch covers both branches; the description is ambiguous, and these are different code paths on iOS.
  (d) Stale-filename display state. The original failure retains a filename alongside an empty blob. Rejecting the blob is necessary; resetting the visible filename / picker UI on rejection is what determines whether retry feels clean or just confusing. Verify on device before rollout.

NARROW ROLL-OUT SCOPE
- Surface: mobile Safari iOS 16 and 17 only, UA-gated.
- Cohort: new applicants only. The two pending applicants from April 12 (2 of 9 affected; 7 of 9 already retried on desktop; 0 declined because of the bug) are not in this rollout unless they retry on their own; their status stays "pending ownership proof" either way.
- Ramp: 100% on the targeted surface, no gradual ramp needed. The change is a rejection/UX guard, not a new affordance, so there's no learning curve to stagger. If you want a ramp anyway, 24h at 10% is enough to confirm the guard doesn't false-positive.
- Out of scope: iOS 15, iPadOS, Android Chrome, desktop (already working). Re-evaluate at day 7.

ELIGIBILITY TREATMENT — unchanged, three explicit points
- The two pending applicants remain pending. They are not declined because of this bug, and they are not auto-advanced because of this fix. Their outcome is determined by whether they complete ownership proof, same as every other applicant.
- Any applicant who hits the new empty-blob rejection and retries successfully continues the normal funnel. No new gating, no new field, no new entitlement check.
- Any applicant who hits the rejection and abandons gets standard abandonment follow-up. The patch removes a path-reliability bug; it doesn't manufacture eligibility where none existed, and it doesn't add a contraction-shaped signal to the lifecycle metrics.

MONITORING — minimum set, named per the segment convention (hs_path__<need>__<measurement>)
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__empty_blob_rejected` — count and rate per 1k ownership-proof attempts on iOS 16/17 Safari. Pre-patch baseline = 0 (event didn't exist). Expect a non-zero rate post-rollout roughly equal to the prior stall rate, then declining as the bug-conditioned cohort clears.
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__retry_after_reject` — applicants who retry ownership proof within the same session after a rejection. Should run high (>70%); low value means the retry UX isn't actually inviting retry or another blocker fires after it.
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__answers_preserved_on_retry` — explicit event. The "preserves other answers" claim is the load-bearing UX promise; measure it, don't infer it.
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__completion_rate_iOS_16_17_Safari` — headline metric. Compare pre-patch baseline to post-patch and to desktop. This is what tells you the funnel actually closed, not just that the spinner cleared.
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__stall_spinner_rate` — original failure mode. Should drop to near-zero on the targeted surface within days.
- `hs_path__ownership_proof_upload__client_error_new` — any new client-side error tagged to this flow. Watch for regressions the patch introduced.

Cadence: daily review for 7 days, then weekly through day 30.

ROLLBACK CRITERIA — minimum, any one triggers
1. False-positive rejection. Any legitimate ownership-proof upload rejected by the empty-blob guard. Threshold: >0.5% of legitimate attempts on the targeted surface, or any single support-traced incident where the rejection blocked an otherwise-good submission.
2. Form-state preservation failure. Any traced incident where an applicant on the rejection path had to re-enter answers on retry. If this claim breaks, the cost-benefit of the fix collapses.
3. Stall rate not decreased. Stall-spinner rate on iOS 16/17 Safari does not drop by at least 80% from pre-patch baseline within 7 days. Means the patch isn't catching the cases it claims to, or it's catching them but the UX still stalls.
4. Mobile Safari completion regression. Ownership-proof completion rate on the targeted surface drops below the pre-patch baseline (not stalls — actual completions). Different from #3; means the patch introduced a new blocker.
5. New P0/P1 client error tied to this flow.
6. Eligibility drift. Any signal that applicants on the rejection path are being routed differently in downstream segmentation than equivalent applicants on the success path. Should not happen; flag-and-investigate if it does.

Keep this behind a feature flag so rollback is a one-action flip, not a hotfix. The two pending applicants are not part of the rollback decision — their status is independent of whether the patch is enabled.

The clause aligns with what's already on your self-transport list. A couple of categories are broader than propane + lighter fluid + cleaning liquids + restricted aerosols, worth a quick scan:

- Compressed-gas cylinders — the clause doesn't carve out non-fuel. CO2 cartridges (seltzer, bike inflators), helium, medical oxygen, anything under pressure counts, not just propane/butane.

- Solvents / hazardous liquids beyond paint and cleaners — acetone/nail polish remover, paint thinner, turpentine, lighter fluid, pesticides/herbicides, pool chemicals, fuel stabilizer, lawn-mower gas can, some car fluids. Anything with a "Danger" or "Flammable" label goes in the self-transport pile, not in a carton.

- Aerosols-labeled-flammable is a specific subset — most cooking spray and pump-spray cleaners are fine; hairspray, spray paint, WD-40, most aerosol cleaners, some deodorants, and insect spray are out.

Since you're separating the self-transport pile before the movers arrive, that's the cleanest moment to do the scan — easier to catch a misrouted can when it's all in one spot than after something's been packed.

INTERPRETATION — HOW THE MOVER CLAUSE APPLIES TO THESE THREE ITEMS

Partially used aerosol art fixative (1 can):
  Art fixative (charcoal / pastel / pencil sealer) is a pressurized container labeled FLAMMABLE. That puts it squarely in the mover agreement's "aerosols labeled flammable" prohibited category. The mover will not load it, and per the agreement it cannot be concealed in a carton.

Partially used butane cooking-fuel canisters (2 cans):
  Pressurized flammable-gas containers. They fall under both the "gasoline / solvents / hazardous liquids" prohibition and, by the same flammable-pressure logic, the aerosol prohibition. They are not loadable by the mover under any condition, even if they feel nearly empty — partial pressure plus residual fuel is still hazardous.

Common thread for all three: none go in a packed carton, none get loaded by movers, none go in curbside trash or recycling, and none should be discharged indoors.

PRE-MOVE HANDLING (today, before tomorrow's 4:30–6:30 PM packing block and well before the movers load)

  1.  Set them aside now in a single labeled bin or box — mark it "HHW — DO NOT PACK" — at Holly, away from packed boxes, heat sources, and direct sun. Keep upright, caps and valves intact. Do not stack anything on top.
  2.  Do not attempt to discharge any of them. Not indoors, not in the garage, not in the driveway. Venting aerosol fixative indoors is an inhalation and ignition hazard and is unlawful in many jurisdictions. Outdoor venting of butane is a fire / explosion risk near structures, vehicles, or people.
  3.  Do not place in regular household trash, recycling, or the Holly dumpster. Partially full pressurized flammable cans are excluded from municipal solid waste; the canisters especially — even "empty" — retain residual gas and pressure and don't belong at the curb.

DISPOSAL — TWO DISTINCT PATHS

(A) Lawful local household-hazardous-waste disposal (recommended for all three)

  This is the path the city expects residents to use and the only routinely lawful disposal route for partially-full flammable aerosols and butane canisters. Austin / Travis County HHW accepts both categories at the drop-off facility and via scheduled residential pickup. Drop-off is the cleanest option before the April 30 walkthrough.

  Even cans that feel "empty" belong at HHW, not the curb — residual pressure and fuel keep them out of the normal waste stream.

(B) Self-transport (only when the destination is HHW or a retailer take-back)

  These items join the existing self-transport pile (propane, lighter fluid, cleaning liquids, restricted aerosols). The self-transport protocol here is the same as for those:

    -  Vehicle trunk, not the passenger cabin. Crack the trunk vent or drive with windows slightly open if the trunk is integral.
    -  Upright and secured — a milk crate or rigid plastic bin with the cans wedged so they cannot tip or roll.
    -  Keep labels visible so HHW staff can identify contents.
    -  Keep the original carton / cap on the butane canisters if you still have it; otherwise wrap the valve area so it can't be actuated by shifting cargo.
    -  Heat: April in Texas means a closed-up trunk in the sun gets very hot. Don't let the car sit; do the errand promptly and unload at the destination.
    -  Don't co-load with food, kids, or pets in the cabin.

  Butane-specific alternative worth checking first: some outdoor / camping retailers (REI, Bass Pro, and similar) run fuel-canister take-back or recycling programs with better recovery than HHW. A quick call before the HHW trip can save the trip. No equivalent take-back exists for art fixative — HHW is the route.

NOT a self-transport option:

The only legitimate self-transport destinations are an HHW drop-off, a retailer take-back, or — for butane only, and only if you actually have an outdoor burner and a real use — burning through the fuel outdoors in a legal appliance and then sending the empty can to HHW. "Use it up just to empty it" isn't worth the time and risk for two partially used cans unless a camping trip is actually on the calendar.

  -  At the April 30 4:00–4:30 PM walkthrough the can and the two canisters should already be gone from the unit — do not leave them behind as Holly's problem.

  Third-cohort rate
    Numerator: 48 of 61 mature admitted accounts completed a supported first integration within the day-7 window.
    48 / 61 = 0.78688...  →  78.7% third-cohort integration rate.

  Combined three-cohort rate
    Numerator: 115 integrations across 153 mature admitted accounts.
    115 / 153 = 0.75163...  →  75.2% combined integration rate across the three non-overlapping weekly cohorts.

  Sanity check on the prior two cohorts
    67 / 92 = 72.8%. So the third cohort (78.7%) is ~5.9 points above the prior combined rate; the rolling three-cohort combined moves up by ~2.4 points (72.8% → 75.2%) once the third cohort is folded in. Both moves are modest in absolute terms and consistent with the third cohort being slightly better than the first two rather than a discontinuity.

DENOMINATOR-FIRST READ

What this establishes before the May 24 review

  1. The denominator is real and non-trivial, and the cohorts are clean. 153 distinct mature admitted accounts across three non-overlapping weekly cohorts (34 + 58 + 61 = 153, no double-count). That is a usable evidence base for a weekly-cohort activation gate — not a single-week anecdote and not a single account.

  2. The rate is computed on the right population. All 153 are admitted accounts with complete day-7 observation windows, not a hand-picked subset. The numerator (115 integrations) is restricted to supported first integrations, not any-touch.

  3. The process-integrity checks passed across the full sample, not just this cohort. No refusal-boundary breach, no duplicate or blank current entitlement state, no unsupported lifecycle branch in any of the 153. That means the 75.2% rate is the rate under clean gate conditions — the lane held.

  4. Support-contact signal is small and stays on the right side of the boundary. 17 contacts across 12 of the 61 third-cohort workspaces. The 14 ordinary setup questions are inside the setup window; the 3 post-admission permissions questions are post-admission, which is the position where the entitlement-boundary posture is being exercised. None are framed as a refusal-boundary breach. This is consistent with, not evidence against, the protected posture holding.

  5. The third cohort alone (61 mature accounts, 48 integrations, 78.7%) is a coherent per-week slice that can be cited alongside the combined 153-account figure rather than folded silently into it.

What this does not establish about the protected continuation decision

  1. It does not establish activation across all admitted accounts — only across those that survived to a mature day-7 window. The 2024-04-15 board-slide note you have in memory flagged this explicitly for the earlier snapshot ("only the earliest 64 of 147 admitted Helio Start accounts had mature day-7 observation windows, so the 52-of-64 first-integration result was not a rate for all admitted accounts"). The same caveat applies here: the 75.2% is a rate among accounts that reached a complete day-7 window, not a rate among all admitted accounts. Pre-window churn, no-show, and drop-off are not represented in either the numerator or the denominator.

  2. It does not establish the rate holds beyond three weekly cohorts. ~3 weeks of evidence is a thin base for a continuation decision that runs further. Seasonal variation, customer-mix drift, and pipeline composition changes are not constrained by this slice.

  3. It does not establish integration depth, sustained usage, retention past day 7, paid conversion, or revenue contribution. First-integration-within-day-7 is a leading indicator, not the outcome the continuation decision is ultimately weighing.

  4. It does not establish causation. 78.7% in the third cohort (and 75.2% combined) does not tell you whether the activation rate is caused by the protected admission path, caused by customer mix, or would survive route-out. There is no counterfactual here — no control cohort, no pre/post comparison on the same population.

  5. It does not establish support-burden sustainability. 17 contacts across 12 of 61 workspaces is a low base rate, but a low base rate on three weekly cohorts does not establish that the contact pattern (ordinary setup vs. post-admission permissions) would hold at higher volume, or that the contacts are not themselves caused by the protections rather than by customer need.

  6. It does not establish that clean-gate-process integrity is sufficient grounds for continuation. "No refusal-boundary breach, no duplicate/blank entitlement state, no unsupported lifecycle branch" establishes the lane stayed within bounds. It does not establish that staying within bounds produces a better customer or business outcome than the alternative lane.

  Net for the May 24 review: the third cohort is a clean, modestly-upward data point on a small but non-trivial denominator, and it keeps the activation-rate evidence on the right side of the gate threshold. It is enough to take to the review as supporting evidence; it is not enough, on its own, to decide protected continuation, because the rate is over mature-window accounts only, over ~3 weeks only, and over first-integration only, with no counterfactual.

RECOMMENDATION

Staggered parallel rollout: 30 accounts randomized 1:1 into 15 treatment and 15 holdout. Treatment accounts start in three weekly waves of 5, with the first wave the week of July 8. Holdouts remain unexposed through the measurement window. Primary analysis is intention-to-treat with cohort and week fixed effects. The held-out 15 supply the counterfactual trend; the cohort and week dummies absorb calendar effects.

WHY NOT PURE PARALLEL 15/15

  The 5-per-week CS handling cap is the binding constraint. Launching all 15 treatment accounts at once is a 3x overage of that cap and is operationally infeasible regardless of statistical appeal. Separately, 15 vs 15 only detects large effects — worth saying out loud before launch, not after a null readout.

WHY NOT A NAIVE 5/WEEK STAGGER WITH NO HELD-OUT ARM

  The "later eligible accounts are temporary comparisons" framing is technically a stepped wedge, but if every account is eventually exposed the only counterfactual becomes each account's own pre-period. That conflates the treatment effect with maturity and time-trend effects and weakens the causal read. A permanent 15-account holdout keeps the comparison explicit.

THE DESIGN

Randomization
  - 30 eligible accounts randomized 1:1 to treatment (n=15) and holdout (n=15).
  - Stratify on prior expansion-signal tier if one exists, so arms balance on the variable most likely to predict the outcome. Pre-register the strata before any prompt is sent.

Rollout (respects the 5/week cap)
  - Wave 1: 5 treatment accounts start the week of July 8. First live prompt lands no earlier than July 8.
  - Wave 2: 5 treatment accounts start the week of July 15.
  - Wave 3: 5 treatment accounts start the week of July 22.
  - Holdouts (15) are not exposed during the measurement window. Pre-commit, in writing, to whether and when holdouts are treated after the readout — this needs to be communicated to CS and Sales before launch so there is no contamination.

Measurement window
  - Pre-register window length (e.g., 8 weeks from each cohort's start) and the primary endpoint before any prompt is sent. Candidate endpoints: qualified expansion-signal event in window; seat-add in window; ARPA lift in window. Pick one as primary, others as secondary, and do not switch endpoints after the readout.

PRE-SPECIFIED ANALYSIS

Primary specification — intention-to-treat at the account level:

    Y_it = alpha + beta*Cohort_i + gamma*Week_t + delta*(Treated_i × Post_it) + epsilon_it

  - delta is the causal estimate.
  - beta absorbs time-invariant differences across the three launch cohorts.
  - gamma absorbs week-of-calendar effects, including any drift across July–August.
  - Identification rests on parallel pre-trends between treatment and holdout across the three launch weeks — pre-register a visual pre-trend check and a stop-rule for when parallel trends fail.

Secondary specifications (robustness, not substitutes)
  - Pooled cross-section DiD with treatment × post fixed effects.
  - Cohort-by-cohort treatment effect estimates (3 effects, one per wave). If they diverge materially, report the divergence rather than pool.

MDE disclosure
  - Pre-register the minimum detectable effect at 80% power for the chosen primary endpoint and expected outcome variance, before launch. If the MDE exceeds the realistic effect size, the readout framing has to acknowledge a null is uninformative. A clean comparison does not rescue an underpowered one.

CAVEATS WORTH PUTTING IN THE BRIEF

  - Denominator is 30 (15 vs 15). The readout language should say so and not disguise concentration of expansion dollars.
  - Calendar effects are modeled, not eliminated. If a meaningful shock lands during the measurement window, the week fixed effects absorb it but the read should flag it.
  - Holdout contamination risk is real. CS or Sales "helping" a holdout during the window breaks the design — the deferred-treatment commitment is the cheapest insurance.
  - This is design work, not an operating retained-mid motion. The brief should not frame the pilot as a retained-mid rollout until the readout is in.

ALTERNATIVE IF PERMANENT HOLDOUTS AREN'T VIABLE

  Stepped wedge where all 30 eventually receive treatment in 6 weekly cohorts of 5. Use a Hussey–Hiemstra-style stepped-wedge specification (cohort and time fixed effects, treatment indicator that switches at each cohort's start). Identification is weaker (within-account pre/post plus cross-cohort variation) and the model is more complex, but it avoids holding accounts out indefinitely. Reach for this only if Sales or CS cannot accept a 15-account holdout through the window.

NEXT STEP

  If you want this written into BRIEF-2024-04-expansion-assist-pilot-design, say go and I will update the brief with the design, the pre-registered analysis specification, and the MDE placeholder.

Bottom line up front: skipping on the two smallest cogs under firm load is the classic signature of a stretched chain (and possibly a worn cassette), not just grime. A clean + lube will tell you whether it's dirt or wear — but if the skip survives a clean, do not ride it to work. Walk it to a shop or drive/rideshare instead.

CLEANING (tonight, drivetrain back on the bike)

  - Wipe the chain first. Pedal backward slowly with a clean rag pinched against the lower run of the chain. Flip the rag, do it again. You're pulling the loose gritty paste off; don't scrub hard.
  - Clean the cassette. Hold a rag through the spokes against the cassette and pedal backward, or use an old toothbrush along the cog gaps while turning the wheel backward. The goal is removing surface paste, not a deep degrease.
  - Wipe the derailleur pulleys. A quick wipe of each jockey wheel and the cage. Spin them — they should turn freely with no crunch.
  - Skip the solvents tonight. WD-40, degreaser, or even dish soap can leave a residue that mimics wear symptoms. If you must use anything wet, rinse fully and let it dry before lubing.
  - Don't remove the chain or the wheel. Nothing about this symptom justifies pulling the drivetrain apart at home.

INSPECTION (after wipe-down, before lube)

  - Stiff chain link. Pedal backward slowly and watch every link flex. A link that pops up instead of hinging smoothly is a stiff link and can mimic a worn-cog skip. Note its location.
  - Small-cog tooth profile. Look directly down at the two smallest cogs in good light. New teeth are symmetric — flat on top, even sides. Worn teeth look like shark fins or hooks, curved and leaning to one side. Compare against a middle cog if you want a reference. Any visible hooking = shop visit before next commute, do not ride under load.
  - Chain length feel. Lift the chain off the largest cog at the front and let it hang. If it droops noticeably or you can see daylight through the cog teeth, the chain is stretched. A shop wear-indicator tool is the proper check, but visible droop is enough reason not to commute.
  - Hanger and derailleur. Glance at the hanger (the tab sticking out of the dropout the derailleur bolts to). It should sit straight. A bent hanger can shift only the upper or lower end of the cassette badly even when shifting feels crisp elsewhere — but crisp shifting across other cogs argues against this.

LUBRICATION (after cleaning, after the chain is dry)

  - One drop per roller, pedaling backward slowly so each link passes over the bottle. Then 30 seconds of backpedaling, then a final rag wipe so the outside of the chain is dry to the touch. Wet outside = magnet for tomorrow's grit.

LOW-LOAD TEST (next day, quiet street, low traffic, daylight)

  - Start in a middle cog. Confirm shifting is crisp across the middle of the cassette under easy pedaling. If shifting is glitchy here, something else is going on — shop.
  - Shift to the second-smallest cog. Pedal lightly for 30 seconds. Then medium firm. Note any skip.
  - Shift to the smallest cog. Light pedaling only. If it skips even once under light load, end the test — that's a clear NO-GO.
  - If light load is clean, try firm pedaling on the smallest cog for a few pedal strokes. Any skip = NO-GO.
  - Coast and brake-test as usual on the way back. The test is about the skip, not anything else.

CLEAR CRITERIA — DO NOT RIDE TO WORK UNTIL A SHOP CHECKS THE CHAIN AND CASSETTE IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE

  - Skip on the smallest or second-smallest cog survives a clean and lube, even once.
  - You can see hooked/shark-fin teeth on the two smallest cogs.
  - The chain visibly droops when lifted off the front ring, or you see daylight through cog teeth when the chain is engaged.
  - You found a stiff link that you can't free by hand (gentle back-and-forth flexing of just that link).
  - The skip happened under startup torque (first pedal stroke from a stop or out of the saddle), not just steady cruising — startup skips are the ones that drop a foot.

OTHERWISE OK TO RIDE, BUT WITH THESE LIMITS UNTIL YOU DO GET TO A SHOP

  - Stay in the middle 60 percent of the cassette. Avoid the two smallest cogs entirely.
  - Spin easy on any climb. Don't stand and mash.

PALETTE ASSIGNMENTS
  Ultramarine (U)        -> cool blue. Shadows, door cool side, deepest accents.
  Burnt sienna (BS)      -> brick, pot, warm mid-tones. Also the "neutralizer" that pushes U toward green.
  Quinacridone rose (QR) -> warms brick, makes clean violet with U, reserved small clean accents.

TWO-COLOR MIXES (avoid three-color mixes on the palette - that is where mud lives)
  Door green-gray      : U + tiny BS, about 4:1 U-heavy. Glaze in two thin passes
                         instead of pre-mixing a heavy puddle.
  Cool blue-violet     : U + QR, about 2:1 U-leaning. Keep BS completely out of the shadows.
  Warm brick wall      : BS straight, diluted 1:4 to 1:8 for sunlit faces. Touch of QR
                         only where the reference shows a pink-warm brick.
  Terracotta pot       : BS straight; a half-drop of QR at most for warmth. Reserve the
                         strongest BS concentration for the shadow side of the pot.
  True neutrals        : U + BS + QR together - use only for the darkest recesses
                         (inside the door shadow) and keep the area small. Three-color
                         mixes go flat and gray fast.

LAYER ORDER (lightest first, dry between passes)
  1. Sunlit brick and lit face of pot - dilute BS. Dry fully.
  2. Door body - pale U+BS glaze, U-heavy. Dry.
  3. Door shadow side and architectural shadow lines - same mix, less water.
  4. Porch-floor cool shadows - U+QR, one confident pass. Wet-on-dry for crisp shadow
     edges; wet-on-wet only where the reference shows soft falloff.
  5. Pot body - BS, possibly a touch of QR. Stop at the rim.
  6. Deep accents - concentrated U in the deepest door recess, one small QR-only note
     (flower in pot, or a single warm speck against the door).

RESERVED CLEAN ACCENTS (do not paint these - let the postcard paper speak)
  - Sunlit top edge of the brick wall
  - Rim and lit face of the terracotta pot
  - One small paper-white catchlight on the door
  - One tiny QR-only note where the reference has the warmest pop

MUD-AVOIDANCE RULES
  - Never pre-mix all three on the palette. If you want a true neutral, mix two and
    let the third touch the brush tip only.
  - If a mix reads brown when you wanted green-gray, you added too much BS - rinse
    and lean U.
  - If a green-gray looks olive-dead, it bled into adjacent wet pigment. Next pass,
    wait for full dry between the door glaze and the brick.
  - Glaze shadows last so they sit on top of dry brick, not into wet brick (which
    rewets the warm and dulls it).
  - Treat each mix as a "feature" - one mix per region. Reusing the same puddle for
    bricks and pot is what turns brick brown and pot gray.

If you want a single rule of thumb for the whole afternoon: keep BS out of the shadows,
keep U out of the brick, keep QR out of the door, and save the postcard white for the
four accents above. The whole study will hold together with cleaner color than a larger
palette usually gives you.
