Root-cause read first, then the plan.

Hypothesis (consistent with what you observed): your router is on the front-room side and the workroom sits one interior wall away with the door closed. The "stable in front room, unstable in workroom, better near the doorway" pattern is classic 5 GHz attenuation through an interior wall (plumbing, duct, or dense framing) — and gets worse the moment you load a dashboard (buffering, retransmits) or push upstream on a video call (asymmetric, your phone/radio's weaker link). Forcing 2.4 GHz is the cheapest first probe because it penetrates walls ~3-4x better than 5 GHz; the trade-off is lower peak speed and more neighbor interference, which is usually fine for a video call + dashboard load.

Stepwise test plan (do in this order, ~30 min total)

1. Quantify the baseline. On the workroom laptop with the door closed and laptop in normal desk position, run:
   - ping -c 100 <router IP> (look at packet loss % and jitter/avg, not just min)
   - a speed test (note both down and up)
   - one full Zoom/Meet call standing by itself, ~10 min
   Then repeat in the front room. You now have a number to compare against later, not a vibe.

2. Try the cheap fix first: force the workroom laptop to 2.4 GHz only (most OSes let you prefer 2.4 in the Wi-Fi adapter settings, or rename the SSIDs so 2.4 and 5 are distinct and pick the 2.4 one). Repeat the ping test. If 2.4 GHz holds a call cleanly, you may not need anything else — only the 5 GHz radio was marginal.

3. Move the modem/router, not the laptop. Constraints:
   - Line-of-sight (or near it) to the workroom doorway when the door is open
   - Elevated (waist height or higher — not on the floor, not behind a TV)
   - Away from metal, microwave, fish tank, brick exterior wall
   - Still reachable by the incoming service line (don't relocate the modem itself if it's an all-in-one the ISP requires at the demarc — move it within the room, or split modem/router if needed)
   Good front-room candidates: a high shelf on the wall shared with the workroom, or a spot on the front-room side of that shared wall. Re-run test 1 from the workroom with door closed.

4. Door + position matrix. With the new router spot, test:
   - Workroom, door closed, desk position
   - Workroom, door open, desk position
   - Workroom, door closed, laptop at the doorway
   If "door open" fixes it and "door closed" doesn't, the door itself is a contributor (hollow-core doors with foil-backed insulation can be surprising). If doorway position alone is fine, a small AP/repeater right inside the workroom doorway may be enough without a full wired run.

5. Check for existing Ethernet. Look in the front room and the workroom for unused RJ45 jacks. Newer builds sometimes have a drop per room that's just not connected. If a workroom drop exists and the router end is in the front room, you can wire an AP in minutes with no new cabling.

Decision criteria for whether to install the wired access point

Proceed to a wired AP if any of the following are true after tests 1-4:
- Workroom RSSI is worse than about -65 to -70 dBm at the desk with door closed (Windows: `netsh wlan show interfaces`; macOS: hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon).
- Ping packet loss > ~1% or jitter (stdev) > ~30 ms during a sustained video call from the workroom desk.
- Speed test upstream in the workroom is < ~5 Mbps while front room is materially higher, AND it does not recover with 2.4-only or router relocation.
- Relocation is constrained — you've found one good spot, but the service line, ISP equipment location, or aesthetics cap you from improving further.

If 2.4 GHz alone gives a stable call and you're willing to live with slower dashboard loads, you can defer the AP. If the dashboard is a daily heavy lift, treat dashboard performance as part of the bar, not just calls.

Wired AP install outline (weekend)

- Run a single Ethernet run from the router to the workroom, along baseboards or through the doorway (no new holes if you can avoid it; cable raceway is fine). Cat6 is overkill; Cat5e is fine for home AP use.
- Place the AP on the east wall (you already have two outlets there, so power is solved), elevated, central to where you actually sit, not behind a monitor or metal filing cabinet.
- Use the same SSID and password as the existing router, but disable router Wi-Fi if your new AP can take over, or set them to non-overlapping channels (e.g., router on 1/6/11 + AP on the other two) so they cooperate rather than fight.
- On install day: same ping + call test from the workroom desk with door closed. You should see RSSI better than -55 dBm and near-zero packet loss; that is the bar.

If you want to keep the day-2 paper trail tight, the only thing worth writing down from today's test is the baseline ping/speed numbers and the router's current location — everything else is noise until you've moved it.

Arithmetic check

40 contracted = 26 weekly active + 14 inactive. Reconciles.
26 active = 9 admins/builders + 12 recurring operators + 5 reviewers. Reconciles (9+12+5=26).
14 inactive = 6 planned (next quarter) + 8 no named near-term use. Reconciles (6+8=14).
Right-size to 32 = 26 active + 6 planned. Reconciles (26+6=32).

All four totals tie. No math error in CS's inventory.

What the numbers actually say (and what they don't)

The arithmetic is clean, but the decision can't rest on the inactive count alone. Three things matter before any option is presented:

1. This is a sharp contraction, not a steady state. On 2024-02-15 Acme had 88 weekly active seats; on 2024-04-29 they have 26. That's a 70% drop in roughly ten weeks. The 14 currently inactive are not a long-standing overhang — they reflect a recent, large reduction in usage. That changes how the 8 unnamed seats should be read: they are most plausibly the trailing edge of that contraction (recently de-prioritized users, contractors coming off project, paused teams) rather than long-reserved-but-never-touched allocations.

2. All nine admins/workflow builders are retained. The structural backbone of the account — the people who configure and own the workflows — is fully intact. That is the single most important fact for renewal posture, and it is true regardless of which option is chosen.

3. The six planned joiners are named, time-bound demand for next quarter. They are not "unused" — they are queued. Treating them as candidates for removal would directly conflict with the customer's stated near-term plan and would create a visible churn-of-seats story at renewal.

The 8 unnamed seats are the only group where usage alone is genuinely insufficient evidence. They warrant a question, not a verdict.

Decision framing for Friday's conversation

Option A — retain 40 with a quarterly assignment review.
  Posture: status quo with a process overlay.
  What it actually does: preserves optionality; defers the question.
  Risk: "quarterly review" frequently becomes a calendar event with no owner and no decision rule. If the same 8 seats are still unnamed at the next review, you've repeated the conversation without resolving it. Also signals to procurement that we are comfortable carrying unallocated capacity on their contract, which weakens our position if a future right-sizing conversation arises.
  When it's the right call: only if there is a named owner, a defined decision rule, and a deadline — e.g., "by 2024-08-15 each unassigned seat has a named user or is released."

Option B — right-size to 32, preserving 26 active + 6 planned.
  Posture: structured reduction that honors known demand and removes only the unanchored 8.
  What it actually does: aligns the contract to validated usage + named pipeline, without penalizing the customer for the contraction or signaling "use it or lose it."
  Risk: small — primarily that the 8 unnamed seats turn out to have legitimate purpose we didn't surface (e.g., a hiring pipeline CS isn't aware of, cross-team access for a partner, seasonal staff). That's why the validation step before presenting the option matters.
  When it's the right call: the default, unless the 8 seats are validated as load-bearing before Friday.

Framing posture to take into the room

  - Lead with workflow coverage, not seat count. The relevant question is "do the 26 active users cover the workflows that matter to Acme, and do the 6 planned joiners cover the gap that's coming next quarter?" — not "are 40 seats being used this week."
  - Treat the 8 unnamed seats as "needs a purpose," not "wasted." The difference is whether the conversation produces a real answer or a defensive one.
  - Do not present weekly inactivity as the basis for removal. It is the prompt for a question; the answer lives in the customer's own plans.
  - Anchor the right-sizing math on the 26 + 6 = 32 structure, not on "you have 14 inactive seats." The first framing is additive and customer-aligned; the second is reductive and adversarial.
  - Note the timing relative to the champion's 2024-06-03 return. The decision can be framed as something to confirm with the champion rather than something decided in their absence — that keeps the relationship intact regardless of which option is chosen.

What to bring into Friday

  - A role-level mapping of the 26 active users (per the standing requirement) — admins/builders, recurring operators, occasional reviewers — tied to the workflows each role touches.
  - The 6 planned joiners identified by name/role/expected start, if CS has that; if not, that is the first thing to ask Acme in the meeting.
  - A direct, non-leading question about the 8 unnamed seats: "Are these reserved for a specific hire, team, or contractor we should know about, or are they unassigned?" The answer determines whether Option B is presented as 32 or as something smaller.
  - A stated decision rule for whatever option is taken, so the conversation doesn't reset in 90 days.

Recommendation

Default to Option B (32 seats) conditional on the 8 unnamed seats not being validated as load-bearing in Friday's conversation. Option A is acceptable only if it ships with a named owner and a hard reassessment date. Either way, do not let the framing be "14 seats are inactive" — that overstates what the data supports and weakens the renewal conversation.

Short answer: don't ride it to work Monday, and take it to a shop.

Why: cleaning + lube was the correct first step, and since the symptom didn't change, grime is no longer a plausible cause. The pattern — skips only on the two smallest cogs under moderate pressure, crisp shifting everywhere else, no visible bent link or broken tooth — is the classic fingerprint of either a stretched chain wearing those smallest cogs thin, or worn cassette teeth on those smallest cogs specifically (the smallest cogs take the most torque and wear fastest). The two usually fail together, which is why the skip stays parked on those two cogs regardless of how cleanly you've maintained the rest of the drivetrain.

Riding risk: skips under moderate pedal pressure — not just a hard sprint — are a no-go for a commute. Under load, a skip can drop a foot or throw the chain.

What to ask the shop to check:

  1. Chain wear — measured with a chain checker tool, not eyeballed. The decision number is 0.5% on most wear indicators; 0.75% means the chain is gone and has almost certainly already damaged the cassette. If they quote a percentage, ask which scale their tool uses.
  2. Cassette tooth profile on the two smallest cogs — look for the characteristic "shark fin" or hooked tooth shape. New chains on a worn cassette will skip until the cassette is replaced; a worn chain on a new cassette will quickly ruin the new cassette. So the diagnosis order matters: measure chain first, then look at the cassette.
  3. Chain length — verify it wasn't over-stretched in a way that a new chain of the same length would skip. If the chain is replaced, length should be set from scratch, not assumed from the old one.
  4. B-screw / derailleur hanger alignment — quick check, cheap to do, and a slightly bent hanger can make a marginal chain/cassette combo look much worse than it is. Worth ruling out before replacing parts.

What to ask them to do: report chain wear as a number, tell you whether the two smallest cogs show hook wear, and recommend chain-only, chain + cassette, or chain + cassette + hanger based on what they actually find. Don't authorize a cassette replacement on a chain that's still in spec — and don't authorize a chain replacement on cogs that are clearly hooked without doing the cassette at the same time. Those two mistakes are the most common ways shops (well-meaningly) spend customers' money twice.

In the meantime, get to work however else you usually would on a Monday — Holly → 2nd & Brazos is a short bike commute, which is the only reason this is worth fixing quickly rather than waiting for a weekend appointment.

The fix for glare on wet paper is side-light plus a bounce — not a curtain.

Orientation: rotate the table 90° so the window is to your side, not in front of you. Side light is actually better for watercolor than front light: it shows wet vs. dry areas clearly and your hand doesn't shadow the work. Front light is the worst case for judging color and value, which is exactly the glare you're hitting. If you can put the window on your left (assuming right-handed), that's the classic studio arrangement, but either side works fine once the foam board is filling shadows.

Light control: lean a white foam board on the shadow side of the table, angled to bounce window light back onto the paper. Photographers and painters use this all the time. About $3 at any art or office supply store, no hardware, thirty seconds to prop up.

Why not the sheer curtain yet:
- It's a real project — rod or clips, measuring, possibly drilling into the rental wall
- Most sheers warm the color temperature slightly, which throws off color mixing
- It permanently dims the room, even on overcast days
- It doesn't actually fix wet-paper glare as cleanly as side light does

The foam-board approach is also better than a curtain for color accuracy, because nothing is filtering the light — you're just redirecting it. The full daylight spectrum still reaches your paper and your mixes.

When to revisit the curtain: if after a few sessions the afternoon sun still feels punishing, or if heat becomes a problem, a neutral-white sheer (not cream or tan) or a simple roller shade is the right add. Save it for then.

Net: rotate the table ninety degrees, lean a foam board on the shadow side, paint. Under two minutes, no unpacking project.

The mechanic's read matches the textbook failure mode for your drivetrain: at ~0.75% the chain is well past the ~0.5% decision point, and once the chain is that stretched the small cassette cogs get sharpened into a shape the new chain can't seat on. Skip under load on exactly those two cogs is the symptom — so the diagnosis is solid, and it's why the shop is steering you away from chain-only.

Comparing the two options:

- $68 chain-only. Almost certainly false economy in your case. The shop's own warning is the tell: a fresh chain on already-worn small cogs usually keeps skipping on those same cogs, which is precisely where you said the skip happens and precisely the gears you use in the faster stretch of your commute. If it doesn't fix it, you've spent $68 and still need the cassette work — plus a fresh chain on a worn cassette tends to accelerate wear on those cogs, so the follow-up job may end up more expensive than doing both at once.

- $214 chain-and-cassette with adjustment and loaded test. This addresses both halves of the problem (stretched chain + worn cogs), the adjustment re-indexes the derailleur to the new cassette so shifting is clean across the range, and the loaded test verifies the fix under the exact condition that was failing. Net extra cost over chain-only is $146, but it's the option that actually resolves the symptom you described.

On whether the diagnosis supports riding before the work: no, it doesn't. The skip is mechanical wear, not contamination, and mechanical wear doesn't self-correct — it gets worse with load. Riding on it is the case where a skip can escalate into a chain drop or a jammed link under hard pedaling, which is a real hazard in the faster part of your commute where you're using those small cogs. The shop measuring wear rather than telling you to keep riding is consistent with the bike not being safe to commute on until the work is done.

Practical path: drop the bike for the $214 chain-and-cassette job with adjustment and loaded test, commute by another mode until it's done. If $214 is tight this week, the $68 chain-only isn't worth doing as a stopgap in your case — you'd be paying to confirm the diagnosis rather than to ride it.

One thing worth asking the shop before they start: have them set the new chain length from scratch and verify length isn't a contributing factor, and confirm the two smallest cogs are the ones being replaced rather than just the visibly hooked ones — sometimes the third cog is borderline and they'll only flag it once the new chain is on.

Recommendation, in three layers, lightest to most defensive:

Layer 1 — Cutoff aligns with the refresh boundary.

Move the reporting cutoff from "9:00am" to the 9:00:00 hourly refresh tick. Owen's 9:05 export then reads the just-refreshed state, so the snapshot's contents match the derived-state table by construction. The 9:00 cutoff and the 9:00 refresh collapse into one boundary, and the "snapshot says X, table says Y" gap stops being a thing by definition.

Layer 2 — Freshness watermark on every export.

Stamp each snapshot with three fields:
  as_of: 2024-XX-XX 09:00:00 (refresh HH:00)
  next_refresh_at: 10:00:00
  snapshot_window_minutes: 60

A consumer reading the export can answer "is this current?" without consulting a separate timestamp. If as_of is older than the current time by more than snapshot_window_minutes plus slack, the export is provably stale. Owen's 9:05 file self-documents its own freshness; he doesn't have to remember which refresh tick it came from.

Layer 3 — Post-snapshot transition panel.

The raw event layer already records the seven 9:02–9:35 finalizations — Daniela owns preserving final routing events in the append-only raw event layer, so the data is already there and trusted. Surface them in the export as a side panel:

  cases_with_post_snapshot_transitions: 7
  [case_id, final_state, transition_at]

This is the part that prevents the "still-valid earlier pending state" from being misread as a routing gap. Owen's 9:05 export reads: 12 pending as of 9:00:00, plus the 7 cases that finalized between 9:02 and 9:35 with their final routes. The reconciliation Owen was doing by hand is now in the export itself, derived from the same raw events the derived state uses.

Why this does not bring back Owen's manual reconciliation:

The post-snapshot transition panel is generated automatically from the raw event log at export time, not assembled by Owen. The watermark fields are part of the export format, not an extra step. Owen still pulls the same file at the same time — the file just now carries its own freshness label and its own post-snapshot diff. If he wants, he can ignore both and read the 12 pending count the same way he did yesterday.

What this is NOT claiming to do:

It does not eliminate the possibility that a case is admitted incorrectly. It does not change the hourly refresh cadence of the current-state table. It does not prevent Owen from doing reconciliation if he chooses to — it makes reconciliation redundant only for the refresh-lag class of discrepancy. If a downstream read needs intra-hour currency (say, a 9:15 status check on a single case), the right move is a targeted raw-event query, not a faster derived-state refresh. The fix is a labeling change at the export boundary, not a rearchitecture of the state pipeline.

One operational check before shipping:

Confirm the export job reads as_of from the refresh job's write timestamp on the relevant state partitions rather than computing its own as_of independently. If the export computes its own clock-driven cutoff, the watermark can drift from the refresh by tens of seconds and reintroduce a smaller version of the same gap. Deriving as_of from the append-only raw event layer's last-write timestamp on those partitions keeps the watermark and the derived state reading from the same source of truth.

  Spreads the whole $93 across all edible output, so trim/shrinkage is

    Chicken per plate:    7 × $0.2849       = $1.99
    Plate cost (food):    $1.99 + $3.45     = $5.44

  Charges only the raw weight physically going onto the plate. Trim
  shows up as a separate loss line, not embedded in plate cost.
    7 oz × $3.10/lb = 0.4375 lb × $3.10 = $1.36
    Plate cost (food): $1.36 + $3.45     = $4.81
    Understates true cost by ~$0.63/plate vs. method 1.

3) Where $18 lands vs. the 30% ceiling
  Full-case basis:   $5.44 / $18 = 30.25%  ← just over the ceiling
  Bird-used basis:   $4.81 / $18 = 26.70%  ← under, but ignores shrink
  → At $18 with current costs, you're effectively at-the-line on the
    honest number. Any small variance (portion creep, side cost creep,
    yield slip) tips you over.

  $5.44 ÷ 0.30 = $18.15

  Holding everything else constant, raw chicken per-lb swings:
    $3.10 (now)   plate $5.44   target price @30% = $18.15
    $3.50 (+13%)  plate $5.70   target price @30% = $19.01
    $3.75 (+21%)  plate $5.86   target price @30% = $19.54
    $4.00 (+29%)  plate $6.02   target price @30% = $20.08

             drifts up to ~$3.50/lb. Reasonable cushion.
    $20.00 — gives ~27.2% food cost today and absorbs a ~20% raw

  If $18 is the price you want to lead with (positioning vs. nearby

LOW-STRESS PLAN FOR FUTURE TRUCK MORNINGS

Anchor "den" setup
  - Keep the workroom pre-staged as Kibo's go-to space on known truck days: his familiar blanket, water bowl, white-noise machine on a timer, and a long-lasting chew or stuffed Kong.
  - Make the room positive, not punitive. Toss treats in there on calm mornings so he associates it with good things, and consider feeding his main meal in there on recycling days to build that link.

Pre-emptive, not reactive
  - Find out Cherrywood's recycling day and roughly what time the truck comes; municipal routes are usually on a predictable weekday morning slot.
  - On that day, get Kibo into the workroom 10–15 minutes BEFORE the truck typically arrives, with the white noise already on and street-facing blinds/curtains closed.
  - Once the barking has started, the moment to intervene has passed. Prevention is what reduces the behavior over time.

Reduce the trigger
  - Close blinds or curtains on the street-facing windows during truck windows so he can't see the approach.
  - Keep white noise or low-volume music/TV running on truck mornings to mask the engine and hydraulic sounds.
  - The fact that the workroom is on a quieter side of the unit is already working in your favor.

Settle the day, not just the moment
  - Earlier and slightly longer morning walk or play session on trash/recycling days so he starts the truck window tired.
  - Stay calm yourself; your state sets his.
  - Don't yell or scold, and don't soothe or pick him up while he is actively barking — both can reinforce the cycle. Wait for a pause, then reward calm.

Longer term (optional, only after he's fully settled at Cherrywood, ~4–6 weeks)
  - Sound desensitization: a recording of a garbage/recycling truck at very low volume during meals, gradually increasing over weeks. If you'd rather not run that project yourself, a positive-reinforcement trainer can coach it.


SIGNS THAT WARRANT A VET OR BEHAVIORIST INSTEAD OF SETTLING-IN SUPPORT

He's still in week-one-of-a-new-home territory, so some heightened startle is normal and your response (den, blanket, water, white noise, 5-minute recovery) was textbook good. Escalate to professional help if you see any of the following.

Escalation or spread of the trigger
  - Barking episodes getting longer, louder, or more frequent.
  - Recovery taking much longer — e.g., still panting or pacing 30+ minutes after the truck has passed.
  - New triggers appearing: other trucks, doors slamming, neighbors' footsteps, household appliances, thunder, fireworks.

Stress symptoms showing up between events
  - Tucked tail, pinned ears, lip-licking, yawning, whale eye, shaking, hiding, or refusing his usual spot on the couch.
  - Appetite drop lasting more than a day or two.
  - Sleep disruption, especially restlessness or pacing after dark.
  - Destructive behavior when you're not home or when he's alone.
  - House-soiling after a long reliable record.

New compulsive behaviors
  - Tail-chasing, flank-sucking, shadow or light chasing, persistent paw-licking to the point of skin damage. These tend to worsen without intervention.

Any aggression
  - Growling, snapping, or biting toward people or other animals, especially if it didn't exist before the move. Don't try to manage this with training alone; get a behaviorist involved.

Physical red flags (vet first)
  - Hot spots, broken skin from scratching.
  - Weight loss or gain.
  - Vomiting, diarrhea, changes in thirst or urination.
  - Limping, stiffness, or reluctance to jump — easy to mistake for "being dramatic" but often pain.
  - Since he's a recent mover, if you haven't already, schedule a routine wellness check. Physical issues commonly surface as behavior changes during stress, and ruling out pain, endocrine issues, and hearing changes is the right first move.


DECISION RULE OF THUMB

One short, recoverable episode in week one of a new home that responds to a known intervention = settling-in support, no escalation needed.

Anything that escalates, persists, spreads to other contexts, or shows up between events = call the vet first to rule out medical causes, then ask for a referral to a veterinary behaviorist (DACVB) if behavior is the driver. A DACVB is a specialist-level credential; a general dog trainer is not a substitute if the picture starts looking like the list above.

Recommendations for the Expansion Assist randomized stagger, addressing Owen's four questions.

1. WHEN ELIGIBILITY IS LOCKED

Lock the 30-account roster and the start-week assignment at a single T-lock date: recommend June 17 (T-21 days before first send on July 8). T-lock serves three purposes: strata (prior expansion-signal tier) are pre-registered and visible; randomization within strata is executed and frozen; CS sees the full 6-week cohort and can flag pre-exposure conditions before any prompt is sent.

Between T-lock and a given account's start week, status changes (churn, downgrade, sales contact) are labels, not triggers for replacement. The randomized assignment is what stays frozen.

2. RANDOMIZED ACCOUNTS STAY IN THE PRIMARY ANALYSIS — INTENT-TO-TREAT

Primary unit of analysis is the randomized assignment, not the prompt receipt. Every account that was randomized remains in its assigned cell in the cut, regardless of what happens before exposure. Per-protocol (only counting accounts that actually received the prompt as designed) is a supportive secondary analysis, not the primary one.

The reason: any "did they receive the prompt" filter reintroduces the selection bias that randomization was supposed to eliminate. Per-protocol effects estimate what the prompt does when delivered cleanly; ITT effects estimate what assigning an account to receive the prompt does, including the no-show and contamination cases. For a 5-per-week operational motion, the ITT estimate is the one that maps to the rollout decision.

Expansion MRR per account should be reported on the ITT basis with the label set below visible in the cut.

3. LABELING PRE-EXPOSURE INELIGIBILITY AND COMPETING SALES CONTACT

Suggested labels, all `pre_exposure_*`:

  pre_exposure_churned        — formal churn before assigned start week
  pre_exposure_downgraded     — seat count or tier dropped below retained-mid
  pre_exposure_sales_contact  — sales-led expansion conversation initiated
  pre_exposure_unreachable    — eligible but CS cannot make contact
  pre_exposure_other          — catch-all, requires free-text reason

`pre_exposure_sales_contact` is the analytically important one. Sales contact before exposure creates ambiguity: any measured expansion could be EA, sales, or both. Recommended handling:

  - Account stays in ITT (do not exclude)
  - Cut reports ITT expansion MRR with and without pre_exposure_sales_contact accounts (sensitivity analysis)
  - Name the contamination in the cut, do not hide it

4. REPLACEMENTS — DON'T, IN THE PRIMARY COHORT

Replacement breaks randomization. The moment you substitute a new account for one that churned, the 5 accounts exposed in a given week are no longer a random sample of the originally-randomized cohort. Owen's comparability concern is correct — that is the cost of replacement.

Two cases:

Case A — no reserve pool exists (30 is the entire eligible population).
Don't replace. Accept that some weeks may have fewer than 5 prompts if attrition occurs. Label attrition, keep ITT, report per-protocol as supportive. This is the cleaner design.

Case B — a reserve pool exists beyond the 30.
Reserve must be separately randomized, not pre-assigned as a backfill. Reserve cohort runs in parallel, analyzed as its own ITT with its own strata pre-registration. Reserve is used to estimate what fresh-randomization behavior looks like at the margins; it does not "fix" the primary cohort's attrition.

I'd recommend Case A even if a reserve is technically available, unless there is a strong reason to need a specific per-week exposure count.

ASSUMPTIONS I'M MAKING

  - "Eligibility" = retained-mid definition, locked at T-lock
  - 5/week x 6 weeks = 30, but the design tolerates a week with fewer than 5 if attrition occurred
  - Strata (expansion-signal tier) are pre-registered before T-lock
  - CS reviews the roster between T-lock and start week and applies labels as conditions emerge

OPEN QUESTIONS TO CONFIRM BEFORE LOCKING

  1. Is there a reserve pool beyond the 30, or is 30 the entire eligible population? (Determines Case A vs B above.)
  2. What is the retained-mid definition (seat count, ARR band, usage-signal tier), and is it the same at T-lock as at start week? If it can drift between, add a `definition_drift` label.
  3. Does "sales-led expansion conversation initiated" mean an SDR/AE has logged an opportunity, or any sales-team contact logged in CRM? Pick one and pre-register it before T-lock.
  4. Accounts that hit `pre_exposure_unreachable` — are they eligible for retry in a later week (shifting them out of their assigned week), or do they stay in their originally-assigned week even if unexposed? Recommend: stay in assigned week. Shifting breaks the stagger.

Clinical read first, since this frames everything: based on what you've described — gradual onset in the final mile, no twist or pop, full weight-bearing, no swelling/bruising, and only 2/10 pain descending stairs — this looks like a mild soft-tissue irritation on the lateral side (most often the peroneal tendon area or the lateral ankle soft tissues in general), not an acute ligament rupture or a fracture. That's reassuring, but it still wants the conservative path below rather than "run through it."

Self-care for the next 48-72 hours
  - Relative rest from running. Normal walking is fine; if walking itself is uncomfortable, that's a useful early signal — pay attention to it.
  - Ice 15-20 minutes, 2-3x/day, for any post-activity or end-of-day ache. A thin cloth between ice and skin. Stop if it irritates.
  - Gentle mobility only: ankle alphabet (trace letters with your big toe), slow circles both directions, light calf stretches if they're pain-free. No ballistic stretching.
  - Compression sleeve or a simple elastic wrap if it feels supportive; not too tight. Elevate after longer periods on your feet.
  - NSAIDs are optional — short course at a label dose is reasonable if discomfort interferes with sleep or daily steps, but they're not required.
  - Footwear check: when did you last rotate or replace your current running shoes? A new ache in a familiar location during a normal-distance run is a reasonable prompt to look at shoe mileage and any lateral heel drift. (You flagged left heel lift back in February — worth glancing at both shoes now.)

Should you skip your next run
  Yes. Plan at minimum 2-3 full days off running, then a self-check before any test run. A useful set of gates:
    1. Walking is fully pain-free, including stairs.
    2. Single-leg balance on the right foot for 30 seconds is steady and pain-free.
    3. Single-leg heel raises (3 sets of 10-15, slow) on the right are pain-free.
    4. No pain or stiffness the morning after the heel-raise test.
  If all four pass, do a short easy test run — about 2 miles at conversational pace, flat terrain, same shoes. No strides, no hills.

Return-to-running ramp (assuming the first test run is clean)
  - Test run 1: ~2 miles, easy.
  - Test run 2: 2-3 days later, ~3 miles at easy pace.
  - Test run 3: 2-3 days after that, return to your usual easy distance.
  - Resume normal mileage and any intensity work over the following week, only if each step stays at 0/10 during and 0-1/10 the next morning. If anything lights up, drop back one step and hold there for an extra day or two before retrying.
  - If both test runs are clean, you're effectively back to baseline within roughly 7-10 days. If they aren't clean, that's the cue to be evaluated rather than to keep grinding through.

Signs that justify prompt medical evaluation (same-day or urgent visit)
  Any one of these, and stop self-care:
  - A pop, snap, or giving-way sensation (at any point — now, or later if symptoms change).
  - Inability to bear weight, or a new limp that develops over the next day or two.
  - Visible swelling, bruising, or deformity around the lateral malleolus or foot.
  - Point bony tenderness — specifically the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus, the base of the 5th metatarsal, or the navicular. (This is the practical version of the Ottawa Ankle Rules — if pressing on the bone itself hurts, that's an X-ray conversation, not a wait-and-see.)
  - Pain at rest, or pain that's getting worse day-over-day rather than better.
  - Pain that wakes you from sleep or that you can't ignore when you're off your feet.
  - Numbness, tingling, or burning along the outside of the foot or into the 4th/5th toes (sural nerve territory).
  - Foot that looks pale, blue, feels cool, or has delayed capillary refill.
  - Locking, catching, or a sense of the ankle giving way on level ground.
  - Hop test: unable to hop on the right foot, or it reproduces sharp pain.
  - Fever, or any skin break over the area that looks red/warm.
  - No meaningful improvement after 5-7 days of real relative rest, or symptoms that flare back each time you try a test run.

One honest caveat: I'm giving general conservative guidance based on the features you described, not a diagnosis. If the picture changes in any of the ways above, or if you'd rather have a clinician look at it sooner rather than later, that's a perfectly reasonable call — ankle and foot complaints are exactly the kind of thing a sports med or podiatry visit handles routinely.

Why this matters

If the insurer's allowed amount is $0 and patient responsibility is $0, the provider's $185 demand is not a legitimate patient balance under your plan. Paying it would be paying for something your insurer has explicitly said is not a covered separate charge.

  3. Ask for one of two outcomes:
       a. Adjust/write off the $185 to match the insurer's allowed amount, OR
       b. If they believe the follow-up was separately billable, have them resubmit with a -25 modifier (separate and significant E/M) or appeal the N20 denial with documentation.
  4. Get any adjustment or appeal commitment in writing (patient portal message or email).
  5. If the provider refuses and keeps billing you, file a complaint with your state Department of Insurance. Sending you a bill for an amount your EOB says you do not owe is reportable conduct.

**Inputs**

- Cooked yield: 19.6 lb = 313.6 oz
- Per plate: 7 oz cooked chicken + $3.45 sides/garnish
- Menu price: $19.00

**Complete plates and leftover**
- 313.6 oz ÷ 7 oz/plate = 44.8
- 44 complete plates (44 × 7 = 308 oz plated)
- Leftover cooked chicken: 313.6 − 308 = **5.6 oz**

- $93.00 ÷ 313.6 oz = $0.2966/oz cooked chicken (precisely $0.296556)
- Per-plate chicken cost: 7 × $0.296556 = $2.0759 ≈ **$2.08**

- $2.0759 + $3.45 = $5.5259 ≈ **$5.53**

**Food-cost percentage at the $19 menu price**
- $5.5259 ÷ $19.00 = 0.2908 ≈ **29.08%**

**Gross contribution per plate after food cost**
- $19.00 − $5.5259 = $13.4741 ≈ **$13.47**

**If all 44 complete plates sell**
- 44 × $13.4741 = $592.86 ≈ **$592.86 gross contribution** (food cost recovered: 44 × $5.5259 = $243.14; revenue: 44 × $19 = $836.00)

DENOMINATOR-FIRST INTERPRETATION

The right unit of analysis for both activation and credential stalls is admitted workspaces, because pending, assistance, and ineligible outcomes never reach the credentialing step. Using 92 as the denominator would dilute both figures with applicants the intake check is specifically designed to route elsewhere. On the admitted base of 68:

   - Filtering at the front door: the 15 routed to assistance because connector authority was missing or uncertain never enter the admitted denominator at all — they are the check working as intended, converting a likely future stall into supported routing.
   - Reducing residual stalls: even among those who did get admitted, the credential stall rate fell by roughly two-thirds, suggesting the remaining admits are more often genuinely credential-ready.

4. The check has not eliminated credential stalls. 3 of 9 nonactivators in this cohort are still credential-related (33% of stalls). The intake question catches most cases but not all — partial coverage, not full coverage. That is consistent with the 5/9 answer mix seen in the intake read (Yes / No / Not sure) and is a reason the question stays in the funnel rather than being retired.

6. CS contact density (11 contacts across 8 admitted workspaces) is a friction signal worth noting descriptively — it sits alongside the activation rate, not above it — but it does not change the intake-check read.

BOTTOM LINE

On the admitted denominator (68), this cohort shows a real reduction in credential-related stalls (4.4% vs 12.2% prior baseline) and a high descriptive 7-day activation rate (86.8%). Those two numbers together support continuing the connector-access intake check. They do not, by themselves, support any claim about mature retention, paid conversion, or revenue performance — those need separate evidence past day 7.

Core principle: no label, no signal. Differential pre-exposure treatment requires a CSM to *know* an account is queued. The protocol removes the signal from anyone who doesn't need it, and narrows the window for those who do.

VISIBILITY TIERS

  Tier A — Program owner (Owen + 1 named ops seat + designated CS lead)
    - Sees: full 30-account roster, all 6 start-week assignments, within-week order, reserve treatment, audit column.
    - Locked at 2024-06-17 snapshot. Post-lock edits require reason + timestamp.

  Tier B — Assigned CSM, rolling 1-week prep window
    - Sees ONLY: accounts they personally own that are `hs_ea_preparing` (next week) or `hs_ea_active` (this week), plus the within-week order for those accounts.
    - Hard cap: view cannot display more than 5 `hs_ea_active` rows per week. If attrition drops the week below 5, no replacement from outside the cohort — that's the existing attrition rule.

  Tier C — Everyone else (incl. assigned CSMs for weeks 3+ out)
    - Sees: nothing. Future-week accounts carry no treatment label from their view. They appear as ordinary accounts. The within-cohort comparison role (per the design) is preserved automatically — those accounts look like controls to their CSM until their assigned Monday.

LABEL STATES (scripted transitions, Monday 00:00)

  - `hs_ea_preparing` — appears on the Sunday before the assigned Monday. Assigned CSM may review notes, confirm entitlement, verify contact path. No prompt, no expansion action.
  - `hs_ea_active` — appears on the assigned Monday. CSM executes per protocol.
  - (no label) — accounts whose assigned week has passed revert to routine. Future-week accounts never had a label from this view.

  Reserve treatment stays Tier A only. CS never sees reserve assignments.

ESCALATION EXCEPTION
  If a CSM opens an escalation ticket on any EA-cohort account (billing, security, churn risk), the ticket auto-attaches the current label state. Labels are allowed to travel through audit/escalation channels — the restriction is on the *proactive prep view*, not on incident response.

OPERATIONAL MECHANICS

  1. Single source of truth for assignments: one sheet/view, snapshotted at 2024-06-17. Tier A only.
  2. View-layer enforcement: Tier B is a filtered view, not a separate sheet CS can scroll past. If your ops tool can't filter by viewer role, use a per-CSM tab with a script that hides future-week columns.
  3. Weekly audit by Owen: confirm label transitions fired on time, no `hs_ea_active` row appeared before its Monday, and no CSM view shows more than 5 active.
  4. ITT preserved: label state follows the original assignment regardless of whether the prompt actually fires that week.

WHAT THIS BUYS

  - 5/week cap and 7/8 boundary: preserved (view-enforced).
  - Intent-to-treat + reserve treatment: preserved.
  - Differential pre-exposure treatment: materially reduced. Future-week accounts carry no signal to their CSM; current-week accounts are visible for one prep week; comparison-period accounts are indistinguishable from controls.
  - Pilot operability: preserved. Each CSM gets a real prep window, escalation paths work, Owen can audit and respond to anomalies.

HONEST CAVEATS

  - Protocol depends on view-layer filtering actually working. A flat shared sheet won't enforce this — needs role-based views or per-CSM filtered tabs. Worth confirming with whoever owns ops tooling before locking it in.
  - The 1-week prep window is a judgment call. Tighter (0-week) hardens protection but compresses CSM prep time; looser (2-week) softens it. One week is the practical compromise — flag if you'd rather go tighter.
  - "Reduced" is not "eliminated." A CSM who sees `hs_ea_preparing` may still read the account more carefully or mention it in a team sync. Owen should note this in the readout interpretation — any pre-exposure engagement on a labeled account is worth logging, because it's the residual channel for differential treatment.
  - If account ownership changes mid-pilot (CSM leaves, reassignment), the new owner inherits the visibility rule for that account's assigned week only — no retro look-back at earlier-week labels.

4. Post-admission support. Support load per admitted account after admission. Owen already owns the support-load cut; this is the steady-state version of it.

Three things, keeping Mom's recipe as-is:

1. Safe internal temperature: 165°F (74°C). That's the USDA floor for all poultry, thighs included. Some cooks pull dark meat at 170–175°F because the connective tissue softens further past 165 and thighs are forgiving above it, but 165 is all you need for safety. Moderate heat + a single turn should clear it comfortably without drying the meat out.

2. Where to place the thermometer: push the probe into the thickest part of the thigh from the side, so the tip runs roughly parallel to the cutting board and sits centered in the meat. Keep the tip away from bone — bone conducts heat and reads higher than the meat actually is, so a bone-touch reading can fool you into stopping early. Test the biggest piece (or two); smaller ones finish first.

3. Keeping the cooked chicken clean from raw marinade: the 2 Tbsp you set aside BEFORE the chicken went in is the whole trick — that portion never touched raw poultry, so brushing it on at the end is safe as written. Two habits to preserve that:
   - Use a clean spoon or brush for the reserved sauce. Don't reuse the brush or tongs that handled the raw-marinating chicken or its bag.
   - The marinade the chicken sat in is fine to leave cooking in the pan (it reaches high heat with the chicken), but if anyone wants to spoon pan juices over the finished thighs, bring that liquid to a brief boil first — easier still, just use the reserved 2 Tbsp and skip the pan-juice spooning.

The "reserve 2 Tbsp before adding chicken" step is exactly the move that makes the "brush at the end" instruction safe. You're already doing it.

SESAME-ALLERGY GUEST — JUNE 1 PRIVATE DINNER
Working draft for Sam's review.

Quick read of the sheet: the soy-ginger chicken glaze itself contains sesame oil. That changes the picture — this is not a garnish-removal situation, it's either an alternative entrée or a sesame-free reworking of the glaze. Anything weaker understates the risk.

WHAT LEAVING OFF THE GARNISH DOES NOT FIX
  - The entrée's base glaze contains sesame oil, so the dish is sesame-containing by ingredient, not just by garnish.
  - Cross-contact from shared surfaces, utensils, fryer oil, holding containers, and the plating area.
  - Airborne sesame from any toasting happening that night in the same kitchen space.
  - Staff-hand cross-contact between the standard batch and the allergen plate.
  - Sesame showing up in adjacent components on the same plate or at the same table: sides, sauces, bread service, dessert, finishing oils on other courses.

RECONFIRM WITH THE GUEST (lead time lets you do this well)
  - Severity and history: any prior anaphylaxis, asthma, other Top-9 allergens? Do they carry an EpiPen?
  - Threshold: strict-avoidance only, or "may contain" tolerable? (Many sesame-allergic guests are strict.)
  - Their preference: a fully different entrée prepared on dedicated equipment, or a sesame-free version of the same flavor profile. Pick one with them, don't choose for them.
  - Scope: just the entrée, or every course including dessert, bread, and dressings?
  - Discreet identification at service: how they want to be flagged without being singled out at a 20-top.
  - Whether they want to be told what's been done to the dish, or just served a plate they're comfortable with.

RECONFIRM WITH SAM (chef-owner sign-off before Saturday)
  - Final call on parallel allergen-safe entrée vs. reworked sesame-free glaze. Lock it.
  - Full sesame audit for the whole night, not just the entrée: marinades, finishing oils, sauces, dressings, bread/dip, dessert, garnishes on any course. Anything toasted in the kitchen that night puts sesame in the air.
  - Equipment list for the allergen plate: dedicated board, knife, tongs, spoon, sauté pan — color-coded or labeled, not "the clean one in the back."
  - Sequencing: allergen entrée prepared before any sesame work starts, or in a physically separated area after. Whichever — pick one and stick to it.
  - FOH briefing: who on the floor knows, who places the plate, who delivers, and the verbal confirmation at the pass that it's the allergen plate.
  - Emergency plan: nearest epinephrine, who calls 911, hospital routing. Confirmed before service, not after.

PREP AND SERVICE SEQUENCE (conservative version, assumes parallel allergen-safe entrée)

Today → Thursday
  - Audit menu, finalize the allergen entrée, lock recipe and equipment list.
  - Brief kitchen and FOH on the plan, the guest, the dish, plate identification.
  - Confirm emergency plan and epinephrine location with FOH lead.

Friday (day-before)
  - Final ingredient check: open sesame-free containers, confirm they're not the shared-prep half.
  - Dry-run the allergen plate: time the cook, confirm equipment, confirm plating.

Day of service
  - Sanitize the allergen workstation fully before any sesame work begins in the kitchen.
  - Stage dedicated equipment, labeled.
  - Cook, plate, cover, label, hold — either before all sesame work, or after, in a separated area with re-sanitized surfaces and fresh tools. No reuse of anything that touched sesame.
  - Allergen plate is plated last, sealed/covered. Lead server confirms at the pass that it is the allergen plate before it leaves the kitchen.
  - Server delivers discreetly and confirms with the guest at the table.

DEFAULT IF ANY OF THE ABOVE IS NOT ACTUALLY IN PLACE ON SATURDAY: do not serve the guest a modified soy-ginger chicken. Serve a known-clean protein on dedicated equipment, full stop.

What the supplied letter could have resolved, and why it does not here
- The letter is the kind of artifact that resolves an ownership mismatch when the workspace has a single identifiable owner who is not the applicant. In that posture, the letter would do three things at once: name the actual workspace owner, authorize the applicant to apply on that owner's behalf, and identify whose connector an administrator will authenticate in week one.
- In this application the letter does none of those fully. The intended workspace would manage deployments for three clients, and the letter is from only one of them. There is no indication that the named client is the workspace owner rather than one of three customers the agency plans to serve from it. The connector access the applicant confirms is for the agency's own systems, not for any client's, so the connector piece of the ownership picture is also unresolved.
- Corroborating evidence in the abstract does not close these gaps. To resolve the ownership mismatch, the corroboration would need to identify which entity owns and will operate the workspace, confirm that entity has authorized this application, and identify the connector account an administrator will authenticate on that entity's behalf. The applicant has signaled none of that.

Why the agency exclusion is unchanged regardless of further authorization
- The exclusion is structural, not authorizational. Helio Start is for the entity that will use the workspace to run its own business. An applicant whose workspace would be operated by the agency to manage deployments for multiple clients is using Helio as a service-delivery surface, and that posture is excluded from the ordinary path whether the applicant carries one authorization letter or three.
- An authorization letter from a client speaks to that client's permission for the agency to act on its behalf. It does not convert an agency-led multi-client deployment into a single end-user operator. Even fully executed letters from all three clients would not change the routing; they would at best confirm that CS should set up agency-admin arrangements per client rather than one shared workspace.
- The connector access already confirmed is also not curative. The applicant can authenticate a connector for the agency's own systems. For a workspace owned by a client, week-one connector authentication must be confirmed by an administrator authorized on that client's connector account, which is a separate question the letter does not answer.

Recommended CS next step
- Route out using the approved agency route-out wording. CS determines the actual workspace structure (most likely one workspace per client with agency-admin access, per the 2023-10-10 agency-admin case pattern), captures the agency administrator's name and email, and confirms connector authentication per client workspace with each client's own administrator.

USAGE NOTES
- The customer-facing reply should not describe the ownership-mismatch versus agency-exclusion distinction; that framing is internal. The customer-facing piece should be the standard agency route-out acknowledgement only.
- If the applicant later supplies evidence that names a single workspace owner and that owner's authorization, re-open the ownership question, but the agency-exclusion analysis above still governs unless the workspace is reframed as a single end-user operator.

DIAGNOSIS

The mock renders every status event as a separate row in the current-state grid. An application with more than one event therefore appears once per event, not once per application:

- A-117 has two events (08:03 provisional_pending, 08:22 final_assisted). Latest is final_assisted. Mock double-counts it in pending AND assisted.
- A-219 has two events (10:01 provisional_admitted, 10:19 final_ineligible). Latest is final_ineligible. Mock double-counts it in admitted AND ineligible.
- A-204 has one event (09:14 final_admitted). Only ever appears in admitted. This row is the only one the mock gets right.

Root cause: the aggregation groups by status over the raw event table (COUNT(*) GROUP BY status) instead of partitioning by application_id and taking the latest event per application. Effect is double-counting in every bucket that receives a transition, and inflated denominators on any rate computed off those totals.

CORRECTED CURRENT-STATE LOGIC

Treat hs_application_status_events as an immutable audit table. Derive a latest-status-per-application view on top of it. Each application belongs to exactly one bucket.

Per-application rule:
  1. Filter events to the as-of window (event_ts <= @as_of_ts).
  2. Order by event_ts DESC, tiebreak by event_seq DESC (or ingest_ts if business ts collides).
  3. Take row_number = 1 per application_id. That row's status is the application's current state.
  4. Bucket each application into exactly one status group.
  5. An application with zero events in the window is not present in any bucket. Do not invent a default state.

Equivalent window query:

  WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT application_id, status, event_ts, event_seq,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
             PARTITION BY application_id
             ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_seq DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM hs_application_status_events
    WHERE event_ts <= @as_of_ts
  )
  SELECT status AS current_status,
         COUNT(DISTINCT application_id) AS application_count
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn = 1
  GROUP BY status

  - final_admitted: 1 (A-204)
  - final_ineligible: 1 (A-219)
  - provisional_pending: 0 (no application currently in this state)

CORRECTED EXCEPTION-VIEW LOGIC

The exception view surfaces transitions and integrity anomalies as a sibling read. It must not feed back into the current-state counts — both views derive off the same event log but neither mutates it.

Columns: application_id, prior_status, current_status, prior_event_ts, last_event_ts, transition_class.

Transition classes worth surfacing:

  - provisional_to_final (expected progression): A-117 (provisional_pending -> final_assisted). Use for stage-duration reporting.
  - final_downgrade (provisional outcome strictly better than final outcome, e.g. provisional_admitted resolved as final_ineligible): A-219 qualifies. Worth flagging separately because this population was operationally communicated one way and resolved another way; downstream messaging and CS treatment may need to diverge from a normal provisional_to_final path.
  - same_final_repeat (data integrity): two events for one application with identical final_* names. None in this mock. Treat as a hard alert if it appears.
  - final_to_final_change (data integrity): two distinct final_* statuses for one application. None in this mock. Treat as a hard alert.

Equivalent exception query:

  WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT application_id, status, event_ts,
           LAG(status)    OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_seq) AS prior_status,
           LAG(event_ts)  OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_seq) AS prior_event_ts,
           ROW_NUMBER()   OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_seq DESC) AS rn
    FROM hs_application_status_events
    WHERE event_ts <= @as_of_ts
  )
  SELECT application_id, prior_status, status AS current_status,
         prior_event_ts, event_ts AS last_event_ts,
         CASE
           WHEN prior_status LIKE 'provisional_%' AND status LIKE 'final_%'
                AND prior_status NOT LIKE 'provisional_admitted' THEN 'provisional_to_final'
           WHEN prior_status = 'provisional_admitted' AND status = 'final_ineligible' THEN 'final_downgrade'
           WHEN status LIKE 'final_%' AND prior_status LIKE 'final_%' AND status =  prior_status THEN 'same_final_repeat'
           WHEN status LIKE 'final_%' AND prior_status LIKE 'final_%' AND status <> prior_status THEN 'final_to_final_change'
           ELSE 'other'
         END AS transition_class
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn = 1 AND prior_status IS NOT NULL

hs_application_status_events is the audit log. Do not collapse, dedupe, or delete rows to make the grid correct. Both views are derived reads. If an event row is wrong, correct it in the event log and re-derive; never suppress events from history to fix a view.

Fix for the damaged corner (least invasive first):

1. Re-wet and press under weight. Lightly mist or touch a damp (not wet) brush to just the lifted-fiber spot and wait 30–60 seconds for the paper to soften. Lay a clean sheet of glassine or smooth tracing paper over it, then weight flat under a few heavy books overnight. Raised fibers usually settle back, and on a fully dry wash the pigment shift is negligible. This is the standard salvage on cold-press and works the vast majority of the time.

2. Kneaded eraser for any fibers still raised after pressing. The putty kind (not vinyl), gently dabbed and rolled across the spot, can coax fibers flat without lifting dry pigment. Light touch.

3. Live with it. A roughly 1/8-inch rough edge sitting just inside an 8x10 mat opening is rarely visible once the piece is matted, especially with a normal 1/16" or greater mat reveal. If you're matting the work, this is often the right answer.

4. Avoid touching up with a re-wash over the spot. Fresh pigment lays down differently than the original dry wash and almost always makes the spot more visible, not less.

Better tape removal for future sheets:

The fiber lift is almost always caused by one of three things: the adhesive fully cured (paper dried for days/weeks), the tape wasn't actually designed for paper, or the pull angle was too steep.

Concrete changes that fix it:

- Use real artist's tape (3M Safe-Release, the yellow "artist tape," or frisket paper tape). Generic low-tack painter's tape behaves inconsistently on cold-press — its adhesive grabs surface fibers in some areas and not others, which is exactly the kind of uneven lift you saw.

- Remove the tape the same session, or within roughly 24 hours. Don't leave it on for weeks. Fully cured adhesive is the most common cause of fiber lift.

- Pull at a low angle — 45° or shalllower, back over itself — not straight up. Go slowly. If you feel real resistance, stop, hit the stubborn spot with a hair dryer on low for a few seconds to soften the adhesive, then continue.

- Before painting, burnish the tape down firmly with a bone folder or the back of a spoon so adhesion is uniform across the strip. Many watercolorists intentionally leave the outermost 1 mm of the tape edge unburnished so that edge releases first and leads the peel.

- If you do hit a stubborn spot mid-pull, slide a clean palette knife or bone folder along the tape edge to break the fiber bond before continuing to pull.

- For the cleanest edges possible, skip taping loose sheets entirely and use a pre-stretched watercolor block. The manufacturer has sealed the edges, you paint into the block, and when the sheet is dry you slide a palette knife between the block and the top sheet to release it. No adhesive involved, edges stay crisp, and you avoid this whole class of damage.

- Pre-test any new tape on a scrap of the same paper. Different paper batches behave differently even with the same tape.

[3] Tile B - Day-7 Activation
    - Separate observation, separate cohort, separate denominator
    - Window: day-7
    - No arithmetic join with Tile A or Tile C; no implied progression to or from first-paid
    - Status: interim, descriptive only

[4] Tile C - Connector-Check Observation (diagnostic)
    - Headline: 92 completed applications observed for connector access; 68 admitted workspaces within that check
    - Denominator: 92-application sample ONLY
    - Window: observation window of the check (state explicitly)
    - Status: separate diagnostic observation; not a funnel stage
    - Non-membership line (required): this sample is NOT shown as upstream of Tile A or Tile B; overlap with the 52-workspace first-paid cohort is unestablished
    - Placement: sits beside or below Tile A, never above it. Above-first-paid placement is what makes the funnel read as ordered.

[5] Tile D - Final Routing

    - Denominator: the relevant intake population (state which)

    - No funnel placement relative to Tiles A, B, or C

Two accounts in a locked primary cohort losing eligibility before any exposure is a specific disposition class with a clean operational answer. Here's the spec.

1. Label for the two primary-cohort accounts

  Semantic label: "pre-exposure eligibility loss" (a.k.a. "pre-exposure ineligibility")

  This is distinct from:
    - post-exposure attrition (became ineligible after seeing a prompt)
    - eligible non-responders (eligible at exposure, did not act)
    - reserve activations (separate cohort, never in primary)

  The label must make three facts explicit: eligible at randomization, ineligible at the exposure window, no prompt sent.

  If you want a flag name following the EA naming convention (workstream + construct type, leaf term may repeat), the documented EA construct type is `ea_act_v3__`. A clean flag would be:

    ea_act_v3__pre_exposure_ineligibility

  Attach to each account: account ID, date became ineligible, direction of seat change (dropped below 75, or rose above 200), date of last eligibility confirmation, confirmation that no prompt was sent.

2. Operational use of reserve accounts

  Reserves are activated, not used to "replace" the two primary records. The language matters because the next reader needs to see that the primary cohort was not silently swapped.

  Rules:
    - Reserves activated under this disposition enter the exposure schedule on the same terms as primary-cohort accounts.
    - July 8 earliest-live boundary applies. No reserve can go live before July 8, regardless of activation reason.
    - 5-account weekly cap applies to ALL live exposures in a given week (primary + reserve). Activating a reserve does not let you exceed 5 in a week.
    - Reserves activated under this class are reported as a separate cohort in any readout, not folded into the primary 30.
    - Reserves keep their original reserve-list draw order; activation does not re-sort them.

  If exposure-slot pressure builds in a week, the fill order is:
    1. eligible primary-cohort accounts ready for live exposure
    2. eligible reserves activated under documented dispositions
    3. eligible primary-cohort accounts deferred within the cap

3. Preserving the primary ITT analysis

  The 30-account primary cohort denominator is locked at randomization. It does not change when a primary account becomes ineligible pre-exposure.

  Concretely:
    - ITT analysis uses all 30 originally randomized accounts in the denominator, including the two that became ineligible.
    - The two contribute zero to "exposed" outcomes (no prompt was sent), and that is the correct ITT contribution: randomized, not exposed.
    - They are reported as a disposition subclass inside the primary cohort, not excluded from it.
    - "n exposed" in the primary readout = primary accounts actually exposed. Reserves activated are not in this numerator.
    - The primary estimate is the ITT estimate over n=30. Activated reserves do not enter this denominator.

  If you want a per-protocol or as-exposed sensitivity, report it alongside ITT with the disposition subclass called out so readers can see the two paths are not merged.

4. The failure mode to avoid (silent replacement)

  The exact failure mode reserves exist to prevent is this:

    - Pull the two primary records out because they're no longer eligible
    - Drop two reserves in to "keep n=30"
    - Re-analyze as if nothing changed

  That breaks the original randomization, hides the eligibility decay from the readout, and lets the July 8 boundary and 5/week cap drift in practice. The locked cohort is the contract with the reader; reserves are how you maintain operational pacing, not how you keep the cohort tidy.

  Specifically, do not:
    - remove the two accounts from the primary analysis denominator
    - substitute reserves into the 30-account cohort record
    - advance the July 8 earliest-live date to "make room" for activated reserves
    - push the 5/week cap above 5 in any week to absorb reserve activations faster

5. Reporting structure

  In any readout that touches the primary cohort:

    Primary cohort (n=30, locked at randomization)
      Eligible at exposure window: X
      Pre-exposure ineligibility: 2
      Exposed: X
      Pending in exposure window: remainder

    Reserves activated (separate)
      Activated for pre-exposure ineligibility: 2
      Activated for other documented dispositions: as applicable
      Exposed: as applicable
      Pending: remainder

  That makes the disposition visible, keeps the cohort contract intact, and keeps the operational bookkeeping honest. The 30 stays 30, the two stay primary-but-not-exposed, and the reserves carry the pacing load without inheriting the primary label.

What you're describing — one vomit episode, alert, normal breathing, soft non-painful belly, no repeated retching, still interested in water, and no bones, onion, garlic, or skewers in what he ate — is reassuring. It sounds like simple dietary indiscretion from a rich food rather than an emergency right now. Here's a practical plan.

Tonight

  Continue calm home monitoring in a quiet spot where you can keep an eye on him without hovering. No food for the next 2-4 hours — if he vomits again in that window, extend the fast; if he doesn't, move to the bland-diet step below. Set a mental checkpoint: any new symptom (retching, belly pain, lethargy, refusing water) over the next several hours means a call to your vet or the nearest ER.

Food and water

  Water: offer small amounts at a time — a few laps every 15-30 minutes rather than a full bowl. Gulping a lot right after vomiting commonly triggers another episode. If he keeps water down for an hour or two, free access is fine.

  After the short fast, reintroduce food with a bland diet: boiled skinless chicken breast (no skin, no fat, no salt or seasoning) mixed with plain white rice, roughly 1 part chicken to 2 parts rice. First meal should be small — a few spoonfuls, not a full portion. If that stays down 2-3 hours, offer a slightly larger portion. Feed 2-3 small bland meals today and tomorrow, then transition back to his normal food over 2-3 days. Hold treats, fatty food, table scraps, and anything fried or rich until his stomach has been clearly normal for a full day.

Call an urgent vet (your regular vet's after-hours line or an emergency clinic) if any of these appear

  - Repeated vomiting — more than 2-3 times total, or vomiting that doesn't stop, especially on an empty stomach.
  - Dry heaving or trying to vomit with nothing coming up. In dogs, that can be a sign of bloat (GDV), which is a true emergency.
  - Belly becomes hard, swollen, or painful to the touch, or he adopts the "praying position" — front legs down, hindquarters up — which signals abdominal pain.
  - Restlessness, pacing, or inability to settle and lie comfortably.
  - Marked lethargy or weakness — not just sleepy, but genuinely unresponsive or uninterested in you.
  - Refusing water for more than a few hours, or any sign of dehydration (sticky/tacky gums, skin that doesn't snap back when gently pinched).
  - Blood in vomit (red streaks or coffee-ground appearance) or blood/black tarry stool.
  - Pale gums, rapid or labored breathing, collapse, or obvious distress.
  - Trembling or shaking without an obvious reason.

One extra thing to watch over the next 24-72 hours: fatty meals can trigger pancreatitis in dogs, and it usually shows up 1-3 days later rather than immediately. The same red flags above apply — especially repeated vomiting, belly pain, lethargy, and refusing food — so keep an eye on him gently through the rest of the week even if tonight looks fine.

Not a vet and not a substitute for one — if anything in the red-flag list shows up, don't wait it out. A call that turns out to be nothing is always better than losing a window where treatment would have been straightforward.

Let me work through the UPS sizing for the Cherrywood workroom network gear.

Step 1 — Compute each device's stated maximum wattage:
- Modem: 12 V × 1.5 A = 18 W
- Access-point injector: 48 V × 0.32 A = 15.36 W
- Combined label maximum: ~33.4 W

Step 2 — Add reasonable overhead. Real-world PoE injectors and cable runs lose a few percent, devices occasionally spike above nameplate, and you want headroom so the UPS isn't running at 100% (which shortens battery life and runtime). A common rule is 20–25% headroom:
- +20%: ~40 W
- +25%: ~42 W

Step 3 — Translate to a UPS watt rating. UPS vendors round up to standard sizes; the next clean step above ~40 W is typically 100 W (smallest "real" home-office UPS class). A 100 VA / ~60 W unit is too tight on margin, so the practical recommendation is a ~150–300 W UPS — a 150 VA/90 W or 300 VA/180 W class unit gives comfortable margin and is the smallest size commonly sold with a USB monitoring port.

Step 4 — Watt-hours for ~90 minutes of runtime. Energy = watts × hours:
- Ideal energy at combined max: 33.4 W × 1.5 h ≈ 50 Wh
- With 25% overhead built in: ~42 W × 1.5 h ≈ 63 Wh
- UPS inverter is ~80–85% efficient, so the battery must store: ~63 / 0.85 ≈ 74 Wh

Realistic recommendation:
- UPS rating: ~150 W (300 VA) class — smallest tier with comfortable margin and a monitoring port
- Battery capacity: ~80–100 Wh, which on a 300 VA class UPS usually means a unit advertised around 450–600 VA (roughly 300–450 Wh capacity), because most UPSes in this range have batteries much larger than the load needs, giving you well over 90 minutes on a ~33 W load.

Quick sanity check — a typical 600 VA / ~330 Wh UPS running ~33 W yields roughly 5–8 hours of runtime, so 90 minutes is comfortably inside its envelope. That gives you a wide margin if you ever add a small VoIP ATA, switch, or fan, and the battery isn't being deeply cycled during short outages.

Plain-text summary you can act on:
- Combined max draw: ~33 W (modem 18 W + AP 15 W)
- Recommended UPS: 150 W / 300 VA minimum, ideally a 600 VA (~330 Wh) class unit
- Expected runtime at ~33 W load: ~90 minutes target sits easily inside that — well under half the unit's typical runtime envelope

Temporary Backup-Access Protocol — Expansion Assist (July 15–19 absence)

Recommendation: sliding-window handover, NOT a flat 14-day reveal.

Core idea
The 7-day view and the 24-hour frontline rule are independent constraints and stay intact. What changes is who holds the view and how it advances during the gap. The backup never sees more than 7 days at any single moment — the window rolls forward each morning instead of being widened on July 12.

The protocol

1. Role scope — distinct, time-boxed, narrower than the lead
   - New scope: ea_ops_backup
   - Grants: read the EA assignment queue, reassign accounts inside the visible window, enforce the 5-account weekly cap, log actions with a required justification field.
   - Does NOT grant: edit the 7-day window policy, edit the 24h frontline unlock, view beyond 7 days, modify flag rollout, edit cohort targeting, change cap value.
   - Auto-expires end-of-day July 22. No standing access.

2. Reveal schedule
   - Fri July 12: reveal the standard 7-day window (July 12–18) to the backup. Backup acknowledges. This is the same window the lead would see — no extra exposure.
   - Mon July 15 (absence start): sliding-window handover active. Backup's view = next 7 days from that morning (July 15–21).
   - Tue–Fri July 16–19: each morning, view rolls forward by 1 day. Always 7 days, never more.
   - Mon July 22: lead returns, backup scope expires automatically, lead resumes standard 7-day view.

3. Weekly-cap handling
   - Cap stays a 5-account budget per ISO calendar week (Mon–Sun). Backup draws from the same bucket as the lead — no separate cap. If the lead already burned 2 of 5 the week of July 15–19 before leaving, the backup has 3 left. Documented in the handover note on July 12.

4. 24-hour frontline limit — preserved automatically
   - Frontline visibility is a separate product-emitted rule, unaffected by who holds the ops view. Backup actions on assignments do not change when reps see the account. The rep-side unlock at T-24h before scheduled exposure stays as-is.

5. Audit
   - Every backup action logs actor=backup, timestamp, justification. Lead reviews the log on July 22 return.

Why this beats the original ask
- The July 12 flat 14-day reveal would have exposed July 12–25 in one shot — 8 extra days beyond policy and 4 days past the lead's return.
- Sliding-window keeps the canonical 7-day atomic. Information overlap with the lead's normal view stays at ≤1 day at any moment (handoff days).
- Backup can still run the queue Mon–Fri because the window always includes the current workday plus the next 6.

Edge cases to flag in the handover note
- Account deferred across July 19 → July 22: legal under the sliding window; lead inherits on return.
- Assignment created by backup that lands on July 22: valid if it satisfied the 24h rule at creation. Lead sees it inside the standard view on July 22.
- If absence extends past July 19: do not extend ea_ops_backup — re-evaluate, do not silently widen.

What to explicitly NOT do
- Pre-reveal 14 days on July 12 (the original ask).
- Lower the 24h frontline threshold to "give the backup more room" — that's a separate breach.
- Hand the backup ea_ops_lead scope and revoke later — too broad, harder to audit.
- Treat the absence week and the return week as one combined cap period.

Net: one new narrow scope, one Friday acknowledgement, four rolling-window mornings, auto-expiry Monday return. Policy constraints preserved; the queue stays operable.

The "pasted on" is almost always two things stacked: the rim is too dense relative to the surrounding wash, so it reads as applique rather than glow, and the edge is hard on the cool side, so there's no transition zone for the eye to slide through. Trying to fix that after the orange is down is what creates the mud — you'd be rewetting the seam and lifting into both layers at once, which is exactly where burnt sienna and ultramarine neutralize into gray-brown.

Sequence:

1. Soften the cool-side edge first, before any warm touches the paper.
   - Clean damp brush (water only), run it along the inside edge of the dry blue-gray where the rim will sit. Don't flood — just reactivate the very edge.
   - Touch a tissue to the lifted pigment so it feathers out instead of creeping.
   - Let it dry fully.

2. Rethink the rim mix. Redo the scrap test at painting strength, not dropper strength — the orange that looked pasted on is probably twice the concentration it'll want on the paper. Lead with quinacridone rose, not burnt sienna. Rose against ultramarine stays luminous; sienna against ultramarine heads straight to neutral. A touch of sienna for warmth is the accent, not the base.

3. First warm pass: thin, and shaped wet, not edged.
   - Tea-strength mix: mostly water, a touch of rose, a kiss of sienna.
   - Paint the rim area, but let the warm edge bleed slightly INTO the softened cool zone — not over the whole shadow, just the seam. The cool stays cool behind it; only the transition warms.

4. Dry completely. Second pass only on the brightest sliver.
   - Same mix, slightly stronger. Apply just to the lit edge itself. Leave the transition from pass 1 alone — this is what gives the glow gradient without a value jump.

5. Optional: a whisper of dilute ultramarine into the deepest shadow to seat the cool back. The rim reads as light because the shadow is convincingly cool.

Avoid:
  - Glazing warm over a still-damp cool seam — that's where the mud lives.
  - Leading with burnt sienna. Rose first, sienna as accent.
  - Softening after the orange goes on. Soften first, glaze second.

Backlit studies live or die on the seam. Get the cool edge soft and dry before the warm goes anywhere near it, and the rim will glow instead of stick.
