No shell here — I'll work the math inline (it's small enough to do carefully by hand) and ground the recommendation in the published numbers, the load assumptions, and standard UPS behavior.

Load first (real, not spec):
- Cable modem, idle/light traffic: ~9–12 W
- Wired access point (home, 2×2, a few clients): ~6–10 W
- Real-world combined: ~15–25 W typical, ~25–30 W with traffic spikes or PoE-passthrough AP. I'll treat **20 W as the planning number** and **25–30 W as a stress check**.

Linear-inverse scaling from the published 30 W figure is roughly right for SLA UPS in this class (manufacturers publish the curve; for modest deratings from the rated load it's close enough to use for an apples-to-apples comparison between these two).

  Scenario            | Option A (min) | Option B (min)
  new, 20 W           |      ~75       |     ~150
  new, 25 W           |      ~60       |     ~120
  new, 30 W (spec)    |       50       |     100
  2-yr-old, 20 W (~25% aging) | ~56 | ~113
  2-yr-old, 25 W (~25% aging) | ~45 |  ~90
  3-yr-old, 25 W (~35% aging) | ~39 |  ~78

Sizing comparison vs the 90-minute target:

Option A (425 VA / 225 W, sealed battery)
- Comfortable headroom on power: 225 W ceiling is ~9× your expected load, so you're never anywhere near the watt limit. Good.
- Runtime margin is thin. At a new 20 W load it clears 90 min; at a new 25 W load it sits at ~60 min, and at 30 W it lands exactly at the published 50. Once the battery ages (see below), the 90-min target slips out of reach even at light load by year 2–3.
- Sealed, non-replaceable battery: the unit has a fixed service life. Once capacity falls off a cliff (typically year 3–4 for SLA in a warm room), the whole UPS goes to e-waste.

Option B (850 VA / 450 W, user-replaceable battery)
- Bigger VA/W than you need electrically (the 225 W model would already cover the load), so on raw "do the watts fit" criteria it's oversized. Fine — that overhead is the cost of runtime.
- At a new 20–25 W load it clears 90 min by ~50–60%; at the spec 30 W load it exactly hits the published 100. After 2–3 years of aging it still meets 90 min at typical load, and a $20–40 replacement battery in year 3–4 resets the clock instead of replacing the unit.

Recommendation: Option B.

For a 90-minute target on gear this light, Option A only works if (a) your actual load stays near 15–20 W, and (b) you replace the whole unit on a ~3-year cycle. Option B buys you the runtime margin you actually asked for, and the user-replaceable battery turns the 5–7 year question into a $30 part swap rather than a new purchase. The extra VA/W you "don't need" is paying for runtime headroom and serviceability, not capacity you'll never use.

How much confidence to put in the published runtime number:

Less than the spec sheet implies. Three things eat into it, and they compound:

1. Conversion loss in real conditions. The "minutes at 30 W" figure already includes inverter and efficiency losses, so it's a delivered-to-load number, not a battery-only number. That's good. But it's measured at 25 °C with a fully charged, brand-new battery. Drop the room to 30+ °C (a media cabinet in summer is commonly that) and capacity falls another ~10–15%.

2. Battery aging. SLA batteries in always-float service lose capacity gradually, then fail fast around year 3. A reasonable working assumption is ~20–25% loss at 2 years, ~30–40% at 3 years. Treat the published runtime as a "new battery, mild ambient" number.

3. Load above the rating. Spec sheets are honest at 30 W, but real APs spike during association/handshake storms, and a cable modem pulling downstream bonding channels can sit closer to 18–22 W continuously. Budget 20–25 W as the planning load, not 30.

Net: treat the published minutes as a **new-unit, mild-conditions** benchmark. Plan on getting roughly **70–80% of the published figure** once the battery is 18–24 months old and the room is warm. Under that lens, Option A's 50 min becomes ~35–40 min — well short of 90 — while Option B's 100 min becomes ~70–80 min, still tight against a 90-minute target but achievable if your real load stays near 20 W and you replace the battery around the 3-year mark. If you want a comfortable buffer rather than a just-barely-pass, the right move is Option B plus a planned battery swap at year 3, and a 20 W (not 30 W) assumption when you're thinking about whether to ride out a long outage.

Working note — dry bloom on a sky wash is a concentration edge, not a stain you can erase. Goal is to soften the edge, not remove the pigment. Ultramarine is moderately staining, so anything aggressive will set it deeper. Try the steps in order and stop as soon as the edge reads soft.

1. Don't rewet yet. The paper is dry — that is the safer state to work from. Any isolated re-wetting will just produce a fresh bloom when it dries.

2. Dry pass first. Take a clean, fully dry mop or large soft brush and pass lightly across the bloom edge. If any pigment dust lifts onto the brush, you have a small window to keep going dry. Most of the time nothing moves — that is fine, just confirms the pigment is locked.

3. Controlled local lift (the move that actually helps). Use a clean brush, dampen it, then blot it almost dry on a towel so it is barely moist, not wet. Working direction matters: stroke from the soft sky INTO the hard edge, never from the bloom outward — you want to dilute the concentrated edge into the surrounding wash, not push it further. One pass, lift, blot the brush on a tissue, repeat. Keep the working area small and keep the tissue moving so lifted pigment doesn't redeposit.

4. Stop and let it dry before assessing. Most blooms lose their "hard line" character after step 3 and read as a soft halo instead. That is usually enough on an airy sky.

5. Only if the edge is still sharp: even re-wet as a last resort. With a wide flat brush, dampen a generous patch of sky centered on the bloom — the margin has to be wide enough that the new drying edge lands well outside the original mark, otherwise you just trade one bloom for another. Immediately wick the surface with a clean tissue or soft sponge, then let it dry flat and undisturbed.

If after step 3 or 5 the mark is still legible as a defect, stop working the bloom itself. Overworking is the larger cost than the mark. Integration options, in order of restraint:

- Read it as a soft cloud form. A pale bloom sitting halfway up a sky is conventionally a cloud edge — leave it and let the eye accept it.
- If it reads as an accident rather than a cloud, add one or two companion marks of similar value elsewhere in the sky (a second soft cloud, a pale wisp near the roofline on the other side). Two or three soft marks of similar weight will read as intentional sky variation; one isolated bloom reads as a mistake. This is a compositional fix, not a tonal one.
- Do not glaze the whole sky to unify it. That is exactly the overworking you want to avoid, and on ultramarine it will just shift the value of the whole wash darker.

A few don'ts worth keeping in mind for the rest of the session: don't scrub with a stiff brush, don't use a wet brush on a small area, and don't keep going once the edge is soft. If the mark survives step 3, restraint is the better craft choice than persistence.

I don't have a terminal/python tool available in this session — let me solve this with exact integer arithmetic on paper and present the result transparently.

The math (worked by hand, in cents to avoid float error):

- Pool: $720.00 = 72,000 cents
- 7 shares → 72,000 ÷ 7 = 10,285.7142857… cents per share
- True double-share (Sam): 2 × 10,285.7142857… = 20,571.4285714… cents = $205.7142857…

Cent-rounding analysis:

- Sam's share rounds to either $205.71 (20,571¢, short by 0.43¢) or $205.72 (20,572¢, over by 0.57¢).
- Each standard staff share rounds to either $102.85 (10,285¢, short by 0.71¢) or $102.86 (10,286¢, over by 0.29¢).

Only one rounding combination for Sam can be reconciled with the staff total to hit exactly $720.00:

Sam at $205.71 leaves 51,429¢ for the five staff. Five × 10,285¢ = 51,425¢ (4¢ short), so four staff at $102.85 and one staff at $102.86 → 4×10,285 + 10,286 = 51,429¢. ✓ Total: 20,571 + 51,429 = 72,000¢. ✓

Sam at $205.72 would leave 51,428¢, but five × 10,286¢ = 51,430¢ (2¢ over) and four × 10,286 + 10,285 = 51,429¢ (1¢ over). No integer combo sums to 51,428¢, so this branch is infeasible.

Therefore the unique cent-correct allocation is Sam $205.71, four staff $102.85, one staff $102.86.

Seven-share split — recommended allocation (totals exactly $720.00):

- Sam (lead, 2 shares): $205.71
- Staff member A: $102.86 (the unavoidable +1¢)
- Staff members B, C, D, E: $102.85 each

Verification: 205.71 + 102.86 + 4 × 102.85 = 205.71 + 102.86 + 411.40 = 720.00 (72,000¢) ✓

How the cent difference is allocated:

The $720.00 pool does not divide evenly by 7 (true share ≈ $102.8571), so a 1¢ excess over the all-rounded-down scenario (5 × $102.85 = $514.25) must land somewhere. Two design choices were considered:

1. Put the extra cent on Sam (Sam $205.72, all staff $102.85): Sam would be 0.57¢ above his true double-share value, but this combination doesn't sum to a whole-cent $720.00, so it's rejected.
2. Put the extra cent on one of the five equal-share staff (Sam $205.71, four staff $102.85, one staff $102.86): this is the only combination that reconciles to exactly $720.00 and keeps Sam at 0.43¢ under his true double-share — closer to his theoretical value than option 1 would have been.

Which staff member absorbs the extra cent: the policy text you gave doesn't specify (it only fixes Sam at "two shares" and the others at "one share"), so by default the cleanest convention is seniority/tenure order — i.e. the longest-serving of the five non-lead staff takes the +1¢. If Sam has a preferred order (e.g. by station, clock-in time, or last event's tip-out rotation), swap the $102.86 line to that person. The arithmetic is unchanged.

Sam can submit this with the closeout; the cent rule above is the one that satisfies "totals exactly $720.00" and "Sam at twice a standard share as closely as possible" simultaneously.

EXPANSION ASSIST — candidate-set freshness & fail-closed rule
(for tomorrow's design review)

Principle: when a behavior signal is stale, or when the CS
suppression sources conflict, the default is OUT of the candidate
set. We don't let either case pass; we make the build pipeline or
CS close the gap before the account re-enters.


BEHAVIOR SIGNALS — per-signal max snapshot age

Each of the three behavior signals is read with an explicit
freshness window at candidate-set build time. A snapshot older
than the window fails the signal to "not pass" — same status as a
true failure, not a soft warning.

  - Integration depth: <= 7 days. Structural signal; the window
    exists to catch a silently disconnected integration, not
    because depth itself churns that fast.

  - Active-admin behavior: <= 48 hours. Admin activity shifts
    inside a week; anything older means we don't know whether
    admins are still active.

  - Usage ceiling: <= 48 hours. A 9-day-old snapshot (acct_014)
    almost certainly reflects a stalled pipeline, not a stable
    product state. Tight on purpose — if acct_014 genuinely
    hasn't emitted, the right fix is restoring the event flow,
    not widening the window.

Missing snapshot -> "not pass." We do not infer pass from absence.


CS SUPPRESSION — conflict resolution

Two sources of truth, both read at build time:
  - the nightly suppression field in the candidate table
    (existing read)
  - CS source-of-truth: currently-open renewal, expansion,
    active-adoption, or churn-risk work

Resolution matrix:
  - nightly=suppressed, CS source=agrees         -> suppress
  - nightly=unsuppressed, CS source=silent       -> unsuppressed
  - nightly=unsuppressed, CS source=active work  -> suppress
                                                   (this is
                                                   acct_027;
                                                   nightly lags,
                                                   CS is closer
                                                   to real-time)
  - nightly=suppressed, CS source=silent         -> trust
                                                   nightly
                                                   (don't false-
                                                   positive)

Failure mode: if the build pipeline can't reach CS source-of-
truth at build time (timeout, schema mismatch, schema drift),
default to suppress for the cycle. Better to miss a candidate
than route EA copy into an account CS just opened renewal on.


EXCLUSION LOGGING

Every exclusion under this rule carries: signal name, snapshot
age or conflict timestamp, CS work-id where applicable, and the
build cycle that produced it. Owen's shadow counts need this to
distinguish "true not-pass" from "data-stale not-pass" in the
pilot read-out — otherwise the suppression rate is unreadable,
and the 9-day-stale vs. genuinely-low case collapses into the
same bucket.


RE-ENTRY

Automatic on the next build cycle once the snapshot refreshes
(behavior) or CS closes the active work (suppression). No manual
re-clear; the rule is just "is it fresh and consistent right
now."

The mock's defect is that it puts five different constructs on one funnel axis. Each of those constructs has its own actor, its own emission source, and its own null reason — collapsing them loses exactly the signal the report needs.

WHY THE FUNNEL MISMEASURES (matching the three problems you named)

  1. Eligible-but-never-exposed is invisible. In a funnel, an account that is eligible but suppressed at the planned-exposure time silently counts as "did not convert" — same as one that saw the prompt and ignored it. The mock has no field for exposure status or suppression reason, so those accounts are structurally indistinguishable from genuine non-converters. The pilot's 9-of-46-suppressed observation is exactly the population the funnel hides.

  2. Prompt exposure, help request, and CS handoff are different events from different actors. Exposure is system-emitted. A help request is user-emitted (and can happen with or without exposure). A CS handoff is human-emitted (and can happen with or without a help request, or via proactive outreach). Sequencing them as funnel stages asserts a chain that does not exist.

  3. The funnel shape asserts causality. The EA program is observational/shadow — there is no controlled exposure to attribute expansion to. An eligible→expanded rate computed from observed co-occurrence is not a conversion rate; it is a coincidence rate dressed up as one.

REDESIGN PRINCIPLES

  - One row per account. Preserve the sequence at the account level; do not summarize it into stages.
  - Each construct is its own timestamped field (or null + reason). No "stage reached" boolean.
  - Exposure status is a first-class attribute, not implied by the absence of a later timestamp.
  - Suppression at planned exposure time is logged explicitly so the eligible-but-not-exposed population is visible, not hidden in funnel falloff.
  - Aggregates are per-transition with honest denominators. Never a single eligible→expanded rate.

PROPOSED ACCOUNT-LEVEL SCHEMA

  Identity / context
    account_id
    cohort_label                          (the behavior-flag segment the account was sampled from)
    current_state_at_report_run           (per Ines: name the account's present state, not its signup age)
    ea_act_v3__unit                       (the EA unit being measured, per naming convention)

  Eligibility
    eligible_at
    eligibility_rule_version              (pin which rule produced the flag — rules will change)
    eligibility_superseded_at             (nullable; if the account later loses eligibility)
    eligibility_superseded_reason

  Usage-ceiling trigger (product-emitted, per EA readout)
    usage_ceiling_crossed_at
    usage_ceiling_metric
    usage_ceiling_threshold

  Exposure (the layer the mock is missing)
    planned_exposure_at                   (nullable if no plan was ever made for this account)
    exposure_status                       enum: exposed | suppressed | planned_not_yet_due | planned_window_missed | not_planned
    exposed_at                            (null unless status = exposed)
    exposure_suppression_reason           controlled vocab; current suppression terms, not retired active_admin_*
    ea_act_v3__prompt_variant             (only meaningful when exposed)

  Help request (separate from exposure)
    help_requested_at
    hs_path__<need>                       (per naming convention; pin which help-signal path)

  CS handoff (human layer)
    cs_handoff_at
    cs_handoff_trigger                    help_request | proactive_outreach | escalation
    cs_owner

  Expansion outcome (measured, not inferred)
    expanded_at                           (null if it did not happen)
    expansion_kind                        seat | plan_upgrade | attach — keep "expansion" specific
    expansion_arr_delta                   optional, labeled descriptive only (Q4 NOTs flagged revenue-credit as out)

ACCOUNT-LEVEL SEQUENCE — TWO EXAMPLE ROWS

  Account a-7321 (suppressed at planned exposure)
    eligible_at:                    2024-05-02
    usage_ceiling_crossed_at:       2024-05-19
    planned_exposure_at:            2024-05-21
    exposure_status:                suppressed
    exposure_suppression_reason:    active_adoption_signal
    help_requested_at:              —
    cs_handoff_at:                  —
    expanded_at:                    —

  Account a-7410 (full sequence)
    eligible_at:                    2024-05-04
    usage_ceiling_crossed_at:       2024-05-22
    planned_exposure_at:            2024-05-24
    exposure_status:                exposed
    exposed_at:                     2024-05-24
    help_requested_at:              2024-05-26   (hs_path__onboarding_setup)
    cs_handoff_at:                  2024-05-26
    expanded_at:                    2024-06-09

  The two rows have visibly different shapes. Neither is forced through the same funnel stages. a-7321's non-expansion is correctly attributed to suppression, not to "drop-off." That distinction is exactly what the original report would erase.

AGGREGATE VIEWS — PER TRANSITION, NEVER ONE FUNNEL

    coverage:                      usage_ceiling_crossed / eligible
                                    (is the trigger firing on the right population?)

    exposure_rate:                 exposed / accounts whose planned_exposure_at has passed
                                    (among accounts that should have been exposed, what fraction were?)

    suppression_mix:               distribution of exposure_suppression_reason
                                    (the 9-of-46 suppression observation becomes a real view, not a footnote)

    help_request_rate_post_exposure:    help_requested / exposed
    handoff_rate_post_help:             cs_handoff / help_requested
    expansion_rate_post_handoff:        expanded / cs_handoff
    expansion_rate_post_exposure:       expanded / exposed        (descriptive, not causal)

  Do NOT compute:                  expanded / eligible.
                                    That single rate is the defect the original funnel produces — it folds non-exposure, suppression, no-help-request, and no-handoff into a denominator-mismatched numerator. Naming it `conversion_rate` would also pull the report back toward the pipeline/forecast vocabulary that is out of scope for the EA readout.

WHAT THE REPORT MUST NOT PRODUCE

  - A single eligible→expanded conversion_rate.
  - Any aggregate that treats non-exposure as failure.
  - Causal language. The program is observational; describe what happened after exposure or after handoff, not what exposure "drove." Use post_exposure / post_handoff, not attributed_to / driven_by.
  - Lifecycle/age segmentation substituting for current_state_at_report_run (the Ines note).
  - Bare field names that drift back from the ea_act_v3__ / hs_path__ prefix discipline.

OPERATIONAL NOTES FOR OWEN

  - The schema needs product-emitted events (usage_ceiling_crossed, help_requested) joined to the EA account table on account_id, with the join pinned by event-emission date so retroactive re-emissions don't rewrite history.
  - eligibility_rule_version and usage_ceiling_threshold belong on the row, not in a separate config table, so the report is reproducible as rules evolve.
  - exposure_suppression_reason must be a controlled vocabulary. Free-text reasons will fragment the suppression_mix view.
  - Drop the proposed `prompted_accounts` and `conversion_rate` columns entirely; replace with the per-transition view set above.

Kibo sounds okay in the moment — a brief favor on a tiny superficial pad scrape, no bleeding/swelling/foreign body, weight-bearing, and letting you handle the paw all read as minor. That said, I'm not a vet; if anything below makes you uneasy, the call is yours.

Clean and protect, today

1. Lukewarm water rinse first — just to wash off grit. A gentle stream from a cup or low-pressure sprayer is enough. Skip hydrogen peroxide and alcohol on the pad; they damage healing tissue and sting.
2. Mild cleanser around (not into) the scrape if there's debris. Dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% (the light blue color, like a dog's wound wash) or a tiny amount of plain unscented dish soap works. Rinse well.
3. Pat dry with a clean cloth. Don't rub.
4. Optional antiseptic: chlorhexidine solution as above, or a pet-safe spray like Vetericyn. Avoid human triple-antibiotic ointments unless you've used them on Kibo before without trouble (some dogs react).
5. Inspect closely under good light. Pad scrapes can hide a small pebble or grass awn in the center. If you see anything embedded that won't wipe away, stop and call the vet.
6. Bandaging or not: a small, dry, non-bleeding pad scrape usually does better open — paw bandages get wet and dirty fast and most dogs chew them. If you do bandage: non-stick pad, then vet wrap (loose — two fingers fit at the top), then a clean sock taped above the dewclaw so it can't slide down. Change daily.
7. Discourage licking for the first day. Supervise, or use a cone / inflatable collar if he goes at it. Saliva macerates the wound and slows healing.
8. Recheck the pad in 12–24 hours.

Walks today

Shorten them, yes. The brief favor means the pad stings on full weight, especially on rough or warm surfaces. Today:

- Skip the ~3-mile loop. A short relief walk on soft, shaded grass is plenty.
- Avoid hot pavement — midday asphalt can both sting an open scrape and re-injure it. If you can't hold the back of your hand to the pavement for 5 seconds, it's too hot.
- Stay on even, clean ground. No gravel, no thorny underbrush, no creek mud today.
- Re-evaluate at the next outing: if he's not favoring at all, you can step length back up gradually over a couple of days. If he favors again, hold the short walks and keep monitoring.

Vet call — call if any of these show up

- Favoring that persists or returns beyond 24–48 hours, or any refusal to bear weight.
- Swelling, spreading redness, or heat around the pad or up the leg.
- Discharge — yellow, green, or foul-smelling.
- Bleeding that doesn't stop with a couple of minutes of gentle pressure.
- A deep cut (gaping, more than a small surface scrape), full-thickness pad wound, or anything that looks like it goes through to the fleshy underside.
- A visible foreign body you can't flush out, or any torn, cracked, or broken nail nearby.
- Increasing pain — pulling the paw back, growling when you approach it, panting/resting when he normally wouldn't.
- Licking that you can't interrupt.
- Systemic signs: lethargy, appetite drop, shivering, unusually warm ears.
- Honestly: any change that just doesn't sit right. You know his normal.

Two small things worth mentioning to the vet if you do call: that the favor lasted only ~2 minutes and resolved on its own, and that there was a brief limp episode after the walk but the pad itself only shows a superficial scrape. Those details help them triage by phone.

Three talking points. Each one answers Priya's question directly rather than restating the checklist.

1. When I stop a build for unresolved timestamp semantics.

Concrete case from the EA pilot: the day-60 copy trigger. The decision in the pilot doc is that the trigger has to name the account's current state, not its signup age. Ship it off signup_date and we fire day-60 copy at accounts that haven't had a real activation window — Ines already flagged that copy as unusable. The build stops until one question is resolved: is day-60 measured from signup, first_active, or first_paid? Until that's answered and signed off by CS and Finance (the same cohort feeds the day-90 retention number on the reopen list), the cohort query doesn't ship. I'd rather hold the work for two days than publish a number that quietly misrepresents both the customer experience and the retention curve.

The principle I want the team to take: I stop when two systems need to reconcile on the same event and the join key isn't defined identically in both. The cost of guessing is paid by the next person who reads the output.

2. When independent validation is non-negotiable.

Anything that crosses out of our team gets a second pair of hands. 3. How I surface a late Finance dependency instead of working around it.

No silent defaults. Every cross-team dependency gets one line in a shared doc — owner, deliverable, due date, what it blocks — and I review that list every Monday. If Finance slips, I send the DRI a Slack same day with two options, not a question: (1) publish the brief with a stated assumption and Finance issues a v2 amendment, or (2) slip the brief publish by N days. The message names the decision and the deadline ("need a call by tomorrow 10am"), not "just checking in." When the dependency arrives late, the lateness is visible in the published brief itself — "uses Finance's preliminary cohort-ARR mapping delivered 6/26; final mapping may shift ±X%." The reader sees the constraint. Late delivery has a cost, and the cost is named, not absorbed.

Here's the read on the diagnosis and what's worth pinning down before mom signs anything.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENTS ACTUALLY SAY

The unit is doing what the technician is describing. An 18°F supply-to-return split sits inside the normal 16–22°F band, and normal compressor amperage with no detected leak means the sealed system and the compressor itself are healthy right now. Both reported faults are consistent with each other and with age: a weak capacitor makes the compressor and fan motors hard-start, the inrush current arcs across the contactor contacts, and the contactor pits and eventually drops out under load — exactly the "stops in afternoon heat, restarts and cools" pattern. So the $468 fix targets the actual cause. The question is whether anything else is close to failing, and whether the repair is warranted well enough to trust.

REPAIR vs. REPLACEMENT AT A GLANCE

Repair ($468, capacitor + contactor):
- Addresses the diagnosed fault at the right cost.
- Compressor and sealed system are currently good; replacing them discards life.
- 11 years is mid-range (typical lifespan 15–20), so several years of service is plausible.
- Capacitor and contactor are both wear items; both being degraded at once suggests the unit has been running with electrical stress, which can shorten compressor life even when amperage looks fine today.
- A failed repair in peak heat is the worst-case scenario: an 11-year-old unit with no backup plan and a tech dispatched once already.

Replacement ($9,240, full system):
- New components, new warranty (typically 10 years parts on a matched install), lower operating cost on a higher-SEER unit, no near-term failure risk.
- Discards a compressor and sealed system that the tech's own measurements say are healthy.
- The quote needs to be unpacked — outdoor unit alone is not the same scope as a matched indoor coil + line set + disconnect + pad + permit, and scope drives whether the new warranty actually attaches.
- 20× the cost of the repair; a contractor's incentive to recommend it is high.

The repair is the rational default unless the answers to the questions below change the picture.

QUESTIONS MOM SHOULD GET ANSWERS TO BEFORE COMMITTING

Warranty
1. Repair warranty: parts only, or parts and labor? For how long — 30/90 days, one year? If either part fails in the first 60 days, is the second visit free?
2. Does the repair warranty cover consequential damage — i.e., if the new contactor is mis-torqued and takes out the compressor, who pays?
3. Replacement: parts, compressor, and labor warranties each, in writing, with the exact term. Many manufacturer warranties require online registration within 60–90 days of install to activate; if mom misses that, the warranty is effectively gone.
4. Is the warranty transferable if she sells the house, and what does the contractor's own labor warranty look like separate from the manufacturer's?

Failure risk
1. Refrigerant type — R-22 (phased out, increasingly expensive to recharge) or R-410A? This alone can flip the calculus: an R-22 system that develops a leak in two years is a write-off, not a repair.
2. Indoor coil and air handler condition — was either inspected, or only the outdoor unit? A pitted contactor doesn't tell you anything about the evaporator coil or blower motor.
3. Contactor assessment — visual inspection only, or tested under load? Pitting can be cosmetic; under-load test confirms whether it's actually dropping voltage.
4. Compressor trend — is amperage nameplate-true or creeping up? Any history of hard-start events? A rising RLA is an early-warning indicator the repair doesn't address.
5. If the repair is done and the compressor fails within six months, what's the standalone compressor-replacement quote vs. the full-system quote? That delta tells you the real cost of "repair first."
6. Thermostat and electrical: is the disconnect properly sized, the breaker healthy, the whip intact? A weak feed can mimic capacitor/contactor symptoms.

Replacement scope
1. Itemized quote: outdoor condenser, indoor coil (matched or reusing old?), line set (new or flushed?), thermostat, electrical disconnect, pad, permit, haul-away, refrigerant recovery. The number changes a lot depending on what's in and what's out.
2. SEER rating of the proposed unit — minimum-code 14.3 or higher-efficiency 15.2/16+? Higher SEER is worth real money over the life of the system but raises the upfront.
3. Is the indoor coil being replaced? Best practice on a matched system is yes; some manufacturers void the compressor warranty if the old indoor coil is reused with a new outdoor unit.
4. Line set: new or reused? If reused, was it flushed for the new refrigerant spec?
5. Any ductwork, return-side, or electrical upgrades in scope, or is this a like-for-like swap? A common upsell is a "necessary" duct modification; ask whether it's actually required or value-add.
6. Rebates and credits: utility rebates, federal tax credits for qualifying high-efficiency equipment (Section 25C has applied historically to heat pumps and some AC), manufacturer promotions. The same $9,240 can drop meaningfully with a 25C claim if she qualifies.
7. Timeline — if this is a non-emergency quote, getting a second quote in the same week is the single best move. Same scope, two bidders, usually a 10–20% gap.

BOTTOM LINE FOR MOM

Ask the contractor to put the repair warranty in writing with a 90-day parts-and-labor term, confirm the refrigerant type and the indoor coil/blower condition in writing, and get one competing replacement quote with an itemized scope before deciding. If the refrigerant is R-410A and the indoor side checks out, the repair is the right call. If it's R-22, or the indoor coil has visible issues, the replacement math gets a lot closer than the headline numbers suggest.

Short answer: yes, get a PT (or sports-medicine) eval before the 6/22 walk-jog, and treat Saturday's session as deferred until you're cleared.

The clinical-eval triggers you wrote down — mod/sharp in-run pain, gait change, swelling, bruising, instability, can't bear weight, limp >24h, night or rest pain — are the red-flag list. You have none of those, so this isn't urgent. But two things push this from "fine to walk-jog" to "yellow, hold and evaluate":

1.  A reproducible 2/10 lateral ankle ache on single-leg hop after ~13 days. Hopping is the closest non-running stress to running impact — it tends to surface what running will surface.
2.  The same on descending stairs. That loads the ankle in plantarflexion with eccentric control, the same position the lateral-ligament complex and peroneals work in during late stance and push-off.

Pattern: walking is silent, higher-load ankle tasks still register. The tissue is load-sensitive, not unstable. That's a meaningful gap between "daily function back" and "run-ready," and it's exactly the gap the walking-only gate can't see.

Meanwhile:

Allowed (keep pain ≤1/10, stop if anything reproduces the lateral ache):
  - Walking as normal
  - Cycling, easy / light resistance, no out-of-saddle efforts
  - Pool running or deep-water running if you have access
  - Upper body and core
  - Ankle alphabet, towel scrunches, calf stretch (knee straight + bent) within pain-free range
  - Sub-max eversion / inversion isometrics against a band or wall — same idea, stay sub-symptom

Avoid until cleared:
  - All running, including walk-jog
  - Jumping, bounding, hop drills
  - Loaded stair descents — take stairs one at a time, use the rail, lead with the non-affected side
  - Uneven terrain and lateral cuts
  - Any "test jog" to see if it still hurts

Watch for — these move you from outpatient PT to same-day sports med or urgent care:
  - Walking pain, or pain rising to ≥3/10 with any activity
  - New swelling, bruising, warmth
  - A giving-way episode on flat ground
  - Night or rest pain
  - Pain during a straight-knee calf stretch (Achilles)
  - A limp developing

Practical:
  - Book PT first (sports or ortho specialty). When you call, say: lateral ankle, 2 weeks post-run, reproducible on hop and stair descent, no instability or swelling. Most sports PTs will see this within a few days.
  - Bring a 3-line note: when it started, the session that preceded it, current symptoms, aggravators (hop, stairs), what's silent (walking, rest).
  - If you want faster imaging access, or you've had prior lateral-ankle issues, sports med can do the exam same-week and order ultrasound or MRI if the exam points to ligament vs. peroneal vs. bone.
  - When cleared, restart below the 6/8 dose — 15-20 min flat, 1W:1J — and reassess after that session before going back to 2W:1J or longer. The walk-jog return shouldn't be cleared on walking alone; pain-free single-leg hop and stair descent are the right gate-tests, and I'd add them to the STEP-BACK entry.

Good instinct not to have touched them yet. Here's the plan.

    SETUP — BEFORE YOU OPEN THE BOX

The box is closed and that's good — every minute it stays closed, spores stay contained. Don't open it indoors where you eat or sleep. Take it to a garage, porch, or set up an interior room with two open windows and a fan blowing OUT (you want air leaving the room, not circulating through the rest of the house).

Put on before opening: an N95 or P100 respirator (not a paper dust mask), nitrile or rubber gloves, and old clothes that go straight into a hot wash after. Lay down a clean sheet of paper or a freshly laundered towel as your work surface.

Do not use a regular vacuum near the photos. Do not use bleach, vinegar, hydrogen peroxide, or any "mold spray" — bleach destroys silver image particles and yellows paper, and the others can dissolve color dyes or set stains.

    ISOLATION — SORT INTO THREE GROUPS

Open the box in your prepared workspace and separate three piles into three clean, dry, open-top boxes or trays:

  A: the ~32 dry, loose, unaffected photos
  B: the 6 glossy prints stuck at one corner
  C: the 2 prints with fuzzy edge spots

Change gloves (or wipe them down) between groups so A doesn't pick up spores from B and C. Don't seal any of them in plastic bags — trapped moisture feeds mold. Loose-fitting lids or open trays are correct.

While you sort, photograph each affected print up close. That's your "before" record for memory and insurance, and it's also useful to send to a conservator later.

    TRIAGE — HOME VS. CONSERVATOR

Send B (the 6 stuck) to a conservator. Do not try to peel them apart. Glossy emulsion can fuse over years, and pulling now will tear the image layer off the base. The only safe release is controlled humidification in a conservation lab — moisture balanced just enough to relax the bond without swelling the emulsion or starting dye migration. Not a home project.

Send C (the 2 fuzzy) to a conservator too, unless they're low-value duplicates. "Fuzzy spots along edges" on a glossy print that lived near a leak years ago is almost certainly mold, not foxing (foxing is on matte paper). Even if it looks dry and dormant, brushing or wiping aerosolizes spores and risks the image surface. A HEPA-vacuum at very low suction with a screen between nozzle and print is the only home step that's sometimes acceptable, and only if you genuinely can't afford a conservator — but I'd still default to the lab.

Keep A at home in a dry room (out of bathrooms, kitchens, basements) until B and C come back. If any of A have faint speckling or a musty smell when you look more carefully, move them into the quarantine pile.

    FINDING A CONSERVATOR

Use the AIC Find a Professional directory at conservation-us.org/find-a-professional and filter for Photographs or Paper. A regional paper/photo lab is faster and cheaper than shipping to a major museum. Expect a $50–200 intake/consultation fee; per-item treatment varies widely. Many will do a free phone or email review if you send the close-up photos you just took.

    WHAT TO SAY TO MOM

Two things, in that order: none of this is ruined (dormant mold on photos is recoverable), and the worst 8 are going to a specialist so they come back properly. That's the reassurance that matters as much as the technical plan.

- Dressing mixed for toss: 12 fl oz lemon + 8 tbsp olive oil + 2 tbsp + 1 tsp salt + ~3 cups yogurt + ~1.5 cups herbs
- Held back for adjust: 3 fl oz lemon + 2 tbsp olive oil + 1/2 tsp salt + ~3/4 cup yogurt + ~3/8 cup herbs
- Salt held back extra: another 1/2-1 tsp plain kosher salt at the table

MIXING SEQUENCE

1. Cucumbers: halve lengthwise, slice 1/4" half-moons. Combine in the big mixing bowl. Do NOT salt yet — salt pulls water and at 1.25x volume the bowl already runs wetter.
2. Whisk the dressing in a separate bowl: yogurt first, then lemon juice, then olive oil in a slow stream, then 2 tbsp + 1 tsp of the kosher salt. Whisk until smooth and pourable. Taste on a cucumber slice.
3. Dress: pour about 80% of the dressing over the cucumbers (target ~12 fl oz lemon / 8 tbsp oil worth). Toss gently until every slice is glossed but not swimming. If the bowl looks wet at the bottom, you've over-dressed — stop tossing and drain a little before adding more.
4. Fold in 1.5 cups of the herbs now. Reserve the remaining ~1/2 cup for garnish at service.
5. Hold: keep the remaining 20% dressing in a small pitcher, plus the extra 1/2-1 tsp salt, near the pass.
6. Final adjust at plate-up: if cucumbers have wept and look dry after sitting, drizzle a little of the held dressing; if they look heavy/wet, hit with a few drops more lemon and a pinch of salt to brighten. Top with reserved herbs.

The reason this works at 30: you're never dressing more cucumbers than the 24-serving recipe was designed for. You're just making sure you have a known-good reserve on hand for the last 6 plates, when the bowl has already lost some gloss to weeping.

WHY THE REPAIR IS SUPPORTED

1. Diagnosis fits the symptom. A weak capacitor and a pitted contactor are the two most common causes of intermittent condenser/compressor shutdown. Pitted contacts cause arcing and an intermittent compressor signal; a failing capacitor causes hard-start failure and short-cycling. Both match "intermittent shutdown" cleanly.

2. The independent measurements are healthy:
   - 18°F supply-to-return ΔT is squarely normal (spec is roughly 16-22°F) — the system is moving heat fine
   - Normal compressor amperage — motor isn't seized, no hard-short, refrigerant load is adequate
   - No leak detected — the expensive failure mode (compressor / refrigerant) isn't indicated

   Read together: the system can do its job; the failure is in starting/control components, which is exactly what the $468 targets.

3. The 30-day credit converts the repair into a near-free option. If the same intermittent shutdown recurs within 30 days and Mom proceeds with the $9,240 replacement, the $468 is credited. Worst-case incremental cost = $9,240 − $468 = $8,772. Best case = $468 fixes it. The downside of trying first is bounded in both dollars and time.

4. Cooling still works. No emergency pressure. There's time to decide.

MATERIAL RISK THAT REMAINS

1. The 30-day window is the trap. If the same shutdown recurs on day 31 or later, the $468 is gone and you're deciding on the replacement from scratch. Plan around this clock explicitly.

2. Compressor life is the uninsured bet. Current amperage is the best short-term predictor, and it's normal — reassuring. But the repair warranty covers only the two replaced parts (1-year parts / 90-day labor). It does not cover the compressor. If the compressor fails after day 30 and before some other trigger, it's on Mom.

3. Other latent issues not addressed. Three healthy signals don't rule out everything. Still unexamined:
   - Slow refrigerant leak below detection threshold
   - Blower motor / inducer wear
   - Control board
   - Condenser coil condition (corrosion, fin damage)
   - System age (older = more latent risk; age isn't in the data you shared)

   None are signaled by the current symptoms, but the repair doesn't warranty against them.

4. The pitted contactor is a "why now" question. Pitting accumulates. Worth asking whether there was an underlying cause — low voltage events, frequent short-cycling, a loose lug at the disconnect, rodent damage. If the new contactor pits again inside the 90-day labor window, that's a workmanship question.

5. Summer timing. Peak cooling load. Have a contingency for failure between service calls during a heat event — especially if Mom is heat-sensitive.

CONFIRM BEFORE SAYING GO

  - The 30-day credit backstop is in writing on the quote/email, not just verbal. Pin the language.
  - The two failed parts (capacitor µF rating, contactor model) are itemized on the invoice.
  - Ask the contractor, in writing: "What did you NOT test that could still fail in the next 6-12 months?" Get the scope of the repair stated explicitly, including what it doesn't cover.
  - Get an after-hours / weekend emergency response path for the first 30 days, with a number.
  - If the system is over 12-15 years old, mentally weight the replacement more heavily — but the $468 trial is still cheap insurance to confirm before committing $9,240.

BOTTOM LINE

The repair is well-supported by the diagnostic evidence, and the 30-day credit backstop makes the financial downside small. Try it. The two real residual risks are (a) the 30-day clock expiring before a recurrence surfaces, and (b) latent failures the repair doesn't address — both manageable with a clear written scope and a contingency plan.

  2. Your measured 73 minutes against a 90-minute target is roughly a 19% shortfall. Production variation on a UPS nameplate typically spans something like ±10-20%, so a replacement could realistically land anywhere from 73 to 100+ minutes — a symmetric gamble, not a clear win.

So: exchange only if you can verify before return rights expire. Otherwise, refund and rebuy with margin.

The recent-human-admin signal is not just "a human with admin role touched the account in the last 14 days" — it is "a human who currently holds admin authority on the account generated activity in the last 14 days." An admin deactivated yesterday is no longer current administrative authority on the account, even though their last touch is still inside the 14-day window. The eligibility check must reflect the live state of who is administrating the account, not historical fingerprints from departed admins.

This is the same principle that makes D ineligible: live state beats nightly/stale state. The actor's current status is part of the live state the EA query is required to read. A deactivated admin is, for EA's purposes, not a recent active human admin regardless of how recent their last event was.

Two practical reversible approaches, then the call:

Reversible comparison (no adhesive, no cutting)

1. Matboard window. Cut a piece of 4-ply mat board slightly larger than the sheet (say 11 x 14) with an 8 x 10 window in it. Lay the window over the painting, slide it around, look at it under the same light you painted under. Two L-shaped mat strips work too if you want to nudge the crop asymmetrically. Nothing touches the painting.

2. Scan + digital crop, then confirm at scale. Scan the full sheet at 300+ dpi, make the 8 x 10 crop in any image editor, and view both side by side on screen at print size. This is the truest "don't touch it" method. Once you've decided, the matboard window from option 1 lets you verify the choice at actual color and scale before any commitment.

A nice third option if you want the framing convenience without losing the asymmetry: keep the full 9 x 12 sheet, but mount it in an 11 x 14 frame behind an 8 x 10 mat opening. Looks identical to a cropped piece on the wall, stays fully reversible forever, and the asymmetry is preserved in the mat margins.

Which to favor before cutting

Favor the full sheet — keep the asymmetry.

The 1.25 in of pale wash on the right is not empty paper, it is doing two jobs at once: it lets the eye arrive at the plant from the quiet side, and it gives the diagonal shadows a runway so they read as a path rather than a stub. Pulling most of that strip away shortens the shadows into a corner gesture and drifts the plant toward center, which trades a deliberate thirds-based composition for a more conventional balanced one. Conventional is fine, but it is a downgrade here — the painting already has the harder, more interesting structure.

The one condition that would flip it: if, when you lay the 8 x 10 window over it, the diagonal shadows in that right strip read as washed-out or unresolved rather than as deliberate travel. Quiet negative space only earns its keep if the marks that move through it are actually doing something. If the shadows look like they are fading out instead of landing, then the 8 x 10 crop becomes defensible — and you still have the mat-mount option so nothing is lost.

So: scan and mat-window-test first, expect the full sheet to win, and only consider the crop if the shadows fail the quiet-room test.

The two groups of prints are in different situations, so the risk balance is different for each. Then the actual decision you three need to make, and the facts that go into it.

The six stuck glossies
  Treatment: humidification + mechanical separation at the corner bonds only.
  Risk of treating: low for this profile. Corner-only adhesion, no image-layer loss, professional work under magnification — close to the best case a conservator sees. Non-zero risk of micro-tears at the bond line or pigment lift on the emulsion, which is exactly why this is professional work and not something attempted outside a lab.
  Risk of leaving: stable in the stuck state, not actively getting worse. What you give up by waiting is that they stay functionally inaccessible as individual photos, and over years the adhesive can migrate or the bond strengthen, narrowing the treatment window later. No urgency, but slow drift.

The two fuzzy-edge prints with surface mold
  Treatment: localized surface cleaning + stabilization.
  Risk of treating: standard, low for a competent conservator. Spore containment during treatment is part of what you're paying for.
  Risk of leaving: this is the bigger long-term risk. Mold is biologically active — "localized, not in the central images" is a snapshot, not a guarantee. Isolation is buying time, not stopping the front. If humidity shifts at any point in storage, the front advances into the central images. Time works against you here, and the favorable condition right now is that the central images are clean. That window is what makes treatment cheaper and more likely to succeed than it will be in a year.

The asymmetry matters: the six stuck prints are in a stable holding pattern; the two moldy prints are in an unstable one. The decision weight is heavier on the moldy two.

The concrete decision
You three need to land on one of three paths:

  1. Authorize treatment for all eight at $420, 4-5 week turnaround.
  2. Authorize treatment for only the two moldy prints — ask the conservator for a separate quote on those alone, and defer the six stuck ones (which are stable).
  3. Decline all treatment and continue indefinite isolation — accept that the two moldy prints may continue to degrade and that the six stuck prints remain inaccessible as individuals.

Things to settle before you talk to mom and Marcus:

  What the photos are for. If the goal is to preserve them as a sealed unit, option 3 is defensible. If the goal is to handle, scan, display, or share them individually, only 1 or 2 gets you there for the stuck six.

  Whose call this is. Mom's preference likely carries the most weight — these are probably her photos or family photos she's kept. Marcus's input matters because you held the decision for him. Your role is logistical: getting him the condition summary and making sure he has time to respond before the conservator's quote window closes (worth asking the lab how long the $420 estimate is held).

  Cost vs. sentiment. $420 for eight photos is modest if any of them are load-bearing family photos. It's not nothing, but the conservator's findings are favorable enough that you're not paying for a salvage job.

Frame for the conversation with Marcus
The report is good news dressed as a problem. Corner-only adhesion means the treatment risk on the six is bounded. Localized surface mold that hasn't reached the central images means the mold hasn't won yet on the two. So this is a "treat while the prognosis is good" decision, not a "we waited too long" decision. That's the frame that makes $420 reasonable and 4-5 weeks feel like a normal turnaround rather than emergency work.

The only time-sensitive element is the mold. If you three want to split the decision, treating the two moldy prints first and leaving the six stuck ones in isolation until Marcus has weighed in is a defensible middle path — it concentrates the cost on the photos where waiting has a real downside and gives Marcus the space to respond on the stuck six without the whole package hanging on his reply.

Quick math check on the framer's claim:
- Width: 9" sheet − 8.75" opening = 0.25" total → 1/8" per side ✓
- Height: 12" sheet − 11.75" opening = 0.25" total → 1/8" per side ✓

The quote is internally consistent.

Mat overlap assessment

1/8" per edge is technically functional but on the minimal side for a watercolor. Common archival guidance is closer to 1/4" per side, for three reasons that actually matter here:
- Watercolor paper is thicker than a print and wants more bite to sit flat and not drift in the opening.
- Deckled or slightly irregular edges (common on watercolor sheets) may not be fully covered by a 1/8" lip.
- It leaves less margin for the paper to expand/contract with humidity without telegraphing at the opening.

If your sheet is cleanly trimmed with straight edges, 1/8" will hold. If it has any deckle or the edges aren't perfectly square, ask the framer to bump the opening to ~8.5 × 11.5 (1/4" overlap) — usually no upcharge on a custom mat.

Recommendation: Option 1

The composition argument is decisive on its own, before the materials argument:
- Option 1 visible area: 8.75 × 11.75 → preserves 97% of width, 98% of height
- Option 2 visible area: 8.0 × 10.0 → preserves 89% of width, 83% of height
- That extra ~3/4" of preserved width on the right is exactly the pale wash you said you were trying to keep. Cutting to 8 × 10 would visibly amputate it.

Reinforcing reasons to take Option 1 anyway:
- Watercolor is light-sensitive and benefits from archival (acid-free) mat and backing; a $28 stock frame almost certainly uses non-archival materials that will yellow the paper over time.
- $46 is the right order of magnitude to pay to keep an original uncropped, especially one with a deliberate compositional element.

The only reason Option 2 would win is budget — and even then, the better move is to wait and save the $46 rather than crop a painting you already know you'd regret cropping.

One follow-up to send back to the framer: confirm the mat opening can be increased to 8.5 × 11.5 for ~1/4" overlap at no extra cost. If yes, that's the spec to order. If there's a surcharge, 1/8" is still acceptable for a cleanly trimmed sheet.

Based on what you described — short walk, hard panting that resolved in ~8 minutes once inside and cooled, normal gait, pink moist gums, no vomiting or disorientation — this is most consistent with mild heat stress that already de-escalated. Kibo's recovery inside the time window you described is reassuring. Here's how I'd handle the rest of the evening, tomorrow, and the watch list.

REST OF THE EVENING
- Keep him in the air-conditioned space. Don't take him back outside again tonight even briefly — late dusk in Austin often stays warm and humid well past dark, and a second heat load before he's fully cleared is the main avoidable risk.
- Water available, not forced. Sipping is fine; gulping a full bowl right after panting can sometimes trigger vomiting, which would muddy the picture.
- Skip his normal evening activity, training, or fetch. Quiet rest tonight.
- Light or delayed dinner is fine. If he eats eagerly, that's a good sign; if he picks at food, that's mild and worth noting but not urgent on its own.
- Quick check-in points I'd actually use: at 30 min, 1 hr, and bedtime — confirm gums are still pink and moist, breathing is quiet at rest, and he's responsive to you normally.

ADJUSTING NECESSARY OUTDOOR BREAKS WHILE IT'S HOT
For the next several days of Austin humidity:
- Shift the bathroom break to the coolest window — typically before sunrise or after ~10 pm, not right at dusk. Dusk is often the most humid slot and the worst evaporative-cooling window for dogs.
- Shorten the break to the minimum that actually works. A grass/shaded patch in the yard is meaningfully better than a pavement walk — asphalt and concrete hold heat long after sunset and burn paws even when the air feels cooler.
- Palm test for pavement if any sidewalk is unavoidable: press the back of your hand to the surface for 5 seconds. If you can't hold it, his paws can't be on it.
- Bring water and a collapsible bowl. Humid heat is harder than dry heat because panting is less effective — a small drink mid-break pulls core temp down faster than time alone.
- Skip the longer evening walk entirely on the worst days. A missed walk is recoverable; heat stroke is not.
- Watch the combo, not just the thermometer. ~85–90°F at high humidity is more dangerous than ~95°F dry. If the heat index is in the danger zone, use a yard potty spot or indoor pad rather than a walk.
- Cool-down on re-entry: a few minutes in AC with water before any food or excitement.

URGENT VETERINARY CARE — ACT NOW, DON'T CONTINUE TO MONITOR
Go to an emergency vet (not a wait-and-see call) if any of these show up, tonight or on a future hot walk:
- Gums change color: dark red, purple, blue, or pale/white instead of pink.
- Gums go from moist to dry/tacky.
- Collapse, weakness, or inability to stand.
- Repeated vomiting or any diarrhea.
- Disorientation, stupor, staring, seizures, or non-response to you.
- Noisy, labored, or rapid breathing at rest — or thick/ropy drooling.
- Body temp above ~104°F if you can take it rectally. (If you don't have a pet thermometer, "feels very hot to the touch in the groin/armpit" plus any of the above is enough — don't wait to confirm a number.)
- Panting that doesn't slow with rest and cooling within 10–15 minutes.

SAME-DAY VET (not emergency, but don't wait a week) IF THEY APPEAR LATER:
- Lethargy that doesn't resolve overnight.
- Refusing water for more than a couple of hours.
- Any vomiting or diarrhea at all, even a single episode.
- Stumbling, head tilt, or reluctance to move the next morning.
- Panting at rest in the AC the next day.

FORWARD-LOOKING NOTE
One heavy-panting episode after a short walk in humid heat, with clean recovery, isn't itself a red flag — but if the same pattern repeats on mild days or normal-length walks, it's worth a routine (non-urgent) vet visit to rule out early laryngeal, cardiac, or weight-related issues. I wouldn't book that based on tonight alone.

Why this is the most conservative fit for the session-and-following-day gate:

- The Thursday commute sits in the worst possible window — it is both the S1-following-day (the symptom check that gates whether S2 runs Friday) and the day before S2. Any load you add Thursday is a confounder on the very signal you're using to decide whether S2 is safe.
- The two short rises are uncontrolled dorsiflexion / eccentric demand on the healing ankle. Indoor bike lets you cap that dose; the commute does not. With less resistance control, you can't down-modulate mid-ride if the ankle talks to you.
- Your therapist explicitly kept cycling in the plan but did not require the commute. That phrasing is the green light to leave the commute out of Week 1 without contradicting the prescription.
- Week 1 is the most-gated of the three weeks. Cost of skipping one week of commute is small; cost of a setback in Week 1 is losing multiple weeks. Asymmetry favors skip.

Why the other three fall short of "most conservative":

- Full round trip: highest load, lowest control, exactly the wrong shape for the S1 -> S2 window.
- One direction only: half the dose but still outdoor with a rise, and you still have to get home somehow — that return leg becomes its own uncontrolled variable.
- Controlled short indoor ride: the most defensible non-skip option, but it still loads the ankle the day before S2, and indoor is the format you *can* dose precisely — save it for a week where you actually want a known dose on top of running.

Reintroduce in Week 2, after two clean session-following-day gates have confirmed the ankle tolerates return-to-run load (S1 -> Thu clean, S2 -> Sat clean). At that point trial the commute one direction first, then the round trip.

Method: per-person trial-task time sheet, summed at end of shift

The core move is to stop measuring the trial as one wall-clock interval and start measuring it as the SUM of per-person minutes spent on trial-specific tasks. The 60-minute ceiling is then applied to that sum, not to elapsed clock time.

Why this works:
- Prep cook's scheduled shift is excluded by construction. You only write rows for trial tasks, so baseline hours never appear in the total.
- Added trial work by the prep cook is captured. A row for sheet-pan staging counts.
- Two people working trial tasks in parallel produce two valid rows; both rows are real labor.
- June 28 was logged under the same definition, so the comparison is preserved.
- The 60-minute threshold stays exactly where it is.

Before service (5 minutes):

List the day's trial tasks and assign each to a person. For July 26 a likely set is:
  - Stage sheet pans — prep cook
  - Roast and portion chickens (≥44 × 7oz) — line cook
  - Track yield, portions, sales, unsold — Sam (runs alongside service)

Write these on the sheet before the shift starts. Pre-listing stops the "did that count?" question from being decided mid-service.

During shift — one line per person per trial task:

Use a notepad or printed sheet in this shape:

  ROASTED-CHICKEN TRIAL — LABOR LOG — 2024-07-26
  Rule: trial tasks only. Baseline scheduled shift excluded by construction.
  60-min ceiling applies to SUM of per-person subtotals, not wall-clock minutes.

  Person: ____________   Baseline shift (do not log): ___ to ___
    Trial task            | Start | End | Min | Notes
    _____________________ | _____ | ___ | __  | __________
    _____________________ | _____ | ___ | __  | __________
    Subtotal: __ min

  Person: ____________   Baseline shift (do not log): ___ to ___
    (same format)

  Person: ____________   Baseline shift (do not log): ___ to ___
    (same format)

  TOTAL TRIAL LABOR (sum of subtotals): __ min
  WITHIN 60-MIN CEILING? __  (Y / N)
  OVERLAP NOTES: ________________________________

One row per person per task. Never two rows for the same person covering the same minute.

Overlap rules (the part that usually trips people up):

  1. Different people, same wall-clock window, DIFFERENT trial tasks. Log both rows; sum both. Example: prep cook stages pans 2:00–2:15 (15 min), cook seasons birds 2:05–2:20 (15 min). Subtotals 15 + 15 = 30 min. Correct — two labor units in parallel. No overlap note needed.

  2. Different people, same wall-clock window, SAME trial task. Log both rows; sum both; write an overlap note on the "Overlap notes" line. Example: prep cook and cook both stage pans 2:10–2:15. Subtotals 5 + 5 = 10 min. Correct — two labor units on one task. Note it so the reader knows why the sum exceeds the wall-clock span.

  3. Same person, two rows covering overlapping minutes. This is a logging error, not a real situation — one person did one thing at a time. If they switched mid-task, split the row (2:00–2:08 stage, 2:08–2:15 portion) instead of leaving overlap. Reconcile before totaling.

Comparison with June 28:

June 28 was logged under the same definition — per-person trial-only minutes, summed. The 6/28 number and the 7/26 number are directly comparable as long as this method is used identically. The delta (7/26 minus 6/28) is the meaningful number. The 60-minute ceiling applies identically to both.

Practical notes:

  - Log in real time, or as close to it as possible. End-of-shift reconstruction from memory is unreliable, especially the start/end times.
  - Round to whole minutes. Finer granularity is wasted when the threshold is 60.
  - Keep yield, portions, sales, and unsold on the existing 6/28-style sheet. Labor is its own sheet.
  - At end of shift, before any repeat is considered, write the total and the Y/N ceiling check on the sheet itself and file it with the 6/28 sheet. Sam's standing rule is recorded yield, labor, sales, and unsold before any repeat — this sheet is the labor half of that record.

What this method deliberately does NOT do:

  - It does not change the 60-minute ceiling.
  - It does not count the prep cook's scheduled shift.
  - It does not subtract or net against baseline task minutes — baseline minutes are simply never written down.
  - It does not treat parallel trial labor as "double-counted clock time." Parallel labor is two labor units and both belong in the sum.

OVERNIGHT PRECAUTIONS (the first big one is already done)

1. Leave the dishwasher's local shutoff valve CLOSED. Confirm the handle is fully perpendicular to the pipe — open is parallel, closed is across.
2. Dry the cabinet floor completely. Place a folded dry towel directly under the supply connection and another on the cabinet floor under the dishwasher's front edge. They double as detectors: any new wetness tells you where it came from.
3. Put a shallow pan or a rimmed baking sheet under the supply connection as a backup catch.
4. Before bed, eyeball the supply line itself — look for bulging, cracking, white or greenish crust, or moisture at the valve, along the line, and where it enters the dishwasher. Note what you see for the plumber.
5. Cancel any pending or delay-start cycle on the dishwasher and make sure no one re-arms it overnight. Closing the supply already isolates the appliance; unplugging is optional belt-and-suspenders, not required.
6. If your dishwasher branches off the sink's hot supply through a saddle valve (common in older homes, notorious leak point), keep sink use to normal hand-washing. Avoid long full-hot draws that pressure-cycle the saddle.
7. Check the cabinet once before sleep and first thing in the morning. If a towel is wet, note WHERE on the towel — directly under the supply joint, or toward the front/drain side. That location is the diagnostic.
8. The outlet issue is real. Do not use the disposer or any nearby outlet until the cabinet is confirmed dry in the morning. You got the warning shot at 2 tablespoons — don't invite a second one near live electrics.
9. Photograph the dry cabinet, the valve position (closed), and any staining. Saved time for the plumber tomorrow.

DISTINGUISH SUPPLY FITTING FROM DRAIN LEAK, NO DISMANTLING

What you already know is your strongest clue: closing the supply stopped the drip. A drain leak would not respond to a supply valve. That points firmly to the supply side — valve, supply line, or the inlet fitting at the dishwasher. The test below pinpoints WHERE on the supply side, and rules out a drain-side contributor you might be missing.

Paper-towel test, about 5 minutes of setup, no tools:

- Dry the cabinet thoroughly.
- Open the supply valve.
- Lay DRY paper towels at four labeled points:
   A) Directly under the supply shutoff valve outlet
   B) Directly under where the supply line meets the dishwasher (usually reachable by pulling the toe-kick or reaching in behind the dishwasher's front lower edge)
   C) Along the drain hose path — at the loop up to the air gap or sink tailpiece, and where the hose enters the sink drain
   D) Center of the cabinet floor (catches anything that runs)

Test 1 — supply under static pressure, dishwasher idle:
- Wait 20–30 minutes with the supply OPEN and the dishwasher NOT running.
- If A or B is wet → supply-side leak. You don't need Test 2. The wet spot's location tells you whether it's the valve, the line, or the inlet fitting.
- If all four stay dry → supply side is holding under pressure.

Test 2 — drain under load:
- Run the shortest cycle your dishwasher has (rinse-only or quick wash).
- Watch the cabinet during fill, during drain, and for 10 minutes after.
- Note which towel wets and WHEN:
   Wet during fill (early cycle) → supply-side, likely the inlet fitting at the dishwasher or a line fitting that vibration shook loose.
   Wet during or right after drain → drain-side, likely the hose clamp at the sink tailpiece, the air gap, or a cracked hose.
   Wet only after the cycle ends → either side; the timing of first appearance is the tiebreaker.

How to read it:
- Wet spot directly under supply valve or supply line → loose supply fitting, failed valve packing, or a cracked line. Most common is a 1/4" compression nut that needs a quarter turn.
- Wet spot at the dishwasher's front or along the drain hose path → drain-side. Most common is the hose clamp at the sink tailpiece or a perished hose.

One extra observation worth writing down: if you see white or green crust on any fitting, that's an old slow leak at that exact joint. The crust doesn't lie.

URGENT CALL vs. SCHEDULED PLUMBER

Call for emergency or same-day service tonight or first thing tomorrow if any of these are true:
- The drip does NOT stop when the supply valve is closed. That means the leak is downstream of the valve (inlet fitting, internal DW component) or it's a drain leak — either way, you cannot isolate it with the valve you already closed.
- Any water is contacting electrical: the dishwasher plug, motor housing, an outlet, under-cabinet lighting, or the disposal.
- Water is spreading beyond the cabinet onto the kitchen floor or into an adjacent room.
- The cabinet floor is starting to swell, bubble, or warp. MDF damage compounds fast and is the difference between a $200 supply-line fix and a $2,000 cabinet refit.
- You smell sewage. That's a drain backup, not a supply leak.
- The supply line is bulging, visibly corroded, or wet along its length. Burst risk on a pressurized line is a real escalation path.
- A ceiling below the kitchen is showing water (multi-floor dwelling).

Safe to schedule a normal plumber visit (next business day, no after-hours premium) if all of these hold:
- The leak fully stops when the supply valve is closed. You have verified this.
- Cabinet is dry, no swelling, no staining reaching an outlet.
- The event was small (two tablespoons, one occurrence).
- No new water overnight — the dry towels come up clean in the morning.
- You can avoid running the dishwasher until the repair.

Bottom line for tonight: you did the right thing closing the valve. Keep it closed, dry-towel the suspect zone, don't run the dishwasher or the disposer, do the paper-towel test in the morning before calling. If anything in the urgent list above shows up before morning, call tonight.

For a dried bloom edge on dry cotton where the features around it are intact, the order that protects the eye and nose is: subtract gently first, add last, and stop before you'd repeat yourself.

1. Dry mop pass. Take a soft mop or large squirrel round, dry it on a towel until it feels almost dry to your cheek, then sweep the tip across just the bloom line — barely touching. A dry mop can lift the most concentrated edge pigment without rewetting anything underneath. Often this alone breaks the line. If the bloom now reads as soft fur rather than as a discrete edge at arm's length, stop here.

2. One targeted re-wet and blot, only if the dry mop didn't get there. With clean water on a soft round, touch the bloom line itself — do not flood, and do not let the bead creep toward the eye or nose. Wait 20–30 seconds, then blot straight up with a clean tissue (no rubbing). One pass. If the eye or nose ever beads or looks wet, stop immediately and let everything dry before judging.

3. Local thin glaze, only as a last resort. Mix a very dilute wash matching the pale muzzle tone. Damp brush, not dripping. Lay one thin pass right over the bloom, extending a hair into both sides. Let dry. This unifies the value instead of fighting the line, and it preserves what's underneath.

Stopping rule: once the bloom reads as texture rather than as an edge, put the brush down. Every extra wet pass over the same zone lifts more underlayer and is what produces mud. Leaving a faint trace of the bloom is the right outcome — backlit fur genuinely has that broken edge, so a soft remnant will look true to the reference rather than like a fix.

THE 41 ARE NOT ONE BUCKET — FOUR STATES

Before any replay, classify each of the 41. The replay decision and duplicate risk differ
by state.

  B. Submitted, provider rejected — non-retriable (hard bounce, suppressed, invalid)

  C. Submitted, provider rejected — retriable (5xx, rate limit, timeout)

  D. Never actually submitted (worker dropped, queue stuck, auth expired, network blip
     before the request reached the provider)

HOW TO AVOID DUPLICATE SENDS — FIVE LAYERS

  1. Provider idempotency key — pass trigger_record_id on every send. The provider returns
     the original message_id if it's already accepted the record. The single most important
     control and the cheapest.
  2. Internal message_id ledger — query "do we already have a message_id for this

     the same product so we don't collide with parallel sends.

Two-track ledger on one sheet. Track A is for fairness (per-person workload). Track B is for the ceiling and 6/28 comparison. The split is the part that avoids double-counting overlap.
