DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE — SAFARI signup_start vs REAL SIGNUP DECLINE
================================================================

Framing
-------
The aggregate picture (signup_start ↓ in Safari, sessions flat, application-session creation flat) already leans toward tracking loss (H1) rather than real decline (H2). Goal of this sequence: confirm H1 or surface H2 before any product action. Run cheapest checks first; each step should yield a binary signal before you instrument the next layer.

Tier the work. Don't start with deep instrumentation — most of these cases resolve in Phase 1.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 1 — TRIAGE (≤ 30 min, often resolves it)
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Browser split of the signup_start drop
   - Filter signup_start by browser+version for the affected day vs the prior 7-day baseline.
   - EXPECTED H1: drop concentrated in one or two Safari versions only.
   - EXPECTED H2: drop spans multiple browsers proportionally, or Safari disproportionately but with the rest of the funnel also down.

2. Pricing-page view comparison (same Safari cohort)
   - Compare pricing_page_view volume for Safari on the affected day vs baseline.
   - EXPECTED H1: pricing_page_view normal; only signup_start is lost at the funnel transition.
   - EXPECTED H2: pricing_page_view also down (real traffic loss) OR pricing_page_view normal but conversion-to-application_session also down (real friction).

3. Application-session creation, broken down by Safari User-Agent
   - You said aggregate application-session is near 7-day average — that's necessary but not sufficient. Repeat the cut on Safari specifically.
   - EXPECTED H1: Safari application-session creation also normal. (Most decisive signal in the entire sequence — the user reached the signup endpoint and was persisted, so the front-end event was simply lost.)
   - EXPECTED H2: Safari application-session creation is ALSO down by similar magnitude. Now you have a real Safari-specific issue.

4. Time-of-day shape
   - Plot Safari signup_start hourly vs the 7-day hourly baseline.
   - Real declines usually have a sharp inflection tied to a deploy or copy change. Tracking failures often look like a flat dropoff or staircase as caches/storage expire.

5. One end-to-end Safari pass
   - Walk the funnel in a real Safari (or BrowserStack / Safari Technology Preview). Did signup_start fire? Did the network request reach the analytics endpoint? Did the application-session cookie set? Capture with Console + Network tab open.

If Phase 1 points firmly at H1, you can often stop here. If any signal is ambiguous, continue.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 2 — BROWSER-SIDE (Safari-specific, only if H1 is on the table)
----------------------------------------------------------------

A. Safari version mix
   - Did a new Safari (or iOS Safari) version land in the last 7 days? Check release notes for ITP, storage, or Beacon changes that took effect.

B. ITP / storage behavior
   - Safari caps JS-set cookies on cross-site contexts to 7 days; localStorage in third-party iframes is blocked. If signup_start is fired by a third-party analytics script loaded in an iframe, ITP can drop its identity state.
   - Test: does the analytics SDK maintain identity across visits? Has the SDK recently moved to a different transport (first-party CNAME, server-side)?

C. Content blockers
   - Safari ships with aggressive default content blocking; users also add 1Blocker / AdGuard / DuckDuckGo. Test from a clean Safari profile with no extensions. Confirm the analytics ingest domain isn't on any default blocklist.

D. Beacon reliability
   - If signup_start is sent via `navigator.sendBeacon` on page-transition, Safari can drop it when:
       • the destination is cross-site and there's been no user interaction with that origin
       • the page is being restored from bfcache
       • an unload handler is slow
   - Confirm whether the page transition fires the beacon deterministically in Safari.

E. iCloud Private Relay
   - A spike in Private Relay traffic changes the IP mix toward Apple-owned ASNs and breaks session stitching in analytics. Check the Safari cohort's IP ASN distribution.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 3 — ANALYTICS-SIDE
----------------------------------------------------------------

A. Ingestion health by User-Agent
   - Compare analytics ingest endpoint request volume by UA class for the affected day vs baseline. If client firing appears normal but server receipt dropped, events are lost between client and analytics (beacon drop, network, SDK error).

B. SDK version rollup
   - Group Safari signup_start by SDK version. A missing or under-firing version is a strong root-cause signal — usually coincides with a release that changed consent, transport, or batching.

C. Sampling / data-layer diff
   - Confirm the pipeline isn't sampling differently for Safari, and that the data layer push still includes expected fields for Safari traffic.

D. Re-compute the funnel in the warehouse (do not trust the dashboard event)
   - Run pricing_page_view → application_session_created directly in the warehouse, restricted to the Safari cohort, for the affected day. If this funnel shows normal conversion, the dashboard's signup_start event is the broken layer.

E. Cross-property comparison
   - If multiple properties use the same SDK, compare Safari signup_start across them. A regression across all properties is SDK-side; only Helio is app/integration-side.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 4 — BACKEND-SIDE (mostly confirmation; H1 evidence)
----------------------------------------------------------------

A. Application-session creation by browser (already noted in Phase 1, repeat here for emphasis)
   - This is the source-of-truth check. Safari app sessions normal = H1.

B. Status-code mix by browser on signup routes
   - 30-second check: are Safari signup requests returning more 4xx (CORS, CSRF, cookie domain) than other browsers? A CORS preflight failure specific to Safari could drop both the analytics event AND the real submission — but app sessions are flat, so this is unlikely.

C. First-party cookies on Safari
   - Confirm the session cookie is being set on Safari on a fresh visit. ITP will drop a cookie that's set without SameSite=None or via JS on a cross-site context.

D. Grep backend logs for Safari User-Agent on signup routes
   - Look for anything new: auth failures, captcha triggers, rate limiting hitting Safari specifically.

E. Origin / Referer policy
   - Safari's default Referer policy has tightened in recent versions. If the signup endpoint enforces Origin or Referer, Safari requests could be silently rejected. Verify with one curl-from-Safari test.

----------------------------------------------------------------
DECISION MATRIX — when to call it
----------------------------------------------------------------

Call H1 (Safari tracking failure) only when ALL of these hold:
  - signup_start down in Safari
  - pricing_page_view normal in Safari
  - application-session creation normal in Safari (the decisive check)
  - warehouse re-computed funnel normal
  - ingest volume for signup_start from Safari dropped

Call H2 (real decline) only when:
  - signup_start down in Safari AND
  - application-session creation in Safari is ALSO down by similar magnitude
  - (and ideally pricing_page_view also down, or a clear deploy/copy change maps to the inflection)

Anything between those patterns is "inconclusive, keep watching" — not a product intervention, not a rollback.

----------------------------------------------------------------
ON `pricing_page_v3` CLEANUP — explicit guardrail
----------------------------------------------------------------

Do not include the pricing_page_v3 cleanup in the causal hypothesis unless at least one of the following is true:
  1. Some active code path, data-layer push, GTM/Segment tag, or analytics ingest transform still references `pricing_page_v3`. (Audit the codebase + tag manager + the analytics pipeline. If you find a reference, that's the cause — but separately, not because of the cleanup.)
  2. The cleanup coincided with a deploy that changed how signup_start fires, the SDK initializes, or the data layer pushes. The registry cleanup alone — with no traffic, no rollout rules — does not change Safari behavior.

A neutral verification step is appropriate: grep for `pricing_page_v3` in code, tags, and pipelines. If no references, treat the cleanup as unrelated and move on.

----------------------------------------------------------------
HANDOFF TO OWEN
----------------------------------------------------------------

After Phase 1 (and a quick warehouse funnel re-check from Phase 3D), you should be able to hand Owen one of:

  - "Tracking artifact, not a real decline — [evidence: warehouse funnel flat, app sessions flat in Safari, ingest dropped]." Owen files it as an analytics/SDK ticket, no product action.
  - "Real decline — [evidence: app sessions down in Safari specifically, deploy X at HH:MM maps to the inflection]." This becomes a P1 product investigation, Riley + Owen.

Don't escalate to P1 on the dashboard number alone. The aggregate "near 7-day average" doesn't rule H2 in by itself; the Safari-specific application-session check does.

Tick removal, aftercare, and monitoring for Kibo — based on the situation you've described.

REMOVAL SEQUENCE
1. Calm Kibo and have someone help hold/steady him if he's wiggly — behind-the-ear site is sensitive.
2. Part the fur so you can see the tick's mouthparts meeting the skin.
3. With your fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick as close to the skin as you can get — ideally at the head/mouthparts, not the body.
4. Pull upward with slow, steady, even pressure. Do not twist, jerk, or squeeze the body. A slow pull of 20–30 seconds is normal; the tick may resist briefly then release.
5. If mouthparts break off and stay embedded, try to pluck them out with the tweezers. If you can't get them cleanly, leave them — the skin will usually work them out. Don't dig.
6. Avoid the old folk remedies: no petroleum jelly, oil, heat (matches/cigarette), nail polish, or alcohol before removal. They can make the tick regurgitate into the bite, increasing pathogen transmission.

AFTERCARE
- Clean the bite site with rubbing alcohol or povidone-iodine, then soap and water.
- Apply a small amount of plain triple-antibiotic ointment if you have it (optional).
- Wash your hands thoroughly, then disinfect the tweezers with alcohol.
- Photograph the bite site now so you have a baseline for comparison if it changes.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TICK
- Do not flush or crush it. Save it.
- Place it in a small sealed ziplock bag or jar with a damp paper towel, or submerge in rubbing alcohol (this both kills and preserves it for ID).
- Label with date (2024-07-27) and location on body (behind left ear).
- Why save it: if symptoms develop, your vet can identify the species (deer tick / lone star / American dog / brown dog) which determines the disease risk profile and what to test for. Even a crushed or partial tick can sometimes be ID'd under magnification.

LOCAL SIGNS AT THE BITE SITE — call vet if you see:
- An expanding red rash, especially a target/bullseye shape (erythema migrans = Lyme indicator)
- Redness, swelling, or warmth that worsens after 24–48 hours rather than fading
- Drainage, pus, or crusting
- A lump that grows or doesn't resolve over 2–3 weeks
- Persistent itching or Kibo scratching the site raw

WHOLE-BODY SIGNS — call vet promptly; urgent/ER if severe:
- Lethargy, reluctance to move, fever-warm ears/dry nose
- Loss of appetite lasting more than a day
- Shifting-leg lameness or joint pain/swelling (classic Lyme presentation in dogs)
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- Breathing changes, coughing
- Swollen lymph nodes (under jaw, behind knees, in front of shoulders)
- Pale or yellow-tinged gums
- Unusual sensitivity to touch, neck pain, or back pain
- Wobbly gait, facial droop, disorientation, or seizures (neurologic — urgent)
- Unexplained bruising or bleeding (rare, but seen with some tick-borne illnesses)

TIMING WINDOW
Different tick-borne diseases have different incubation periods in dogs:
- Anaplasmosis: 1–2 weeks
- Ehrlichiosis: 1–3 weeks
- Rocky Mountain spotted fever: 2–14 days
- Lyme disease: 2–5 months (most dogs exposed don't get sick, but watch for lameness, fever, kidney issues later)
- Watch for at least 30 days actively; keep the tick preserved for ~2 months in case late questions come up.

FOLLOW-UP TESTING WORTH KNOWING
Your vet can run a 4Dx snap test roughly 4–6 weeks after the bite that screens for Lyme, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, and heartworm. Many primary care vets will suggest this as a baseline, especially if the tick was attached for >24 hours or engorged. Worth mentioning at Kibo's next routine visit or sooner if you have any concern.

Given that Kibo was in the Cherrywood yard (tall grass / brush edge = higher tick-exposure habitat), it's worth doing a quick body check for any additional ticks tonight (armpits, groin, between toes, under tail, around eyes/ears) since they often travel before embedding.

No need for an emergency visit today based on what you've described — Kibo is behaving normally, the tick was caught, and you have the right tools. Just save the tick, watch the site and his behavior, and you'll be in good shape.

Good news first: a single transparent glaze on fully dry paper is the most liftable state watercolor offers. The horizon opening is intact, the cool violet sky is untouched, and the warm bank isn't scrubbed in — granulation is still sitting in the paper's tooth where pigment remains. A two-pass lift plus cool glaze should resolve it without reworking the study.

One note before the sequence: warm lower cloud banks on backlit Austin storms aren't wrong — your read of the scene was probably accurate. The problem is the bank reading as solid and equally weighted as the horizon opening, so the light can't win. Cooling it and breaking the solidity lets the eye return to the pale strip where it belongs.

Sequence:

1. Bone-dry check. Wait another day if there's any coolness to the paper. Lifting on a not-quite-dry glaze reactivates binder and lifts unpredictably.

2. Mask the horizon opening. A torn paper strip or light frisket band over the pale opening keeps your working brush from pushing warm pigment into it. Worth doing even with good brush control — a slip on a rewet pass is easy.

3. First lift — restrained. Clean water, size 8 or 10 round, damp not wet. Work small sections (1–2 inches). Pull outward, away from the horizon. Blot immediately with a dry mop or paper towel — don't let lifted pigment resettle. Re-dampen, re-clean the brush, move to the next section. Goal is to break the solidity, not strip to white. Two or three passes is usually enough.

4. Dry fully before glazing. Half hour minimum, longer in humid weather.

5. Cool glaze. Mix a pale cool gray-violet — ultramarine with a touch of raw sienna, or cerulean with a sliver of ultramarine, or payne's gray thinned to tea strength. Test on scrap. The glaze should read as a tint, not a wash. Wet-on-dry, small sections, stopping short of the horizon opening (mask again if needed). One thin coat usually does it.

6. Optional second pass once dry. If the bank still competes, a second thinner glaze deepens the cool without re-darkening. A granulating cool pigment (cerulean, moonglow) is the right choice if any tooth got flattened in the lift.

What to skip:

- Scrubbing. That's exactly how you turn a liftable glaze into the unfixable kind, and how you lose granulation.
- Rewetting a wide area. Lift in small sections, blot between each.
- Lifting to pure white. You want reduced warmth and broken solidity, not erasure — the granulation needs pigment to sit in.

The horizon light reads brighter once the bank around it cools and quiets. Most storm studies resolve in one lift-plus-glaze cycle; a second light glaze is the typical finish.

Yes — a 4 mm pink, slightly raised bump with a dry center, five days after tick removal, in the absence of warmth, drainage, enlargement, marked tenderness, and with Kibo eating and behaving normally, fits a minor local reaction very well. The two most common explanations:

  1. Tick-bite granuloma / local irritation. The bite site can stay mildly reactive for 1–3 weeks as the skin clears tick saliva and any microscopic mouthpart fragments. A small dry papule or scab is the typical look.

  2. Retained hypostome fragments. A tiny piece of the tick's mouth sometimes breaks off in the skin and produces a persistent small foreign-body papule that slowly works itself out. Not dangerous, just slow.

Less likely given what you're seeing: a true bacterial infection (usually warmth, swelling, pus, or pain) or early erythema migrans of Lyme disease (classically an expanding target lesion well over 5 cm, not a static 4 mm papule).

CARING FOR THE SITE WITHOUT IRRITATING IT

  - Default is to leave it alone. Don't squeeze, pick, or scrub.
  - Gentle cleaning once daily is fine: lukewarm water, mild dog-safe soap, soft cloth or gauze, pat dry. Don't soak.
  - Avoid on or near the bump: repeated hydrogen peroxide (damages healing tissue), rubbing alcohol, iodine scrubs, essential oils, tea tree, and over-the-counter antibiotic ointments unless your vet has recommended them — some dogs react to topical antibiotics.
  - If Kibo is scratching or rubbing the spot, a soft e-collar or a T-shirt over the area for a few days prevents self-trauma.
  - Don't start systemic antibiotics, steroids, or any "preventive" medication on your own.
  - Photo-check daily under the same lighting and distance. Optionally mark the edge of the bump lightly on surrounding fur once to confirm it's truly static.

CHANGES THAT PROMPT A ROUTINE (NON-EMERGENCY) VETERINARY CALL

Schedule a standard appointment within a few days if any of these appear:

  - The bump enlarges, becomes more raised or firm, or develops a target / bull's-eye ring of redness expanding outward from it.
  - It persists beyond 2–3 weeks without shrinking.
  - New crusting, ulceration, oozing, bleeding, or a shift from dry to moist.
  - Local tenderness when touched, or Kibo starts persistently scratching it.
  - Mild systemic signs: a dip in appetite, slightly lower energy than baseline, mild lameness or stiffness (especially shifting-leg lameness — a Lyme clue), or palpable swelling of nearby lymph nodes.
  - If the tick was attached for more than ~24–48 hours, or you live in a Lyme-endemic area, it's reasonable to ask your vet proactively about tick-borne disease screening at the 4–6 week mark. Optional, but sensible.

CHANGES THAT PROMPT URGENT OR EMERGENCY VETERINARY CARE

Go in the same day (ER after hours) for any of the following:

  - Sudden facial, muzzle, or throat swelling, or hives spreading across the body — possible anaphylactic-type reaction (rare this late, but not impossible).
  - Difficulty breathing, rapid breathing at rest, or pale or blue gums.
  - Significant lethargy, weakness, collapse, or unwillingness to stand.
  - Repeated vomiting, profuse diarrhea, or refusal to eat for more than 24 hours.
  - Fever-like signs: warm ears, shivering, or panting at rest in a cool room. If you're comfortable taking a rectal temperature, anything over about 103.5°F (39.7°C) is a vet-today threshold.
  - Any neurologic change: wobbliness, head tilt, confusion, seizures.
  - Ascending weakness or paralysis (classic tick-paralysis picture — worth knowing even if uncommon; especially relevant if another tick is found attached).
  - The bite site rapidly swells, becomes hot and painful, or develops a foul-smelling discharge — suggests abscess or spreading cellulitis.

A NOTE ON WHAT I CAN'T DO

I'm not a veterinarian, and this is general information rather than a diagnosis. What you described is reassuring, but if anything changes — or if you'd simply like peace of mind from a hands-on exam — a quick vet visit is the right call.

Short answer: the hallway wall is the safest of the three. The west-facing living-room wall gets the most damaging exposure (direct afternoon sun), and the kitchen wall trades light safety for moisture risk — and moisture is the bigger long-term threat to watercolor on paper even with a sealed float mount.

Why the hallway wins on balance:
- Indirect light means dramatically lower total luminous exposure. UV-filtering acrylic blocks roughly 97–99% of UV, but it does not block visible-light damage, and visible light does most of the fading work over years. Cutting total light, not just UV, is what actually extends pigment life.
- Steadier humidity means fewer paper expansion/contraction cycles, which is what causes cockling, hinge stress, and foxing in float-mounted sheets over time.
- The acrylic face is still doing its job here; it just isn't being asked to do the impossible.

Why the other two are worse:
- Living-room wall, 3:00–5:00pm direct west: two hours of unfiltered direct visible light plus heat loading on the acrylic face. Heat accelerates both pigment fade and any adhesive or seal creep in the mount.
- Kitchen wall, no sun but cooking humidity: water vapor and cooking aerosols migrate past a frame edge over months. Float mounts are dust-sealed, not vapor-sealed. Steam episodes are the fastest path to foxing and to swelling that can lift a sheet off its mount.

Practical placement precautions, treating UV-filtering acrylic as one layer of protection rather than a complete solution:

Light and heat
- Hang in the hallway, but pick the segment that is farthest from any west- or south-facing window and not directly across from a bright light fixture.
- If a window in that area gets afternoon sun, hang the frame on the wall section that sits outside the bright pool on the wall — a few feet laterally makes a real difference in cumulative exposure.
- Keep the frame out of any direct sunbeam, even brief ones. UV acrylic does not excuse sun.
- Avoid hanging above or directly behind a radiator, heat register, or fireplace. Heat cycling degrades the acrylic face and stresses the seal.

Humidity and air
- Target a stable indoor relative humidity around 40–55%. Watercolor paper is hygroscopic; the goal is to avoid swings, not to hit a single number.
- Avoid exterior walls with known thermal bridging or cold spots — these can sweat behind the frame on cold nights and feed mold you can't see until the sheet is removed.
- Leave a small air gap behind the frame (standard D-rings and a slight standoff) so the back can breathe; do not press-seal the frame against the wall.
- Do not hang in a bathroom, above a kettle, or anywhere with steam events, even with the acrylic face.

Handling and cleaning
- Don't touch the acrylic surface with bare fingers — skin oils etch acrylic over time. Handle by the frame edges only.
- Clean the acrylic with a soft microfiber and a cleaner labeled safe for museum acrylic (no ammonia, no window cleaner with solvents). Dust first, then wipe gently.
- Inspect the mount every 6–12 months: look at the sheet through the acrylic for early foxing (tiny brown specks), any edge lift, or condensation痕迹 between the sheet and the acrylic. Catching a seal failure early is the difference between a recovery and a restoration.

Display strategy if you ever want it on the living-room wall
- Treat the living-room wall as a short-term display only: a few weeks at a time, then rotate back to the hallway for a longer rest. This cuts total light dose significantly and is the standard practice for works on paper that you actually want to live with.
- If you do rotate it, hang it on the living-room wall outside the 3:00–5:00pm direct sun arc (which may simply mean that wall is unusable during those months and fine in winter when the sun is lower).

One honest caveat: UV-filtering acrylic is excellent at its specific job and gives you real years of additional life. The mistake is treating it as a complete environmental shield. The two failure modes it cannot address — visible-light fade and humidity-driven paper degradation — are exactly the two your three candidate locations vary on, which is why the hallway is the clear pick.

Classification rule for the 52-workspace Helio Start support export, before Owen joins it to refund-adjusted cash.

1. Cutoff is the workspace-level admission timestamp (admitted_at). Every workspace in the cohort has one; that is the deterministic anchor.

2. Three classes, resolved in this order:

   a. Pre-admission assistance. Contact_type values: connector-authority, sales-evaluation, demo-prep, pilot-setup, security-review, contracting, billing-onboarding (pre-payment). These answer a sales-side operating question and never enter the support-effort metric, regardless of contact_date. The 11 connector-authority contacts fall here by type. Include them in a separate column if Owen wants to track pre-admission assist minutes, but they do not go into the per-account support numerator.

   b. Billing contacts. Contact_type values: invoice, dunning, payment-failure, refund-request, plan-change, tax-form, chargeback. These answer a cash-collection question. They are excluded from the support-effort metric entirely (different operating question from product support), but they are NOT the same as pre-admission — keep them in their own column so refund-adjusted cash can reconcile against them downstream if needed.

   c. Post-admission product support. Everything else, where contact_date >= admitted_at. This is the only class that populates the support-minutes numerator.

3. Tiebreakers when type is ambiguous or null:

   - contact_date < admitted_at → pre-admission (default to sales-side unless type says otherwise).
   - contact_date >= admitted_at AND type is null/ambiguous → post-admission product support.
   - never reclassify a clearly-typed billing contact as support, and never reclassify a clearly-typed pre-admission contact as support.

4. Zero-contact workspaces stay in the denominator with minutes = 0. Rationale: support-effort is reported as support minutes per admitted account across the mature 52. Dropping zero-contact accounts would inflate the per-account burden and bias the read on organic-bounded economics. Zero is a real observation here — it means the cohort self-served, which is information, not missing data.

5. What the join needs to be unblocked:

   - One row per workspace_id, with admitted_at, refund-adjusted cash (gross minus refunds, same window), pre_admission_minutes (informational, not joined), billing_minutes (informational), and post_admission_support_minutes (the numerator).
   - All 52 workspaces present, including zero-contact ones.
   - The 11 connector-authority contacts sorted into pre_admission_minutes, not post_admission_support_minutes.

Until those four conditions hold, the combined acquisition evidence is incomplete and Owen should not run the join — silently combining the 11 with post-admission support would inflate the support-effort read by however many minutes those contacts carried, and that inflation would propagate into whatever per-account support assumption feeds the Q3 organic-bounded economics.

Here is a question and angle that open responsibility and intimacy along a different axis from last month's frame (needed vs. known) — pivoting instead to a contract or consent reading.

DISCUSSION QUESTION
    Whose work disappears when the narrator refuses to ask for help, and what kind of closeness does that hidden work actually produce?

INTERPRETIVE ANGLE
    The refusal is not only self-protection; it is also a quiet transaction with the people around the narrator. Other characters reward competence with appreciation and with the relief of being cared for without having to reciprocate. In return, the narrator receives a love that is contingent on remaining capable — close, real, but conditional, and paid for in labor no one sees. So the scene is doing two things at once: the narrator has quietly taken on a responsibility that ought to be shared, and in exchange has accepted an intimacy that knows them only as the useful self.

    Pride, in this reading, is the wrong frame. The more precise frame is consent — consent to being loved in a particular way, and to the cost of being loved in no other. The productive pressure on the group, then, is not "is the narrator proud?" but: do the other characters know what they have agreed to, and would the narrator accept any of the available alternatives?

A few ways the group could push it further, depending on where the discussion wants to go:
    - Is the narrator's competence freely offered, or has it been trained into them by the same people who now reward it? The transaction may be older than this scene.
    - If the narrator stopped being useful, who in the room would lose the most — the narrator, or the people who have built their days around the narrator's reliability?
    - There is a difference between refusing help as autonomy and refusing help as a condition of belonging. The scene may not let us tell which one is operating, and that ambiguity may be the point.

Four realistic options for a two-week usage-spike window. None kick in unless the customer picks one.

4.  Shape the migration to current plan
    If the migration has any scheduling flexibility, throttle or sequence it to stay under current cap. No plan or billing change. Best when the spike is a want, not a need, and the team has room to stage the work.

The lower premium isn't actually cheaper — it's just pre-paid risk shifted to your claim day.

The math
- Premium savings: $36/year
- Extra out-of-pocket per claim: $1,500
- Break-even: ~42 claim-free years to offset a single claim event

Why the "save $36" framing is wrong
Insurance exists for the bad day, not the average one. Renters claims that actually get filed are typically theft, fire, water damage, or liability — and most of them are well over $2,500 (otherwise the hassle of filing isn't worth it). On the day something goes wrong, you're comparing $1,000 out-of-pocket vs $2,500 out-of-pocket. The $36/yr you "saved" evaporates the first time you file.

The right question isn't "which premium is lower?" — it's "can we absorb $2,500 in a bad month without stress?" If yes, the $36 is genuinely free money. If no, the $312 is buying you $1,500 of liquidity protection on the day you'd actually need it.

Recommendation: keep the $1,000 deductible at $312/yr. The $36 annual savings requires ~42 years of perfect claim-free luck to come out ahead, and you don't buy insurance expecting perfect luck.

One tiebreaker if you want it: look at your emergency fund. If you have enough cash that a $2,500 surprise wouldn't register, the higher deductible is a defensible micro-optimization. If a $2,500 hit would mean putting it on a card or pulling from savings, the $36 isn't worth the loss-aversion cost.

A practical sequence, one print at a time so identity never has to be reconstructed after the fact:

PRE-SESSION (before any print is touched)

  Set the temp ID scheme first. Eight prints, two populations — use a prefix that encodes the population and a number that encodes sequence:
    TP-G-01..06  for the six separated glossy prints
    TP-M-07..08  for the two cleaned mold-edge prints
  Print eight slips in advance with checkbox columns: front captured, back captured, condition logged, file verified, re-sleeved. Slips are filled in during the session, not at the end.

  Prepare the capture station: scanner/computer on, color target and scale at hand, file-naming convention locked (TP-G-03_front_01.tif etc.), working folder created, backup target identified.

  Confirm the prints have settled after rehousing — do not run this on the same day as the rehousing session. The two mold-edge prints especially benefit from a quiet interval.

  Seed identity status on every slip from the start, even if "uncertain — see condition notes." Do not assign confident IDs in this session; that is the Sunday identification work, separate from capture.

PER-PRINT SEQUENCE (do all eight this way; do not batch by step)

  1. Pull. Remove one print from its rehousing sleeve. Place on a clean surface with the printed temp ID slip visible alongside it.

  2. Condition notes. Transcribe the conservator's rehousing notes that apply to this specific print onto the slip. Distinguish on the slip:
       - conservator's findings (verbatim or paraphrased, attributed)
       - your handling observations only (new observations, not corrections)
       - identity status: confirmed / tentative / unknown, with what is actually known
     Keep uncertain identities explicitly uncertain — "tentative: studio portrait, female subject, ca. 1910s, no inscription" is fine; "this is Grandmother" is not.

  3. Front capture. Scan/photograph the front. First shot of the session includes color target and scale. Confirm focus and exposure on screen before moving on. File name = temp ID + _front + sequence.

  4. Back capture. Flip carefully. If there is writing, capture it (raking light if the writing is faint). If there is no writing, capture once anyway and note "no inscription observed" on the slip — the captured no-inscription state is itself a record.

  5. Verify the files before re-sleeving. Open the captured file(s) on screen and confirm:
       - correct print (not swapped with neighbor)
       - in focus, properly exposed, full frame
       - file name matches the slip
       - file size sanity check
     Only proceed once the file is confirmed. If anything is wrong, recapture now — once the print is back in its sleeve, you lose the easy access.

  6. Re-sleeve. Return the print to its rehousing sleeve. The sleeve should carry the same temp ID so identity is preserved without re-opening.

  7. Mark the slip. Check the boxes for this print. Move to the next.

SESSION-END

  Count: front files = 8, back files = 8 (or back-no-inscription entries = 8), slips complete = 8. If any count is off, that print is the one to revisit before closing the session.

  Save the condition log. Backup the capture folder to a second location before powering down.

WHAT TO AVOID

  - Same-day scanning after rehousing — the prints are stable but you are not.
  - Two prints on the workspace at once.
  - Capturing all fronts then all backs — swap risk is real with eight similar-looking items.
  - Re-sleeving before the file is verified.

Short answer: yes, leave the scab. Cleaning is essentially optional at this stage. What you describe — flattened, no pink, dry scab, no inflammation signs, normal behavior — is the normal resolution phase, and the more useful thing to watch over the next few weeks is Kibo's overall behavior, not the wound.

1) The scab

  Let it fall off on its own. A dry scab at two weeks is the body's own bandage over closed, remodeling tissue; picking, peeling, rubbing, or scrubbing it will reopen the wound and restart the inflammatory phase. Don't apply hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, or topical antibiotic ointment unless a vet has specifically asked you to — all of those are cytotoxic to the new tissue that's forming underneath. A vet-approved antiseptic spray (chlorhexidine or similar) is fine if you want to do something, but it's not necessary.

  The real remaining risk is self-trauma. Kibo can reach the spot with a hind paw, and a single scratch cycle from a hard reach can rip a fresh scab off in one motion and push you back a week. Watch for short, focused scratching bouts aimed at that exact spot. If you see them, an e-collar or a light vet-recommended covering is cheaper and easier than restarting the wound.

2) Cleaning

  Not really useful at this point. The wound has epithelialized; cleaning is for open or dirty tissue. If the scab gets visibly soiled (mud, grit), a brief rinse with sterile saline — or 1 teaspoon of non-iodized salt in 1 cup of cooled boiled water — gently patted dry, is fine. Don't soak it, don't scrub it, don't use soap or peroxide on it.

3) What would justify a vet call despite the improvement

  Local-site changes:
    - Scab falls off and the skin underneath is red, swollen, weeping, or warm
    - The lump reappears, enlarges, or becomes firm/persistent (a tick-bite granuloma can sit there for weeks to months; usually harmless but worth a look if it doesn't keep shrinking)
    - New drainage, pus, or odor
    - The area becomes painful or Kibo starts guarding it
    - The scab hasn't fully resolved by ~4 weeks

  Systemic / behavioral changes (more important than the wound itself at this point):
    - Lethargy, inappetence, or fever lasting more than a day
    - New lameness, joint swelling, or shifting-leg stiffness
    - Bruising, pinpoint red spots on gums or belly, or pale gums
    - Any neurologic sign — head tilt, ataxia, facial droop, seizure
    - Vomiting or diarrhea that's not a one-off

  Why this matters more than the wound: tick-borne illnesses (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, Lyme) typically incubate 1–4 weeks after the bite. You're at two weeks right now, which is the early edge of the symptomatic window. The bite site healing normally does not rule out a transmitted infection — pathogen transfer happens at the moment of the bite, not from the wound looking bad later.

  A reasonable frame: leave the scab alone, keep an eye on Kibo's behavior and locomotion through the 4-week mark, and call the routine vet if anything in either list shows up. If you see sudden neurologic changes, bleeding, or a rapid drop in energy, that's an urgent visit rather than routine.

A 3-pass glazing sequence on dry paper, each pass fully dry before the next.

Mix: a chromatic cool gray that leans blue, not neutral. Two workable options:
- Ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna (the sienna grays it AND keeps it chromatic — straight Payne's reads neutral and reproduces your "pasted" problem)
- Cerulean + a touch of burnt sienna (softer, more atmospheric)
For rust fur, ultramarine-leaning is the cleaner complement.

Pass 1 — Cast shadow shape, weakest tint
- Water-to-pigment: very high, just tea-colored
- Brush: medium round or mop
- Paint the cast as a shape: broadest and darkest-adjacent where Kibo meets the floor (ambient occlusion), tapering as it recedes
- Inner edge: stop ~1–2 mm SHORT of the fur. The shadow's edge runs parallel to but offset from the figure — never butting against it. This margin is what protects the rim of light.
- Outer edge: lift off with a thirsty brush so it feathers to nothing into the floor (real cast shadows have soft outer falloff, not a hard perimeter)
- Dry fully

Pass 2 — Strengthen ONLY the core ambient occlusion
- Same mix, ~1.5x pigment load
- Confine to the narrow band directly under belly / chest / paws where body meets floor
- Everything else stays at Pass 1 value
- The value jump between core and outer shadow is what creates "sits ON the floor" rather than "stuck TO the floor"
- Dry fully

Pass 3 (optional) — Reflected warm bounce at the far edge
- Your original rust mix, very dilute (paler than Pass 1)
- A whisper along the OUTER edge of the cast shadow only, not near the figure
- Binds the shadow to the floor's local color and kills any remaining decal feeling
- Skip if the floor itself is already warm — it can over-warm the shadow

Why this anchors without contaminating:
- Cool-vs-warm contrast is what your eye reads as spatial separation, not value alone — a neutral shadow next to warm fur has nothing chromatic to push against
- The 1–2 mm margin is preserved paper, so the rim-of-light halo survives intact for later facial/edge work
- Stops short of the figure entirely, so the existing rust wash is never re-wet

When you do add the facial details later, work them on the figure itself, not on the cast.

A conservative plan for the 40 stabilized photographs:

REASSURANCE FIRST
Six hours at 67% RH, no condensation, no visible change, is a brief, moderate excursion, not an emergency. Because the boxes were closed, the interior RH inside them lagged the room air — actual box conditions were probably closer to 55-60%, not the full 67. The biggest avoidable risk now is a rapid RH or temperature swing, which causes more damage than the original high-humidity event. Slow, stable re-equilibration is the goal, not speed.

RELOCATION
Move the closed boxes to the most climate-stable interior spot available — a closet or interior room in the conditioned part of the home that:
  - sits on an interior wall (not an exterior wall or a plumbing wall)
  - is out of direct sunlight
  - is away from kitchens, bathrooms, laundry, and any exterior door
  - is on a mid-floor if possible — not a basement, not an attic

Do NOT move them to a garage, attic, basement, car, or any space whose RH or temperature differs from the rest of the home. A 10-15 degree F or 20+ percentage-point RH swing during relocation is worse for the prints than a few more hours where they are now. Leave the boxes closed. Do not open them to "air them out" — every opening is a new equilibration event the prints have to absorb.

MONITORING WITHOUT DISTURBING
  - Place a small hygrometer/thermometer in the room near the boxes — not inside or touching the boxes, just on the same shelf or surface a foot or two away.
  - If you have a datalogger (Govee, SensorPush, Inkbird, even an inexpensive one), put it next to the boxes and let it record. Room RH should drift back toward the home's normal range (ideally 40-50%) within hours of the AC being restored.
  - Resist the urge to check inside. The closed boxes will equilibrate slowly over 24-72 hours once room conditions stabilize. That slow drift is exactly what you want.
  - Photograph the boxes in place now, dated. If anything changes later, you have a visual baseline.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A PHOTOGRAPH CONSERVATOR
Stop and call one before doing anything else if, when you eventually inspect the prints (after conditions have been stable for 24-72 hours), you find:
  - any fuzzy, dusty, or cottony growth on surfaces or inside sleeves — white, gray, green, or black. This is mold.
  - a musty, sweet, or "old basement" smell when the box is opened
  - tacky or sticky surfaces, especially on color chromogenic prints — gelatin or dye migration
  - any surfaces bonded to sleeves or to other prints — do not attempt to separate them
  - new cockling, curling, or warping beyond what was already there
  - milky, cloudy, or hazy appearance on a print surface
  - visible dye movement, bleeding, or color smearing
  - any crystalline or powdery deposits on surfaces

To find a qualified photograph conservator, the American Institute for Conservation (culturalheritage.org) maintains a "Find a Conservator" directory — filter by specialization in photographs or photographic materials. Most will do a paid remote assessment from good photographs if transport is a concern.

WHEN YOU DO EVENTUALLY INSPECT
Wait at least 24-72 hours after AC is restored and room RH has returned to normal. Then:
  - open the boxes in the same stable room, not somewhere different
  - wear clean nitrile gloves
  - use raking light from one side to reveal surface changes
  - check the most vulnerable prints first — color chromogenic prints, glossy surfaces, anything you already knew was fragile
  - do not separate anything that has bonded together — note it and call a conservator
  - do not wipe, brush, or clean any surface

DOCUMENT AS YOU GO
Date and photograph the boxes now, the room RH/temperature over the next few days, and the condition of each print when you eventually inspect. This record is valuable if you later decide to have any professional work done.

ONE LAST "DON'T" LIST
Do not put them in a freezer. Do not add silica gel inside the closed boxes. Do not use a space heater, hair dryer, or dehumidifier pointed at the boxes. Do not put them in a car. Do not wipe or brush anything. All of these create the rapid gradient that is the actual threat here.

Short answer: replace the tire before your next loaded commute. Visible casing through a sidewall cut is the textbook "this tire is done" indicator, and a boot is for getting home, not for ordinary riding.

Why visible casing matters:
- The sidewall casing (nylon/polyester cords) is what holds the tire's shape under load and inflation pressure. An 8 mm cut with casing showing means those structural cords are severed in that spot. The tire still holds pressure because the inner tube is plugging the hole, not because the tire is sound.
- A sidewall cut is also a stress concentrator. Under rider weight + inflation pressure + cornering forces on a loaded commute, small sidewall cuts grow. A bulge may not be visible now, but the failure mode is sudden — the tube pushes through the cut, the casing lets go, and you're off the bike.
- Tread punctures you boot. Sidewall cuts that expose casing, you replace.

What a boot is actually for:
- Emergency-only: finish the ride, get home, or limp to a shop. Park Tool, Sheldon Brown, and the major tire makers all describe boots the same way.
- A boot is not a structural repair. It just covers the hole from the inside so the tube doesn't bulge out. It does not restore the cut casing, and it tends to shift or fail under sustained load.
- One defensible use case: boot it for one short, direct, low-traffic commute ride so you can buy a replacement during the workday, then ride home on the new tire. Do not boot it and keep commuting on it for a week.

For your situation specifically:
- It's the rear tire, which carries more load (especially if you run panniers or a rack — sounds like you do, given "loaded commute").
- "Holds pressure, no bulge" is reassuring but doesn't change the verdict. The structural failure point is the cut casing, which doesn't heal.
- A commuter rear tire (Schwalbe Marathon, Continental Contact, Panaracer Pasela, Vittoria Randonneur, etc.) is roughly $30–60 and swaps in 10–15 minutes with a single tire lever. Cheap insurance against a sidewall blowout in traffic.

When you do replace it: cut the old tire across the cut before tossing it, so a shop or fellow rider doesn't grab it off the trash as a spare.

If you want, tell me the tire size printed on the sidewall (something like "700x32c" or "27.5x2.0") and your typical commute surface, and I can suggest a specific replacement that matches what you're riding on.

The calculation you're proposing — $18,960 divided by 52 workspaces, $364.62 when rounded — is a per-workspace arithmetic step, not a CAC. What it actually produces is the average observed organic cash per admitted workspace in a mature, matched cohort, with refunds netted out. That's a useful number for talking about retention and lifetime cash in a population that has already been filtered through organic admission and natural attrition. It isn't a paid-acquisition CAC for three concrete reasons.

  1. The numerator is cash collected, not cash spent. CAC is acquisition cost over acquired customers. Here the numerator is refund-adjusted cash these workspaces generated over the mature window — a revenue-side metric. The denominator is the count of workspaces still present in the cohort. The ratio therefore says "how much cash, on average, an admitted mature workspace produced." That's a yield or contribution figure, not an acquisition cost.

  2. CAC measures incremental cost. To call a number a paid CAC, the evidence has to show (a) a paid-media spend incurred on this population, (b) an acquisition mix between paid and organic channels, and (c) a paid-vs-organic response comparison that lets you isolate the workspaces paid media actually caused. This evidence has none of those three. The mature cohort was admitted organically; there is no paid spend in the numerator, and there is no counterfactual separating paid lift from organic baseline. Whatever the division returns, it cannot, by construction, be the incremental cost of acquiring a workspace through paid media.

  3. A mature cohort is the wrong population for a paid test even if you wanted one. It's already been selected by organic admission and filtered by attrition. Any per-workspace figure computed on survivors is conditional on having survived — using it to forecast paid-acquisition economics assumes the paid channel would deliver the same mix and the same retention shape, which the evidence doesn't establish and the Q3 pricing-page organic boundary explicitly leaves open.

Practical consequence: the $364.62 doesn't authorize a paid test, doesn't set a CAC ceiling, and shouldn't be carried to Owen or execs as a paid benchmark. The mature retention, refund-adjusted cash, and account-level support evidence should be kept bundled together so that a real paid-acquisition proposal can later be evaluated against them — with paid spend, mix, and a response comparison in evidence — rather than against an organic average that's been relabeled.

Recommendation: the $58 puncture-protected 700x32.

The deciding factor is your conditions, not the price. The cut that took your current tire out of service is the exact failure mode a puncture belt is built for — sharp debris on city pavement slices through a thin casing far more easily than through a belted one. Picking the lighter tire to save $14 means you're buying the tire most likely to repeat today's outcome.

Tradeoff you're actually making:

  Lighter tire ($44):
  - Faster acceleration and slightly lower rolling resistance at speed
  - Thinner casing, more vulnerable to glass / staples / pothole edges
  - Often dual-compound leans toward dry-road grip; wet braking is typically weaker
  - Lighter feel matters most when you're sprinting or chasing watts — not on a commute

  Puncture-protected tire ($58):
  - Adds roughly 80–150 g of rotational weight and a small rolling-efficiency penalty
  - Belted casing resists the cuts and pinch flats that come with rough pavement
  - Commuter-pattern tires in this category usually have siped/softer-compound shoulders for wet grip
  - Fewer roadside surprises, which is exactly what "predictable commuting" buys

The $14 difference is a one-time cost against a tire that should last 2,000–3,000 city miles. Even one avoided flat (tube + shop labor) erases the gap, and a belted commuter tire in rough urban use commonly delivers a full season without one. The weight savings would only matter if you were racing or chasing KOMs — at commute pace on 32 mm tires, you will not feel it.

Get the $58 tire.

Sanity check on your numbers first: 43 single-issue + 23 mixed = 66 contacts; 66 contacts x full minutes each = 684 total. The method below preserves 684 by construction.

THE METHOD

For each of the 23 mixed contacts, assign exactly one primary tag and one or more secondary tags.

  - Primary tag: the issue that drove the contact (why the customer reached out, or the issue the contact's outcome is recorded under). Carries the FULL contact minutes. One per contact, no exceptions.
  - Secondary tag(s): issues that came up during handling but did not drive the contact. NO minutes. One or more per mixed contact.

Net effect: minutes attach to 66 primary tags (one per contact), sum = 684 by construction. Secondaries are presence-only markers used for issue-co-occurrence, not minute attribution. No double-count, no invented splits.

DECISION RULE FOR PICKING THE PRIMARY (give Owen one rule, not judgment calls)

  - Default: the issue the customer opened with. If the notes show "came in about X, then asked about Y", X is primary.
  - Tiebreaker when the opening issue is ambiguous or the conversation shifted mid-contact: the issue whose resolution the contact's outcome is recorded under.
  - Last-resort tiebreaker (only if both signals disagree and the notes are silent): the issue consuming the largest share of agent time in the notes. Use this only to PICK ONE primary, never to split the minutes.

AGGREGATION / ISSUE-LEVEL OPERATING READ

Three distinct cuts, all defensible from the same data:

  1. Issue volume (any mention) = primary occurrences + secondary occurrences for that issue. "How often does this come up at all."
  2. Issue primary volume = primary occurrences only. "What is driving contacts."
  3. Issue minutes = sum of minutes on contacts where the issue is primary. "Where are we spending time." Sums to 684.

This separation lets you say "permissions is the #1 primary driver" (cut 2) without conflating it with "permissions gets mentioned a lot alongside other issues" (cut 1), and lets you report "X min on permissions" (cut 3) without attributing any minute that wasn't on a permissions-primary contact.

WHAT THE 23 MIXED CONTACTS BUY YOU BEYOND THE 43 CLEAN ONES

  - Cross-issue pattern read. If 12 of the 23 mixed contacts list permissions as primary and automation as secondary, that is a real signal worth routing to product/education, without needing any minute estimate for automation.
  - Root-cause clustering. Secondary tags on permissions-primary contacts (e.g., automation, billing) become a candidate root-cause list for that primary.

CAVEATS TO FLAG IN THE EXPORT DOC

  - Secondary-tag counts are presence-only. Never compare secondary minutes to primary minutes - the former is zero by construction, not zero because the issue is unimportant.
  - "Average minutes per issue" is only defined over primaries. If anyone asks for weighted-by-mention minutes on secondaries, that requires agent-recorded per-topic minutes (a different methodology) and should be declined for this cohort.
  - The 23 contacts are still 23 contacts and 23 x their full minutes. They are not "less real" than the 43 clean ones in any minute accounting.

If you want, I can draft the tagging schema (issue list, primary/secondary columns, decision-rule column for the auditor) so Owen can apply it directly to the 23 mixed records - or apply it myself if the CS notes are loaded into a doc I can read.

Practical sequence, in order. Plain text so it renders cleanly in the terminal.

1.  Verify before the drive moves
    a.  Generate SHA-256 checksums for all 8 TIFF masters on the laptop and save as MANIFEST.txt in the same folder as the masters.
    b.  Generate SHA-256 checksums for the access copies and save as MANIFEST_access.txt alongside them.
    c.  Run a checksum compare on the external drive against MANIFEST.txt. Every TIFF on the drive must match a laptop master byte-for-byte. If anything fails, recopy from laptop and re-verify before the drive goes anywhere.
    d.  This is the answer to Mom's question in its strongest form: a verified second copy with a manifest she (or anyone) can re-check later.

2.  Lock in the directory layout so altered access copies cannot be mistaken for archival masters
    Keep the verified P033-P040 filenames exactly as they are — do not rename. Separate by folder, not by filename suffix:
        P033-P040/
            masters/        <- 8 unaltered TIFFs, archival-quality
            access/         <- treated/enhanced working copies
            manifests/      <- MANIFEST.txt, MANIFEST_access.txt, README, scan logs
    Rule of thumb: anything in masters/ is treated as bit-stable and never overwritten. Working copies always go in access/.

3.  Close the single point of failure on the access copies
    The external drive currently holds only the TIFFs. The access copies live only on the laptop. Add at least one of:
        -  A second external drive that mirrors both masters/ and access/, kept at a different physical location.
        -  Cloud backup (Backblaze B2, iDrive, or a cold-sync folder on a real cloud provider — not a streaming/syncing service that could sync a corruption across all copies).
    The drive going to Mom's house covers the offsite leg for the masters. The access copies deserve the same protection, separately.

4.  Write a short README next to the manifests
    Plain language, one paragraph each:
        -  What masters/ is and the rule against modifying it.
        -  What access/ is and that it may change.
        -  How to re-verify: tool, command, expected checksum file, what to do on mismatch.
        -  Date the arrangement was set and by whom.
    This is what makes the backup legible to a future you and to Mom, without needing to reconstruct intent.

5.  Verification cadence
    -  At handoff to Mom: full checksum compare plus manifest on the drive.
    -  Quarterly: bit-rot check on the external drive against the stored manifest, from any machine.
    -  After any new scan session: extend the manifest, verify the new files, then propagate to all copies in the same sitting — never leave a copy half-updated.
    -  After any laptop-to-drive restore: regenerate the manifest from the authoritative source and re-verify the other copy.

6.  On treating the physical collection as a fallback
    It is one leg, not the spine. The physical originals are slow to access, vulnerable to the same site-level disaster as the laptop, and any re-scan introduces new variables (slight exposure differences, dust, scanner drift). The digital masters are now the primary preservation copy; the physical collection is a re-derivable source if the digital chain is ever broken. Operationally that means: trust the verified TIFFs + manifest as authoritative, and treat the physical as a known-good source you could rescan from if needed — not as the thing you go running back to every time something looks off.

Net of all that, Mom's bar — "is the digital arrangement sufficient?" — is met when steps 1–4 are complete and a re-check from her house on any later visit returns the same checksums.

A load-only rub on a freshly installed 700x32 is a classic diagnostic situation. The wheel/tire/frame system has marginal clearance or marginal stiffness, and rider weight is the missing variable the stand can't supply. Here's how to think through it.

WHAT THE LOAD-ONLY SYMPTOM TELLS YOU

When the wheel spins free on the stand, you're testing static conditions only:
  - tire pressure (you confirmed it holds)
  - static tire clearance in the frame
  - static wheel true
  - static brake pad clearance
  - approximate spoke tension

When you sit on the bike, you add:
  - rider mass compressing the tires (a 32 compresses noticeably more than a 25 or 28)
  - frame flex, especially the rear triangle: chainstays and seatstays flex inward under load
  - bottom-bracket drop under load
  - wheel dish deflection, since the rear wheel is offset toward the non-drive side for cassette spacing and reacts asymmetrically to load
  - possible axle micro-shift in the dropouts if the QR or thru-axle isn't fully torqued

A rub that appears only under load is almost always one of: (1) tire too big for the frame's real-world clearance, (2) marginal wheel dish or spoke tension, or (3) brake caliper centering that was set without load on the wheel.

CHECK ORDER (for the shop, or to walk through with them)

1. Identify what is actually rubbing.
   Tire on chainstay, seatstay, seat tube, or brake pad, or rim on pad. Apply chalk, lipstick, or a thin smear of grease to the suspected surfaces, ride briefly, and see where it transfers. This step is non-negotiable; everything else depends on knowing the contact surface.

2. Frame clearance under load.
   This is the most likely cause with a new 700x32. Many road frames are spec'd for 700x25 or 700x28. Static clearance can look fine, but under rider weight the chainstays flex inward 1-3 mm and the tire squeezes through a window that's actually too tight. Measure with you seated on the bike (or with a load applied to the saddle and bars) the gap between the tire and the nearest frame surface. Spec minimum is usually 4-6 mm; less than 3 mm is asking for rub, and less than about 2 mm can become a contact issue with debris, bumps, or wet-rim flex.

3. Wheel dish and true.
   Rear wheels are dished; the non-drive side spokes carry less effective tension. Under braking and rider weight the rim can deflect more on that side. Check lateral true specifically at the contact-patch quadrant, with the wheel in the frame, not just on a truing stand, since a stand doesn't replicate the dish load. Check spoke tension evenness; an imbalance shows up under load even if static true looks acceptable.

4. Axle seating.
   Quick-release: confirm the skewer is fully clamped (often under-clamped if the installer focused on seating the tire bead). Thru-axle: confirm torque spec and that the axle is fully inserted before levering. A wheel that sits 1-2 mm off in the dropout will rub under load even with perfect true and clearance.

5. Brake caliper centering (rim brakes only).
   If you have rim brakes, the caliper was almost certainly centered with the wheel in the stand, no load. Under load, the rim can shift relative to the pads. Re-center with you on the bike, or at minimum with a load applied. Centering screws should be re-set with weight on. If a pad is already less than about 1.5 mm from the rim, this is likely the issue.

6. Tire pressure.
   You confirmed it holds, but didn't say what value. 700x32 puncture-protected casings are usually stiffer; running too low causes excessive casing flex and a different contact patch. Don't over-inflate to mask the rub; that addresses a symptom, not a cause, and you'll bounce on every imperfection. Stay mid-range in the manufacturer's recommendation.

7. Bead seating.
   You said no visible casing damage or bulge, good. On a new install, also confirm the bead is evenly seated all the way around; the safety line on the sidewall should be equidistant from the rim the whole way. A mis-seated bead changes the tire's effective width and shape and can shift the contact patch.

SHOULD YOU DECLINE TO RIDE

Yes. Take it back to the shop and have them resolve it before you ride on the road.

Reasons:
  - The rub is intermittent and load-dependent, which means it's not predictable. On the stand it's fine; loaded it isn't. Road riding means loads vary constantly, pedaling out of the saddle, climbing, leaning, hitting bumps, and the rub will recur unpredictably.
  - A tire-on-frame rub is paint damage at minimum. If it's tire-on-brake-pad, it can drag or, in the worst case, lock the rear wheel under hard braking. Real safety issue, not a nuisance.
  - A tire-on-chainstay or seatstay rub can wear through paint and into the frame material on aluminum or carbon; on steel, into the tube wall. Slow damage, expensive later.
  - Load-only rub is the shop's problem to diagnose properly. Static-only checks (which is what they almost certainly did at handover) won't catch it. Asking them to identify the contact surface and re-check under load is a reasonable request.

WHAT TO ASK THE SHOP TO DO

  a. Identify the rubbing surface.
  b. Re-check tire-to-frame clearance with you seated on the bike, or with a load applied to the saddle and bars.
  c. Re-true the rear wheel in the frame, with attention to dish.
  d. Re-center rim brakes with load applied (if applicable).
  e. Confirm the axle is fully seated and clamp torque is correct.
  f. Report back what they found, with measurements, before you accept the bike.

If the diagnosis comes back that the frame genuinely cannot accept a 700x32 with adequate margin under load (which is possible, especially if the bike was originally built around a 25 or 28), then the answer is a narrower tire, not ride-it-and-see. Don't accept the bike with marginal clearance as a fix; that's the shop handing you a slow-burn problem.

Here's guidance for Kibo's superficial paw-pad scrape. Note: I'm not a vet — this is general first-aid reasoning; if anything below contradicts what your own vet has told you for Kibo specifically, defer to them.

CLEANING (do this once now, then once daily until healed)

- Rinse the paw under lukewarm running water or in a shallow bowl for 1-2 minutes to flush out grit and any walking debris. A gentle stream from a cup or low-pressure faucet is fine.
- Clean around (not directly on) the scrape with a dilute antiseptic:
  - Chlorhexidine 0.05% solution (the light blue liquid sold for dogs, diluted per label), OR
  - Povidone-iodine (Betadine) diluted to weak-tea color
- Pat dry with a clean cloth. Do not rub.
- If hair around the wound is long and trapping debris, carefully trim it with blunt-nose scissors held flat against the pad, away from the skin.
- Inspect after cleaning: you want to confirm no flap, no embedded material, no deep tissue visible, edges lying flat when Kibo flexes the toes.

AVOID on the wound itself:

- Hydrogen peroxide (damages healing tissue, can delay closure)
- Rubbing alcohol (stings, dries and damages tissue)
- Human antibiotic ointments that contain pain relievers (Neosporin "Plus," anything with pramoxine or lidocaine) — toxic to dogs if licked
- Essential oils, tea tree, or herbal salves

SHORT-TERM PROTECTION

- A breathable dog boot or paw sock is the easiest option if Kibo will tolerate it — fit matters, two-finger room at the top, no rubbing on the wound.
- If no boot, use a non-adherent pad (Telfa or similar) over the scrape, then 1-2 layers of self-adhering vet wrap above the paw. Critical: wrap snug but not tight. After wrapping, check two toes — they should be warm, pink, and you should be able to slip a finger under the top edge. Cold/swollen/red-purple toes = wrap is too tight, unwrap immediately.
- Change the bandage once daily, or any time it gets wet, dirty, or Kibo chews through it.
- An e-collar (cone or inflatable) is worth using if Kibo licks or nibbles at the paw — saliva macerates a healing pad and slows closure.
- A thin layer of plain petroleum jelly or a dog paw balm (like Musher's Secret) on and around the scrape after cleaning can protect against recontamination, especially before outdoor time.

ACTIVITY

- Short, on-leash potty breaks only for the first 24-48 hours. No walks longer than necessary, no running, no jumping off furniture, no stairs if avoidable.
- Keep the paw clean and dry. If you go out, cover with a boot or a clean bandage; remove and air-dry the paw when back inside.
- Avoid hot pavement, sand, gravel, and heavy dirt/mud until the scrape is closed — sand and grit are particularly good at working into a pad wound.
- Re-inspect the pad at the end of each outdoor session.
- Recheck Kibo's gait each morning: weight-bearing should remain normal or improve; any worsening is a signal.

VETERINARY ESCALATION

The signs you described — shallow scrape, oozing stopped with pressure, no flap, no puncture, no debris, normal weight-bearing, no gaping — are reassuring. Watch for the following.

Same-day call to your regular vet (get Kibo seen within ~24 hours) if you notice any of:

- Redness, swelling, or warmth spreading beyond the immediate wound edge
- Discharge that is yellow, green, creamy, or foul-smelling (pus vs. the small amount of clear/pinkish ooze you described)
- Wound edges starting to gape, or any flap forming
- A dark or black patch appearing on the pad (can indicate pressure necrosis or a deeper bruise/contusion under the scrape)
- Progressive lameness, or Kibo starting to favor the paw when he was weight-bearing fine before
- Repeated licking or chewing that you cannot interrupt with an e-collar
- Lethargy, reduced appetite, or fever-warm ears/nose lasting more than a day

Go directly to urgent care or an emergency vet if:

- Bleeding restarts and does not stop after 10-15 minutes of firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth
- You suspect a foreign body you cannot see clearly (foxtail, glass fragment, thorn) — particularly relevant if the walk was through tall grass, brush, or weedy areas; foxtals can migrate into tissue and become dangerous fast
- A deep puncture becomes visible, or the wound is deeper or larger than you initially thought
- Significant tissue loss, a hanging flap, or the pad is partially torn
- Severe pain — Kibo vocalizes when the paw is touched, will not let you near it, or becomes aggressive when you try to examine
- Swelling that tracks up the leg (past the carpus/wrist or up toward the elbow)
- Systemic signs: pale gums, weakness, rapid breathing, vomiting

TYPICAL HEALING

A clean superficial pad scrape that stays clean and protected usually closes over within 5-10 days, with full pad toughness taking a couple of weeks longer. Pad tissue heals slowly because it bears constant load. Patience and keeping it clean/dry are most of the work.

Recommendation: the one-day wash-and-edges clinic.

The binding constraint is schedule risk, and once that's the anchor the other two factors stop arguing for the longer class.

Schedule risk. The six-week class commits six Saturdays to a partner whose September rota is still variable. Even at a moderate conflict rate, you lose enough sessions that the effective feedback-per-attended-session drops well below what the brochure implies, and each missed Saturday is a small negotiation you have to keep having. The clinic asks for one Saturday (Sept 21), and if that one doesn't work you only lose a single date, not a quarter. Saturday load is the variable that matters here; Sunday watercolor stays intact in either case, but the class bleeds Saturday energy and planning attention across the whole stretch in a way the clinic doesn't.

Learning value. The "longer = more learning" reflex is wrong for this hobby. Your watercolor is casual and self-directed: you already have a Sunday practice block, you read alongside it, and you came in through your mom rather than via any formal track. A sustained six-week feedback loop is built for someone trying to build a practice; you already have one. A focused wash-and-edges clinic is a transferable foundation skill that feeds directly into the kind of loose Sunday work you already do, and you get the instructor's eye for one intense session rather than six diluted ones. The clinic also lets you test whether you actually want sustained instruction before committing to a 6-week rhythm, instead of locking in before you've learned that.

Cost. Not decisive, but worth naming honestly: the clinic is $17/hr vs. the class at $15/hr, and the class is $95 more in total. For a casual hobby where the class's main advantage is contingent on attending most sessions, paying for sessions you might miss is the worst of both worlds. The clinic's higher hourly rate is actually buying you certainty, not less value.
