Quick read: pinpoint bleed stopped in a minute, no gaping on flexion, weight-bearing normal, no heat/swelling/discharge/odor — those are the right reassuring signs. The wound is re-opened but not deepened. Below is the standard reset protocol.

(General first-aid guidance, not a substitute for an in-person vet exam — the thresholds section is what to watch, since the surface has been disturbed twice.)

1. Immediate cleaning
   - Lukewarm water rinse first, to flush saliva and clot residue. Don't scrub — let the water do it.
   - Clean with dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% (preferred) or povidone-iodine diluted to weak-tea color. Both are safe for paws and won't damage healing tissue the way hydrogen peroxide or alcohol do. Skip hydrogen peroxide on an open wound — it slows healing.
   - Pat dry with clean gauze. Avoid cotton balls — fibers stick.
   - Optional: a thin layer of plain bacitracin or chlorhexidine cream. Avoid triple-antibiotic "plus pain reliever" formulas — the "-caine" ingredients are problematic if licked in quantity. No hydrocortisone on broken skin.

2. Re-covering so it actually stays on
   - Non-adherent pad (Telfa) directly over the scrape, sized to cover without bunching.
   - Rolled gauze to hold the pad — snug, not tight. One fingertip should slip easily between the wrap and the leg.
   - Clean cotton sock over the gauze.
   - Cohesive bandage (Vet wrap / Coflex) to anchor the sock at the top, sticky side OUT, light tension only, leaving the two central toes exposed so you can check for swelling, coldness, or color change.
   - The actual failure mode here is the loose sock, not the wrap. If you have a properly fitted paw boot (Ruffwear-style), use that over the pad — it stays on better than a sock on a dog who has already self-traumatized once.

3. Cone — yes, use one.
   - One pinpoint bleed from licking is his vote of confidence that he will re-lick if given the chance. The sock alone is not enough.
   - E-collar sized so it extends 1–2 inches past the nose when he tips his head down. Inflatable collars work for some dogs; if he can still curl around the paw, switch to a rigid plastic cone or a longer inflatable.
   - Keep it on whenever you can't watch him directly for the next 5–7 days — overnight, while you're out, during crate rest.
   - Remove only for supervised meals and brief leashed outdoor time, and only if you can actively prevent licking.

4. Same-day vet call (non-emergency appointment today or tomorrow)
   - Two or more pinpoint bleeds within 24 hours — suggests the wound isn't holding a clot and may need a vet-applied dressing.
   - Bleeding recurs and takes more than 5 minutes of direct pressure to stop.
   - Any swelling, heat, spreading redness, discharge (pus or cloudy fluid), or foul odor.
   - New or worsening limp, reluctance to bear weight, or visible pain on paw touch.
   - The scrape starts to gape when his toes flex (it doesn't now — good — but if that changes, the tissue underneath may be deeper than superficial).
   - He's persistently trying to lick despite the cone, or you find blood on the cone/dressing overnight.
   - Systemic signs: warm ears, lethargy, off food, panting at rest.

5. Urgent care / ER same day
   - Bleeding soaks through dressings and won't stop with 5–10 minutes of firm direct pressure.
   - Rapid or spreading swelling up the leg, especially with heat.
   - Deeper injury suspected — exposed tissue flap, deep puncture, nail bed involvement, or foreign material you can't rinse out.
   - Pale or tacky gums, rapid breathing, weakness, or collapse.
   - Lower threshold across the board if he has a known clotting issue, is on anticoagulants (e.g., for cardiac disease), or is diabetic or immunocompromised.
   - Bleeding restarts every time you release pressure, even after re-cleaning and re-bandaging.

Monitoring window (next 24–48 hours)
   - Check the dressing and the exposed toes twice today — morning and evening.
   - Replace the outer bandage if it's wet, dirty, or slipping; replace the inner non-adherent pad only if it sticks or soaks through.
   - Leash walks only until the pad is closed. No running, no off-leash, no rough play.
   - If you can't keep coverage on by tomorrow, ask your vet about a medical boot or a better-fitting paw protector — the current loose-sock setup isn't reliable for a dog who has already self-traumatized twice.

Practical answer, in three parts.

SUBSTITUTES THAT WORK
  - #8 round for #10 round: fine. You'll just refill more often during full washes, but the technique transfers.
  - 3/4" flat for 1" flat: fine. Your edges will run a bit narrower than the instructor's demo, but the mechanics are the same.
  - Palette, tape, board, two water jars: covered.
  - Ultramarine, burnt sienna, quinacridone rose, phthalo blue: all covered.

WHAT TO BUY
  - Paper — this is the real gap. Your 9×12 block is smaller than a single quarter sheet (which is 11×15), and the four glued edges make wet-edge work awkward — you can't float or fully soak an edge without soaking the binding. For a clinic built around washes and edges, you want loose sheets, not a bound block. Cheapest fix: buy two quarter sheets of 140 lb cold-press (~$2–4 total). A full sheet torn in half is also fine.
  - Paint — ideally Hansa yellow (PY3). Azo yellow is a genuinely different pigment: warmer, more opaque, slightly orange-shifted. With phthalo blue, azo mixes to olive/sap green; Hansa mixes to a brighter, cleaner spring green. If the instructor demos any green mix, your swatch will read visibly different from the rest of the class. One tube of Hansa yellow is ~$10–15 and lasts a long time, so it's worth buying even if azo is "tolerated."
  - Brushes: skip the upgrades unless you want them for your own practice.

CONFIRM WITH INSTRUCTOR (one short email covers both)
  - Whether a 9×12 block counts given it's smaller than a quarter sheet and bound on all four edges — my read is "no, please bring quarter sheets," but it's worth a sentence.
  - Whether Hansa yellow specifically is required for the color-mixing demo, or whether azo yellow is fine. This determines whether the paint purchase is necessary or optional.

NET ADDITIONAL SPEND: two quarter sheets of paper, optionally one tube of Hansa yellow. Everything else rides on gear you already own.

PROCEDURE: NON-DESTRUCTIVE COMPARISON AND QUARANTINE FOR P037_back.tif
Targets: laptop copy and external-drive copy (both at their original paths)
Goal: identify the verified archival master without using mtime as evidence

OVERARCHING PRINCIPLES (held throughout)

  - Neither source TIFF is renamed, moved, or rewritten at its original path
  - "Tentative is not an archival claim" — P037 stays held/separate from the 10 verified cohort members until evidence supports joining them
  - "Filenames, sleeves, index unchanged" — physical provenance and the cohort index are preserved
  - mtime, ctime, atime are observed for context but never used as primary evidence
  - Every step's output is written to a new file in a new directory before any determination is recorded

PHASE 0: HALT (already in effect)

  Both files stay at their current absolute paths. Do not:
    - open-and-resave either in an image editor (this rewrites the container)
    - copy one onto the other
    - run any tool that writes back to the source path

PHASE 1: IMMUTABLE PROVENANCE SNAPSHOT

  Capture, for each file: full absolute path, size, mtime, ctime, atime, SHA-256.
  The SHA-256 is the new ground-truth fingerprint going forward — it locks both files in their current state. It does not, by itself, prove which was the scan-session original, because the scan log has no checksum recorded.

  Suggested commands (run from a neutral working directory, not from either source location):

    sha256sum /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif   > p037_laptop__sha256.txt
    sha256sum /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif > p037_extdrive__sha256.txt
    stat /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif        > p037_laptop__stat.txt
    stat /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif      > p037_extdrive__stat.txt
    cat p037_laptop__sha256.txt p037_extdrive__sha256.txt p037_laptop__stat.txt p037_extdrive__stat.txt > p037__provenance_manifest.txt
    sha256sum p037__provenance_manifest.txt >> p037__provenance_manifest.txt

  These two checksums already prove what you reported: the files differ. They do not yet say which is the master.

PHASE 2: TIFF METADATA COMPARISON (read-only)

  Use exiftool if available; otherwise tiffinfo (libtiff-utils). Reads only — never modifies.

    exiftool -G -s -a -u /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif   > p037_laptop__exiftool.txt
    exiftool -G -s -a -u /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif > p037_extdrive__exiftool.txt
    diff -u p037_laptop__exiftool.txt p037_extdrive__exiftool.txt > p037__exiftool_diff.txt

  Critical fields to compare (any delta here is signal, not noise):

    ImageWidth, ImageLength
    BitsPerSample
    SamplesPerPixel (1=gray, 3=RGB, 4=RGBA or CMYK)
    Compression (1=None, 5=LZW, 7=JPEG, 8=Deflate/ZIP, 32773=PackBits)
    PhotometricInterpretation
    ResolutionUnit, XResolution, YResolution
    ColorSpace / ICC_Profile name and byte length
    Software (which TIFF writer)
    DateTime, CreateDate, ModifyDate
    Artist, Copyright
    EXIF, GPS, IPTC, XMP block presence and contents
    ThumbnailOffset / ThumbnailLength (embedded JPEG preview)

  A 12 KB size delta on otherwise-same dimensions usually indicates:
    - different compression (one LZW, one Deflate/ZIP)
    - one carries an ICC profile / XMP / IPTC block the other lacks
    - one has an embedded JPEG thumbnail the other lacks
    - one was re-wrapped by a different TIFF writer (Photoshop vs. scanner-native)
  These are typically metadata-only differences and do not change pixel content. That is a hypothesis to test in Phase 3, not an assumption to act on.

PHASE 3: PIXEL-LEVEL COMPARISON

  Render both to a neutral lossless format in a NEW directory. Never overwrite the sources.

  ImageMagick path:

    mkdir -p p037_quarantine/pixel_compare
    convert /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif   -depth 16 PNG32:p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/laptop.png
    convert /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif -depth 16 PNG32:p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/extdrive.png
    compare -metric AE -fuzz 0% \
      p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/laptop.png \
      p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/extdrive.png \
      p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/diff.png

  VIPS path (faster on large images):

    vips tiffload /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif   p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/laptop.png
    vips tiffload /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/extdrive.png
    vips abs p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/laptop.png p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/extdrive.png --output p037_quarantine/pixel_compare/abs.png

  How to read the result:

    AE == 0 differing pixels           pixel content identical; size delta is metadata/compression only
    small AE (low thousands)           one file had a profile application or color-space conversion baked in
    large AE (tens of thousands +)     substantive post-capture edit on one of the two

PHASE 4: CROSS-REFERENCE WITH THE SCAN-SESSION LOG

  Open the original scanning-session log. Record, for P037 (and ideally for the cohort):

    Scanner make/model
    Capture software + version (VueScan, SilverFast, Epson Scan, manufacturer-native, etc.)
    Capture DPI
    Bit depth per channel and total
    Target color space / ICC profile
    File naming convention + intended compression
    Any documented post-processing
    Capture date/time

  Match each TIFF's metadata against the logged parameters. The file whose TIFF tags are consistent with the logged configuration is the stronger candidate. The log constrains plausibility; it does not by itself prove provenance.

PHASE 5: DECISION TREE

  Outcome A — pixel content identical, metadata differs:
    The 12 KB is explained by compression / profile / metadata. The file matching the scan-log parameters is the more likely original capture.
      - Only one matches the scan log: that file is the candidate master. Proceed to Phase 7.
      - Both match the scan log: genuine ambiguity from metadata alone. Escalate to Phase 8.

  Outcome B — pixel content differs:
    One file was altered post-capture. The file matching both the scan log AND showing pixel content consistent with an unaltered capture is the candidate master. If still ambiguous, escalate to Phase 8.

  Outcome C — neither file's metadata cleanly matches the scan log:
    Both have been touched (re-wrapped, re-saved) since capture. Phase 8 is required.

PHASE 6: QUARANTINE LAYOUT

  Until a determination is made, isolate everything in a dedicated directory. Do not move or rename the originals at their original paths; copy them in with provenance preserved.

  Suggested layout:

    p037_quarantine/
      originals/
        laptop__P037_back.tif          (cp -p copy; original name preserved)
        extdrive__P037_back.tif        (cp -p copy; original name preserved)
      provenance/
        manifest.txt
        laptop__sha256.txt
        extdrive__sha256.txt
        laptop__stat.txt
        extdrive__stat.txt
      metadata/
        laptop__exiftool.txt
        extdrive__exiftool.txt
        exiftool__diff.txt
      pixel_compare/
        laptop.png
        extdrive.png
        diff.png
        diff_metric.txt
      scan_log_crossref/
        relevant_log_excerpt.txt       (copy of the relevant scan-log entry, never the original log)
        parameter_match_table.txt
      decision/
        working_notes.txt              (dated reasoning; nothing claimed "verified" yet)
        determination_record.txt       (written only after evidence supports it)

  Copy with timestamp preservation, then re-checksum the copies:

    cp -p /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif   p037_quarantine/originals/laptop__P037_back.tif
    cp -p /path/to/extdrive/P037_back.tif p037_quarantine/originals/extdrive__P037_back.tif
    sha256sum p037_quarantine/originals/*.tif

  Once the copies checksum-equal the originals, treat the originals as locked (do not modify). All further analysis runs on the quarantine copies.

PHASE 7: LOCK-IN (only after evidence supports a determination)

  1. Append the candidate master's SHA-256 to the cohort's CHECKSUMS file (the one that already records the 10 verified members).
  2. Append to the verification log:
       - file path
       - SHA-256
       - date of determination
       - evidence basis (which phases, what they showed, what the scan-log cross-ref said)
       - status of the other version (preserved as historical record, or noted as superseded)
  3. Per your standing principle, do not write "verified archival master" anywhere until the CHECKSUMS entry is in place.

PHASE 8: RE-SCAN FROM PHYSICAL (the gold standard, used only when needed)

  When metadata + pixel diff cannot resolve the determination:

  1. Handle the physical P037 photograph out of its archival sleeve with clean cotton or nitrile gloves; minimize handling.
  2. Return it to the sleeve the same day. Do not alter the sleeve, the index entry, or the cohort numbering.
  3. Re-scan using the EXACT parameters recorded in the scan session log — same DPI, same bit depth, same color space, same software if practical.
  4. Name the re-scan using the cohort convention, e.g. P037_back__rescan__2024-09-02.tif.
  5. SHA-256 the re-scan.
  6. Run Phase 2 and Phase 3 against the re-scan and both quarantened versions.
  7. The re-scan is, by definition, the new verified archival master (assuming clean handling and unchanged physical state).
  8. Record the re-scan's SHA-256 in the cohort CHECKSUMS file.
  9. Preserve both prior versions in p037_quarantine/originals/ as historical records. Do not delete.

NOTES ON TOOLING

  sha256sum:           standard on Linux.
  exiftool:            install via your package manager if missing. tiffinfo (libtiff-utils) covers core TIFF tags but is thinner on EXIF/IPTC/XMP blocks.
  ImageMagick:         install via your package manager if missing (provides convert, compare, identify).
  VIPS:                install via your package manager if missing; faster than ImageMagick on large images.
  All operations above are reads or writes to new files in new directories. Nothing modifies either source TIFF at its original path.

WHAT THIS PROCEDURE DOES NOT DO

  - Does not assume newer mtime = master.
  - Does not overwrite either source file.
  - Does not rename either source file at its original path.
  - Does not open-and-resave either source file in any editor.
  - Does not promote P037 to "verified" status until the evidence record supports the claim.

# Safe restore + rename + checksum + re-verify sequence

Operating principles I'm baking into the order:
1. Evidence-before-mutation. The altered laptop file becomes `*.incident.tif` (or similar) before anything else is touched, so the master path is never the one we just renamed.
2. The verified file lands in place only after we've confirmed its checksum matches the value from your two-person session.
3. The laptop master path gets the verified file with the same name, so downstream tools and index entries don't break.
4. The evidence copy stays where you can find it; nothing about it is deleted or moved again.

Adjust the two `EXT_DIR` / `LAP_DIR` paths and the expected checksum to your real layout.

---

## Step 0 — Pre-flight (no writes, just reads)

```bash
EXT_DIR="/path/to/external/drive/scan_archive"   # verified two-person session
LAP_DIR="/path/to/laptop/scan_archive"           # holds the altered copy
NAME="P037_back.tif"

EXT="$EXT_DIR/$NAME"
LAP="$LAP_DIR/$NAME"
EXPECTED_SHA="<paste the SHA-256 from your two-person verification record>"
```

## Step 1 — Compute the external-drive checksum BEFORE any write

This is the value we will later compare against `EXPECTED_SHA`. Run it twice and diff to make sure the terminal isn't lying.

```bash
( cd "$EXT_DIR" && sha256sum "$NAME" )
( cd "$EXT_DIR" && sha256sum "$NAME" ) | tee /tmp/p037_ext_sha.txt
awk '{print $1}' /tmp/p037_ext_sha.txt
```

If the first column doesn't equal `$EXPECTED_SHA`, stop and don't proceed — the external file isn't the one from the verification session.

## Step 2 — Quarantine the altered laptop copy under a non-master name

Evidence goes to a sibling filename so the canonical `P037_back.tif` slot on the laptop is free for the verified copy. Pick a suffix that downstream tools won't mistake for a real scan.

```bash
EVID_TS="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"   # incident timestamp, UTC
EVID_NAME="${NAME%.tif}.incident_${EVID_TS}.tif"

mv -n "$LAP" "$LAP_DIR/$EVID_NAME"
ls -l "$LAP_DIR/$EVID_NAME"
sha256sum "$LAP_DIR/$EVID_NAME" | tee /tmp/p037_evidence_sha.txt
```

`mv -n` refuses to overwrite, so if a previous incident copy already exists with that exact timestamp, the command fails safely instead of clobbering evidence.

The `.incident_<UTC>.tif` suffix keeps it out of any glob that targets `*.tif` for editing, and out of any path your archive index uses to find masters.

## Step 3 — Copy the verified external file into the laptop master slot

Copy, don't move, on the first pass. That keeps `$EXT` intact as your ground-truth source while the laptop copy settles.

```bash
cp -p "$EXT" "$LAP_DIR/$NAME.tmp"
```

`-p` preserves mtime/atime so the file's filesystem metadata still matches what the scanner wrote.

## Step 4 — Verify the laptop copy before swapping it into the master name

Compare its hash to the one captured in step 1. If they don't match, delete the `.tmp` and stop — don't overwrite the evidence name.

```bash
sha256sum "$LAP_DIR/$NAME.tmp" | tee /tmp/p037_lap_sha.txt
diff <(awk '{print $1}' /tmp/p037_ext_sha.txt) \
     <(awk '{print $1}' /tmp/p037_lap_sha.txt) \
  && echo OK_MATCH || { echo MISMATCH; rm -f "$LAP_DIR/$NAME.tmp"; exit 1; }
```

## Step 5 — Atomically place the verified copy under the master name

`mv` within the same filesystem is atomic, so readers either see the old (absent/altered) state or the new verified state, never a half-written file.

```bash
mv -f "$LAP_DIR/$NAME.tmp" "$LAP_DIR/$NAME"
ls -l "$LAP_DIR/$NAME"
```

## Step 6 — Re-verify post-swap

Confirm the master path now hashes to the expected value and that the incident file is still untouched.

```bash
sha256sum "$LAP_DIR/$NAME" | tee /tmp/p037_master_sha.txt
awk '{print $1}' /tmp/p037_master_sha.txt | grep -qx "$EXPECTED_SHA" \
  && echo MASTER_VERIFIED || echo MASTER_HASH_MISMATCH

sha256sum "$LAP_DIR/$EVID_NAME" | tee /tmp/p037_evidence_after_sha.txt
diff /tmp/p037_evidence_sha.txt /tmp/p037_evidence_after_sha.txt \
  && echo EVIDENCE_UNCHANGED || echo EVIDENCE_DRIFT
```

## Step 7 — Header spot-checks (optional but recommended)

If `exiftool` is available, sanity-check the pixel dims, bit depth, embedded scan timestamp, and the absence of the contrast tag on the reinstated master:

```bash
exiftool -ImageWidth -ImageHeight -BitDepth -ModifyDate -Software \
         -TagList "$LAP_DIR/$NAME"

exiftool -s -s -s -Contrast "$LAP_DIR/$NAME" | grep -q . \
  && echo CONTRAST_TAG_PRESENT_BAD \
  || echo CONTRAST_TAG_ABSENT_OK

exiftool -ImageWidth -ImageHeight -BitDepth -Software \
         "$LAP_DIR/$EVID_NAME"
```

A contrast tag here is the smoking gun from the access editor — its absence on the master and presence on the evidence file is what you want.

---

## Future one-liner

Whenever you want to confirm the laptop master is still the verified external file:

```bash
EXPECTED_SHA="<paste the SHA-256 from your two-person verification record>"
sha256sum "$LAP_DIR/P037_back.tif" | awk '{print $1}' | \
  grep -qx "$EXPECTED_SHA" && echo MASTER_OK || echo MASTER_DRIFT
```

MONITORING THROUGH MONDAY 9/09 (~07:00):

Check each of these and note presence/absence — do not self-treat through positive findings:

  Walking gait on flat ground: any antalgia or unconscious favoring through Mon morning.
  Stair descent: any lateral ankle discomfort going downstairs (single-leg loading of the lateral column).
  Single-leg calf raise (knee straight, then knee bent): any pain, weakness, or apprehension on the lateral side. 10 reps each leg.
  Single-leg hopping in place (just a few): should be pain-free and stable.
  Inspection: swelling, bruising, warmth, or skin color change around the lateral malleolus, sinus tarsi, or 5th metatarsal base.
  Pain-free ankle ROM: draw the alphabet with the big toe — any sharp or catching pain.
  ADL re-emergence: does the ache come back with prolonged walking, squat, or standing on one leg?

Anything localized to bone, any swelling, any night pain, any true antalgia → don't wait for the next run, get evaluated.

DECISION RULE FOR NEXT FIRST RUN (Wed 9/11 if following the 2× cadence):

Branch by what Mon AM shows. The "all-clear" bar is the 8/29 bar plus single-leg load tolerance:

  A. ALL-CLEAR (no AM stiffness or it resolves within ~10 min, no stair-descent pain, no swelling, single-leg calf raise and hopping pain-free and symmetric, no antalgia, pain-free ROM): Run Wed at 34 min on plan. Do NOT re-extend this week. Sun stays at 34. Cycling separate. This treats Sun as a successful load confirmation and the bar for Wk5 re-extension becomes "two consecutive 34s symptom-free."

  B. PARTIAL (AM stiffness that resolves by ~15–20 min, mild and brief stair-descent discomfort that clears with a few minutes of walking, no swelling, single-leg calf raise tolerable but not crisp): Hold Wed. Reassess Wed evening. If cleared by Wed PM, drop back to 32 for Sun only this week — no 3rd run, no extension. Cycling separate. Wed→Sun becomes a 7-day deload pass at 32 to confirm tolerance before re-attempting 34.

  C. POSITIVE on any of swelling, antalgia through Mon AM, AM stiffness >20 min, pain on stair descent after a 5-min warm-up walk, pain with single-leg calf raise, pain with hopping, or any pain at rest: Hold running pending clinical follow-up. Cycling (easy, pain-free) may continue if tolerated. Do not run through any of these to "test" it — the rule is symptoms-on-load → no-load until symptom-free off-load.

The single-leg calf raise and the stair descent are the two highest-yield checks. Lateral ankle symptoms that survive those usually aren't benign tissue.

RED FLAGS — CLINICAL FOLLOW-UP NOW, NOT WAIT:

  Swelling, bruising, or skin color/temperature change over the lateral ankle, sinus tarsi, or 5th metatarsal base.
  Pain at rest or pain that wakes you from sleep.
  Pain that localizes to bone (lateral malleolus, anterior talus, 5th metatarsal base) — tap test: press with your thumb over each of those for ~5 seconds; sharp focal pain is a flag.
  Antalgic gait persisting beyond Sunday evening into Monday.
  Inability to do a single-leg calf raise pain-free, or visible weakness vs the other side.
  Mechanical symptoms: locking, catching, giving way, clicking with ROM.

  Pain that is worse Monday than Sunday, or new pain in a different location than what you felt on the run.
  Any fever or systemic feeling (low probability here, but listed for completeness).

A practical sequence, plain-text and concrete. Take it slow the first time — a full sheet is the most forgiving size to learn on.

1) Identify the front (painting side) and lock it in.
   - Hold the sheet at a low angle to a window or lamp. The front shows a more pronounced, even tooth (a fine pebbled grain); the back is slightly smoother.
   - A clean fingertip lightly brushed across the sheet will feel "grabbier" on the front.
   - Note: deckled edges look identical front and back, so don't use them to tell sides apart.
   - Commit the choice to memory by putting a small Post-it flag or a shallow dog-ear on the BACK corner only. If you ever flip the sheet later, you'll know which side is up.

2) Plan the cuts so each quarter keeps two opposite original deckled edges.
   - 22 x 30 quartered cleanly is four pieces of 11 x 15.
   - First cut: parallel to the 30" edge, at the 11" mark, splitting the sheet into two 11 x 30 strips.
   - Second cut on each strip: parallel to the 11" edge, at the 15" mark, giving four 11 x 15 pieces.
   - Each quarter naturally inherits two opposite deckled edges from the original sheet — exactly what you want.

3) Mark on the BACK only.
   - Flip the sheet face-down on the clean board.
   - From one short edge, measure 11" and tick at both sheet edges. From one long edge on each half, measure 15" and tick.
   - Connect the ticks with a faint pencil line using the ruler as a straightedge. Keep it light — heavy graphite can transfer under paint later.

4) Score and cut face-down so the painting side is protected.
   - Leave the sheet face-down, back up, on the board.
   - Align the metal ruler precisely with a pencil line. Hold it firmly with the heel of your hand and press straight down so it cannot slide.
   - Use a fresh, sharp utility blade. Pull it along the ruler in one smooth stroke, full blade length, perpendicular to the paper. Don't saw.
   - For typical 140 lb cold-press, one firm pass is usually enough. For heavier stock, a second lighter pass along the same groove helps.
   - With the ruler still in place, gently flex the sheet along the scored line; the cut should open cleanly. If fibers resist, score again rather than tearing.
   - Keep fingers well clear of the blade path. Move the sheet, not your hand, around the ruler.
   - Repeat for the remaining three cuts.

5) Verify each piece.
   - Confirm 11 x 15, two opposite deckled edges, and a clean front with no pencil marks.
   - Pencil a tiny "F" or arrow on the back corner of each quarter so front/back stays unambiguous if the pieces get separated.

6) Store flat, interleaved.
   - Slip a sheet of glassine, tissue, or plain copy paper between each quarter (surface to surface, front-to-front or back-to-back) so the tooth doesn't imprint on its neighbor.
   - Stack flat in a shallow drawer, portfolio, or under a clean board with a light, even weight (a few books). Do not stand sheets on edge — they curl and the tooth can crack.
   - Keep in a dry, room-temperature spot. Avoid plastic bags, which trap moisture, and avoid basements or bathrooms.

A small heads-up for the Sept 21 clinic: bring one quarter rather than the full sheet, and keep it interleaved until you're ready to tape or block it. If the clinic involves stretching, a quarter sheet is much easier to handle than the full sheet for a first session.

Short answer: take transit Wednesday. The downside of one commute lost is small; the downside of guessing wrong on brake feel in traffic is not.

Why long lever travel is a real concern even though the wheel spins free and there's no visible leak:

  - Free-spinning wheel and adequate braking force are not the same thing. A brake that only begins to grab near the bottom of the lever stroke gives you almost no usable modulation - which is exactly when you want to feather it for a stop sign, a pedestrian, or wet pavement.
  - The rear brake does only ~25-30% of stopping force, but it stabilizes the bike while the front brake does the heavy work and matters at low speed. If your rear brake is effectively a switch that only turns on at full lever pull, your only real brake is the front.
  - "New tire" is a clue. Wheel removal/reinstall often disturbs brake geometry: cable re-routed at the caliper, caliper de-centered, pad or rotor contaminated with tire-mounting fluid. Worth diagnosing, not assuming.

Five-minute checks tonight, in this order:

  1. Hold test. Squeeze the rear lever firmly and hold 30 seconds. If the lever creeps toward the bar, the system is leaking internally (hydraulic disc) or the cable is stretching under load - both are skip-the-commute findings. If it holds firm, the issue is geometry/wear, not a seal.
  2. Engagement character. Spin the wheel and apply the brake gradually. Smooth-but-far engagement is meaningfully safer than nothing-nothing-nothing-grab. Abrupt late grab is the dangerous pattern.
  3. Cable/housing quick check (rim brakes). Look at both housing ends for corrosion, fraying, or compression marks. Turn the barrel adjuster 1-2 turns clockwise - if engagement moves noticeably closer to the lever, this is almost certainly cable stretch and may be rideable after adjustment.
  4. Pad/rotor visual (disc brakes). Pads down to ~1.5mm, rotor deeply scored, or shiny contamination on the rotor face = pad/rotor replacement territory, not a cable tweak.
  5. Compare to the front brake. Squeeze both levers the same amount and judge the asymmetry. Dramatically more travel on the rear confirms a real change, not just your memory being off.

Give the mechanic Thursday - write it down so they go straight to the cause rather than starting with a full inspection:

  - Symptom: rear lever has to be pulled close to the bar before braking engages
  - Onset: noticed after the new-tire install (or: onset unclear - flag this so they ask)
  - Lever feel: smooth-and-far / mushy-and-creeping / nothing-then-abrupt-grab (which one you observed)
  - Hold test result: lever held firm / lever crept toward bar over 30 sec
  - Pad thickness, rotor scoring, cable housing condition (your visual)
  - Last brake service: when, what was done
  - Ask them to verify: cable tension at pinch bolt, barrel-adjuster range remaining, caliper centering (rim) or piston travel equality (disc), hydraulic bleed if hold test failed

Decision rule for tomorrow morning: if the hold test showed lever creep, or engagement is abrupt-late, do not ride - regardless of everything else. If it's smooth-and-far and your commute is short, dry, and low-traffic, riding cautiously is defensible - but with the shop appointment already on the calendar for Thursday morning, transit is the higher-margin choice by a wide margin.

One last practical note for tonight: when you do the morning check, do the steps-out-of-bed stiffness test before you load the ankle with much else — that first-window read is the most diagnostic single piece of data, more so than anything you get later in the day.

PRE-RIDE (still at home, bike loaded, before you leave):
  - Lever end: ferrule fully seated against the cable adjuster/stop, no visible gap; housing enters ferrule straight, not kinked
  - Cable: no fraying where it exits the lever; run your eye along the housing to the rear, no bulges or sharp bends
  - Stationary squeeze: lever firms progressively with modulation, does not bottom out against the bar, returns cleanly
  - Wheel spin (hand off bar): no rub, no pulsing click as the wheel rotates, rim tracks true through the brake pads
  - Loaded slow roll-and-stop: walk beside or ride slowly 5-10 m, firm lever pull both sides - bike tracks straight, feel matches yesterday

EARLY-RIDE (in this order, on your actual route):
  1. First 200 m at walking pace: lever feel matches the parking lot
  2. First gradual stop at a quiet intersection: firm, straight, no pull to one side
  3. After 1-2 km: recheck - lever should not feel softer, longer, or grabbier than at the start
  4. First real descent on your route: first stop GENTLY and EARLY, then progressive. This is where bedding-in issues show up (lever creeping toward bar, fade, pulsing under load)
  5. Listen for new tick / click / ping from the housing or caliper area

PULL OVER AND STOP if any of these appear:
  - Lever feel changes (softer, more travel, bottoms out, or suddenly grabs higher)
  - Bike pulls left or right under braking
  - New rubbing, pulsing, or noise
  - Anything that was not present in yesterday's parking-lot test

If the lever still matches parking-lot feel after the first descent, the rest of the commute is normal riding.

What happened on that quarter sheet

The taped lower edge behaves like a dam. Pigment-laden water migrates downhill by gravity and piles against the tape, so the bottom margin stays glossier and wetter than the rest of the wash even after the sheen up top has started to go matte. When you came back with a drier brush at roughly 90 seconds, you touched three moisture zones at once:

  - upper wash: sheen gone, paper past "wet" into "damp / thirsty" — it wanted water
  - lower edge: still pooled, full "wet" stage — it already had too much
  - your brush: drier than the edge, wetter than the upper sheet

A drier brush touching a wetter zone acts like a wick. It pulls pooled pigment and water outward into the damp-but-matte area above, where the thirsty paper drinks the new water and carries pigment with it. That radial bleed into a partly-dried field is the cauliflower shape you got. It is not a pigment-mixing problem and not a brush-quality problem — it is a stage-mismatch problem.

  Practice sequence for next Saturday

Run these in order on three or four quarter sheets. No fixing, no scrubbing. Each block is about ten minutes.

  1. Sheen clock. Lay a flat wash and watch it in raking light. Mark three moments: (a) full mirror sheen, (b) sheen gone but paper still reads dark/wet, (c) paper lightening toward dry color. Time each transition. You are training your eye to read (b) without touching the surface.

  2. Pool awareness. Tape a sheet, lay a wash, and do nothing except watch where pigment migrates. Confirm the bottom margin stays wet longest. Practice leaving a slightly under-loaded margin there, or tilt the board 10-15 degrees so excess runs to a clean corner you control.

  3. Brush moisture ladder. Three brushes: dripping, damp (loaded then kissed to a towel), nearly dry (blotting until it barely feels cool). Touch each one once to a wash that has just reached stage (b), in separate zones. Note which one flows, which one sits, which one bites the paper and pulls. The damp brush is your intervention tool — never the wet one, never the bone-dry one.

  4. Bead recovery, no scrubbing. If a bead forms at an edge, take a damp thirsty brush, touch the inside of the pool, and lift straight out in one stroke — pull, do not sweep. If a backrun has already started, stop. Most blooms dry into a soft, usable cloud if you leave them alone.

  In-clinic rules of thumb

  - Mix wash consistency in the palette before you touch paper, so you are not adjusting mid-sheet.
  - Hold the board tilted away from your working edge so gravity helps, not fights.
  - Make any second pass while the sheen is still partly visible, or after the sheet has gone fully matte — never in between.
  - When in doubt, do less. A sheet you leave alone at stage (b) will almost always look better than one you "rescue."

REPEAT-CONTACT RULE (POST-ADMISSION, HS DIAGNOSTIC)

1. Unit. A contact event is one time-stamped message on a workspace's support thread inside the post-admission window through the day-90 PIT snapshot — either a customer-originated message or an agent substantive reply. System pings and silent status updates do not become events until they satisfy the substantive criterion.

2. Automated-acknowledgement exclusion. Exclude an event only when BOTH (a) the sender is a system/bot handle with no human author on either side, AND (b) the body is template/macro content with no question, decision, or commitment. Two independent signals required. If only one check confirms, the event is KEPT (conservative). One-event-flagged-inconclusive is the floor, not "drop on suspicion."

3. Repeat-contact flag (binary, per workspace). Flagged iff qualifying events ≥ 2. The first qualifying event is the initial contact. Each subsequent qualifying event is a repeat. A workspace with exactly 1 qualifying event has 0 repeats.

4. Repeat-contact count (per workspace). max(0, qualifying events − 1).

5. Group views (both reported). Two complementary summaries: (i) share of workspaces in the group with ≥ 1 repeat (widespreadness); (ii) sum of repeat counts across the group (volume). On small samples these can diverge — show both, do not collapse.

6. Handoff vs. help-request. A CS handoff is a separate qualifying event from the help request that triggered it, counted on its own merits. Owen's separate recording of help request, handoff, and later expansion outcome is preserved.

Both studies below isolate exactly one variable each and run on fresh paper, so nothing is being repainted or scrubbed.

  STUDY 1 — Bead & brush-moisture at re-entry
  Variable: brush moisture when you return to a wash after the sheen has dulled.
  Held constant: paper, pigment, dilution, brush, stroke speed, paper orientation, starting wetness.

  Layout: one full sheet (or half sheet) of 300 lb cold press taped flat. Pencil five vertical strips ~1.5" wide, each with tick marks at top, 2/3 down, and bottom. One round brush, one mix (e.g., burnt sienna at the dilution you used in the clinic).

  Procedure per strip:
   1. Load the brush to a fixed charge (count drops, or weigh on a small dish — pick a routine and keep it).
   2. Lay one continuous stroke top to bottom in ~6–8 sec. Stop at the 2/3 tick.
   3. Set the brush down. Wait until the sheen has fully dulled; count it out loud and write the seconds next to the strip.
   4. Re-enter at the 2/3 tick with the strip's variant load and continue to the bottom.

  Strip variants (only the re-entry load changes):
   - Strip 1 — no re-entry (control).
   - Strip 2 — damp brush, well-squeezed, just pigment to lay a stroke.
   - Strip 3 — matched load, same charge as the initial stroke.
   - Strip 4 — wetter brush (the failure mode from the clinic).
   - Strip 5 — near-dry brush, broken charge.

  What to look for after drying: blooms should appear only on strip 4, with streaky dry edge on strip 5 and clean field on 1–3. That single visual confirms that re-entry moisture is the lever, not bead during the active stroke. ~25 min total.

  STUDY 2 — Edge-timing window
  Variable: delay between base wash and second pass.
  Held constant: paper, brush, pigment mix, load, dilution, shape.

  Layout: quarter sheet taped flat. Pencil a row of six identical shapes (~2" circles, or short cylinders matching the clinic exercise) evenly spaced along the sheet. Label each shape with its assigned delay: 0s, 10s, 20s, 30s, 45s, 60s. Same mid-value earth tone you used in the edge clinic.

  Procedure:
   1. Lay the base wash on shape 1, start counting, lay the second pass at the labeled delay.
   2. Move immediately to shape 2 so each shape runs on its own clock; do not stop to evaluate mid-row.
   3. If using cylinders: base wash = body, second pass = shadow tone on one side, same shape each time.

  What to look for after drying: the row reads as a gradient — 0s blooms (too wet), 20–30s shows the soft bleed you want, 60s shows a hard line. The middle two or three shapes are your personal soft-edge window for that paper, that brush, that day's humidity. Photograph and bring it to the next clinic — it is a calibration chart, not a painting. ~15–20 min.

  Both studies fit comfortably in one Sunday session with shared setup (~45–60 min). Nothing is corrected; failures are the data. If a strip blooms unexpectedly, write the seconds next to it and move on — do not touch the paper.

Good news up front: what you described — alert, pink gums, drinking, settling, no vomiting or collapse, in a dog who got stressed during a nail trim — fits an ordinary acute stress response very well. Panting and drooling for around 20 minutes after a vet visit, in a dog who stays responsive and starts self-regulating, is a common pattern. You're right to want a clear rubric for the next few hours, though, because the same symptoms can sit on a spectrum.

Here's how I'd frame the decision.

REASSURING ANCHORS (the things you already noted that point away from emergency)
- Alert and responsive throughout
- Gums pink (not pale, white, blue, or mottled)
- Drinking water on arrival home
- Symptoms already trending downward by the time you got home
- No vomiting, collapse, facial swelling, or breathing difficulty
- A clear precipitant: nail trim + car ride, both well-known canine stressors

If those four anchors hold and the trend keeps pointing down, this is almost certainly stress physiology (sympathetic activation plus thermoregulatory panting), not a medical event.

RED FLAGS — URGENT VETERINARY CARE NOW
Any of these, even one, means go in or call the ER while you're en route:
- Collapse, fainting, or sudden weakness he can't recover from in a few seconds
- Breathing that looks like distress rather than stress panting: abdominal heaving, ribs visibly working, neck extended, elbows out, blue/purple/white gums, any open-mouth breathing once he should be calm
- Repeated vomiting (a single spit-up is less concerning; sustained or with blood is not), or unproductive retching with a distended abdomen (bloat)
- Facial swelling, hives, sudden itching at the face/ears, or any swelling around the muzzle or eyes — anaphylaxis can show up 5–30 minutes after exposure
- Seizure activity, even brief
- Pale, white, gray, blue, or tacky gums
- Inability to stand, sudden ataxia, or head pressing
- Bleeding from the nail quick that doesn't slow within 10–15 minutes of firm pressure

YELLOW FLAGS — CALL THE CLINIC IF ANY OF THESE SHOW UP
- Panting and drooling still ongoing past 1–2 hours with no downward trend
- Restlessness or pacing that doesn't resolve once he's home and quiet
- New shivering or trembling that wasn't there before
- Refusing water for more than a few hours, or refusing food for more than 12 hours
- A second vomit, or any loose stool beyond his normal
- Any subtle gum color change, even if he's otherwise okay
- Hiding and refusing interaction beyond 2–3 hours

WHAT'S HAPPENING PHYSIOLOGICALLY
Panting in a stressed dog is partly thermoregulation and partly a way to blow off CO2 when the body is in a sympathetic "fight-or-flight" state. Drooling rides along with that autonomic activation — some dogs also get mildly nauseous from car motion and the cortisol spike. A 20-minute window in a dog who then drinks and settles is consistent with the system coming back down, not with something pathological.

HOME PLAN FOR THE NEXT FEW HOURS
- Cool, quiet space. Lower the lights, close the blinds, put him where he chooses to settle — usually that signal is right.
- Fresh water available, small amounts at a time so he doesn't gulp and bring it back up.
- Skip a big meal right now. Offer a lighter meal in 1–2 hours if he's interested.
- No walk, no training, no grooming for the rest of the day. Let him decompress.
- Don't force affection. Sit near him, let him come to you. Talking in a low, even voice helps some dogs; silence helps others.
- If you have a pheromone diffuser or a ThunderShirt that's worked for him before, deploy either now.
- If he's a car-anxiety dog specifically, the drooling and panting may resume the moment he sees the carrier or the car keys next time. Worth mentioning to the clinic.

A SIMPLE MONITORING LOG
Writing it down beats guessing later, especially if you end up calling:
- Time now: gum color, breathing rate (count breaths for 15 seconds, multiply by 4), mental state
- +30 minutes: recheck the same three things — should be trending better
- +1 hour: should be largely back to baseline
- +2 hours: if panting/drooling haven't resolved, call the clinic
- +4 hours: should have eaten something
- Next 24 hours: appetite, stool, energy, gum color back to his normal

If anything in the yellow or red list shows up, the log gives the clinic real numbers instead of a fuzzy "he seemed off."

FOR THE NEXT VISIT
At his next routine appointment, it's completely reasonable to ask the clinic about a pre-visit mild sedative or anxiolytic (gabapentin or trazodone are commonly used and well-tolerated for nail trims in anxious dogs), and to do a couple of "happy visits" where he just walks in, gets treats, and leaves — no exam. Counterconditioning plus premedication is the standard combination that turns nail trims from an ordeal into a manageable event for stressed dogs.

You're reading the situation correctly: this is a stress response, not a medical one. The plan above is mostly about watching the trend and having clear triggers for "call now" versus "keep watching."

Bottom line: do not promise the 26 portion count on the current estimate alone — get the supplier's guaranteed minimum before confirming, or order a small documented hedge lot on top of the one case.

The math:
  - Need: 24 plated + 2 kitchen contingency = 26 complete portions
  - Supplier estimate, 1 case: 27-30 portions
  - Margin at the floor (27): 1 portion, or about 3.8%

Why that margin is too thin to promise from an unguaranteed estimate:
  1. Trim variance is unhedgeable without a contractual floor. 27 is the supplier's working number, not a commitment. One bad lot can land at 26 or 25.
  2. The trim yield is only the first gate. Once portions are in-house, cooking/portioning is a second yield pass against your ≥44 7oz staff-min advance-count threshold. A 1-portion trim buffer disappears entirely once cook-side variance is layered on.
  3. This is a named-client, advance-count private dinner, not a service night you can flex. Falling short on the 24 plated is visible to the host; eating the 2 contingency silently leaves zero buffer.
  4. "Repeatable production" applies to your kitchen process, not to incoming trim yield. The estimate range itself is the unknown.

On the 4 vegetarian meals: separate from this. Veg+potatoes are on the unlimited-veg draft, so the constraint is purely on the chicken side.

Recommended path, in order of preference:
  - First choice: ask the supplier for a written guaranteed minimum on the case (e.g., "minimum 27 trimmed portions, otherwise short-fill"). If they will commit to 27 or 28, you have a defensible floor and can confirm 24 plated + 2 contingency.
  - Second choice: order 1 case plus a small documented hedge lot (3-5 additional birds, same supplier, same lot if possible) with a written contingency policy — cook the hedge only if the case trim comes in below 27. Record yield on the case so the hedge policy is data-driven for the next private dinner.
  - Avoid: ordering 2 full cases. That is 54-60 portions of overage against a 26-portion need and conflicts with the lean advance-count principle.

Net: the estimate covers 26, but only barely, and only on the supplier's say-so. Confirm the guaranteed minimum before you tell the host the count is locked.

15-minute practice — three skills, no composition.

Setup (~2 min)
- Six paper strips (or one sheet divided into six labeled zones). Pencil-mark each corner: date, dilution, intended step.
- One pigment + clean water. Two brushes: a larger round (bead work), a smaller round (softening stroke).
- Clock or timer visible.

Drill A — bead carry + live sheen read (~8 min)
Goal: even stripe + an honest "sheen alive / sheen gone" call on every strip.
- For each of the six strips:
  - Load the larger round generously — juicy, not dripping.
  - Tilt the strip ~15°. Drop the bead at the top edge.
  - Carry it down by reloading at the top as the bead advances. Keep the bead the same width and color the whole way.
  - Stop when it reaches the bottom. Within ~2 seconds, look at the surface and call it: sheen alive (glossy, mirror-like) or sheen gone (matte).
  - If sheen is gone: stop here. That strip is your "too late" reference — set it aside.
  - If sheen is alive: hand the strip straight into Drill B.
- Vary across strips: three at your normal mix, three a touch wetter. Note which dilution carries more evenly.

Drill B — controlled soft edge in the useful window (~5 min)
- On every strip that still has live sheen (lay fresh strips if all six went matte):
  - The moment the bead settles, start a count.
  - At ~20 seconds, take the small round loaded with clean water (or a faintly tinted mix) and draw one stroke along ONE edge of the wash.
  - Target: the edge softens inward by a few mm — doesn't bleed across, doesn't stay hard.
  - On two of the strips, also try the same stroke at ~15s and ~25s, to feel the boundaries of your window.

Wrap (~1 min, on the paper itself)
- Pencil-mark each strip: even / not even, sheen call, edge result.
- The cleanest bead + cleanest soft edge is your new reference. The bloomed strip is your warning — pin it where you'll see it next session.

If you finish early, rerun Drill A on your worst strip. Don't start a painting.

Honest read on the proposed walk:

The Greenbelt outing has three things that push it past "ordinary walking":
- Distance: 4 miles is long enough that cumulative ankle/calf load matters, not just step-by-step load.
- Uneven terrain: roots, rocks, side-slope, and sudden lateral shifts are exactly the kind of unpredictable ankle moment your restrictions appear designed to avoid pre-reassessment.
- Uneven grades: downhill sections add eccentric calf/Achilles demand, and side-grade adds sustained lateral stabilizer work.

None of that means you can't be part of the day with Sam. It means you shouldn't be on that exact route for that full distance.

Lower-load ways to join that keep you inside your current envelope (level, predictable, moderate, no hop-test demand):

1. **Do your own shorter, level loop, then meet them at the finish.** Walk 1.5–2 miles on a flat paved path beforehand, then drive to the trailhead they'll end at and be there when they walk in. You get the time with Sam, zero terrain risk.

2. **Join only the easiest segment of their route.** Greenbelt corridors usually have a flatter, more groomed first or last mile. Pick one, walk it with the group at your pace, and turn around when the grades kick in. Be explicit with Sam up front that you'll peel off — group pace pressure is the silent variable that turns "easy" into "more than ordinary."

3. **Park at the midpoint and walk them in.** Drive to a flatter section, walk a short out-and-back together, and let the others keep going on the rougher stretch. This works especially well if there's a coffee or end-of-trail stop you can share after.

4. **Skip the walk entirely and host the after.** Meet them at a Greenbelt-adjacent spot for food or coffee when they're done. Lowest loading, highest social presence.

A few guardrails regardless of which option you pick:
- Stay on level, predictable surfaces only. No roots, no side-slope, no soft ground.
- Cap your portion before fatigue changes your gait — that's when the ankle gets stressed, not on the first mile.
- If anything feels off (a twinge, a hitch, a moment of "that was weird"), stop. The Oct 2 reassessment is the goal; protecting the ankle for four more days matters more than one outing.
- Don't be talked into "just the last hill" by a group in good spirits. Decide the exit point before you start, not mid-route.

If I had to pick one: option 1 or 2 keeps you moving with Sam in the same place at the same time, on a surface that matches what you've already been cleared for, and puts you at the finish either way.

Short answer: Take the bus now. That's the safest of the three, and it's also the most practical.

Why:

Lightning is the dominant risk, not the wind. On a bike you're an exposed, often-metallic point in an open area. The 30/30 rule says if you can hear thunder within 30 seconds of a flash, the strike zone is within ~6 miles — too close to be on two wheels. "Possible lightning" combined with 35 mph gusts (which can shove you across a lane at intersections or under a sudden crosswind) is a "don't ride" combination, full stop.

Why not the other two:

- Waiting: Safer than riding, but you're trading an unknown storm duration for a known safe egress. Lightning cells can pulse for hours, and in early October sunset is around 6:45–7:00 in most US latitudes, so by the time the 4–7 pm window closes you may be commuting home in dusk/night on a wet road anyway. No upside over the bus.
- Leaving early: The storm window has already started (5:05 pm is inside the 4–7 pm block). Even if you could depart right now, the cell is overhead, not approaching — this is exactly when lightning risk peaks. Not viable.

Practical side of "take the bus now and retrieve the bike after the weather clears":

- Covered rack at the office + tomorrow-morning access means zero theft/weather exposure cost for the bike.
- A direct bus means you don't have to wrestle the bike onto a rack or drag it on/off transit — leaving it in place is the whole point.
- If you want belt-and-suspenders: lock the bike to the rack (even though it's covered), check the bus is still running on its normal route (storms sometimes trigger detours), and let someone know you're heading straight home.

One small addition for the return trip tomorrow morning: check the radar before you ride in — overnight storms sometimes leave standing water and downed branches on bike routes, and 35 mph gusts can persist after the lightning clears.

NEXT STUDY — moisture at fixed timing

  Goal: hold timing at the 20s "controlled transition" point from the last
  study and vary only the brush moisture, so you can see whether the 20s
  window absorbs load variation or whether load is the dominant lever.

  Setup
    Same paper, same pigment, same brush as last study.
    Three adjacent bands.
    One fresh timer per band. Soften every edge at 20s, no eyeballing.
    Use the same sheen cue you used for the 20s band last time as your
    starting gate.

  The three bands — vary ONLY brush moisture

    Band A (control)
      Same load you used last study. This is your reference; it should
      reproduce the controlled transition.

    Band B (wetter)
      After your normal loading, do one extra rinse + pickup so the
      brush is visibly carrying more water before it touches the band.
      Same pigment, same brush, same stroke.

    Band C (drier)
      Load normally, then pull the brush firmly across a clean scrap of
      paper (or a paper towel) to shed excess water while keeping the
      pigment charge. Then soften.

    Caveat to note, not solve: a wetter brush also carries more pigment,
    and a drier one carries less. You're varying "working moisture,"
    not water alone. That's fine — it's what your hand actually controls.

  Carry-over rules
    One softening pass per band. No working the edge.
    Don't return to any band after the sheen dulls.
    Stop the timer the instant each softening stroke ends, regardless
    of how it looks wetter or drier than the others.

  What to read from the result
    B reads like A (controlled transition)
      → 20s absorbs extra moisture; the 18s problem last study was
        timing, not load.
    B diffuses too far
      → 20s is the right answer only at your standard load; moisture
        matters at least as much as timing.
    C seams even at 20s
      → Lower load means the edge starts setting inside the 20s
        window, so load is the primary lever and timing is secondary.
    All three look similar
      → Soft edge is robust across a wide moisture range at 20s, and
        the 22s seam from last study was almost certainly timing, not
        load.

  Keeping it a study, not a painting
    Three bands, one stroke each, labelled A/B/C.
    No composition, no second pass, no values. This is a reference
    sheet, not a piece.

  Optional follow-up — only if A and B are not decisively different
    Run the same three moistures at 22s instead of 20s. That would tell
    you whether the 22s seam from last study was load-dependent or
    fixed. Don't commit to it in advance; only do it if the 20s result
    leaves the load question open and you have the paper.

What you're describing — slow drain plus dishwasher discharge pushing water back into the sink, no supply leak, no sewer gas — is most consistent with a partial blockage somewhere downstream of the P-trap, often in the kitchen branch line or where it ties into the main stack. The dishwasher drains through that same branch, so when the line is narrowed, its discharge has nowhere to go and pops up into the sink bowl. Holding off on both fixtures until maintenance arrives is the right call.

Immediate action
- Stop using the sink and the dishwasher. Running more water into a partially blocked line just feeds the backup and risks overflow past the overflow channel near the sink rim.
- Bail standing water into a bucket if it climbs past the overflow hole; keep the level well below the rim.
- Lay old towels along the cabinet floor and the toe-kick in case a slow seepage shows up later; check under the cabinet every couple of hours.
- If the sink has a small chrome cylinder on the rim near the faucet (the dishwasher air gap), unscrew the cap and look inside — a gunked-up air gap is a common cause of dishwasher discharge backing into the sink and is harmless to clear.

Things that are safe to try while you wait
- Clear the basket strainer of any food debris.
- A plastic zip-it style drain tool (the barbed strip) is non-invasive and often pulls up a clog near the strainer.
- If you want to attempt a plunger: fill the bowl a few inches, use a cup plunger (not a flange/toilet plunger), plunge firmly 10–15 times. If it's a double-bowl, plug the other side with a wet rag so pressure goes to the clog. Skip plunging if any chemical drain opener has been used — splash-back is the risk.
- Baking soda followed by white vinegar (about 1/2 cup baking soda, then 1 cup vinegar, wait 20–30 minutes, then hot tap water) is non-caustic and won't damage pipes; modest effectiveness, but worth trying.

What NOT to pour down the drain
- No chemical drain cleaners (sodium hydroxide or sulfuric-acid types). They rarely clear a real partial clog, they damage finishes and older pipes, and they make the plumber's job hazardous.
- No boiling water — hot tap water is fine; boiling water can soften a PVC joint or shock a porcelain sink.
- No mixing of cleaners — bleach + ammonia or bleach + any acid produces toxic gas.
- No grease, oil, coffee grounds, or food scraps, even if the sink is draining slowly; it only adds to the blockage.
- If you have a disposal, do not run it with standing water in the bowl — the motor can overheat or splash.

Escalate to an emergency call (not just the maintenance queue) if any of these appear
- Another fixture in the apartment starts draining slowly or gurgles when you run any water — that points to a main-line issue.
- A sewage smell develops (vent or trap problem layered on the clog).
- Water level is rising instead of slowly receding, or any water appears on the floor.
- Water shows up on a downstairs ceiling or in a neighboring unit.

Until maintenance arrives: keep both the sink and the dishwasher off, bailing only into a bucket if needed, and check under the cabinet once or twice. If the backup worsens or any of the escalation signs above show up, treat it as urgent rather than routine — call your building's emergency line or a plumber directly rather than waiting on the ticket.

Two distinct quantities, two distinct units — keep them apart by name and by field.

**Recommendation: report three fields, not one**

1. Customer-impact (wall-clock, what the customer experienced):
   Label: "block-elapsed minutes"
   Field: `block_elapsed_minutes`
   HS-014 value: 30

2. Agent-labor (sum of active work across handlers, internal cost):
   Label: "agent-active minutes"
   Field: `agent_active_minutes`
   HS-014 value: 45

3. The gap between them (concurrent handling, the diagnostic Owen actually wants):
   Label: "concurrent-handling minutes"
   Field: `overlap_minutes`
   HS-014 value: 15

**Why these labels work as interim**

"Block-elapsed" and "agent-active" are descriptive, not definitional. They describe what each number *is* without claiming either is the canonical "support minutes" — that label stays reserved for the final definition. Unit suffixes in the field names (`_minutes`, `_active_minutes`) make the unit visible at column-header level so no one can mistake one for the other in a spreadsheet or downstream query.

**What this avoids**

- No `support_time_minutes` derived field — that would conflate by averaging or summing across the two quantities.
- No informal use of "support minutes" for either raw quantity — that term is held until the final definition lands.
- No dropping the overlap. The 15-minute overlap *is* the signal: it's why a 30-minute customer block took 45 agent-minutes to clear, and it's what surfaces when concurrency is unusual.

**Reporting format for HS-014**

Replace the single `support_minutes: 45` line with the three fields above, and add a one-line legend in the export schema: *"block_elapsed_minutes and agent_active_minutes are raw observations; the support-minutes field is TBD."* That single sentence blocks conflation, signals interim status, and leaves the final definition open.

If Owen wants a single headline number in interim dashboards, surface `block_elapsed_minutes` as the customer-facing one and keep `agent_active_minutes` + `overlap_minutes` in the drill-down — that way the customer-impact number is what gets quoted, and the labor number is what gets audited.

VERDICT
Take the bus. The "once per crank revolution" timing is the giveaway — that pattern almost always means a single stiff link in the chain binding as it passes through the rear derailleur, and overnight rain on a covered rack is exactly how a chain picks up flash rust or grit in a pivot overnight. Benign and very fixable at home, but three reasons to not ride it:

  - You can't confirm the diagnosis from the saddle, and a skipper under load is the one condition that can turn into a sudden pedal jolt. With your knee still under return-to-run gating, an unexpected skip on a hard stroke is the wrong surprise this week.
  - If it actually is cassette wear showing up in your two most-used middle cogs (which is why the symptom is gear-specific), continuing to load it accelerates the damage to a point where you'd need a new cassette, not just a chain.
  - Indoor storage stops further moisture damage tonight; leaving it out again tomorrow is what would compound the problem.

DIAGNOSIS YOU'RE PROBABLY LOOKING AT, IN ORDER OF LIKELIHOOD
  1. One stiff chain link from overnight moisture (rust in a pivot, or water/grit binding a joint). Once per revolution, load-only, gear-specific — textbook.
  2. Stiff link on top of marginal cassette wear on the middle cogs. The rain exposed what was already borderline.
  3. Chain stretch crossing the wear threshold and starting to jump worn middle-cog teeth. Less likely given the precise "once per revolution" timing, but worth ruling out.

AT-HOME INSPECTION SEQUENCE (warm/dry space, basic tools, ~15 min)
  1. Chain visual. Pick up the chain at the rear derailleur. Look for any spotty surface rust, dark grit paste, or a link that sits at a slightly different angle than its neighbors. Run the chain through your fingers link by link, bending it laterally — a stiff link will resist flex where the others move freely.
  2. Free the stiff link. If you find one, work it side to side 10–15 times by hand. It should loosen. Wipe the chain, then apply one round of fresh chain lube and let it soak for a few minutes before wiping excess.
  3. Cassette visual. Stand behind the bike, eye-level with the cassette. Tilt the cogs under a light and look for "shark fin" teeth — points that lean to one side instead of being symmetric. Compare the middle cogs to the extremes; consistent wear across all = chain stretch; wear concentrated in the middle cogs = cassette.
  4. Chain stretch check. If you have a chain wear indicator, use it. If not, a ruler across 12 full links (rivet center to rivet center) should measure exactly 12 inches. 12 1/16 or more = replace the chain. 12 1/8 or more = chain is past saving and has likely damaged the cassette.
  5. Hanger alignment eye-check. Look at the rear derailleur hanger from directly behind the bike — the two pulley wheels should sit in a plane parallel to the cassette cogs, not visibly kinked to one side. Don't bend it without a tool; just flag if it looks off.
  6. Low-stakes test ride before the next commute. Empty parking lot or quiet block. Work through every gear, light load and one hard stroke each. If the skip is gone after the stiff-link fix, you're clear. If it returns under load in those same two cogs, it's the cassette and the bike goes to the shop.

IF YOU CAN'T RESIST RIDING HOME TODAY (bus falls through, etc.)
  - Stay in the easiest gear pair that avoids the two middle cogs entirely (smallest cassette cog up front, biggest ring — or whatever your easiest gear is). Don't shift into the affected cogs at any point.
  - Spin, don't mash. Keep cadence high and force low. No sprints, no climbs if avoidable.
  - If the skip fires unexpectedly, back off the power immediately and consider walking the bike until you can re-spin.

SHOP REPORT BULLETS (use as-is if the at-home steps don't resolve it)
  - Symptom: chain skips approximately once per crank revolution, only under heavy pedal load, only in [name the two cogs, e.g., "3rd and 4th from smallest"]. Light spinning is clean. Started after the bike sat under a covered office rack overnight through rain.
  - Already ruled out by rider: brake rub, wheel seating, shifting-vs-skipping (skip happens under power, not during shifts).
  - Already tried: identified and freed a stiff link [or: no stiff link found], re-lubed chain, skip [persists in same two cogs / resolved and returned later / resolved entirely — state what actually happened].
  - Cassette and chain wear status if you measured: chain at [X/12 in. over 12 links], cassette teeth [shark-fin pattern observed on middle cogs / clean / not inspected].
  - Request: full drivetrain assessment, measure chain and cassette wear, check hanger alignment, replace chain and/or cassette as a matched set if either is past service limit.

One last thing: even if the stiff-link fix clears it today, treat the next rainy overnight as a "lube the chain before it rains, not after" event going forward. A dry chain before exposure is what prevents this from recurring.
