ASSESSMENT: IS THE ENZYME SENSIBLE?

Yes — with realistic expectations.

Enzymatic cleaners use bacteria/enzymes to digest organic matter (grease, food residue, soap film). They are safe for pipes (no corrosion, no heat), safe for septic, and won't create a splash hazard for the plumber on Oct 15. That makes them a reasonable interim measure over 3 days.

But they have real limits you should not expect them to overcome:
- They work slowly. Most need 6–8+ hours of undisturbed contact, applied at bedtime.
- They are maintenance-grade, not clog-removal-grade. They will not clear a partial blockage on their own — they soften and gradually reduce organic buildup, which may or may not be enough to relieve the dishwasher-induced backup.
- They do nothing against non-organic obstructions (mineral scale, a stuck object, a flattened pipe section).
- The fact that the sink drains alone but not with dishwasher discharge strongly suggests a partial restriction that the dishwasher's high-volume pump simply overwhelms. That points to a real mechanical issue, not a maintenance one — likely the trap, the branch line, or a transition point in the wall. The enzyme is a softener, not a fix. The plumber visit is the actual fix.

Bottom line: enzyme use is sensible as a "don't make it worse, possibly help a bit" step. Plan on the plumber doing the real work.

PRODUCT-LABEL CONDITIONS THAT MATTER

When you pick up a product, confirm each of these on the label:

1. Active category. Should be bacterial/enzyme-based (commonly Bacillus cultures plus protease, lipase, amylase). Avoid anything listing sodium hydroxide (lye), sulfuric acid, or hydrochloric acid — those are chemical openers, not enzymes, and conflict with your goal of keeping the drain safe for service.

2. Intended use. Kitchen / grease / organic matter. Some enzyme products are formulated for septic or for hair/soap in bathroom lines; kitchen-targeted is what you want here.

3. Dwell time. Should specify an undisturbed contact period of at least 6–8 hours, ideally overnight. If a product claims a 15-minute clear, it is not actually an enzymatic product.

4. Dosage. Use the kitchen-sink dose exactly. More is not better with enzymes — excess just flushes through.

5. Water temperature at dosing. Lukewarm to warm, not hot. Hot water (especially near-boiling) can kill the bacterial cultures before they colonize. The label will specify.

6. Pipe and disposal compatibility. Should state compatibility with PVC, copper, and cast iron, and with garbage disposals if you have one. Most reputable enzyme products do.

7. Septic safety. Should be explicitly stated as septic-safe. Almost all enzymes are, but worth confirming.

8. Shelf life / lot date. Live cultures lose potency. Pick a bottle with a visible date and reasonable remaining life.

9. "Do not mix with" warnings. Will state not to combine with bleach, ammonia, or chemical drain openers. None apply to your situation since you haven't used chemicals, but worth knowing so no one reaches for bleach to "disinfect" the sink.

10. Application frequency if no immediate result. Some labels allow a second nightly dose; some recommend weekly maintenance. Two consecutive overnight doses before Oct 15 is fine.

SAFE INTERIM GUIDANCE: SUNDAY OCT 13 → TUESDAY OCT 15

Sink use:
- Install or use a sink strainer; scrape plates into trash/compost before rinsing.
- No grease, oil, coffee grounds, eggshells, fibrous peels (potato, celery), pasta, rice, or flour down the drain. These are the substrates feeding whatever buildup is in the line.
- After each sink use, run the hot tap for 20–30 seconds to push residue past the trap.
- Never use the sink during a dishwasher cycle.

Dishwasher use:
- Run smaller loads. The backup is volume-driven; halving the discharge roughly halves the surge the line has to absorb.
- If your model has an eco or light cycle, use it — lower pump-out volume.
- Run it at night when possible, so any overflow is discovered in the morning rather than mid-day, and so any standing water can sit without being used.
- After the cycle ends, give the sink 5–10 minutes to fully drain before using the sink.
- If a mid-cycle backup occurs: pause/cancel the cycle, let the sink drain on its own (do not plunge — no chemicals are present but plunging a partially restricted line can splash waste), then resume. Two partial cycles are usually less risky than one full cycle.
- Optional advanced workaround (only if backups persist): disconnect the dishwasher drain hose from the sink tailpiece/disposal and direct it into a 5-gallon bucket during the cycle. This is a 10-minute job if you're comfortable under the sink, but for 3 days it is not necessary unless the dishwasher is unusable as-is.

Enzyme application:
- Apply at bedtime on the night before the visit (Mon Oct 14) or two nights before (Sun Oct 13).
- Pour the labeled dose into the sink drain (not the dishwasher inlet).
- Follow with the labeled amount of lukewarm water.
- Do not run any water — sink or dishwasher — for the full dwell time stated on the label.
- One dose is fine; a second consecutive nightly dose is also fine and may help marginally.

WHAT NOT TO DO

- No chemical drain opener. Lye and acid-based products damage pipes (especially older metal or glued joints), create a splash/burn hazard for the plumber on Oct 15, and are completely incompatible with the "safe for service visit" goal.
- No boiling water down the drain if you have PVC under the sink — it can soften the trap joints. Hot tap water is fine.
- No plunger use, period. Plunging a partially restricted kitchen line with a dishwasher hose connected can push wastewater back through the dishwasher's air gap or into the disposal.
- Do not disassemble the P-trap yourself unless you are experienced. The plumber will do this; introducing a leak or a misaligned washer into a 3-day pre-visit window just adds risk.
- Do not run the dishwasher and the washing machine (if it's on a nearby branch) simultaneously. Wash on a separate day if possible.

ESCALATION SIGNS — CALL AHEAD OF OCT 15 IF YOU SEE THESE

The picture you described (one fixture slow, dishwasher-induced backup, no smell, no multi-fixture issue) is consistent with a localized kitchen branch restriction, which is well-suited to the scheduled visit. But the following would shift it from "scheduled maintenance" to "call sooner":

- Sewage odor from the sink or from any other drain.
- Multiple fixtures backing up at once (toilet gurgling when sink drains, washing machine standpipe overflowing when sink drains, bathtub slow when dishwasher runs).
- Gurgling sounds from other drains when the sink drains.
- Water appearing at a floor drain or at the washing-machine standpipe.
- The kitchen sink stops draining entirely between uses, or holds standing water that doesn't recede.
- Any wetness, staining, or odor under the sink cabinet that wasn't there before.

If any of those appear, the issue has moved beyond the kitchen branch and the Tuesday visit may need to be moved up — call maintenance rather than waiting.

PRE-VISIT HANDOFF (HELPFUL TO DO, NOT REQUIRED)

When the plumber arrives, two pieces of context will save time:
1. The backup is dishwasher-driven, not sink-alone. That tells them the restriction is downstream of where the dishwasher tie-in joins the line, narrowing the search.
2. No chemical drain opener has been used. That tells them they can use a snake, auger, or hot-water flush without acid-neutralization precautions and without a burn risk on opening the line.

If you can, leave the cabinet under the sink clear so the trap and dishwasher hose connection are accessible.

Use the flat collar for today's walk. Here's why and how to do it safely.

Recommendation: collar today, not the harness

A carabiner bridging a cracked plastic clasp is a false fix. The cracked buckle body is still the structural failure point — a carabiner clipped through it doesn't restore the integrity of the plastic. Dogs also apply sudden, jerky loads (lunging at a squirrel, jumping, scratching at the harness) that your hand-press demonstration didn't replicate. Plastic cracks propagate, and once a buckle has a visible hairline crack plus opens under manual twist, the next failure is unpredictable. The flat collar is known-good, fits properly, and already carries his ID tags — for a short, calm neighborhood walk that's the right tool.

Collar-fit check before you clip the leash

- Two-finger rule: slide two fingers flat between the collar and the top of Kibo's neck. If you can't, it's too tight; if you can fit more than two easily, it's loose enough to slip.
- Head-slip test: with the collar buckled, gently try to pull it backward over his ears. A properly fitted flat collar should not slip off when he pulls back.
- Tags positioned: ID + license/rabies tags should hang from the buckle area or a dedicated tag ring, not a loose S-hook that could catch on something.
- Quick check on his neck skin/coat for any matting or irritation from the harness that would tell you how long he's been wearing it.

Hardware audit on the harness (so you know what you're replacing)

- The cracked buckle itself — note whether it's the side-release or a chest-buckle; check the other buckle the same way.
- All other plastic parts: adjusters/sliders, any tri-glides. Stress whitening (chalky look) or any hairline crack means they're aging out too.
- Metal D-ring(s): check the weld points for cracks, bending, or sharp burrs. This is the actual load-bearing hardware when he's on leash.
- Webbing around the D-ring: look for frayed threads, pulled stitching, or any area that's gone stiff or thin.
- Webbing generally: cuts, chew marks, UV brittleness (stiff, faded sections).

Replacement notes

- Order before the next walk that isn't a calm neighborhood loop — don't let the collar become the default by accident.
- When choosing a replacement: a harness with all-metal or reinforced side-release buckles is worth it if Kibo pulls at all. For a calm walker, a standard well-stitched nylon harness is fine.
- If you ever switch back to the collar for an outing that isn't calm/familiar (new routes, other dogs, wind — and per memory Kibo dislikes wind on walks), reconsider. Distraction + flat collar is the riskier combo. In that case wait for the new harness or walk somewhere enclosed.
- If you notice any cough, gag, or throat irritation after today's collar walk, that's a signal the collar was tighter than ideal or that a harness is medically better for him long-term.

Short version: collar today, audit the harness tonight, replace before anything but calm familiar walks.

FOLLOW-UP: MOISTURE SWEEP AROUND THE ONCE-BLOTTED ANCHOR

Goal — find the narrowest cleanest-bristle window by perturbing above and below the once-blotted condition. Hold the 20-second gap and one-touch boundary constant. Same 3x2 shape as the first study so the two sheets compare directly.

GRID (light pencil ticks at cell corners only — no boxes drawn)

  Row 1 — LESS BLOTTED, brush slightly wetter than anchor
    L  loaded brush, one quick swipe across folded towel, no dwell
    R  loaded brush, one brief light press, roughly half the dwell of anchor

  Row 2 — ANCHOR, once-blotted repeated as control
    L  loaded brush, one firm press on towel
    R  loaded brush, one firm press on towel

  Row 3 — MORE BLOTTED, brush slightly drier than anchor
    L  loaded brush, anchor blot plus one second brief press
    R  loaded brush, anchor blot plus a single drag across folded towel

15-MINUTE BUDGET

  0:00 –  2:00   Setup. Two water pots, folded towel, scrap paper, palette charged with one pigment. Pencil ticks.

  2:00 – 12:00   Six cells, roughly 90 seconds each. Per cell: rinse, reload, condition the brush per row protocol, count 20, one touch, set brush down. Move top-left to top-right, then row 2, then row 3. Do not revisit a cell.

 12:00 – 14:00   Rinse brush, lay flat to dry, close the palette.

 14:00 – 15:00   One-line note: which cells equaled or beat the anchor's narrow dark seam.

HOLDS

  20-second gap is non-negotiable — set a visible timer or count aloud; do not adjust to catch up if a cell runs long.
  One-touch boundary — once the brush leaves the paper, the cell is done. No returns after the sheen dulls, no matter what the edge looks like.
  Single pigment, single color per cell, edge-only contact. No composition, no color blending, no second pass. This stays a study.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR

  Row 1 — does the seam widen, or does a backrun return as in the damp-brush cells from the first sheet?
  Row 2 — should reproduce the first study's anchor; if it doesn't, the comparison sheet is compromised and the sweep data is suspect.
  Row 3 — does the seam stay narrow but turn brittle or granular, or does pigment skip on contact?

  If a row-1 cell reads cleaner than the anchor, the next session narrows the sweep between that cell and row 2. If a row-3 cell matches the anchor, you've found a drier-tolerance margin. Either outcome shrinks the window.

LAY-OUT TIP — leave a 2 cm gutter on the right edge of the new sheet so it can sit flush against the first sheet for a side-by-side seam-width read.

RECONCILING THE EOB AND PORTAL BALANCE

Short answer: do not pay the portal balance yet. The EOB is the adjudicated answer for what you actually owe on DOS 10/02/2024 ($35). The portal's $95 is almost certainly a pre-posting figure. Once the clinic receives and posts the insurer's payment and applies its contractual write-off, the portal balance should drop to $35. Paying $95 now risks an overpayment that is slow to refund.

Likely explanations for the $60 gap between $95 and $35:

  (a) Insurance payment not yet posted. The portal status "insurance pending" supports this. Until the clinic posts the insurer's $110 and applies the contractual adjustment, the portal shows the pre-insurance figure.

  (b) Contractual write-off not applied. If the clinic's billed charge exceeded the $145 allowed amount, the difference is supposed to be written off under their contract. If they have not booked that adjustment yet, the gross balance looks larger than the EOB's patient share.

  (c) Multiple CPT lines on the same DOS. The EOB may show only the reassessment line (allowed $145, patient $35). If a second service was rendered and billed the same day (injection, brace, taping, imaging, splint supply), it has its own allowed amount and patient share. $95 could be the reassessment balance plus a second line.

  (d) Patient-responsibility components not split out. EOBs often split patient responsibility into deductible, copay, and coinsurance. Confirm the EOB's breakdown so you can match each piece.

  (e) Prior balance rolled forward. Some portals show a total account balance, not a per-visit balance. A small older underpayment could be lumped in.

IDENTIFIERS AND RECORDS TO COMPARE AND RETAIN

Pull these from each side and line them up side by side:

  Patient and plan
    - Full legal name, date of birth
    - Member ID, group number, plan name (from card and EOB)
    - Subscriber name and relationship, if not self

  Provider and visit
    - Clinic name plus billing entity name (often different)
    - Clinic TIN, rendering provider NPI
    - DOS: 10/02/2024
    - Place of service (e.g., 11 = office)
    - CPT code(s) billed that day
    - ICD-10 diagnosis code(s) on the claim

  Money side, per line and in totals
    - Billed charge (clinic's gross fee)
    - Allowed amount ($145 per EOB)
    - Plan paid ($110)
    - Patient responsibility ($35), broken into deductible / copay / coinsurance
    - Contractual adjustment / provider write-off
    - Claim number and claim status
    - Date insurer processed the claim (10/09/2024)
    - Date the clinic posted the insurance payment
    - Any prior payments or credits on the account

  Documents to keep (paper or PDF, with dates visible)
    - The EOB itself, plus the insurer's remittance advice if sent
    - An itemized statement from the clinic showing CPT, billed, allowed, adjustment, paid, patient balance per line
    - A portal screenshot of the $95 balance and "insurance pending" status, with the date you captured it
    - Any written response from billing (date-stamped email is best)
    - Your insurance card, front and back
    - A one-page reconciliation sheet you update each time

WHAT TO ASK BILLING BEFORE PAYING

Direct these to the clinic's billing department, not the front desk. Ask in writing (patient portal message or email) so there is a record.

  1. "What is the claim number and current status for DOS 10/02/2024 with [insurer]?"
  2. "Have you received the insurance payment for this claim? If not, when do you expect it?"
  3. "Please send an itemized statement showing billed charge, allowed amount, contractual adjustment, insurance payment, and patient balance for each CPT line on this DOS."
  4. "What CPT codes were billed for 10/02/2024? Was anything billed in addition to the reassessment?"
  5. "The EOB shows patient responsibility of $35. Why is the portal showing $95? Is the insurance payment not yet posted, or is the contractual adjustment not yet applied?"
  6. "What is the billed (gross) charge per line, and what is the contractual write-off for my plan?"
  7. "Is the $95 a per-visit balance for 10/02 only, or does it include other account balances? Please split it by DOS."
  8. "When will the portal balance be updated to reflect the EOB?"
  9. "If I pay $95 now and the corrected balance is $35, how is the overpayment refunded and how long does it take?"
  10. "Can you confirm in writing that no further patient balance will be billed for DOS 10/02/2024 once the EOB is fully posted?"

If billing cannot or will not answer 1 through 3 in writing within a reasonable window, call your insurer's member services and ask them to confirm the claim was paid to the provider on the date shown on the EOB. That protects you if the clinic later claims it never received the insurance payment.

DECISION RULE

Until the clinic confirms in writing that $95 is the correct patient balance after insurance posting, treat the EOB's $35 as authoritative for this DOS. Do not pay $95. Do not pay $35 yet either. The cleanest sequence is:

Chain at 0.75% is at the standard replace line on a Park CC-2/CC-3/CC-4. A stretched chain rides deeper into the cassette teeth than designed, and the middle sprockets wear fastest because that's the range you spend the most time in. Visible hooking on those cogs that lines up with your reported skip is the textbook wear pattern — and it's specifically why a new chain alone would still skip on a hooked cassette (correct pitch on already-scalloped teeth). The shop's other checks rule out misalignment as a contributor, so chain + cassette together is correct, and the adjustment + road test close the loop.

Pickup test — about 5 minutes in the parking lot:

  1. Quick link. Tug the master-link plates side to side; no play, no exposed pin. This is the failure that strands you on the road.
  2. Full-cassette sweep, light pedal. Pedal slowly and shift one click at a time from largest cog to smallest and back. Every shift should land with a small click — no hesitation, grind, or clunk.
  3. Front shift if you have one. Big ring to small and back, briefly unloading while it moves.
  4. Loaded skip test in the middle of the cassette. In a mid cog (not the easiest), stand and push moderately hard for 5–6 pedal strokes. No skip or tick under load.
  5. Cross-chain indexing. Big ring + largest three cogs, then small ring + smallest three cogs, quick shifts both ways. Indexing errors show up at the extremes first.
  6. Downshift under load. Ride at moderate speed in a mid gear and drop 2–3 cogs in one sweep, like approaching a hill. Should drop cleanly, no slam.
  7. Slow upshift. Roll at walking pace in an easy gear and shift up one click at a time. Catches indexing problems that hide at speed.
  8. Brakes. One firm squeeze each lever at standstill; firm, no sponge. Roll and listen for rub.

If anything hesitates or skips, ask for another indexing adjustment before you pay. Once it's clean, ride home conservatively for the first few miles: avoid mashing the biggest gear, listen for any tick under load, and re-check shifting after 10–15 minutes once everything's warmed and stretched to working position.

Short answer: that rotation is a shape problem, not an adjustment problem. The 2-finger fit and the closed clasp already confirm the circumference is right; what you're seeing is the chest piece sliding off the bony sternum onto softer tissue, and the fur line is the strap edge-loading instead of lying flat. Tightening the chest strap further will not stop the rotation and will probably make the armpit pressure worse on an outdoor walk, where the thin skin under the front leg is one of the first places a harness causes a real abrasion. I'd treat this as a likely return.

Here is the indoor test that separates the two cases cleanly. Run it before you decide.

THE 5-MINUTE SYMMETRY TEST

Setup (2 min)
  - Put the harness on and settle it so the chest strap sits roughly centered between the two armpits, perpendicular to the spine, with no twist in the webbing.
  - Confirm the 2-finger fit at neck and chest. Mark the starting position of the chest strap with a small piece of masking tape on the strap itself (or take a top-down photo from directly above Kibo while you hold him still for a second).
  - Note which side the leash D-ring sits on.

Movement phase (5 min, indoors, leashed but no pulling)
  - Walk Kibo at a normal pace in a straight line for about 1 minute.
  - Then in a slow figure-eight for about 1 minute (this stresses lateral strap movement).
  - Then sit, down, sit, shake (each paw) — this stresses vertical strap migration.
  - Then a calm 1-2 minute loose-lead walk.

Read the harness and Kibo (do this immediately after)
  - Position drift: did the chest strap end up closer to one armpit than where it started? By how much (use the tape mark / the photo)?
  - Twist: is the webbing flat, or has it folded/rolled onto its edge?
  - Fur: any new compression line, especially along the inner edge of the chest strap or in the armpit fold?
  - Skin: any pinkness, especially in the armpit or behind the elbow? (Part the fur and look.)
  - Behavior: is Kibo trying to back out, freeze, scratch at the strap, or shake the harness off?

WHAT KEEPS IT IN THE "ADJUSTABLE" COLUMN
  - Position drift is small (under about 1 cm / half an inch) and symmetric.
  - No twist, no new fur line, no pink skin.
  - Kibo moves normally and isn't trying to remove it.

If any of those fail, before you return it, try these in order and re-run the same 5-minute test after each:

  1. Reseat the chest strap higher on the sternum (1-2 cm toward the throat). The bony prominence of the breastbone is what "catches" a Y-front chest piece; if the strap is sitting below it, it has nowhere to anchor.
  2. Try the harness on backwards, if the design allows it. On some step-in harnesses, reversing puts the chest piece at a different angle that better matches a narrower-front chest.
  3. Switch which D-ring you clip the leash to (front chest ring vs back ring). Force direction matters for whether the chest piece wants to slide sideways.
  4. Check for a half-twist in the webbing itself — a twisted strap will rotate under load even on a correctly shaped harness.

DECISION RULE

  - If after the above tweaks the chest strap still drifts toward one armpit, still edge-loads (leaves a fur line), or Kibo is actively trying to remove it: return it. The chest piece is the wrong shape for Kibo's chest, and that won't change with adjustment.
  - If the strap stays centered, lies flat, leaves no line, and Kibo ignores it: it's an adjustable fit.

WHY NOT WALK OUTDOORS WITH THE CURRENT STATE

  - The flattened fur line means the strap is already edge-loading. Outdoor walking adds pulling, sniffing lunges, and faster direction changes — all of which amplify edge-loading.
  - The armpit is exactly where real harness injuries start: thin skin, high motion, often where fur is sparsest. A 10-minute calm indoor test already produced a fur line; a 30-minute outdoor walk can produce actual abrasion.
  - A rotated chest strap also lets the whole harness migrate forward, which puts the neck strap closer to the trachea. Not a concern for a calm indoor test, but a real concern if Kibo pulls on a walk or lunges at something.

If you want, tell me the harness brand/model and roughly Kibo's chest shape (narrow and deep, or wider/barrel?) and I can suggest a shape category (Y-front vs H-back vs step-in) that usually fits the rotation pattern you're describing.

SKY STUDY — WASH-ANGLE VARIATION
(holds: one-firm-blot, 20s edge-touch, one-touch. varies: paper tilt only)

GRID
One sheet. 4 cells, ~3"x4". A 1x4 horizontal strip keeps the gravity axis consistent across cells — direct comparison is cleaner than a 2x2.

THE VARIABLE — paper tilt per cell
  A  0°  (flat)
  B  ~7° (gentle)
  C  ~15° (moderate)
  D  ~30° (steep)

CONSTANTS — every cell, every wash
  Same paper, same pigment load (sky mix), same brush.
  Pre-wash blot: ONE firm blot only.
  Edge protocol: 20s hold, ONE touch, no return.
  Sheen-dull wait before each wash. No return-to-wet once the wash is down.

THE TWO WASHES (sequential, wet-on-dry)
  1. Sky base — full cell, at the cell's tilt. Let dry fully.
  2. Horizon band — lower third, slightly deeper value, at the SAME tilt. Let dry.

WHY WET-ON-DRY
Removes "timing of the second wash" as a confound. If you went wet-on-wet, angle and timing would co-vary and you couldn't read the result.

RECORD PER CELL
  - Distribution: even / gradient / pooled / streaked
  - Edge character: sharp / soft / bled
  - Depth top→bottom
  - Blooms: should be 0 — if not, protocol slipped, note it
  - Sky character in one phrase ("still", "settled", "raked", "torn")

WHAT IT ISOLATES
Whether wash angle alone — with moisture, pressure, and timing held — produces a learnable, repeatable difference in sky character. Answers: is tilt a reliable tool in your kit, or does it get swallowed by other variables?

HUMAN AGENT-MINUTES (concurrent stack, auto=0):

  Agent A — 09:18–09:38 ........... 20 min
  Agent A — 09:48–10:02 ........... 14 min
                                 ----------
  Agent A total                      34 min

  Agent B — 09:30–09:45 ........... 15 min
                                 ----------
  Summed agent-min ................. 49 min

  (Overlap window where both A and B are on the case: 09:30–09:38 = 8 min. That 8 min is counted twice — once for A, once for B — because the metric is labor expended, not "wall-clock with an agent attached.")

ELAPSED CUSTOMER-BLOCKED-TIME (wall-clock, auto=0):

  Start:  09:10  customer reports blocked
  End:    10:02  customer confirms cleared
                                 ----------
  Elapsed                          52 min

HOW THE OVERLAP IS TREATED:

  Per the 10/15 data dictionary (Owen + CS): agent-min is a *concurrent stack* — overlapping agent intervals are summed, not unioned. Two agents working the same case for the same 8 minutes represents two units of labor, not one. That is why 09:30–09:38 is double-counted (in A's 20 and B's 15). Elapsed customer-blocked is wall-clock and is therefore indifferent to how many agents are touching the case at once — it runs from report to resolution regardless.

WHY THE AUTOMATED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT CONTRIBUTES NOTHING:

  Two independent reasons, both anchored in the data dict (auto=0 on both fields):

  1. Agent-min is defined as human labor only. The 09:10 auto-ack is a system event with no human minutes behind it, so it is excluded from the numerator by definition — not because it is short, but because it is not human.

  2. Customer-blocked is a wall-clock duration between two human-anchored endpoints (report → confirmation). The auto-ack neither starts the clock (the customer's report does) nor stops it (the customer's confirmation does), so it does not move either endpoint and cannot shorten the interval. Even if it had fired five minutes late, the wall-clock figure would be unchanged.

  The two fields are deliberately not collapsed: agent-min (49) measures labor, elapsed (52) measures customer experience, and a gap between them is normal and expected.

Stored customer name: Acme Dev Shop

WHAT THE NOTICE CONFIRMS

This is the standard Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) excerpt — the kind plans are required to mail by September 30 for the coming year. It confirms three concrete changes effective January 1, 2025:

  Monthly premium:   $14.20 (2024) -> $28.90 (2025)  -> +$176.40/yr on premium alone
  Annual deductible: $545 (2024)   -> $590 (2025)    -> +$45/yr
  Preferred pharmacy network is changing for 2025.

It also explicitly states — by federal requirement — that the figures shown are NOT a personalized estimate of Mom's total annual prescription cost.

Fixed-cost floor of the increase: roughly +$221/year before any change in what she actually pays at the pharmacy counter.

WHAT THE NOTICE DOES NOT ESTABLISH

The ANOC excerpt tells you almost nothing about what Mom will actually spend in 2025. It does not establish:

  - Whether each of her current medications is on the 2025 formulary
  - What tier each drug sits in, or the copay / coinsurance per fill
  - Whether her current pharmacy is still preferred, in-network, or out-of-network
  - Any prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity-limit changes
  - Whether she'll pass through the deductible phase and when
  - Coverage-gap ("donut hole") impact — does she reach it?
  - Whether she hits the catastrophic phase or the new $2,000 out-of-pocket cap
  - Mail-order pricing for her specific drugs
  - Insulin or vaccine cost-sharing (separate rules, see below)
  - Late-enrollment penalty status or IRMAA (income-related) adjustments
  - Eligibility for "Extra Help" (Low-Income Subsidy), which can wipe out premium and most copays
  - Whether a tiering exception would lower her cost for any specific drug

2025 PART D RULES WORTH KNOWING DURING THE COMPARISON

These apply regardless of plan and change the math:

  - $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap on Part D drugs (new for 2025 under the IRA).
    Once she spends $2,000 in true out-of-pocket costs, covered drugs are $0 for the rest of the year.
  - $35/month cap on insulin (no deductible applies to that $35).
  - $0 cost-sharing on ACIP-recommended adult vaccines (shingles, Tdap, RSV, COVID, flu, etc.) on any Part D plan.
  - Medicare Prescription Payment Plan (M3P): she can opt in to spread monthly drug costs across the year instead of paying large sums early. Useful if January–March costs would otherwise spike.

DOCUMENTS TO PULL BEFORE COMPARING

  1. Mom's current medication list — drug name, strength, dose, frequency, quantity per fill, prescribing doctor.
  2. Her current preferred pharmacy — name and address — and a backup she might use.
  3. Year-to-date 2024 Explanation of Benefits (EOBs) or a portal printout showing what she's actually paid so far in 2024, drug by drug.
  4. The full 2025 ANOC (not just the premium/deductible excerpt) — usually 20+ pages, includes tier changes and pharmacy network changes.
  5. 2025 Summary of Benefits — one-page overview of copay tiers and rules.
  6. 2025 Formulary (drug list) — searchable; the plan's website should have it.
  7. 2025 Pharmacy Directory — preferred vs. standard vs. out-of-network for her pharmacy.
  8. 2025 Evidence of Coverage — full benefit document; the Summary of Benefits + Formulary is usually enough unless she's hitting edge cases.
  9. CMS Star Rating for each plan she's considering (1–5 stars; quality + complaint + member-experience measures).
  10. Her current plan's 2024 total drug spend (annualized) — baseline for comparison.
  11. Any "Extra Help" / LIS award letter if she's ever applied; or her current income/assets if she hasn't but might qualify.

QUESTIONS TO VERIFY, DRUG BY DRUG AND PHARMACY BY PHARMACY

  - Is each medication on the 2025 formulary? If yes, which tier? Tier 1 generics are usually $0–$5; tiers 3–5 are where surprises live.
  - What's the copay (or coinsurance %) for a 30-day retail fill? A 90-day mail-order fill?
  - Any prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limit on any of her drugs? If so, is her doctor likely to satisfy it easily?
  - Is her current pharmacy still in-network, and is it still in the *preferred* tier (cheaper copays)?
  - What is the cheapest in-network pharmacy for her specific drug mix? (Big-box stores and grocery pharmacies aren't all preferred.)
  - Will she realistically hit the 2025 deductible in 2025? On what date? (That affects January–March cash flow.)
  - Will she realistically hit the $2,000 OOP cap? If yes, the cap and the payment plan both matter.
  - Does she use insulin? If yes, confirm $35 cap applies regardless of tier/phase.
  - Are any of her vaccines due? Those should be $0 with an in-network pharmacy or provider.
  - If any drug is non-preferred or high-tier, ask the prescriber whether a therapeutically equivalent alternative sits on a lower tier.
  - Has her pharmacy changed ownership or franchise affiliation recently? That can silently move it in or out of preferred status.

TIMELINE TO KEEP IN MIND

  Now through mid-November: pull the documents above, build the medication list, and use Medicare's Plan Finder (medicare.gov/plan-compare) with the drug list + pharmacy + dosage to get a side-by-side projected annual cost for each candidate plan.

  Compare three views, not just premium: total estimated annual cost, deductible + copay trajectory, and worst-case (if she adds a new drug mid-year).

  December 7, 2024: open-enrollment deadline for a January 1, 2025 effective date. After that, she generally can't switch Part D plans for 2025 unless she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period.

  January 1, 2025: any new plan starts; first fill under the new network rules happens here. If she's switching and her old drug requires transition, the new plan is required to provide a one-time transition fill (typically 30 days) so she's not without medication on day one.

ONE PRACTICAL SUGGESTION

Before she compares, calculate her 2024 total out-of-pocket for drugs (premium + deductible paid + copays). That number is the baseline. The 2025 plan comparison only makes sense as "2025 estimated cost vs. 2024 actual cost + the +$221 floor increase." Without the 2024 actual, the new plan looks free or expensive for reasons that aren't real.

The two-finger rule at neck and chest, the centered 10-minute walk, and the firm clasp all check out. The clearance behind the front legs is the spec point you're failing, and on a Y-front the belly strap's vertical position is mostly a geometry fact, not an adjustment fact. The chest and back straps control tension and rotational stability; the belly band sits where the panel's bottom edge puts it. On most Y-fronts the belly strap anchors at a single fixed point on the back panel, so there's no geometric adjustment available. A few models do offer two anchor points — if yours has one, the lower setting is worth trying before you give up on it. Otherwise: loosening the chest strap might drop the band a half-inch, but it also frees the panel to migrate, which is what made the medium rotate toward the armpit in the first place. Honest read: adjustment alone is unlikely to deliver the full two inches without re-creating the failure mode you just replaced. The harness is probably the wrong shape for Kibo, not the wrong size.

The indoor tests that actually discriminate usable from return-now:

1. The trot test. A walk masks strap interference because the foreleg only sweeps back a few inches. At a comfortable trot the elbow extends fully and the back of the forearm passes right under the belly strap. Trot Kibo for 30–40 paces on a flat surface, then watch his near-side foreleg in profile as it comes forward. A hitch, a high-stepping lift, or the strap visibly catching and snapping forward as the leg extends means the geometry is wrong — return.

2. The figure-8 / tight-turn test. Walk him in figure-8s at normal pace. The previous medium failed under torsional load. If this one shifts more than about a centimeter off-center on tight turns, the chest panel isn't seated deep enough to hold position.

3. The 20-minute friction check. Walk or trot for 20 minutes, then slide two fingers under the belly strap at the contact patch behind the foreleg. Skin should feel cool and dry, same as the surrounding area. Any warmth, dampness, or a faint pink line means friction heating is starting — that's what becomes raw by mile three on a real hike. This is the single most predictive test for outdoor use.

4. The paw-offer. With Kibo standing, gently lift a front paw and fold it under as if he's offering it. The strap should not bind or visibly press into the armpit crease. Repeat a few times on both sides.

5. The sustained gentle pull. Hold a leash with light steady tension — the kind you'd have on a loose-leash walk — for a minute while he stands. The strap should not migrate up into the armpit under that load.

Decision rule: pass 1, 2, 4, and 5 cleanly, and the friction check comes back cool and dry after 20 minutes — usable for outdoor walks. Fail any one of them, especially the friction check — return before the first outdoor walk.

If it fails, the pattern (medium rotated, this one sitting too high at the correct chest girth) is telling you the issue isn't size, it's that this model assumes a chest shape Kibo doesn't have. Worth measuring his chest depth — sternum to belly at the deepest point — and looking at deep-chest or sighthound-cut harnesses rather than the next size up.

The auto-stop is keyed to customer-correction conditions, not to opt-outs. It exists to prevent compounding an error already made — e.g., halting further sends once a false statement has gone out so it isn't repeated, or pausing before another duplicate is created against the same account. 35° wick-cadence study

What varies (only): how many times the lower bead is wicked during the 20-second touch.
What stays fixed: 35° tilt, one-firm-blot brush condition, 20-second touch, one-touch rule, paper, pigment + dilution, brush, water, wick tool and method, room session.

Levels — frequency of wick, evenly spaced inside the 20s and all centered at the 10s midpoint so position is not a confound:
  A.  0 wicks — reproduces your current failure (baseline)
  B.  1 wick at 10s
  C.  2 wicks at 7s and 13s
  D.  3 wicks at 5s, 10s, 15s

3 trials per level = 12 strips on one sheet. Drop level A if you want 9; you'll lose the failure-baseline anchor but keep the comparison.

Setup
  - One sheet of your usual paper, taped flat.
  - 12 strips about 2 in wide, randomized order across levels (e.g. B1, C2, D3, A1, C1, A2, D1, B3, A3, D2, B2, C3) so any drift in humidity or pigment freshness does not bias one level.
  - Same pigment and dilution as the failing wash.
  - One brush, re-loaded and re-blotted to the same condition before every strip.
  - Pick one wick implement — damp brush tip, tissue, or roller — and use it identically every time: same direction, same pressure, same contact length. Write the choice and method once at the top of the page; do not change it mid-study.

Per strip
  1. Load and one-firm-blot.
  2. Set board at 35° (verify against the board edge with a protractor or angle app, not the paper — paper can sag).
  3. Apply brush; start the stopwatch on contact.
  4. At the prescribed times, wick the lower bead with the dedicated tool. Do not re-touch the wash.
  5. Lift at 20s; dry flat.

Record per strip (after dry, raking light from the side)
  - Photo.
  - Cauliflower edge count.
  - Backrun length into the drying wash, mm.
  - Edge uniformity 0–3 (0 clean line, 3 heavy broken bloom).
  - Any anomaly — paper flaw, accidental re-touch, blot variability, timer slip.

Pick a winner: cleanest edge and shortest backrun across the three trials at that level. Tie-break toward fewer wicks — less cadence means fewer chances for an accidental re-touch to sneak in.

Optional confirmation strip, separate from the 12
  Re-run the winning cadence at 15°. If it still wins there, you have isolated cadence as the lever. If 15° looks better with a different cadence, angle and cadence interact and the instructor will want both numbers at once.

Workstation cleanup + update prep — sequenced for safety. Run steps in order; do not skip the verification gates.

Today's date: 2024-10-26. Last full backup: 2024-10-19 (7-day gap, so current Desktop state is not yet captured).

Target math:
  Start free:        19 GB
  Need:              27 GB
  Gap:                8 GB minimum
  Target with buffer: ~35 GB free (OS updates sometimes double-dip)


STEP 0 — Inventory before touching anything
  - Open Settings → Storage → show breakdown per folder.
  - Sort Desktop by date modified and flag every file/folder modified after 2024-10-19.
    Anything in that window is "new since backup" and gets the strictest handling.
  - Note the largest 5 items in Downloads. Do not delete anything yet.


STEP 1 — Back up the unbacked window (newest first)
  - Open your corporate backup client (OneDrive for Business, SharePoint sync, or
    whatever IT issued). Confirm it points to a company-managed destination —
    not a personal Google/Dropbox/iCloud account. Company data must stay in the
    company boundary.
  - Force-sync the post-2024-10-19 Desktop items to that destination. This is a
    "delta" backup covering the gap, not a fresh full backup.
  - For active Helio analyses specifically: move them into a synced workspace
    folder (e.g., OneDrive for Business / SharePoint / Google Drive enterprise
    under your Helio tenant). Synced folders are backed up by definition AND
    accessible from other devices, which is the correct long-term home for
    active analysis files. Local Desktop is the wrong place for them.


STEP 2 — Verify the backup before any deletion (do not skip)
  Three checks; all three must pass:
  (a) Sync status: backup client reports "files up to date" / green check, and
      the timestamp on the destination copy matches "after sync completed".
  (b) Spot-check integrity: pick 2-3 of the largest Desktop Helio files.
      Compare file size on local vs destination. They must match exactly.
      Open one CSV or render one image to confirm it is not corrupt.
  (c) Test-restore: use your backup tool's "restore" or "download" function on
      one file to a temporary folder. Confirm checksum/size match and the file
      opens correctly. Then delete the test-restore copy.
  Only proceed if all three pass. If any fail, stop and re-sync before going
  further.


STEP 3 — Low-risk cleanups (no backup needed; safe to delete)
  These are regenerable caches, not data:
  - Video-call cache (Teams / Zoom): clear from inside the app's settings
    ("Clear cache" or delete the cache folder).  ~6 GB freed.
  - Recycle Bin: empty it.                                         ~variable
  - Windows Temp: Disk Cleanup → "Temporary files" → tick all.
    Or delete C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Temp contents (skip files in use). ~1-3 GB
  - Windows Update cache: Disk Cleanup → "Clean up system files" →
    "Windows Update Cleanup". This alone often frees 2-5 GB and is the
    single most useful action before a feature update.

  Running free so far: ~30-32 GB. You are already past the 27 GB threshold.


STEP 4 — Downloads triage (4 GB pool, mixed risk)
  Sort by date. Categorize each item into one of three buckets:
  - Keep: anything still referenced by active work, recent installers you may
    need again, source files for ongoing projects.
  - Move to managed workspace: archived work files older than ~30 days that
    you want to retain but no longer need locally. Same rule as Desktop —
    company-managed destination only.
  - Delete: old installers whose apps are already installed, duplicate copies,
    obviously stale downloads. These are safe to delete after Step 2 passed.

  Expected free: 3-4 GB if you move or delete most of Downloads.


STEP 5 — Move (do not delete) the active Helio Desktop exports
  This is the 9 GB Helio block. The rule you set: do not delete blindly.
  Correct action is MOVE, not delete:
  - Cut the Helio analysis folders from Desktop.
  - Paste into your synced company workspace (same destination as Step 1).
  - Wait for sync to complete and re-run Step 2's spot-check on those folders.
  - Only after sync confirms every byte is at the destination, the local copies
    on Desktop are freed. You do not need to manually delete; cutting +
    pasting + sync achieves the same result as "delete after backup" but with
    stronger guarantees.

  Expected free after Step 5: ~38-40 GB.


STEP 6 — Re-check space
  Settings → Storage. Confirm free space is well above 27 GB before starting
  the update. If short, the likely culprits in order are: a leftover hibernation
  file (powercfg /h off, then reboot), user AppData caches, or shadow storage
  (vssadmin list shadowstorage). Each can free 1-5 GB.


STEP 7 — Run the OS update
  Plug in power. Close heavy apps. Start the update. Do not interrupt.


STEP 8 — Post-update verification
  - Boot cleanly, confirm update version.
  - Open one of the moved Helio CSV/image files from the synced workspace to
    confirm it is reachable.
  - Confirm Desktop is clean of the moved folders (they live in workspace now).
  - Schedule the next full backup if your client does not auto-run.


Key safety properties of this sequence:
  1. No Helio file is deleted before it exists verified-intact in a managed
     company destination.
  2. The active Helio analyses end up better protected than they were (synced
     workspace vs. local Desktop) — this is a permanent improvement, not just
     a one-off space grab.
  3. The 27 GB threshold is crossed by Step 3 alone, before any Helio file is
     touched. Steps 4 and 5 are for buffer and long-term hygiene, not for
     hitting the minimum.
  4. All cleanups use company-managed destinations; no personal cloud accounts,
     no data crossing the company boundary.

If anything in Steps 1-2 does not behave as expected (backup client error,
sync stuck, file size mismatch), stop. Do not proceed to deletion. Post the
specific symptom and I can narrow down the next move.

Practical plan below — organized so you can work through it once and not think about it again until 5:30pm.

PRE-EVENT (do this before 5:30pm if you can)

- Leashed potty walk earlier than usual — aim for 4:45-5:00pm, before foot traffic builds. Short sniff walk, not a run. Goal is empty bladder/bowls and a little mental fatigue, not extra adrenaline.
- Feed his normal dinner at the regular time so he's not hungry at peak stress.
- Fresh water available but not overfilled — heavy panting + sloshing water = mess he has to lie in.
- Save two numbers in your phone NOW, not at 8pm: (1) your regular vet's after-hours line, (2) the nearest 24-hour emergency hospital with address and drive time.
- Optional but worth it: ASPCA Animal Poison Control 888-426-4435 (fee applies). Halloween chocolate, xylitol gum, raisins, and THC edibles are a parallel risk to the noise — keep the candy bowl out of his reach and the door completely closed.

THE RETREAT ROOM (rear bedroom)

This is your whole plan. The bedroom is the right choice — farthest from the front door, smallest window exposure, no street view.

- Move his normal bed in. His scent on it matters more than a "better" bed. Add an unwashed t-shirt of yours and his usual blanket.
- Close the door. Close curtains/blinds fully. If the room has a window facing the street, cover it with a blanket too.
- White noise on before 5:30pm — a box fan is the most reliable; a podcast or brown-noise app at low volume works if no fan.
- Dim lighting. Comfortable temperature (heavy panting = overheating risk).
- If he has a crate and already loves it for longer stretches, use it. If he's only ever been crated briefly, don't introduce one now — the bed on the floor is safer.

DOOR MANAGEMENT (this is the single biggest variable)

You do not need to answer the door. Plan to not answer the door.

- Put a sign on the front door, posted by 5:00pm: "Happy Halloween — please take one (or zero). No doorbell needed, thanks!"
- Add a bowl of candy on the porch with the sign so trick-or-treaters don't knock.
- Mute or disable the doorbell if you can (most smart doorbells have a quiet mode; a wedge under a wired chime works too).
- Porch light off is fine — the sign does the work.

DURING (5:30-9:30pm)

- Stay in the retreat room with him. Your presence is the largest anxiolytic you actually have. Don't bounce out to grab candy or check the door.
- High-value, long-lasting items to keep his mouth busy: a stuffed frozen Kong, a lick mat with peanut butter or wet food, a frozen toppl. Hand-feed small pieces if he'll take them — licking/chewing is self-soothing.
- A safe long chew if he has one he actually settles with. Skip rawhide if he's a gulper.
- If he hides in a corner, let him. Don't pull him out. Sit on the floor nearby and read or scroll — your calm presence is the message.
- If he leans into you, slow chest pressure or steady hand on his side is fine. Low voice, slow exhale audible so he can match it.

DO NOT

- Don't bring him to the door to "show him it's fine." It won't be.
- Don't fit-test a thunder shirt tonight. Pressure without prior familiarization increases anxiety in many dogs.
- Don't leave him alone in the retreat room during the 7:00-9:00pm peak — that's when escape attempts and panic escalations happen.
- Don't scold trembling, panting, or hiding. It's physiology, not misbehavior.

Here's a sequence that keeps the folder intact, postpones the update until protection is real, and never touches personal storage. The phases are ordered so the cheap/zero-risk steps run first and the bigger commitments (disk space for a duplicate, OS update itself) only run after verification.

PHASE 1 — INVENTORY + INTEGRITY BASELINE (zero disk cost, do this first)
  - Record the folder's top-level layout: subfolder names, file count, total size, last-modified timestamps at the folder root. Output goes to a small text file outside Desktop/Helio-Q4 (e.g., your home directory), so the inventory survives even if the folder is later touched.
  - Generate a sha256 manifest: one hash per file, written as a text file in the same safe location. This is metadata only — no company data leaves the device, and the manifest itself is tiny (KB-scale).
  - You now have detection: anything that changes size, mtime, or hash between now and the OS update will be visible. That alone is enough reason to do Phase 1 even if you skip everything below.

PHASE 2 — LOCAL READ-ONLY ARCHIVE (optional, only if you have disk headroom)
  - Create a tar or zip of Desktop/Helio-Q4 to a directory OUTSIDE that folder, on the same managed device. A compressed archive is usually 50–80% of the original size — figure ~4–6 GB for 6.8 GB of mixed exports and images. If the space you freed for the OS update can't absorb that, skip this phase; the manifest in Phase 1 plus IT's response is enough to bridge.
  - Mark the archive read-only (chmod 444 on Unix; lock attribute on macOS). Do NOT mark the original folder read-only — you still need to work in it.
  - Verify the archive by extracting to a temp location and re-running sha256, then diffing against the Phase 1 manifest. If any hash mismatches, the archive is bad; redo it before trusting it.
  - Same-device managed storage is not "personal storage." Compliance posture is identical to the original folder. The point of this phase is restoration if the OS update or anything else corrupts the originals — not off-device protection.

PHASE 3 — HOLD THE OS UPDATE
  - Do not start the installer. If the update is scheduled or staged, defer or cancel the schedule through system settings — don't just ignore the prompt, since some installers will retry automatically.
  - Keep the disk space you freed intact. Do not refill it with downloads, caches, or new exports until protection is confirmed.
  - Note the IT ticket reference alongside the deferral so the audit trail is one place, not three.

PHASE 4 — WAIT ON IT, ON A REASONABLE CADENCE
  - The ticket is open and asking the right question; you don't need to chase it hourly.
  - Re-check ticket status roughly once per business day. When IT responds with an approved managed destination, follow their exact path — including any naming conventions, share permissions, or DLP tagging they specify. Do not improvise a parallel route.

PHASE 5 — PRE-UPDATE VERIFICATION GATE (only after one of these is true)
  - The backup client now reports Desktop/Helio-Q4 (or its managed-destination equivalent) as covered, AND a fresh scan has run, OR
  - IT has confirmed the approved destination and you can see the folder or its current contents reflected there.
  - Then re-run the sha256 manifest against the current state of Desktop/Helio-Q4 and diff against the Phase 1 baseline: same file count, same sizes, same mtimes (or only the mtimes you yourself changed by working in the folder). Any unexplained delta means stop and reconcile before proceeding.
  - Only after the gate clears, start the OS update. After the update completes and the device is stable, re-run the manifest one more time and diff — confirms the update didn't disturb the folder.

TRAPS — things that look like progress but aren't
  - Personal cloud (iCloud personal, Dropbox personal, Google Drive personal, OneDrive personal) — even temporarily, this is data leaving the managed boundary. Don't.
  - Personal USB or external drive, even one labeled "work" — same problem regardless of label.
  - Emailing the archive to a personal address, or to yourself at a personal address — no.
  - Re-running the backup client to "retry" before IT confirms the destination — it may write to the wrong target or simply re-record the exclusion.
  - Editing the backup exclusion list yourself to "fix" it — that's IT's call, and a self-service change to backup scope is its own compliance issue.
  - Deleting originals or "cleaning up" exports to free space — you already freed space; going backward creates data loss with no protection in place.
  - Renaming the folder to dodge the exclusion — moves the problem, doesn't solve it, and may break working-file references your team relies on.

WORKING IN THE FOLDER MEANWHILE
  - Fine. Reading and editing active cohort exports and working images does not change the protection question; the hold is specifically on the OS update and on any movement of the folder off the managed device.

If Phase 1 runs cleanly and IT's response lands within a business day or two, you can usually skip Phase 2 and proceed straight to the Phase 5 gate. If IT will take longer than you'd like, the local archive in Phase 2 is the only restoration option that respects the no-personal-storage line, and it's worth the disk space.

## Case HST-1048 — Worked Values

**Human intervals (the three agent segments):**
- Agent A, segment 1: 1:32pm–2:07pm = 35 min
- Agent A, segment 2: 2:40pm–3:00pm = 20 min
- Agent B: 2:05pm–2:25pm = 20 min

**Overlap check (between A1 and B):** A1 ends 2:07, B starts 2:05 → 2 min of double-coverage. A2 (2:40–3:00) does not overlap B.

**Union of human work** (the field value):
- 1:32pm–2:25pm (A1 + B merged) = 53 min
- 2:40pm–3:00pm (A2) = 20 min
- **Human agent-minutes = 73 min**

If you summed naively (35 + 20 + 20 = 75), you'd be double-counting the 2 minutes where Agents A and B were both on the case.

**Customer-blocked-elapsed (wall-clock, auto=0):**
- 1:10pm–3:20pm = 2h 10m = **130 min**

## How the Overlap Is Treated — and Why Auto Contributes Zero

**Concurrent human work is unioned, not summed per-agent.** The human agent-minutes field measures *customer-facing staffed coverage*, not total labor input. Two agents working the same ticket at the same instant is one minute of staffed coverage, not two — the customer's experience is a single minute of being actively worked. Counting it per-agent would inflate the metric whenever the queue hands off mid-conversation and would let us "buy" a better number just by adding bodies during overlap windows. Taking the union of the intervals keeps the field honest as a coverage/responsiveness measure and is exactly the "concurrent, auto=0" definition Customer Success locked in for the diagnostic data dictionary.

**The 1:10pm automated acknowledgement contributes nothing — to either field.** Per the same dictionary, both human agent-minutes and customer-blocked-elapsed carry auto=0: automated touches are excluded by construction. The auto-ack is a system event fired the instant the case opened; it is not a human action, so it can't count toward human agent-minutes, and it is auto-classified, so it can't count toward the blocking-elapsed wall-clock window either. (The blocked window already starts at 1:10pm — the auto-ack is the *trigger* that opens the case, not something inside the window to be summed.)

**The two fields are deliberately not collapsed.** 73 min of human coverage inside a 130-min blocked window tells you staffing density during the incident (humans were actively on the case ~56% of the blocked time); collapsing them into one number would destroy that signal. Hence the data-dict rule: human agent-min ≠ customer-blocked-elapsed, never collapsed — same rule that produced HS-014 = 45+30 rather than a single 75-min figure.

**Final values for HST-1048:**
- Human agent-minutes: **73**
- Customer-blocked-elapsed: **130 min (2h 10m)**

FOOD-SAFETY DECISION — TUESDAY 2024-11-05

1) The cooked chicken and rice: DISCARD.

Reasoning (conservative, no smell/appearance):

- The 46°F reading on Sunday is 6°F above the 40°F danger-zone threshold. Without a reading BEFORE that point, you cannot rule out that the refrigerator was at or above 40°F — possibly much warmer — for some or all of the 2 hr 15 min the food was in it.

- The USDA 2-hour rule (FoodSafety.gov) treats time above 40°F cumulatively. Once that cumulative clock is unprovable, the conservative call for perishable cooked food is discard.

- Cooked rice carries a specific, irreversible risk: Bacillus cereus. Spores survive cooking; if the rice cools slowly through ~130–100°F or is held warm, spores germinate and some strains produce an emetic toxin that is HEAT-STABLE — reheating will not destroy it. Once the toxin forms, cooling does not reverse it.

- Cooked chicken supports Staphylococcus aureus (heat-stable enterotoxin), Salmonella, and Clostridium perfringens. None of these are reliably detected by smell or appearance. The emetic B. cereus toxin from rice is specifically odorless and flavorless.

- The food was in the questionable environment 2 hr 15 min, which is itself over the 2-hour boundary even before any extra warm-up time is assumed. With unknown pre-46°F temperature and zero margin, the answer is discard regardless of how the food looks or smells now.

- Moving the chicken and rice to the cooler at 8:15pm and holding them at ≤38°F does not undo any toxin that may have already formed. Cooler status from 8:15pm onward is not the deciding factor.

What would change the answer: a continuous thermometer log showing the refrigerator interior was ≤40°F from Sunday 6:00pm through 8:15pm. You don't have that log, so the unknown is the deciding factor.

2) What can return to the now-verified-cold (37°F) refrigerator:

- Everything else currently in the ice-filled cooler can go back, provided it has been continuously ≤40°F since being placed there and it is a perishable that tolerates re-chilling (raw meat, poultry, fish, dairy, eggs, other cooked leftovers, opened sauces, cut produce, etc.).

- Anything that stayed inside the refrigerator through the failure window needs a case-by-case rule:
   - Have a continuous log showing ≤40°F → keep.
   - No log → apply the same conservative rule used for the chicken and rice: perishable, high-water-activity, high-protein items (raw meat, poultry, fish, dairy, eggs, cooked leftovers, cut fruit, vegetables in water) should be discarded unless you can document they stayed cold.
   - Shelf-stable items are unaffected by a refrigerator temperature event: unopened canned goods, sealed dry goods, intact whole fruit (apples, potatoes, onions, garlic), hard aged cheese (parmesan, romano), intact uncut melons, whole uncut vegetables, honey, salt, sugar, vinegar, hard alcohol.

- Freezer (1°F, cycling normally): safe. Anything that stayed frozen is fine. Anything that thawed and then sat at room temperature is a separate discard question — you didn't describe any, so I'm assuming frozen items stayed frozen or were refed into the cooler promptly.

Practical next steps:

- Bag the chicken and rice, seal it, and discard. (Sealed so a pet or anyone else doesn't retrieve it.)
- Wipe and dry the cooler before putting it away.
- Relocate the remaining cooler contents to the refrigerator now that it's holding 37°F.
- Going forward, a refrigerator thermometer with min/max memory (e.g., a ThermoPro/Thermoworks digital unit, or a connected SensorPush) gives you the "what was the temp before this reading" answer you lacked on Sunday. An internal fridge thermometer alone reads the current moment; a min/max or logging unit reads the worst moment since you last reset it.

PHASE 8 - POST-UPDATE VERIFICATION AND CLEANUP
  17. After you are back at the desktop, open the managed folder and confirm the reconciled CSV (and at least one sampled image) is still reachable and opens correctly.

  - Do not delete the Desktop copies before the sampled CSV and image still open from the managed folder after sync resume (step 15).

That is the full sequence: pause, hash, backup, copy-overwrite, re-hash, resume sync, re-verify, delete Desktop, run OS update, re-verify reachable, schedule backup, delete temp backup. Salvage for the lifted strip:

1. Mist the lifted area lightly with clean water from a distance, or touch a damp brush to the back of the sheet so moisture wicks through. Goal: relax the raised fibers back down — do not soak the sheet.
2. While damp, coax the strip flat with a clean fingertip or a soft brush. Light touch only; no rubbing.
3. Lay a sheet of glassine or clean scrap paper over it and weight evenly (a few books, light pressure). Dry flat, ideally overnight.
4. Inspect dry. A faint ridge may remain — leave it; do not sand or scrub it out.

If the strip is torn rather than just lifted (a fiber piece is missing), rewetting will not recover it. Mask it as a known defect or rework the edge; do not try to glue fibers back.

Recommended approach: a short bland home-cooked bridge, not a same-brand swap.

Even a small bag of a different kibble is still an unfamiliar protein/fat/fiber mix that Kibo's gut hasn't seen — you'd be trading one abrupt change for another. The bland bridge is the standard short-term veterinary recommendation precisely because it's predictable and easy to digest. A 24-30 hour bridge with a healthy, normally-eating dog is a low-risk move.

Feeding plan (assuming twice-daily feeding — adjust if Kibo eats 3x/day):

1. Monday morning: last portion of regular kibble, normal amount.
2. Monday evening: small bridge portion (~1/3 of normal meal size) to test tolerance.
3. Tuesday morning: full bridge portion at normal meal size.
4. Tuesday afternoon/evening when the shipment arrives: transition back to regular food over 2-3 days — start with ~25% new kibble + 75% bridge, ramp up gradually.

The bland bridge itself:

- Boiled skinless, boneless chicken breast, shredded. Poach in plain water — no oil, butter, salt, or seasoning.
- Plain white rice, cooked in water only.
- Roughly 1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice.
- Serve warm or room temperature.
- Total daily volume should match his regular intake, split across the meals above.
- Keep fresh water available throughout — hydration matters more than the exact food.

Before starting, two quick checks:

- If Kibo has any known chicken or rice sensitivity, swap the protein — plain cooked ground turkey (rinsed/ drained) or scrambled egg work on the same principle. If unsure, a quick call to your regular vet is worth it.
- If he has any chronic condition (kidney disease, pancreatitis, diabetes, food allergies), call the vet before changing meals, even briefly.

Signs that should prompt a vet call during the bridge:

- Any vomiting, especially repeated or non-stop.
- Diarrhea — particularly if watery, frequent, bloody, or black/tarry.
- Refusing food and water for more than 24 hours, or refusing water alone for more than 12.
- Marked lethargy — really not engaging, won't get up, seems dazed.

What you're seeing — fine bubbles, no odor, normal pressure, no particles — is dissolved air from repressurization, not contamination. Cloudiness that settles from the bottom up in a clear glass confirms air (sediment stays suspended). Property-level valve work is also lower-risk than a main break, which is why no boil notice is expected. The flushing plan is mainly to purge air and any stirred-up sediment and to protect your water heater.

FLUSHING SEQUENCE (cold first, hot last)

1.  Remove aerators from the kitchen cold tap and any other cold taps you'll run. Aerators trap sediment.

2.  Kitchen cold tap, full open, no aerator. Run 10–15 minutes, or until a glass filled from it clears from the bottom in under a minute.

3.  Other cold taps, nearest to farthest from the main entry. 3–5 minutes each at full open:
    -   bathroom sinks (cold only)
    -   bathtub cold (full flow, no aerator — moves the most volume)
    -   outdoor spigot if present
    -   fridge water line — dispense 2–3 full glasses; discard the first full batch of ice and let the ice maker refill once clear
    -   washing machine — run a cold rinse cycle empty, then stop once the supply line is flushed

4.  Flush each toilet once or twice by holding the handle down.

5.  Hot side. If the water heater was actually drained during the work, refill it per its startup procedure before opening any hot tap (running hot with an empty heater can burn out an electric element). If it wasn't drained, just flush the hot lines:
    -   one hot tap at a time, run until clear
    -   bathtub hot at full flow is the fastest way to push volume through the heater
    -   expect the first 5–10 minutes to look airier than the cold side

6.  Run the dishwasher empty on a hot rinse cycle to clear its supply line and any stagnant water inside.

7.  Reinstall aerators. If a faucet sputters after reinstallation, pull the aerator again — a particle is likely stuck in it.

8.  Replace the fridge water filter if it's more than 3–4 months old; it almost certainly caught some sediment.

DO NOT USE YET

-   Don't drink, cook with, or brush teeth with tap water until cold lines have run clear, and use your stored water as a conservative buffer for the next 24 hours — especially for anything uncooked (salad washing, ice, drinks).
-   Don't open hot taps for the flushing sequence until the cold lines are clear — sediment pulled into the heater tank can clog the anode or settle in the tank.
-   No Neti pots, no CPAP humidifier, no baby formula with tap water. Stored or boiled only.
-   Skip the washing machine and dishwasher with real loads until you've run them empty.
-   For Kibo: stored water is the right call. Dogs tolerate minor upsets, but post-main-work water can cause transient GI issues. Don't refill the water bowl from the tap yet.
-   Aquariums: disinfectant residual can shift when the system is refilled. Wait 24–48 hours or treat with a water conditioner before topping off.

CALL MAINTENANCE OR STOP USING THE WATER IF YOU SEE

-   Yellow, brown, red, or black tint that doesn't clear after 15–20 minutes of full-open cold flushing
-   Visible grit or particles
-   Any odor other than a faint chlorine smell — musty, sewage, rotten egg, fuel, or chemical all warrant a call
-   Pressure that drops below normal after the initial restoration, or no pressure on a fixture that previously worked
-   Any leak — under sinks, around the water heater, at the meter, on any visible pipe (pressure transients commonly open old joints)
-   A boil-water or do-not-drink notice from the property manager or utility (overrides the whole plan — boil for at least 1 minute, or use stored/bottled)
-   Cloudiness that returns hours later after clearing
-   Metallic taste that persists after the water visually clears
-   Anyone in the household — you, Sam, or Kibo — develops GI symptoms within a day or two of using the water

If the kitchen tap settles to fully clear within the next few minutes of running and nothing else develops, you're in the benign-air category and can finish the sequence today.

Bottom line: do not ride this bike, even a short distance. An 8 mm sidewall cut with exposed casing is structural failure waiting to happen. Sidewalls flex on every rotation; once casing cords are cut, the cut propagates under load and the tube can blow out without warning. The fact that the tube is still holding pressure is not a safety signal — tire integrity and tube integrity are separate questions, and the tire is the failed component here. Blowouts on rear tires cause sudden loss of traction and crashes.

Safe sequence before you leave with the bike:

1. Photo first, deflate second. Once pressure is off, the cut changes shape and you lose the "as-found" record. With the tire still inflated:
   - Straight-on shot of the cut, with a coin or ruler in frame for scale.
   - Sidewall shot wide enough to read the tire size marking (something like "700x32c" or "27.5x2.2") and the brand/model.
   - One shot with your thumb gently pressing the cut open, to show depth and how much the casing is exposed.
   - One shot of the tread on the same tire for wear reference, and the front tire for comparison.

2. Mark the cut location so you can show the shop tech without re-finding it. A small piece of masking tape stuck to the rim near the valve or on the sidewall opposite the cut is enough.

3. Release all the air. If you have a valve-core tool, unscrew the core and let it hiss out; otherwise press the valve and let it drain. Don't pry the cut open to "let air out faster" — you're just enlarging the injury.

4. Leave the tube in place, uninflated. Don't pull the tire off the rim in the parking area unless you have a clean surface and a spare tube; you don't want to introduce a second problem.

5. Transport. Rideshare or transit with the wheel still on the bike is fine. If you're worried about the rim getting bumped, shift the chain to the largest cog so the derailleur hangs safely, and if you have a frame strap or bungee, secure the front wheel so it doesn't pivot. Lay the bike rear-wheel-up on its saddle and bars only if the bike is clean enough — otherwise just wheel it. The wheel does not need to come off for this.

What to send the shop when you message them (text or photos):

  - Tire size as printed on the sidewall (the marking I mentioned above).
  - Bike model and year if you know it; otherwise a photo of the head tube or top tube decal.
  - Tubeless or tubed, and if tubed, what tube type (presta vs. schrader — visible at the valve).
  - How long the tire has been on and roughly how many miles, if you have any idea.
  - Riding surface (mostly road, gravel, mixed).
  - The four photos from step 1.
  - One sentence describing the failure mode: "Sidewall cut, ~8 mm, casing visible, cut opens under finger pressure, tube still holding air as of this morning."
  - Ask whether they have your tire in stock or can order it, and whether they recommend replacing the tube at the same time (you usually should — once a tube has been pinched by a sidewall breach it's considered compromised even if it's currently fine).

Realistic outcome: that tire is done. A sidewall cut with visible casing is not patchable; the sidewall has no tread cap to bridge it and patches there don't survive. Plan on a new tire and a new tube, and expect the shop to also want to inspect the rim for any damage from whatever caused the cut in the first place.

Conservative at-home care for a superficial pad scrape — what you described sounds appropriate for home management, with clear escalation triggers below.

CLEANING (first day, then once daily until healed)

- Cool water rinse first to flush any remaining grit; lukewarm is fine if the paw has been out in cold air.
- Clean with dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% (the blue liquid, light blue dilution) OR povidone-iodine diluted to weak-tea color. Either works; don't combine.
- AVOID hydrogen peroxide on an open wound — it damages healing tissue and slows repair. Avoid alcohol; it stings and is cytotoxic.
- Pat dry with clean gauze or a clean cloth. Don't rub the scrape.
- Optional thin layer of a pet-safe antibiotic ointment (bacitracin or veterinary triple antibiotic). Only useful if Kibo can't lick it off — see below.
- If you want to cover it, use a non-stick pad + light vet wrap + a thin layer of tape at the top. A wet or dirty bandage is worse than no bandage, so change daily and keep it dry. For a shallow scrape, leaving it open to air after cleaning is often the safer choice.

LICKING MANAGEMENT (this is the #1 reason these become infected)

- An e-collar (the cone) is the most reliable control. If you don't have one, a properly sized inflatable collar or a clean sock secured with vet wrap over the paw can help, but be aware dogs can chew through socks quickly.
- Bitter-tasting sprays (Bitter Apple, etc.) sometimes help but are not foolproof.
- Don't let Kibo lick — even a clean mouth introduces bacteria and disrupts healing.

ACTIVITY GUIDANCE

- Short on-leash bathroom walks only for the first few days (5–10 min). No off-leash, no running, no jumping, no rough play.
- Avoid gravel, hot pavement, sand, mud, and standing water — all can contaminate or re-injure the pad.
- A dog bootie or clean sock over the paw for outdoor trips keeps debris out; remove indoors so the paw can air out.
- Check the wound twice daily — visual + a gentle look for heat, swelling, discharge.
- Expect 7–10 days to heal. Pads heal slowly because they're under constant load.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A VETERINARIAN CALL

Any of these, even if Kibo still seems fine overall:

- Spreading redness, especially red streaks moving up the leg (lymphangitis).
- Increasing swelling, warmth, or obvious pain when you touch near the scrape.
- Discharge — pus, cloudy fluid, foul odor, or persistent wetness.
- Bleeding that restarts or won't stop with gentle pressure after 5–10 minutes.
- New or worsening limping / reluctance to bear weight.
- Foreign material still embedded that you can't rinse free.
- Wound gets larger instead of smaller after 2–3 days, or shows no improvement by day 3.
- Depth exposing underlying tissue (fat, muscle), or the scrape crosses over a joint.
- Torn, cracked, split, or partially detached nail — that's a different injury with different management.
- Systemic signs: lethargy, refusal to eat, vomiting, fever behavior (warm ears, shivering).
- Licking you genuinely can't control, even with a cone and a sock.

A shallow scrape with the gravel already rinsed away, no swelling, and normal weight-bearing is the right kind of problem to manage at home — but pad injuries are deceptively easy to contaminate because the paw is in contact with the ground every time he steps. The cone (or equivalent) and short, clean walks are doing most of the work here.

Short interpretation — separating observed from causal:

OBSERVED (descriptive, Q3 only):
  Partner (73.3%) > Organic (65.0%) > Paid social (46.7%).
  Largest gap is Partner minus Paid (~26.7 pp); Organic minus Paid is ~18.3 pp;
  Organic minus Partner is ~8.3 pp. Pattern is monotone: Partner highest,
  Paid lowest.

UNEQUAL DENOMINATORS — read these before trusting the ranking:
  Partner's n=45 is roughly a third of Organic's n=120 and half of Paid's n=90,
  so the Partner estimate is the noisiest. A back-of-envelope 95% CI width
  scales with 1/sqrt(n), so Partner's CI is ~1.6x wider than Organic's and
  ~1.4x wider than Paid's. Practical consequence: the Organic-vs-Partner gap
  (8.3 pp) is well inside sampling noise on this base; the Partner-vs-Paid
  and Organic-vs-Paid gaps are larger and more likely to be real differences
  in the eligible populations. Don't read "Partner is the best channel" off
  these numbers — the gap to Organic isn't reliable at n=45.

WHAT THIS IS NOT — causal channel-quality conclusions are not supported:
  1. Selection / composition confound. The three "eligible" pools are built
     by different mechanisms: Organic users self-select via search intent,
     Partner users arrive through an existing relationship, Paid-social users
     are reached by an ad auction. Activation differences may reflect who is
     in each pool (intent, awareness stage, demographics, device, geography),
     not what the channel does. This is the central reason the cut is
     descriptive, not causal.
  2. Eligibility definition may differ across channels (e.g., "completed
     signup" vs "reached by ad" vs "referred by partner"). Without a single
     shared eligibility rule, the rates are partly apples-to-oranges.
  3. No controls for time, campaign type, creative, or product surface.
  4. Significance is not causation. Even if all three gaps were p < 0.01,
     the descriptive design still doesn't license a "channel X is better"
     claim without composition controls.

SAFE LANGUAGE FOR OWEN'S BRIEF:
  "In Q3, paid-social eligible users activated at a lower rate (46.7%) than
  organic eligible users (65.0%); partner eligible users activated highest
  (73.3%) on a substantially smaller base. Differences are descriptive of
  the eligible populations in each channel and do not imply channel-level
  causal effects on activation."

WHAT WOULD MOVE IT FROM DESCRIPTIVE TO CAUSAL:
  a within-cohort comparison holding user characteristics fixed (propensity
  match, regression with channel fixed-effects + user controls), or an
  experiment that randomizes channel exposure. Until one of those exists,
  treat the 26.7-pp Partner-vs-Paid spread as an upper bound on the real
  channel-quality effect, not an estimate of it.

Hypothesis: Of the locked conditions, only tape-removal direction varies. The test is whether that single change shifts how the clean low pull sits against the masked edge on a full dry passage.

Locked across every panel (do not vary):
  - Paper: same sheet, same weight, same area
  - Pigment mix, dilution, water source
  - Brush (size, shape, load)
  - The longer successful steep-angle wash
  - One firm blot
  - 20-second bead-wicking interval
  - One-touch edge control
  - Clean low pull back over itself at ~45°, on a fully dry passage
  - No heat, no paper swap, no wash-variable change

The single variable:
  - Direction of tape removal only.

Layout — one sheet divided into four equal panels (A / B / C / D), same session, same water, same brush-load sequence. Each panel is a replicate of the locked procedure; only the final step changes.

Panels — tape-removal direction:

  A.  90° straight up (perpendicular to paper), slow steady pull  — baseline
  B.  180° folded back flat against itself, pulled parallel to surface, away from the wash edge

  D.  Low 45° angle, pulled parallel to the edge (mirror of the brush technique)

  8. Remove tape per the panel's assigned direction, slow and even

  - Tape-removal speed is slow and even across all four — direction is the only thing that varies
