Context: this is Kibo's 2025-02-06 vet claim — $128 total, $50 medication line allowed (applied to deductible), $78 consultation line denied as "behavioral services excluded." Today (2025-02-23) is the provisional start of the appeal window. Below is how the denial could be reconciled with the policy, followed by the exact questions to pin it down before you decide accept vs. appeal.

Possible reconciliations

There are three honest ways a $78 consultation can be excluded while a $50 medication from the same visit is allowed. Each one points to a different action.

1. Misclassification — the policy does not actually exclude this visit
The consultation was a routine medical workup (e.g., GI, ear, skin, endocrine). The insurer's adjudication system likely read a keyword in the chart notes — "anxiety," "reactivity," "fear," "behavior," "training" — or hit an internal trigger code, and auto-routed the line to the behavioral exclusion bucket. The medication line cleared because its code didn't trip the trigger. This is the most common version of this denial and is fully appealable on the strength of the vet's actual diagnosis code and chart notes.

2. Partial match — the visit was mixed
The chief complaint started as behavioral, but the vet identified an underlying medical cause (e.g., hypothyroidism driving behavioral change, pain driving reactivity, allergy-driven itching causing compulsive licking) and prescribed medication for the medical condition. The medication line paid; the consultation was excluded because the policy excludes behavioral consultations as a category even when they yield a covered prescription. The fight here depends on whether your policy has a medical-cause carve-out (many do, but it's narrow).

3. True exclusion — the policy genuinely excludes this consultation
The visit was primarily behavioral and the policy has no carve-out that reaches it. In that case the $78 is correctly excluded and accepting is the rational move; appealing would just burn the clock. The way to distinguish this from #1 and #2 is the policy wording itself (below).

Decision rule of thumb
- Chart notes show a covered medical diagnosis → reconciliation #1, appeal.
- Chart notes show a medical cause driving the behavior → reconciliation #2, appeal only if a medical-cause carve-out exists in your policy.
- Chart notes show a purely behavioral visit with no medical diagnosis → reconciliation #3, accept.

The question list is what tells you which bucket you're in.

Exact questions to ask before you decide

Policy questions (to the insurer, in writing — cite the EOB and claim number)

1. Quote the exact policy provision that defines "behavioral services" — section number, page, verbatim text.
2. Quote the exact provision that excludes behavioral services — same format. Is the exclusion in the base contract or in an endorsement/rider?
3. Does the exclusion apply to (a) the consultation/exam time only, (b) treatments, or (c) both?
4. Is there a medical-cause carve-out — i.e., behavioral symptoms caused by a diagnosed medical condition (thyroid, pain, allergy, neurological)? If yes, quote it.
5. Is there an accident-trigger carve-out — behavioral symptoms caused by a covered accident?
6. Does the exclusion apply if a covered medical diagnosis was made during the same visit but the chief complaint was behavioral?
7. Is there an optional behavioral-coverage rider available, and was it offered and declined at enrollment?

Coding questions (to the insurer)

These four already discharge the direct blockers from Daniela's 2025-02-24 production-observability review and the 2025-02-14/02-18 replay evidence gap.

Gaps — acceptance criteria that should be in the proposal before implementation and before any production replay approval

A. Privacy / access-posture criteria (the proposal says "no customer field values" but doesn't pin the boundary)

  A1. Access scope explicitly stated. The proposal should state which operator roles see the metadata and confirm that read access does not extend to anyone outside today's Customer.io / lifecycle-export audience. Without this, "bounded read-side" is an intent, not an acceptance criterion.
  A2. Field-value redaction proven by test. Acceptance should require a test case in the shadow replay that shows a held row displays metadata + reason code while the underlying customer field values are not present in the operator payload (or are masked). The 2025-02-18 clean shadow replay only proved agreement on values/as-ofs/freshness; it did not prove the visibility fix can't be wired to leak values.
  A3. No regression in existing access controls. Acceptance should require that any operator who previously couldn't see a field's value still can't see it after the change.

B. Freshness-alarm contract alignment

  B1. Reuse, don't fork, the existing 2h/4h thresholds. Stated, but acceptance should require that the operator view reads its threshold from the same source the freshness alarm uses (so a future tuning change touches both surfaces in one release). Otherwise we end up with two thresholds drifting.
  B2. Same authority for source-as-of and consumer-as-of. The proposal exposes both, but it doesn't say how they're reconciled when they disagree. The replay evidence rules require per-row capture of "lifecycle-preflight as-of, Helio Start as-of, Expansion Assist selection timestamp, and freshness score" — the operator view should label which of these it is showing so the operator doesn't confuse a consumer-side as-of (which can lag) with a source-authoritative as-of.
  B3. CRITICAL behavior preserved. Acceptance should restate that a CRITICAL freshness state triggers a page but does not release held rows; the operator view is a display surface, not a release authority. Otherwise a future reader could infer that visible-but-critical means "send anyway."

C. Held-row semantics

  C1. Reason code must be a first-class row field, not a derived payload. The 2025-02-24 review established this as a hard requirement; acceptance should require that the reason code is queryable/filterable as a column, not buried in a JSON blob.
  C2. Held rows remain held pending a fresh check by the consumer. The visibility fix must not let the operator infer release eligibility from a now-green display. Acceptance should require an explicit label like "held — visibility only" so an operator can't mistake a cleared freshness display for a release decision.
  C3. Per-row state-change history not required, but the current state must be unambiguous. The proposal exposes a snapshot; it should not expose any UI affordance that suggests "click to release."

D. Eligibility-recheck at send time (this is a real gap, not a nicety)

  D1. The proposal is about preflight visibility, but campaign release criteria already require an eligibility re-check at send time, not only during preflight. Acceptance should state that the operator view does not change, weaken, or substitute for that send-time re-check. The 2024-10-08 governed onboarding-help send had a post-send audit failure on exactly this point — suppression was checked at preflight but not rechecked at send. The visibility fix shouldn't make that easier to miss.

E. Replay-evidence reconstructability

  E1. The whole point of the fix is that replay evidence for a held row can name which governed field caused the hold. Acceptance should require: for every held row in the controlled replay, the evidence artifact contains (field name, source as-of, consumer as-of, source owner, freshness result, reason code) — i.e. exactly the fields the operator view will show. If the replay evidence format doesn't match the operator-view schema, the blocker just moves from the operator view to the evidence artifact.
  E2. The 2025-02-14 replay must remain marked FAILED until this fix lands. Acceptance should reference the existing FAILED-state gate on the 2025-02-14 replay and require a new replay artifact after implementation that supersedes it. The 2025-02-18 clean shadow replay closes the timestamp-unification prerequisite but is only a prerequisite, not production-release authorization — that distinction needs to be explicit in the acceptance criteria.
  E3. The release request must still attach the full replay-window account roster and a source-coverage attestation covering every account touched by Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, or lifecycle preflight. The visibility fix doesn't remove this obligation; it just makes the per-row evidence legible. Acceptance should restate it.

F. Cross-surface consistency

  F1. Field labels must match Helio Start reporting and Expansion Assist selection. The proposal is the third surface showing this metadata; acceptance should require that "source as-of," "consumer as-of," "freshness result," and "owner" mean the same thing on all three. Otherwise a release artifact will still be ambiguous when it has to compare across surfaces, which is exactly the failure mode that produced the 2025-02-14 timestamp disagreement.
  F2. Shared lifecycle state contract unchanged. The proposal is a surface change, not a shared-state change. Acceptance should state that explicitly so future reviewers don't have to re-derive it. Helio Start reporting and Expansion Assist selection already expose per-field as-of and freshness — this brings preflight to parity, not to a new contract.

G. Rollback and operational behavior

  G1. Rollback path preserved. Lifecycle preflight restores its prior selector through Customer.io configuration; that path must continue to work. Acceptance should require that rolling back the visibility change does not require a separate rollback mechanism (it should be a Customer.io config revert, same as today) and that no held-row state is created, changed, or cleared as a side effect of the rollback.
  G2. Kill-switch behavior unchanged. The 2/19 rollback design uses a kill switch that stops transport; acceptance should require that the operator view does not introduce a new path that bypasses the kill switch.
  G3. Held-versus-released visibility on every row. Before-cutover requirement: held-vs-released state visible per row with a reason code. The proposal adds the reason code on held rows; acceptance should require the released rows to also show per-field metadata (even if "fresh") so an operator can distinguish "passed because fresh" from "passed because no check ran."

H. Audit / observability

  H1. Per-field state changes are not silently editable from the operator view. Acceptance should require the view is read-only and that any state change goes through the existing release path (so freshness-alarm tuning uses the same release path as other lifecycle-export behavior changes).
  H2. The freshness-alarm audit log's "auto_source_recovered / manual_op / system_init" clear-mechanism taxonomy should still apply when the underlying alarm clears while the operator view is open. Acceptance should require that the operator view updates to reflect the cleared state on the same transition the audit records, and that the audit retains the stale interval.

I. Scope-of-fix statement (the meta-criterion)

  I1. The proposal says "bounded read-side fix." Acceptance should enumerate exactly what is in scope (the six fields above) and what is out of scope (no new write paths, no new consumer authority, no new threshold tuning, no schema changes to the shared lifecycle state contract, no changes to who can see customer field values). Without this, a future "small extension" can quietly turn a visibility fix into a contract change.
  I2. The contractor engagement ends 2025-02-23 with access-grant expiry 2025-02-28. Acceptance should require that implementation work does not depend on contractor access past 2025-02-28 and that any code/config changes are owned by Daniela/Ines from day one. This is governance, not engineering, but it should be in the acceptance criteria.

Bottom line
The proposal is correctly scoped at the right altitude — read-side metadata only, no customer field values, same freshness thresholds. The eleven gaps above are the minimum I'd want pinned before signing off on implementation, and the seven that touch replay evidence (A2, B1, C1, D1, E1, E2, E3, F1) are the ones I'd flag as hard prerequisites before any production replay approval. The four privacy criteria (A1–A3) and the two scope-of-fix criteria (I1, I2) are the ones I'd want Daniela to confirm in writing before code lands.

Ines's draft has real problems against the Helio Start setup-message conventions. Here's the read.

**State is misrepresented**
- "Connection failed" / "couldn't verify" treats *pending* as *failed*. A connector that's still propagating, or where owner-authorization is pending, hasn't definitively failed. Telling the customer it failed when the system is still checking will misroute them — they'll retry an action that isn't actually broken, and ignore the step that *is* the gate.
- That distinction matters operationally: per the 2024-04-26 read, ~2 of 7 pending cases are "unable to authenticate the selected connector" — i.e. the customer can't fix it on their own account, but the message still has to land cleanly. Framing it as "failed" pushes them down the wrong path.

**Gate isn't named**
The setup-message convention requires the message to name the pending external-system owner-authorization gate so a later confirmation is expected and understandable. Ines's draft doesn't name the gate at all — it just says "your integration" and "the connection." The customer can't tell from the message whether they need to act, the workspace admin needs to act, or the third-party system just needs time to propagate.

**Workspace-state framing is inverted**
The held-precedent subject ("Your Helio Start workspace is set up — final authorization pending") reflects the actual state: the workspace *is* up, only the authorization is pending. Ines's body — "Once the connection succeeds, your workspace will be ready" — implies the workspace isn't set up yet. That creates a later-confirmation surprise when the workspace appears without a fresh "ready" email.

**Action is ambiguous**
"Reconnect it now" doesn't tell the customer *what* to reconnect, *which* connector, or *who* needs to authorize it. For the owner-authorization-pending case (the most common pending state), the customer's own reconnect attempt is a no-op — the blocker is on the third-party admin side. The message should point at the right actor.

**No expectation-setting for the catch-up path**
Per the convention, the message exists *because* a later confirmation may arrive (status catching up after the propagation lag, or owner authorization landing after a delay). Ines's draft doesn't set that expectation at all — if state flips after this email, the customer has no model for what just happened.

**What the draft should do instead**
- Subject: workspace is set up, authorization is pending — not "failed."
- Body: name the gate (external-system owner authorization), identify the connector, and identify who needs to act (workspace admin vs. connector owner). Don't tell the customer their connection failed when it hasn't.
- Set the expectation that a confirmation may follow once authorization lands.

Now the ruling, in plain terms:

Source hierarchy, applied to this case:

The album index's creation date is unknown, so it cannot be treated as contemporaneous to the print. That strips it of the controlling-source priority a contemporaneous album caption normally enjoys (the same principle that made the P023 album caption outrank Mom's and Marcus's later recollections). The physical back inscription, by contrast, is contemporaneous by definition — it was written on the print itself.

So for the date field, the back outranks the album index. But the back says "Barton — 61?" — the question mark is the original writer flagging their own uncertainty, so we don't promote that to a confident 1961 either.

Net result:

- Year: held as uncertain. The '61? and '62 are both leads; this evidence does not resolve between them. Do not pick one.
- Location: Barton Springs (consistent across both sources).
- Names ("Marcus and Keiko"): preserved as tentative, sourced to the album index. The back supplies no contrary name evidence, so the album index's names stand as a lead — not as a confirmation.
- Tentative IDs: preserved verbatim, not overwritten.
- Provenance: the '61? / summer '62 conflict is recorded as an open question, not silently resolved.

Practical next step before any access-copy caption is written: this print still needs a P### assigned, a Marcus rescan to confirm the back inscription literally (compare against the "M— at Barton Springs, maybe '58?" transcription discipline used for P039), and ideally a third source to break the year tie — a sleeve inscription, another album entry with a known creation date, or a contemporaneous family record. If nothing breaks the tie, the access-copy caption should read along the lines of "Marcus and Keiko (identification tentative) at Barton Springs, year uncertain (1961 or 1962 per conflicting family sources)."

The general principle this case crystallizes — and which I've stored in supermemory for future photo work — is: an album index with an unknown creation date loses controlling-source priority for date, and the contemporaneous physical back inscription becomes the controlling source instead.

CATALOG ENTRY — A-008 (tentative)

Object ID: A-008
Working identification (tentative): Zilker Park, May 1964
Physical medium: photographic print (1), stable
Archived digital file: present; byte-identity resolved 2026-01-18 to this accession
Tentative physical-back inscription: present, location on print (lower right margin, Grandma's hand)
Album index entry: present, page and column location logged per Mom's hand-transcription (2026-02-27)
Provisional date: May 1964 (per album index, not yet corroborated independently)
Catalog status: TENTATIVE — identification and date held, not asserted

PROVENANCE NOTE

This accession rests on three independent strands of evidence, each preserved in its current form because none, on its own, fixes the identification or the date.

(1) Album-index evidence. The index card corresponding to this print was located by Mom on 2026-02-27 during the ongoing review of Grandma's album paperwork. The card carries the inscription that has previously been read as "Zilker, May 1964." The card is the documentary anchor for the working identification and for the May 1964 date.

(2) Handwriting attestation. Marcus Tanaka has examined the index card and confirmed that the inscription is in Grandma's handwriting. This is recorded as a positive attribution to the writer, not as a date of writing.

(3) Physical-back inscription. The print itself bears a tentative inscription on the back, also in Grandma's hand. This duplicates (in abbreviated form) the album-index content and provides a parallel strand of evidence on the object itself rather than only in the album paperwork.

What remains unresolved is whether the inscription was made contemporaneously with the photograph, i.e., at the time the print was placed in the album (or shortly after), or was added later. Marcus's handwriting confirmation establishes only that the inscription was written by Grandma; it does not establish when. A grandmother reviewing her own albums years later could have added an inscription in the same hand that was used when the album was first assembled, which is precisely the kind of evidence that cannot, by itself, fix a date.

The reading lands the obvious meaning but I think the passage is doing something more interesting than "finally choosing to stay," and the zipped bag is the reason.

Three details push against it:

1. The bag is still zipped. Choosing to stay, in most registers of the gesture, looks like unpacking — hanging the clothes back up, emptying the bag, dismantling the readiness. She doesn't. The contents are undisturbed. Whatever she prepared to leave *for* is still prepared.

2. It's beside the bed, not put away. A committed stay would put the bag in a closet, under a bed, back on a shelf. She parks it at hand. Within reach of the next morning.

3. The streetlights. She doesn't decide — she waits through a civic, indifferent threshold. Streetlights come on every night regardless of her. She lets an ordinary marker of time pass and then reverses when nothing arrives to push her out. That's the grammar of deferral, not the grammar of choice.

So I'd read it as: she suspends the leaving rather than cancels it. The decision doesn't happen in this passage — what happens is that the day ends without a trigger, and the bag comes back inside by default. The packed bag beside the bed is the sentence's last image, and it's an image of something still *ready*, not something abandoned.

A question worth bringing to the group: what would the passage look like if she *had* chosen to stay? Probably the bag would be open, or it would be downstairs, or she wouldn't think of it at all. The fact that the narrator notices where it is — zipped, beside the bed — tells us the leaving is still a live option she's keeping warm.

Draft:

That's the reading that holds up best for me too — the gesture isn't declarative, it's durational. Keeping the bag packed preserves the exit as a real option rather than a performed one, and the move indoors is exactly the kind of small spatial act that delays the moment a decision has to become a fact. Nothing in the passage forces the postponement to resolve into either a yes or a no; it can sit there, and the sitting is the point.

Where I want to stay with it: the packed bag inside and the packed bag by the door are the same bag, but they're not the same sentence. The text knows that, and I think it's asking the reader to know it too rather than to choose.

Is the postponement a deferral toward leaving, or a deferral toward staying — or is the difference between those two something the character hasn't yet been forced to name?

Three drafts below, process-honest. I've left clear placeholders for the painting-specific bits so you can drop your own observations in and keep your voice. Nothing promotional — kept it that way per your note.

1) "What did you notice first in this scene?"

The light. [PAINTING-SPECIFIC: where it fell, what it touched — e.g., the strip on the counter where the window light landed before anything else did.] Once I'd seen that, the rest of the scene organized itself around it — which edges to keep, which to let soften.

If they push on why light comes first: in watercolor, the first commitment is usually a reserved white or a light shape. So I look for the light first by habit, even before I think about subject.

2) "How did you keep the cool window light from flattening the warmer counter edge?"

Honestly, by not trying to paint both of them equally. The window side stays mostly paper — light washes, lost-and-found edges, a few darker notes where something crosses it. The warm counter holds more pigment, and the warmth does some of the work of separating them without me needing a hard line.

[OPTIONAL, if you want a sharper answer: edges. The transition stays soft where the light fades, and only gets harder where the counter edge meets the shadow under it. That one harder edge is what keeps the warmth from sliding into the cool.]

3) "Does painting at home change what you choose to observe?"

Yes. Plein air, or working somewhere unfamiliar, I'm usually racing the light — I notice the big shapes first because they'll be gone if I don't catch them. At home there's no clock on the scene. I notice smaller things — the way a glass sits on a counter, the edge of a shadow that only shows up at this hour. The trade is that home work can get too quiet; the place I have to push myself is choosing what to leave out.

KEEPING AND RECONCILING MOM'S OFFICIAL FORM 1099-INT FOR $12.01

This is general guidance for working with a corrected-or-discrepant 1099-INT, not personal tax advice.

1. WHAT "OFFICIAL" MEANS HERE

   On a 1099-INT, the official figure is the amount the payer filed with the IRS in Box 1 (Interest income). When a payer reissues a 1099-INT to fix a mistake, the new form is marked "CORRECTED" at the top and supersedes the original. Mom's "$12.01 official" is therefore whatever amount the payer filed, on the form stamped CORRECTED if one exists. If there's no CORRECTED form in hand, the original is the official of record.

   The earlier 17-cent-lower figure (so $11.84 if the new official is $12.01) was either:
     (a) the original 1099-INT before the payer noticed and reissued, or
     (b) Mom's own interest-totals worksheet / December statement estimate.

   Distinguishing (a) from (b) matters: only (a) means a payer-side corrected form is in play. (b) is just a Mom-side estimate that doesn't override the payer's filing.

2. WHAT TO RETAIN (KEEP, DON'T DISCARD)

     The CORRECTED 1099-INT for $12.01, with the payer's name, TID, account number suffix, and tax year visible.
     The ORIGINAL 1099-INT showing the earlier amount, if Mom still has it.
     Both December 2024 and January 2025 statements from the account, plus any year-end interest statement the bank mailed.
     Any payer's correction letter or notice explaining the change ("corrected amount," "revised interest," etc.).
     A short dated note recording: which form arrived when, what changed, and the source Mom trusts (the payer's filing, not her own estimate).

   The CORRECTED form is the one to use for filing, but the original is the receipt for the payer's correction — keep both together.

3. THE 17-CENT DIFFERENCE IN CONTEXT

   A 17-cent change on $11.84 is roughly 1.4% of the original amount, or about 0.013% of the typical federal AGI in Mom's profile. Reasons payers reissue at this magnitude:
     Late-December interest posting after the original print run (very common for savings accounts and broker cash sweeps).
     Year-end accrual true-ups on money-market or brokered-CD positions.
     Backup-withholding or fee adjustments that flow back into the interest line.
     Reclassification of a small amount from "interest" to "other income" or vice versa.

   None of these necessarily means Mom owes more tax or that anything was wrong on her side. For a 1099-INT, $12.01 vs $11.84 changes taxable interest by $0.17; federal income tax on $0.17 of additional taxable interest, at Mom's bracket, is on the order of a few cents. The IRS does not require an amended return over differences of this size.

4. WHAT TO VERIFY BEFORE DECIDING ANY FILING FOLLOW-UP

   a) Is the new form actually marked CORRECTED?
        Yes — the corrected 1099-INT replaces the original for filing and for Mom's records.
        No, and the dollar figure is just Mom's own estimate — there's no payer-side correction and the original still governs.
        Not sure — Mom should pull the form and look at the top of the document, not rely on a memory of it.

   b) Does the TID (payer's TIN/EIN) on the corrected form match the original?
        If yes, the payer corrected their own filing.
        If no, that's a serious flag: it could mean the wrong payer reissued, or the account number is misread — escalate before filing.

   c) Does the account number suffix on the corrected form match Mom's actual account?
        Truncated account numbers are normal and the last 4-5 digits should be familiar.

   d) Is the corrected amount consistent with Mom's monthly statements and year-end summary?
        Sum the 12 (or 13) monthly interest postings on her statements and compare to the corrected Box 1. If the sum matches $12.01, the corrected figure reconciles end-to-end and there's nothing to chase.

   e) Has the payer already filed the correction with the IRS?
        Almost always yes — the corrected 1099-INT is the payer's filing. But if the payer's correction letter says anything like "we will refile with the IRS separately," that's worth keeping with the form.

   f) Is there any backup-withholding change (Box 4)?
        If Box 4 changed too, the federal-tax-withheld line on the return needs the new figure; the difference (likely $0 here) goes through the normal withholding reconciliation.

5. WHETHER FILING FOLLOW-UP IS NECESSARY

   In general:

   If the return has already been filed using the original $11.84 figure, the corrected 1099-INT creates a $0.17 mismatch between Mom's return and the payer's IRS filing. The IRS's automated matching will flag it (a CP2000 notice is possible but not certain at this magnitude), and:
        If Mom receives a CP notice explaining the $0.17, the notice itself contains the correction workflow — respond to the notice, not by filing a separate 1040-X on her own initiative.
        If no notice arrives, the IRS often doesn't assess anything for differences this small and the matter closes administratively.

   Filing a 1040-X (amended return) for a $0.17 interest discrepancy is allowed but disproportionate: it adds 8-12+ weeks of IRS processing time, restarts the matching cycle, and is unlikely to produce a different outcome than responding to a CP notice if one ever comes. Standard guidance: don't preemptively 1040-X a corrected 1099-INT at this size; respond to whatever the IRS sends.

   If the return has not yet been filed, simply use the CORRECTED $12.01 figure on Schedule B / Form 1040 and stop — there is nothing to amend.

6. THE ONE THING WORTH CONFIRMING IN WRITING

   Ask the payer (bank's customer service, in writing through the online message center or a dated email) for a one-line confirmation: "The corrected 1099-INT for tax year 2024 reports $12.01 in Box 1 and supersedes the earlier $11.84 figure." Keep that confirmation with the corrected form. It is the receipt for the payer's correction and is the cleanest answer if anything is ever questioned later.

Summary: keep both forms, the statements, and the payer's correction notice; use the corrected $12.01 for any current or future filing; don't 1040-X preemptively for a 17-cent interest change — respond to an IRS notice if one ever arrives; and get the payer's correction in writing.

## 1. Scope and intent

This proposal asks permission to run a single, bounded guest-facing exposure of the braised dish in order to collect the guest-demand evidence the chef-owner identified as missing. It is not a menu application and does not assume any future placement, regular execution, or recurring authorization. The only intent of this proposal is to close the guest-demand evidence gap, on terms the chef-owner can revoke at any moment.

## 2. What stays locked from the kitchen-only repeat (unchanged production constraints)

Every production parameter proven in the 2026-03-01 kitchen-only repeat carries over verbatim. None of these are relaxed for the guest-facing test.

-  Cost ceiling: ≤ $218.40 per execution (repeat landed at $215.60; ceiling kept, not tightened, so a single real-world variance cannot silently blow the budget).
-  Station-timing: same station, same target time. No time-buffering borrowed from prep to compensate for service-window drag. If the test shows station-timing cannot hold under service conditions, that finding itself is the evidence and goes back to the chef-owner.
-  20-minute hold stability: 4×20-minute holds without separation, identical to the repeat. If a hold is broken during service, the test is paused, not improvised around.
-  Kitchen-only staging: prep, cook, and hold stay in the T2 kitchen-only zone; the dish does not migrate stations for the test.

## 3. What is new — and intentionally narrow

Only the following three changes convert the proven kitchen-only execution into a guest-facing test. Anything outside this list is out of scope and requires a fresh chef-owner decision.

3.1 Fixed portion count: 20 portions, one service only. 20 is chosen because it (a) clears any "kitchen-cooked-only" sample-size objection, (b) stays inside one service window so no second-day carryover contaminates the data, and (c) is small enough that a full recall or halt is operationally trivial. The number is a ceiling, not a target — if 20 cannot be plated within the station-timing target, the test is reduced, not extended.

3.2 Guest communication: silent placement on the existing daily menu board, no server upsell, no table-side recommendation, no specials recitation. Guests who order it order it under the same conditions as any other dish that day. This is deliberate: it tests pull, not push.

3.3 No assumption of recurrence: language used at FOH, in the prep sheet, and in any post-test note is "one-service test," not "trial," "soft launch," or "pilot." A "trial" label tends to get reused week-to-week and quietly becomes recurring placement; the chef-owner has not authorized that and this proposal does not request it.

## 4. Pre-test readback (what gets confirmed before the first portion goes out)

Before service starts, Sam reads back to the chef-owner (or designated lead):
 (a) portion count locked at 20,
 (b) cost ceiling $218.40 unchanged,
 (c) station-timing target unchanged,
 (d) 4×20-min hold plan unchanged,
 (e) no menu language change, no FOH script, no server directive,
 (f) no carryover to a second service.

If any item is not as stated above, the test does not start.

## 5. Evidence to be captured (the whole point of the test)

Single-page readback delivered to the chef-owner within 24 hours of service close:

-  Portions plated vs. portions sold (sell-through).
-  Service-window timing vs. station-timing target (delta in minutes).
-  Hold-stability: did all 4×20-min holds complete without intervention.
-  Actual food cost vs. $218.40 ceiling.
-  Any server observation re: guest questions or reactions (recorded verbatim, not paraphrased into "positive/negative").
-  Any complaint, refund, or remade plate, with time and table.

No interpretation, no recommendation, no "next step" in this readback. Interpretation is the chef-owner's call after seeing the evidence.

## 6. Post-test state — explicit

Regardless of how the test goes:
-  The dish is NOT on the menu.
-  There is NO recurring authorization.
-  There is NO standing prep slot, NO standing hold slot, NO standing FOH note.
-  No "while supplies last," "back by popular demand," or any carryover language is added to subsequent menus.
-  Any future discussion of menu placement or recurring execution is a fresh chef-owner decision, opened only after the chef-owner has reviewed the §5 evidence.

## 7. What this proposal is NOT asking for

-  Not asking for menu placement.
-  Not asking for recurring authorization.
-  Not asking for a standing test slot ("every Saturday we run 20").
-  Not asking for FOH scripting, server training, or marketing language.
-  Not asking to relax any of the cost / station-timing / hold-stability constraints proven in the repeat.

## 8. Chef-owner decision points (the only asks)

Cautious spot-cleaning sequence for watercolor pigment on sealed wood:

Good news first: you blotted immediately, the finish is intact, and a "pale shadow" means the seal did most of its job. Watercolor pigment is stubborn by design (it's made to stain paper permanently), so the goal is to lift what's loose without attacking the seal. Work in graduated steps and bail at the first sign of trouble.

STEP 1 — Mild soap lift (safest)
  - A few drops of plain dish soap (Dawn-style) in a small cup of water
  - Dampen a soft microfiber cloth — barely wet, not dripping
  - Blot (don't rub) the shadow for 5-10 seconds, then lift straight up
  - Rinse the cloth, wipe with a fresh damp cloth, then dry immediately with a clean dry cloth
  - Repeat 2-3 times max

  Move on if: shadow doesn't fade after 2-3 gentle passes.

STEP 2 — 70% isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab (moderate)
  - Test FIRST on the same surface in a hidden spot (under the table edge, behind a chair) — wait 30 seconds, check for dulling, tackiness, or whitening. If anything changes, do not use on the visible area.
  - Lightly dampen a cotton swab (not soaked)
  - Touch the shadow, working from the outside edge inward so you don't spread it
  - 5-10 seconds of contact, then blot dry with a clean cloth
  - Repeat 2-3 times max, fresh swab each pass

  Note: if IPA dulls or softens the test spot, your finish is likely shellac or a wax-sensitive seal — stop, IPA isn't safe for it, and you should leave the shadow alone.

STEP 3 — Stop here, full stop
  - Do not escalate to magic eraser / melamine foam: it will micro-scuff and dull most seal finishes.
  - Do not use acetone, nail polish remover, bleach, vinegar, or any abrasive.
  - Do not soak the area — water under the seal causes white haze or lifting.

STOP IMMEDIATELY if you see any of:
  - Dulling or loss of sheen in the spot
  - Tackiness or softness when you touch it (finish is being dissolved)
  - Whitening, hazing, or color shift in the wood
  - The shadow spreading instead of lifting
  - Any rough feel where it was smooth before

AFTER ANY STEP:
  - Dry the area completely
  - Leave it untouched for 24 hours before setting anything on it
  - If the finish looks slightly dull after cleaning, a tiny buff with paste wax (or the polish you'd use for the rest of that piece) can sometimes even out the sheen — only after it's fully dry and only if the test spot tolerated it

WHEN TO ACCEPT THE SHADOW:
  - If steps 1-2 don't lift it within their few attempts, leave it. A faint blue shadow is cosmetic and reversible only by refinishing; a damaged seal is not.
  - Staining blues (Prussian, Phthalo, Indigo) are specifically formulated to be permanent and may have caught in a micro-imperfection the seal can't fully shed.
  - You can have the spot spot-refinished later by a furniture pro if it really bothers you, but it's not urgent and not worth finish damage today.

If you want, tell me what the piece is (table top, easel, frame, floor, etc.) and I can tighten the advice — different seal types (polyurethane vs. hard wax oil vs. shellac vs. conversion varnish) tolerate this differently and the right "test first" spot changes.

The plan below assumes you do not yet know the specific contaminant (pathogen vs. toxin vs. foreign object vs. nutrient deficiency), which is the single biggest driver of priorities. Step zero is to identify it from the recall notice, then weight the rest of the plan accordingly.

================================================================
0. READ THE RECALL NOTICE FOR THESE FIELDS
================================================================
- Reason (pathogen name, toxin, vitamin/mineral excess or deficit, foreign material, label mismatch)
- Scope (your lot only vs. all lots of SKU vs. brand-wide)
- Date the recall was issued and "best by" / lot code range
- Manufacturer contact and refund/claim procedure
- Whether human handling is a concern (Salmonella, Listeria — yes; aflatoxin — no)

Keep the printed notice or a screenshot. You'll want it twice: for the vet, and for the manufacturer's claim process.

================================================================
1. EXPOSURE — what you have, what's still unknown
================================================================
What you told me:
- One meal consumed on 2025-03-22 from lot L25-0317A
- Asymptomatic at observation time
- Remaining bag quarantined, bowl and scoop washed
- Switched to a sealed unaffected lot

Still unknown (matters for risk):
- Approximate amount eaten (cups/grams). Larger single-dose intake raises stakes for acute toxins and obstruction; a small portion of a pathogen-contaminated bag still carries infection risk.
- Whether other pets or household members handled the food. If the recall is pathogen-based, hand-washing and surface cleaning for humans applies.
- Kibo's baseline health (kidney, liver, GI) — relevant if a vet wants a baseline blood draw.

================================================================
2. MONITORING — what to watch, by time window
================================================================
The window you are in right now (0–24h post-meal) catches the acute hazards. Don't wait for "obvious" symptoms; mild early signs are the most useful trigger.

Immediate red flags (vet same-day, not wait-and-see):
- Vomiting 3+ times in 24h, or any vomit with blood or coffee-ground appearance
- Bloody or black/tarry stool, or diarrhea lasting >12h
- Refusing water for >12h, or any sign of dehydration (skin tent, tacky gums)
- Any neurological sign: ataxia, head tilt, tremors, seizure, sudden sedation
- Yellowing of gums, inner ear, or sclera (jaundice)
- Collapse, pale gums, rapid breathing
- Visible distress, restlessness, or a posture change (hunched, "prayer position")

Sub-acute window, days 2–7 (most relevant if recall is mycotoxin / aflatoxin or vitamin D excess):
- Lethargy, inappetence that persists more than a day
- Increased drinking or urination (vitamin D, kidney)
- Dark urine, pale gums, bruising (liver)
- Waxing-and-waning GI signs

Chronic window, weeks 2–6 (only relevant for aflatoxin or nutrient deficiency recalls):
- Persistent appetite or weight change
- New skin/coat changes
- Any behavior change that doesn't resolve

Practical monitoring method:
- Twice-daily check-ins for the first 72h: appetite, water intake, energy, stool consistency, gum color
- Photograph anything unusual (stool, vomit, gums) with a timestamp — the vet will ask
- Don't reset Kibo's normal routine for "watching" him; behavioral change is itself a signal and routine loss confounds it

================================================================
3. CLEANUP — you've done the main steps; here's the gap list
================================================================
Done:
- Bag quarantined
- New sealed lot in use
- Bowl and scoop washed

Add:
- Wash bowl and scoop with hot soapy water, then sanitize (dilute bleach ~1:32, or a veterinary-grade disinfectant like Rescue or Virkon). Rinse and dry.
- Wash anything the bag touched: countertop, floor under the bag, food-storage bin (inside and out), any measuring cup.
- Wash hands after any future handling of the quarantined bag, especially for pathogen recalls.
- Storage of the quarantined bag: keep it sealed (clip or zip bag inside another bag), label it with the lot code and date, store somewhere dry. Do not throw it out yet — the manufacturer may request the lot, your vet may want to test contents, and you'll want it for any reimbursement.
- Photograph the bag label (UPC, lot code, best-by date) and the recall notice.

If a child or another pet in the home had access, treat that as a parallel exposure — same cleanup logic applies.

================================================================
4. VETERINARY ESCALATION
================================================================
Call today or next open hour, even though Kibo is asymptomatic. Reasons:
- The vet can tell you what the recall reason implies for a single-meal exposure at Kibo's size and history.
- They may want a baseline blood draw (liver values, calcium, kidney) now so any later change has a comparison. Baseline is much more useful than a single post-symptom panel.
- Pre-emptive note in the chart speeds things up if you do end up going in.

When you call, have ready:
- Lot code (L25-0317A), brand/SKU, recall reason if you have it
- Approximate amount eaten, exact time/date
- Kibo's weight, age, current medications/supplements
- That he is asymptomatic now and on a different lot

If symptoms appear:
- Call the clinic first. Describe what's happening. They'll triage phone-vs-visit.
- Bring the sealed recalled bag (or a photo of the label) and the recall notice to any visit.

If your vet is closed and symptoms are red-flag: emergency clinic. Don't wait for morning.

================================================================
5. ADMIN / DOCUMENTATION (do this once, costs nothing, saves later)
================================================================
- Save the recall notice (PDF or screenshot) in a folder you can find.
- Note in one place: date, lot, amount eaten, lot switched to, manufacturer, any vet contact.
- Check the recall notice for a refund / reimbursement procedure. Many voluntary recalls refund with proof of purchase and lot code; the quarantined bag is your proof.
- If the recall reason is pathogen-based and anyone in the household is immunocompromised, pregnant, or has a young child, mention this to their physician — Salmonella and Listeria are zoonotic from contaminated pet food.

FOOD-RECALL RESPONSE PLAYBOOK (Kibo / dog)
================================================
Use the recalled product's UPC, lot code, and best-by date as your single
anchor — every step below keys off that record.


1. IMMEDIATE RESPONSE (first 30 minutes)
----------------------------------------
  a. Stop feeding. Pull the bag/treats/cans from the rotation now — even
     partial bags. Do not finish the open bag "to see."
  b. Capture the identifier triple:
       - Brand + product name
       - UPC (full 12-digit)
       - Lot code AND best-by date (photograph both; lighting matters,
         use flash)
     Photograph the front and back of the bag, plus the receipt.
  c. Seal the food in a plastic bag and set aside — do NOT throw out yet.
     Keep it available so the vet or FDA investigator can reference it,
     and so you can confirm your dog didn't access the bin.
  d. If Kibo already ate any in the last 12 hours:
       - Note time of last known ingestion
       - Estimate volume (cups, treats, treats per day)
       - Note any current symptoms, however mild, with timestamps
  e. Cross-check storage: pantry, garage, car, treat jars, training-bag
     pockets, toppers, top-up samples. Anything from the same brand+lot
     is recalled, not just the bag you noticed.


2. MONITORING WINDOW
--------------------
Default watch:  72 hours from last ingestion (most acute GI signs)
Extended watch: 14 days for aflatoxin / mold-mycotoxin recalls
Salmonella watch:  5-7 days (humans in household can also get sick)

What to log, twice daily (morning + evening):
  - Appetite (normal / picky / refused)
  - Water intake (normal / increased / decreased)
  - Energy / gait (normal / lethargic / wobbly)
  - Stool (formed / soft / diarrhea / blood / mucus / color change)
  - Vomit (none / bile / food / blood)
  - Gums color (pink / pale / yellow)

  Yellowing at any point = ER, do not wait for the morning vet.


3. CLEANUP STEPS
----------------
Order matters — clean bowls last, not first.

  1. Bag and remove all recalled food (sealed, off-limits to all pets
     and wildlife; trash in an exterior bin if no pet access).
  2. Discard or quarantine anything the food touched:
       - Open-package treats, toppers, kibble dust
       - Shared scoops (recommend replacing, food-contact plastic
         harbors salmonella/listeria in crevices)
  3. Wash food-storage container and lid in hot soapy water, scrub seams,
     then sanitize 10 minutes in:
       - Diluted bleach 1 tbsp per gallon of water, OR
       - Undiluted white vinegar (for metal/wood that bleach damages)
     Rinse and air-dry fully.
  4. Wash bowls and slow-feeder inserts: hot soapy water + sanitize,
     rinse, dry. Same for water bowl.
  5. Wipe down the feeding station surface and floor mat with the same
     sanitizer. Bleach-spray a 2-foot radius around the bowl.
  6. Wash your hands and any human dishes/utensils that contacted the
     food. Re-run the dishwasher on sanitize cycle for any pet bowls
     that go in (separate load from human dishes).
  7. Launder feeding mats, towel liners, crate pads Kibo rests on while
     eating — hot cycle with bleach-safe detergent.


4. SIGNS THAT REQUIRE VET OR URGENT CARE
----------------------------------------
Call your vet (same-day) for:
  - Refusing food > 24 hours OR refusing water > 12 hours
  - Repeated vomiting (3+ times in 24h) or any vomit with blood
  - Diarrhea > 24 hours, OR any stool with blood/mucus/black/tarry look
  - Noticeable lethargy, hiding, or reluctance to move
  - Loss of coordination, stumbling, head tilt
  - Tremors, twitching, or single-episode seizure-like event

Go to the ER (do not wait for your regular vet) for:
  - Yellow gums, yellow whites of eyes, or yellow skin (jaundice —
     aflatoxin / liver involvement)
  - Pale or gray gums
  - Collapse or inability to stand
  - Active seizure, or multiple seizures
  - Bloated / distended abdomen with restlessness or unproductive
     retching (rules out bloat, which is unrelated to recall but
     can mask symptoms)
  - Difficulty breathing
  - Blood in vomit that looks like coffee grounds (digested blood)

When you call or arrive, hand the vet:
  - The photographed lot info
  - The estimated amount ingested and time window
  - The symptom log
  - The sealed bag (or a clear photo of the lot panel)


5. REMINDERS SPECIFIC TO KIBO
-----------------------------
  - Behavioral consults are covered as vet evals under the annual
    deductible per your policy — a recall-related exam counts the same
    way, so use the clinic without a separate behavioral carve-out
    worry.
  - Kibo's anxiety baseline is yours to read best: small behavior
    shifts (clingier, more panting, off the spot) that look "mild" to
    a stranger are signal-grade for him. Flag them on the log.
  - Bring a familiar item if you do have to go in — ERs are loud, and
    for him that stacks.


6. AFTERMATH / DOCUMENTATION
----------------------------
  - Report the lot to the FDA: fda.gov/safety/report-problem (MedWatch
    online). Include brand, lot, symptoms, date(s).
  - Save receipts — most reputable brands refund recalled product and
    will reimburse vet bills tied to confirmed ingestion of their lot.
    Keep vet invoices, lot photos, and any symptom log.

    confirming the recall match.

One loose stool after grass chewing, a week past asymptomatic recall exposure, and otherwise well — plan below. Context that may help your framing: Salmonella signs from a food exposure typically show within 6–72 hours, so today's stool is more plausibly the grass than the recall, but you're right that any new GI sign is worth watching carefully and worth logging.

HYDRATION
- Keep water freely available as normal. Don't restrict — for one loose stool, dehydration risk outweighs over-drinking risk.
- If he gulps and vomits water back, switch to small frequent laps: ice cubes, or a tablespoon or two every 15–30 minutes, working back up to free access.
- Quick at-home hydration check, do once now and repeat if anything drifts:
    Skin tent: gently pinch scruff over the shoulders and release. Should snap flat in under a second.
    Gums: pink and slick. Tacky or dry is a concern.
    Eyes: not sunken.
    Urine: still being passed; noticeably darker, or no urine 8+ hours, is a concern.

FEEDING
- Don't fast. He's eating with interest, which is a good sign.
- If you want to be cautious, split his normal portion into 2–3 smaller meals across the day instead of one big meal.
- Bland backup if stool worsens: plain boiled skinless chicken plus plain white rice, roughly one-third chicken to two-thirds rice, for 24–48 hours, then mix back to his normal food over 2 days.
- No new treats, no table food, no dairy, no rich or fatty add-ons.

HYGIENE  (Salmonella is zoonotic, so this matters regardless of cause)
- Pick up stool immediately; bag and bin, don't leave it in the yard.
- Wash your hands after handling him, his bowls, or stool.
- Wash food and water bowls in hot soapy water daily; sanitize weekly with dilute bleach (about 1 tablespoon bleach per quart of water), rinse well.
- Keep him from licking faces, especially kids or anyone immunocompromised.
- Rinse the grass area he chews with water if you can, to dilute residue.
- A bath isn't needed unless he rolled in stool.

MONITORING  (log these so you can give the vet a clean story if you need to call)
- Stool: count per day, consistency (soft, loose, watery), color (yellow, bloody, black-tarry), mucus, any blood.
- Energy and alertness, especially whether he greets you normally.
- Appetite: full meals vs leaving food.
- Vomiting: count and timing relative to meals or water.
- Temperature if you have a rectal thermometer; normal is 100.5 to 102.5°F. Above 103.5 or below 99 is a vet-now sign.
- Repeat the hydration checks.

THRESHOLDS — REGULAR VET, call within 24 hours (next business day, or sooner if it's an easy non-urgent call)
- 2 to 3 loose stools in 24 hours, all clearly off baseline.
- Slightly reduced appetite for one meal but otherwise bright.
- Mild one-off lethargy that resolves within an hour.
- A small amount of mucus or a single streak of fresh blood on one stool.
- Any soft stool that persists into day 2.

THRESHOLDS — URGENT CARE OR ER, now
- 3 or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours, or any stool overnight while you can't observe.
- Any vomiting, especially repeated or with blood.
- Fresh blood in stool beyond a single streak, or any black or tarry stool.
- Fever above 103.5°F, or temperature below 99°F.
- Won't get up, hides, or won't respond normally.
- Refuses water for 6+ hours, or any dehydration sign on the at-home checks.
- Abdominal pain: hunched posture, won't let you touch the belly, or repeated stretching and looking at the flank.
- Pale, white, yellow, or brick-red gums.
- Bloating or rapid abdominal distension (this is a separate emergency even if unrelated to the GI signs).

RECALL-SPECIFIC NOTE
- Put the exposure date in your log so any vet you call has the timeline in one sentence.
- If anything Salmonella-shaped develops in the next 1 to 2 weeks (fever, bloody diarrhea, profound lethargy, vomiting), mention the recalled-food history explicitly — it changes what the vet tests for.
- A fecal PCR or culture can give a definitive answer; reasonable to discuss at a normal appointment if anything drags on, no need to rush it today.

The wet-vs-dry read you got is a value match dressed as a hue difference. While wet, warmth does the separating work; once both areas dry to the same value, the warmth collapses into the surrounding field. So the study needs to load one side with a darker VALUE (not just a different temperature), and hold the three constants you named.

VALUE-LOCK DRYING TEST
One sheet, three cells, one value ladder.

SETUP
Light pencil grid dividing the sheet into three cells (top to bottom or side by side). Reserve one edge for the value ladder.

HOLD CONSTANT
  - Paper: same sheet, same brand and weight
  - Brush load: same brush, same loaded volume per stroke, same stroke count per swatch
  - Pigments: one cool (ultramarine, cerulean, or your usual) and one warm (burnt sienna, yellow ochre, or your usual), used throughout
  - Wash timing: paint the cool and warm halves of each cell within ~30 seconds of each other so they share a wet/dry arc
  - Swatch shape: same-size rectangle per cell, cool on the left, warm on the right, separated by a thin dry gap so they do not bleed

CALIBRATION (do this first)
  Paint a 1:8 swatch of each pigment in a corner. If 1:8 reads as a clean mid-value on your paper, use the ratios below as written. If 1:8 reads near-white or near-black, shift every ratio one notch lighter or darker and re-label your wells.

THE THREE CELLS

  Cell 1 — Control
    Cool 1:8, warm 1:8, single wash each.
    Replicates the test that converged. Expected: dry values match.

  Cell 2 — Warm heavier
    Cool 1:10, warm 1:6, single wash each.
    Tests whether loading the warm side denser preserves the gap.

  Cell 3 — Cool heavier
    Cool 1:6, warm 1:10, single wash each.
    Tests whether loading the cool side denser — and tells you which direction reads better to your eye.

VALUE LADDER (along the reserved strip)
  Five small swatches using the same two pigments at:
    1:12, 1:8, 1:5, 1:3, neat (no water added)
  Label each step. This is the ruler you will read the dry cells against.

PROTOCOL
  1. Pre-mix and label all dilutions in clean wells.
  2. Paint Cell 1, then 2, then 3 in order — same brush, same stroke count per swatch.
  3. Jot pigments used and room humidity on the sheet margin (dry-down shifts with both).
  4. Photograph each cell at 30 seconds post-stroke (wet) and again at full dry (~60 minutes, or when paper reads matte not sheen).
  5. Read each dry cell against the value ladder. Note which cell holds the largest wet-to-dry value gap, and which side (cool or warm) is doing the separating work.

WHAT THIS ISOLATES
  Whether asymmetric dilution in the wet stage is enough to lock the value gap through drying.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ISOLATE (follow-ups if all three cells converge when dry)
  - Glazing: re-run with both halves at 1:8, then lay one more 1:8 wash on the warm half once bone-dry. Cleanest test of post-dry layering.
  - Pigment choice: a fresh sheet with a different cool/warm pair tells you whether the problem is the value convergence or your current pairing.
  - Edge dynamics: real counter edges are lines, not fields; the convergence at a shared boundary has its own behavior that flat swatches do not capture.

That's a clean empirical result — controlled comparison isolating the one variable that mattered. A few thoughts if useful:

The mechanism makes sense: when warm and cool converge in value, the eye reads them as the same plane and the warmth visually neutralizes into "flat mid-tone." A value step gives the warm edge its own structural role (the lit interior reads as a separate plane from the recessed cool window), so the warmth survives without needing to be louder chromatically.

This also tracks with general watercolor physics — saturation losses on drying hit warm pigments (especially earth tones and oranges) harder than cool washes, so chasing warmth chromatically is fighting drying. Chasing it structurally via value is more stable.

If you ever want to test the next variable, the obvious follow-up is what you already held constant: paper, brush load, and wash timing. Worth noting those were the controlled variables, so the result is genuinely about value vs. saturation, not confounded by edge wetness or pigment load.

The pattern you're tracking — repair, rerouting, label — is doing something interesting because the label isn't separable from the practice. The residents' workaround is genuinely adaptive in the sense that it works and it persists, and the planner's "resilience" framing is what makes it legible to officials, which is often what allows a workaround to survive contact with the institution. On that reading, the language is functional for the people doing the rerouting.

The avoidance reading has weight too, and it lives in a different place: not in whether the practice works, but in what the label lets the institution stop doing. If "resilience" becomes the official story, then the drainage that keeps flooding the underpass doesn't have to be anyone's project anymore. The reframing absorbs the failure into a system property. So the two readings aren't symmetric — one is about what residents gain, the other about what the institution gets to not fix.

What I'd watch for across the three scenes is whether the planner's framing changes anything material: does it unlock funding for the workaround, does it suppress a complaint, does it show up in a budget line as "community resilience" instead of "drainage repair"? If the label is doing institutional work, that's usually where you can see it. If it's purely rhetorical and the drainage still gets fixed on its own timeline, the adaptation reading holds more weight.

The thing I'd resist is collapsing them. The novel might be precisely about a label that is both true and evasive at once — true about the residents, evasive about the cause — and your unwillingness to settle is probably the right way to read it.

Reading: Sam's standing is settled; what's unsettled is the substance behind four typical quarter-close artifacts. Each has a common gap that a well-placed question can close without re-litigating role.

(1) Calculation statement — the ambiguity
The headline figure is only as good as the inputs that aren't shown in the statement itself: cutoff date, included scope, treatment of edge cases (refunds, credits, mid-period upgrades, proration), and gross-vs-net adjustments. Without that, the number can't be reconciled to the underlying ledger.

(2) Reserve disclosure — the ambiguity
"Reserve" can mean several different things (allowance for doubtful amounts, refund reserve, contingent/escrowed amounts, holdbacks), each sized differently (percentage, statistical, judgmental) and signed off by different people. The disclosure rarely shows the category breakdown or whether methodology changed from the prior quarter.

(3) Payment timing — the ambiguity
"Paid in Q1" can mean disbursed by cutoff, accrued by cutoff, or merely scheduled by cutoff — and the cutoff policy itself is often not stated alongside the figure. The answer can differ by line (payroll, vendor, customer refund, settlement).

(4) Correction process — the ambiguity
If a discrepancy surfaces after close, the policy usually isn't spelled out: who can initiate, whether the correction adjusts the closed quarter or posts in Q2, who has approval authority, and what the audit-trail documentation looks like.

Four questions Sam can ask (precise, noncombative; role-accepted as a given):

A. Calculation — "On the Q1 calculation statement, can you confirm the input cutoff date, the treatment of [the specific edge case relevant here — e.g., refunds processed in the last five business days], and how the reported figure ties to the underlying ledger total?"

B. Reserve — "For the quarter-end reserve, could you share the breakdown by category — refund reserve, allowance, holdback, contingent — and the methodology used to size each, plus any change from Q4 2024?"

C. Payment timing — "For [the specific line, e.g., Q1 customer refund disbursements], does 'paid in Q1' mean disbursed by the cutoff date, accrued by it, or scheduled by it — and where is the cutoff policy documented?"

D. Correction — "If a discrepancy is identified after the Q1 close, what is the process — does it adjust the closed quarter or post in Q2, who has approval authority, and what documentation does the audit trail require?"

Yes — that pattern fits trapped air very well. Milky cloudiness that clears from the bottom of a glass upward in roughly 30 seconds, with no sediment, color, or odor, is the classic signature of microbubbles (dissolved air coming out of solution as pressure equalizes after a shutoff and refill). Bubbles cling to the glass walls first, then buoyantly rise — that's why the clearing reads bottom-up. Keeping Kibo on pre-shutoff water was the right call; air-laden tap water is unpalatable but not harmful.

Conservative cold-water flushing sequence (cold only until you've confirmed clarity, because the hot side pulls through the water heater and can mask a real issue or stir sediment):

  1. Remove aerators from the kitchen and bathroom cold taps so any dislodged debris exits instead of clogging the screen. Set screens aside.
  2. Open the cold tap nearest where service enters the unit (usually the kitchen) fully, and let it run 3–5 minutes into a sink or bucket. You should hear sputtering taper to steady flow as air purges.
  3. Move to the next farthest cold tap (bathroom sink), then shower/tub cold, then any laundry or outdoor hose bib. 2–3 minutes per fixture at full open.
  4. Flush every toilet once (refills the tank and clears the supply stub).
  5. Fill a clean clear glass from the kitchen cold tap and confirm clarity from bottom-up within ~30 seconds, no specks, no tint, no smell.
  6. Only after step 5 looks clean: run hot briefly (~30–60 seconds) at one fixture to clear air from the hot branch. If your water heater was actually drained during the shutoff, follow the building's relight instructions before running hot for long.
  7. Reinstall aerators. Discard any ice in the freezer and run the icemaker through 2–3 cycles so the supply line and bin flush.
  8. If you have a point-of-use filter (under-sink, fridge, pitcher), replace the cartridge now — trapped air in a filter slowly outgasses and can keep water cloudy and taste flat for days.

Stop and contact management (do not assume air) if you see any of:

  - Discoloration that doesn't clear in a few minutes: yellow, brown, orange, or reddish tints, or water that darkens after sitting. Suggests rust/disturbance in the service line or building riser — needs the property to flush at the main.
  - Persistent visible particles or sediment (grit, flecks, flakes) after a full cold flush. Air bubbles vanish; particulates don't.
  - Any non-chlorine odor: sulfur/rotten egg, metallic, fuel/oil/petroleum, or sewage. Chlorine smell is normal right after a shutoff and should fade; the others aren't.
  - Pressure loss that doesn't recover after the full flush, or repeated heavy sputtering that returns minutes after you stop running water. Can indicate a failing PRV, building-side issue, or a service-line problem.
  - Any leak: under sinks, around the water heater, at toilets, at the supply stops, on walls or ceilings, even a small drip. Air doesn't cause leaks; a shutoff and refill often reveals weak fittings or aged valves.
  - Cloudiness that's only in the hot side, or hot-side rumbling/clanking. That's water-heater sediment, not air in the lines.
  - Recurring cloudiness after multiple full flushes over 24 hours. Suggests the air source is ongoing (pressure tank, building pump, or service-side issue) and warrants management involvement.

If everything clears and stays clear after step 5, Kibo can switch back to tap water on the next fill.

Bottom line: keep the bike out of commute use until a shop has looked at it. Chain skip under load climbing is a drive-train problem, and it can repeat at a stop sign, a hill start, or in traffic — that is the exact moment you do not want the chain to jump. Walk, bus, or drive it; do not commute on it.

Why "conservative" matters here: you cannot reliably diagnose a skip from a stationary visual alone (skip is a dynamic symptom), so the goal of the inspection is to narrow it down and to collect information for the shop, not to clear the bike for riding.

Stationary inspection sequence (bike on a stand, flipped upside-down on the bars+seat, or just leaned against a wall — your choice; do NOT pedal hard under load):

1. Stiff-link check. With the chain on the chainring, slowly turn the cranks by hand backward and watch the chain run across the rear cassette. Any link that does not hinge freely — look for a kink, rust spot, or a side plate that sits proud of its neighbors — is a suspect. Stiff links often cause skip under power.
2. Chain wear (the most common cause of skip under load). Use a ruler or tape measure: count 12 complete links (pin to pin) and measure end-to-end. 12 fresh links = exactly 12.0 inches (304.8 mm). If you measure 12-1/16" or more, the chain is stretched and is the prime suspect. If you have a chain-check tool, 0.5% = replace soon, 0.75% = replace now. Skip is usually the chain OR the chain plus a worn cassette.
3. Cassette tooth inspection. Crouch behind the rear wheel and sight across the cassette cogs at eye level, ideally with light coming from behind you. Worn cogs look like shark fins or hooks; new cogs are symmetric and shelf-like. Focus on the cogs you spend the most time in (middle of the cassette). If you see hooked teeth, the cassette is shot and a new chain alone will skip on it.
4. Chainring teeth. With the chain off (or just looking through it), check the big and middle chainring teeth for the same hooked/shark-fin shape, especially on the side that takes power (front of the tooth for the big ring). Chainring wear is less common on commuters but not rare.
5. Rear derailleur hanger alignment. Eye-ball the derailleur cage from directly behind the bike. The two pulleys should sit in a clean vertical line under the cassette cogs. If the cage is visibly twisted to one side, the hanger is bent — that alone causes skip and bad shifting, and it is also the part most likely to be bent by a low-speed tip-over you may not remember.
6. Cable feel at the shifter. Click through every gear with the bike stationary. Each click should produce an immediate, crisp cage movement. If a shift is mushy or the cage does not move, suspect cable/housing friction before suspecting wear — but report it either way.
7. Chain lube condition. Wipe a section of chain with a clean rag. If it comes back bone-dry and gray, or black and tarry, the lube state is contributing and worth telling the shop.

What to tell the shop, verbatim:

  - "Chain skipped twice under firm pedal pressure while climbing on my commute."
  - "Brakes, tires, and steering felt normal; no crash."
  - "I stopped riding and walked the last half mile rather than retesting."
  - Date, approximate mileage on the current chain (if you know), and whether the chain or cassette has been replaced recently.
  - Anything you noticed above: stiff link, hooked teeth, bent-looking derailleur cage, mushy shifter.

What not to do before the shop visit:

  - Do not ride under load to "see if it still does it."
  - Do not throw a new chain on yourself without inspecting the cassette — a new chain on a worn cassette will skip immediately and can also accelerate cassette damage.
  - Do not twist limit screws or the B-tension to "fix" it. Adjustment cannot repair worn teeth; it can mask a real problem until the chain jumps at speed.
  - Do not ignore it because it skipped only twice. Twice under load is enough.

Realistic expectation: the most likely shop verdict is worn chain plus worn cassette, replaced together. Less likely: bent hanger, stiff link, or cable/housing issue. Either way, until the work is done, this bike is a weekend-ride bike at most — not a commuter.

Two-week runway, 4.1 GB free, four protected categories. Work in phases, smallest blast radius first, with an explicit verification gate before any downloaded media or app data is removed.

PHASE 1 — REVERSIBLE, NO DATA LOSS

  1. Browser caches
     Settings → Safari → Clear History and Website Data
     Settings → Chrome → Privacy → Clear Browsing Data → Cached Images and Files
     Both regenerate on next visit. Expected gain: 200 MB – 1 GB.

  2. Offload unused apps (the system-managed feature, not per-app)
     Settings → General → iPhone Storage → enable "Offload Unused Apps"
     Removes the binary, keeps the icon and data. Reinstall restores full state including logins. Auth and travel apps you use regularly won't be touched.
     Expected gain: 1 GB+ typical.

  3. Streaming app caches
     Spotify, Netflix, YouTube, Apple Music, Audible, Podcasts — each has a cache-clearing option in its in-app settings. This is NOT the same as removing downloaded offline content (that's Phase 3).

  4. Mail trash + Mail cache
     Mail app → Mailboxes → Trash → Empty.
     Settings → Mail → Accounts → turn Mail off and back on if the cache is stuck. Travel confirmations live in Inbox/Sent — leave those alone.

  5. Recently Deleted photos already in trash
     Photos → Albums → Recently Deleted → Delete All.
     These are already in the 30-day trash. Clearing them reclaims space earlier; it is not deleting from your library.

  Typical Phase 1 total: 2–6 GB. Often enough by itself.

PHASE 2 — VERIFICATION GATE

Run this list BEFORE touching downloaded media or any app's data. This is the explicit checkpoint you asked for.

  Travel confirmations are reachable in under 10 seconds:
    - Airline boarding pass in Wallet (open airline app, confirm pass is added)
    - Hotel reservation (email + hotel app, or in confirmations@)
    - Rental car / ground transport
    - Itinerary backed up in at least two places (email + an app, or email + a PDF in Files)

  Authentication apps still work and are recoverable:
    - Open each one (Authy / Google Authenticator / 1Password / etc.)
    - Confirm a TOTP code generates
    - Confirm a recovery path exists: cloud backup enabled in Authy, printed recovery codes in a safe place, master password memorized
    - Note these apps explicitly in the "do not touch" list for Phase 3

  Message history you'll need is cloud-backed:
    - iCloud Messages on (Settings → [name] → iCloud → Messages)
    - WhatsApp / Signal backups current
    - You can find any conversation you'll need while away (Marcus, logistics, anyone coordinating the trip)

  Downloaded media — re-downloadable on Portland wifi:
    - Marcus's place, hotel, coffee shop — assess realistically
    - If you anticipate flaky wifi, KEEP the offline copy of anything you'll actively use during transit or in-transit moments (flight entertainment, boarding-pass-area transit map)

  App data — backed up:
    - For any app whose cache/data you'd clear in Phase 3: does it sync to iCloud or app backup? If yes, local cache is safe to clear.

  If anything in this list fails, stop and resolve it before moving to Phase 3.

PHASE 3 — REVIEWED REMOVALS

After Phase 2 passes. Largest first, protected categories untouched.

  1. Downloaded offline media
     Spotify / Apple Music → downloaded playlists
     Netflix / YouTube / Disney+ / Prime → downloads
     Podcasts → downloaded episodes
     Audible → downloaded books (purchased — re-downloadable forever from your library)
     Kindle → downloaded books (same)
     Apple/Google Maps → offline regions — DOWNLOAD Portland-area BEFORE you delete anything, or do this last and only after re-downloading is verified

     Rule: anything from a streaming subscription is freely re-downloadable; anything you bought lives in your library forever.

  2. Files app → On My iPhone
     PDFs, ZIPs, installers. Travel confirmations sometimes live here — open before deleting anything unfamiliar.

  3. Messages → Review Large Attachments
     Settings → Messages → scroll to bottom → Review Large Attachments
     Deletes the attachment file only; the text and conversation remain. Safe because Phase 2 confirmed cloud backup.

  4. WhatsApp / Telegram / Signal media
     In-app Storage settings. Same logic as iMessage — chat history stays, attachments go.

  5. Voice Memos
     Audit and export any keeper to Files or email before deleting. Trip notes are useful.

  6. App caches unreachable in Phase 1
     For an app with no in-app cache clear: delete the app, reinstall (login + library survive if account-backed). Do NOT do this for any app on the protected list.

  7. Visual voicemail cache
     Phone app → Voicemail → scroll to bottom → Delete Voicemail. Save any audio you need first.

PHASE 4 — PRE-TRIP FINAL CHECK

  - Storage: aim for 8–10 GB free (room for trip photos, offline maps, mid-trip downloads)
  - Auth apps: still working
  - Boarding pass + hotel + ground transport reachable in 10 seconds
  - Offline Maps: Portland + airport area downloaded
  - Family photos: iCloud Photos or Google Photos backup verified on (this should already be true — verify, don't change policy)
  - Kibo's care plan / pet sitter contact saved somewhere that doesn't depend on the phone (printed, or shared with Sam)

PROTECTED — DO NOT TOUCH AT ANY POINT

  - Family Photos library
  - Authentication apps (Authy, Google Authenticator, 1Password, etc.)
  - Travel confirmations (email, Wallet passes, Files PDFs)
  - Message history you may need while away

OPTIONAL BONUS, NO DELETION REQUIRED

  Settings → Photos → Optimize iPhone Storage. Keeps smaller versions locally, full resolution in iCloud. Frees 1–5 GB commonly. Only do this if your iCloud Photos backup is on and current — your family photos are preserved, just not stored as full files on the device.

If Phase 1 gets you to 8+ GB free, you can stop there and not touch Phase 3 at all.
