Good catch before any damage shows up. "Ordinary cardboard" in direct contact with a watercolor is the single most common amateur-framing mistake, and the fact that there's no staining, odor, buckling, or transfer yet means you've caught it at the ideal point — early enough that simple, reversible DIY isolation is the right call, not a treatment job.

Why the cardboard is the problem (short version): groundwood / wood-pulp board contains lignin, which oxidizes over time and off-gasses acids that migrate into adjacent paper. The result is yellowing, embrittlement, and eventually brown staining that radiates inward from the edges. "Acid-free" cardboard from a craft store is often only surface-neutralized and may still be lignified; the only truly safe substrates are 100% cotton/alpha-cellulose, pH-neutral, alkaline-buffered boards.

Conservative options, in increasing order of effort:

1.  Interleave with buffered tissue (minimum, do this today)
    -  Hollinger buffered tissue (calcium-carbonate-buffered, pH ~8.5–9) is the standard
    -  Place a single sheet between the watercolor and the cardboard, fully covering the artwork with a small margin so no edge of the painting touches the board
    -  Buffered tissue neutralizes migrating acids, so even if you do nothing else for now it halts ongoing damage
    -  Note: unbuffered is required for charcoal, pastel, photographs, and certain dye-based media, but a normal watercolor with stable pigments is fine with buffered
    -  Sources: Gaylord Archival, Hollinger Metal Edge, Talas, Light Impressions (online; small sheets are inexpensive)

2.  Replace the cardboard with a conservation-grade backing board
    -  Best: 100% cotton rag matboard, neutral pH, alkaline-buffered — Rising Museum Board, Bainbridge Alpharag, Crescent RagMat. Cut slightly larger than the artwork (about 1/8 to 1/4 inch margin all around) so the board edges never abrade the paper
    -  Acceptable cheaper alternative: archival corrugated board (e.g., Gaylord Heritage Corrugated) — provides rigidity without acid migration
    -  Avoid: standard foam board, "acid-free" craft-store foam board unless it explicitly states 100% cotton / lignin-free, corrugated plastic (Coroplast) is inert but cheap-feeling and less archival-grade for fine art
    -  Cut with a clean mat knife on a protected surface; deburr the edges

3.  Add a window mat (the proper long-term housing)
    -  A matboard with a rectangular opening creates an air gap so the painted surface never touches either the glazing or the backing
    -  Mount the artwork to the back of the mat with Japanese tissue hinges and wheat starch paste (both reversible, both archival). Two hinges along the top edge is standard; the sheet should hang freely
    -  Use UV-filtering glazing if you'll hang it — Optium Museum Acrylic or Tru Vue Museum Glass. Regular glass or acrylic passes UV that fades watercolor pigments
    -  This is the level most framers trained in "conservation framing" can deliver; look for a PPFA Certified Picture Framer or a shop that explicitly offers archival/conservation mounting

Handling precautions while you're working on it right now:
    -  Clean, flat work surface — not carpet (lint), not the kitchen counter mid-meal
    -  Wash and dry hands thoroughly; nitrile gloves are preferred over cotton (cotton can snag paper fibers). If no gloves, handle by opposite corners only, never touch the painted surface
    -  Lift the sheet with two hands, supporting under it — don't flex it
    -  Don't lay it face-down on anything
    -  No tape, paper clips, rubber bands, Post-its, or glue anywhere near the artwork
    -  No paper towels (lint, sometimes acidic); a clean microfiber cloth or lint-free cotton is fine for the board, not the painting
    -  Don't talk/sneeze/cough directly over the sheet
    -  Keep it out of direct sun and away from any heat source while you work
    -  If you ever suspect flaking or lifting media, don't flip the sheet — work face-up only and stop

Things you might be tempted to do that are wrong:
    -  Plastic sleeves / Ziploc bags for storage: PVC off-gasses; polyethylene is fine short-term but not archival
    -  "Acid-free" kraft or black paper from a craft store: often only surface-treated, still acidic in the core
    -  Mounting with spray adhesive, double-sided tape, or glue stick: not reversible, will damage the sheet
    -  Lining or ironing the paper: leave entirely to a conservator

Signs that justify stopping and calling a paper conservator (American Institute for Conservation directory at culturalheritage.org, "Find a Conservator" → specialization: paper) — any one of these is a stop-work signal:
    -  Foxing — small reddish-brown spots, often with a darker center (fungal or iron byproducts)
    -  Tide lines, staining, or yellowing/browning radiating inward from the edges of the sheet (the signature of acid migration already underway)
    -  Buckling, cockling, or warping that wasn't there before, or that won't relax under gentle weight overnight between blotter sheets
    -  Media lifting, flaking, powdering, or smudging under a soft brush — rare in watercolor, but possible if overworked or if it's been exposed to moisture
    -  Tears, creases, losses, or thinning areas in the paper
    -  Musty or sour odor, or any fuzzy/spotty growth (mold) — contains the sheet in a clean folder, don't try to clean it, and call a conservator
    -  Old tape, glue residue, mounting hinges you didn't apply, or pressure-sensitive adhesive staining (often visible as a dark rectangle or strip)
    -  Insect activity — small holes, fine frass, webbing
    -  Any handling damage introduced during the work

A professional framer (not a conservator) is the right call when the goal is presentation/display rather than repair: archival matting, hinging, and framing behind UV-filtering glazing for a piece you intend to hang. A conservator is the right call for treatment, damage repair, or assessment of something with real value.

Practical recommendation for this session, given it's Sunday watercolor block and the piece is already separated from the glazing:
    -  Stop with the cardboard in contact; don't put it back together
    -  Cut a sheet of buffered tissue or a piece of cotton-rag matboard to size, and place the watercolor on it face-up, uncovered
    -  If you have a clean folder or interleaving paper, slip it loosely over the top to keep dust off
    -  Plan the mat-and-frame step for a separate session with fresh hands and a clean surface — it's worth doing well rather than rushing between brush strokes
    -  If during any of this you spot one of the warning signs above, set the piece aside and call a conservator before doing anything further

One last consideration specific to this piece: "Before the House Wakes" sounds like a titled, intentional work rather than a study — if it's part of an ongoing body of work or anything you might exhibit or sell down the road, the marginal cost of getting the housing right now is much smaller than the cost of trying to undo acid damage later. Conservation framing with UV-filtering glazing is genuinely worth it for titled work you intend to keep.

Two worked examples below, both drawn from the May 8 prod-shadow shape (9 holds: 7 stale QHA + 2 unresolved ESA; 4 suppressions = VALID active CS adoption/renewal). Aligned to the 5/13 canonical definitions, not the Ines draft.

  EXAMPLE 1 — Final suppression (VALID, active CS work)
  
  Contact:        ACME-renewal-Q2
  Surface state:  Suppression
  Reason:         ACTIVE_CS_ADOPTION
  Field:          customer-success-engagement = in-progress (renewal motion)
  Validity:       tied to CS engagement lifecycle, NOT to data freshness
  What "final" means here:
    The suppression was set because CS has a live counterpart working this
    contact on adoption or renewal. It stands until CS closes the engagement.
    It is not a stale hold. It is not a bad-data flag. When CS closes the
    renewal motion, the suppression lifts on its own — no source check needed.
  Why this is NOT a hold:
    There is no stale/unresolved/conflicting field on this contact. The data
    is current. The contact is paused because a human CS counterpart is
    working them, not because of a data condition.
  Operator takeaway:
    See ACTIVE_CS_* reason code → it is suppression. Do not try to "refresh"
    the contact to clear it. The lift comes from CS closing the engagement,
    not from a fresh source check.


  EXAMPLE 2 — Stale hold → fresh source check → reevaluation → Proceed
  
  Contact:        BETA-stale-qha-091
  Surface state:  Hold
  Reason:         STALE_QHA
  Field:          qualification-data (QHA) last refreshed 2025-03-22
                  (47 days old; threshold 30)
  Validity:       held because the field is stale, NOT because CS is working
                  it, NOT because the contact is suppressed
  Fresh source check (2025-05-08):
    Connector enrichment run returned current QHA — signed-off 2025-05-08,
    all fields within the 30-day threshold.
  Reevaluation result:
    Hold clears. Contact moves to Proceed (now eligible; not "permitted,"
    but no longer blocked by a stale field).
  Why this is NOT a suppression:
    No CS engagement on this contact. The pause was data-driven, not
    human-counterpart-driven. When the field refreshed, the hold went away
    on its own — there was no CS close-out event to wait for.
  Operator takeaway:
    See STALE_* or UNRESOLVED_* reason code → it is a hold. It clears when
    the underlying field gets a fresh source check (connector run, manual
    refresh, or owner confirmation). If a CS-owned reason is also present,
    that is a separate state layered on top of the hold, not the hold itself.


  THE CONTRAST THAT MAKES THEM DISTINCT
  
    Suppression:  human-counterpart-driven; lifts on CS lifecycle event
    Hold:         data-driven; lifts on fresh source check
  
    Both look like "outbound paused," but the lift condition is what tells
    them apart. The reason-code prefix is the fastest signal:
      ACTIVE_CS_*  →  suppression  →  wait for CS close
      STALE_*      →  hold         →  wait for fresh source check
      UNRESOLVED_* →  hold         →  wait for owner confirmation
      CONFLICTING_*→  hold         →  wait for reconciliation

Acceptance checklist (plain text, no markdown):

BEFORE YOU OPEN
  - Photograph the shipping box: all sides, seams, label, tracking number.
  - Note the carrier, sender, delivery date/time.

AS YOU OPEN
  - Photograph inner packaging before fully unwrapping.
  - Photograph the item as-received, including any defect.
  - Keep all packing materials until the issue is resolved.

CONFIRM THE ORDER
  - Pull up the confirmation: item, SKU/variant, qty, ship-to, price.
  - Check what's actually in the box against what was ordered.
  - Write the gap in plain language: "expected X, got Y, condition Z."
  - Note the retailer's return/remake window from policy.

TRY THE REMAKE CAUTIOUSLY
  - Read any included instructions or care notes first.
  - Use the smallest/minimal test the situation allows.
  - Consumable: photograph, then a small taste test. Don't serve to others yet.
  - Tool/device: test on a non-critical surface, not a full deployment.
  - Stop the moment the original defect reappears or a new one shows up.

STOP AND CONTACT THE RETAILER NOW IF ANY OF THESE
  - Visible damage that affects function.
  - Wrong item entirely (not just a variant mismatch).
  - Safety concern: sharp, hot, electrical, chemical, choking, off odor.
  - Same defect the remake was supposed to fix.
  - Missing parts/accessories essential to use.
  - Sign of tampering (broken seal, resealed packaging, unusual smell).

WHEN YOU CONTACT THEM
  - Use the retailer's official channel (order page, support email, phone). Not social DMs.
  - Lead with: order number, one-line description, what you want (refund / replacement / cancel).
  - Attach: the as-received photos, the defect photo, and any test-result photo.
  - Keep a written log of who you spoke to, when, and what was agreed.

Your three signals together clear the threshold: mileage in the lifespan band, lateral heel nearly smooth (rearfoot stability gone), and pronounced midsole creasing (foam compression set, rebound lost). Two of three is enough; all three means the shoe is past useful life. The risk is exactly the one your return-to-running has been protecting against — a subtle loss of cushioning and lateral stability that converts to compensatory gait and re-loads the ankle.

REPLACEMENT FRAMEWORK
  Replace on any 2 of these 3 (you already have 3 of 3):
    - Mileage: in or past the 300–500 mi band (lower end if you're heavier or mostly pavement; higher if mostly soft trail)
    - Outsole: lateral heel smoothed (rearfoot stability gone) or forefoot slick patches (push-off compromised)
    - Midsole: visible creasing/folding lines under the forefoot or rearfoot (foam cell breakdown; shock attenuation gone)
  Replace on these even if mileage is still low:
    - New ache/pain in last 4–6 weeks that wasn't present earlier in the shoe's life
    - "Dead" underfoot feel — same effort now feels harder
    - A trip or near-twist tied to a smooth outsole patch
  Don't replace on mileage alone if midsole and outsole look fine — over-replacing has its own adaptation cost.

TRANSITION PLAN (2×/wk, 30 min, nonconsecutive — held throughout)
  Buy the same model or a known equivalent: same heel-toe drop, similar stack height, same category (stability/neutral/trail). Do not change shoe geometry mid-return.
  Wear-test indoors first: 10–15 min standing/walking to check heel slip, toe-box pressure, arch hot spots, before any logged miles.
  3-week rotation:
    - Week 1: Run 1 in old, Run 2 in new
    - Week 2: Run 1 in new, Run 2 in old
    - Week 3: both runs in new
  Extend to a 4th partial-rotation week if either old-shoe run in the prior 7 days tripped the symptom rule, or if a new-shoe session produced a new sensation (heel slip, hot spot, calf stretch, ankle awareness). A new sensation is treated as a symptom event: log it, run the next-day check, and rotate back to old for the next session if it persists.
  Do not bump duration or frequency in the rotation window. Any future progression to distance or a third day stays out of the new-shoe transition and should happen in fully broken-in shoes.

GUARDRAILS (unchanged)
  Symptom rule still applies: no R-ankle ache during run, at rest that night, or next AM. If any, hold the next run; resume only after two consecutive symptom-free rest days.
  Clinical follow-up if focal ankle pain recurs — i.e., localized to the joint, sharp, or reproducible on a specific motion. Shoe-break-in feel is not the same as joint pain; calf stretch or general DOMS is not the same either.
  Ankle + calf strengthening stays in the rotation independent of the shoe change.
  The old shoes get retired at the end of Week 2 of the rotation, not before — you want a clean comparison of how the new shoe behaves in two sessions before you commit.

One thing worth flagging given the ankle history: run your next new-shoe session on a day where the day-before session was in old shoes, not new shoes. I have the full prior session. Let me verify the math and build the decision framework you asked for. Let me do the arithmetic precisely.

**The two options (6-month term, so $72 savings is per 6 months):**
- Option A: $684 / 6 mo — comp $500, collision $750, rental + towing included
- Option B: $612 / 6 mo — comp $1,000, collision $1,500, no rental, towing included

Annualized savings going B: $72 × 2 = **$144/year**

**Additional exposure under B:**

1. **Collision deductible exposure**: $1,500 − $750 = **+$750 extra out-of-pocket per collision claim**

2. **Comprehensive deductible exposure**: $1,000 − $500 = **+$500 extra out-of-pocket per comp claim**

3. **Loss of rental coverage**: typical 14-day rental after a covered claim at ~$40/day ≈ **+$560 out-of-pocket** when you file a claim and need a loaner. If your credit card has *primary* rental coverage, this drops to ~$0; if only *secondary* or none, the loss is real.

**Break-even math (purely on deductibles):**

  - Extra collision exposure: $750
  - Annual savings: $144
  - Break-even: one collision claim every ~$750 ÷ $144 = **~5.2 years**
  - With comp layered in: $500 + $750 = $1,250 extra deductible exposure vs. $144/yr → **~8.7 years** of claim-free driving to come out ahead on deductibles alone.

So B only wins on premium math if you go *roughly* 5–9 years without a single comp or collision claim. Towing is unchanged, so that's not a factor.

**Loss of rental is the sleeper:** Unlike the deductibles (which only cost you if you actually claim), the rental drop is a *categorical* loss. If you don't have a backup vehicle or primary rental on a credit card, one claim + 14-day loaner can erase years of premium savings in a single event. This is the line item most people under-weight.

---

**Decision framework — based on liquidity and value of rental coverage, not just "cheaper is better":**

Step 1 — Liquidity check (can you absorb a $1,500 shock?)
  - Do you have $1,500+ in accessible savings without disrupting other goals (emergency fund, Kibo's vet reserve, etc.)?
    - Yes → deductible exposure is tolerable; the higher comp/collision deductibles are a real cost only on the day you claim.
    - No → A. The deductible isn't just "worse insurance," it's a forced $1,500 spend at the worst possible moment.

Step 2 — Rental substitute check (this is the $144 vs ~$560 question)
  - Do you have a backup vehicle available within 24 hours (partner's car, second car, family nearby, short-term rental access)?
    - Yes → rental loss is mostly theoretical; B's case strengthens.
  - OR: does any credit card you carry include **primary** rental coverage (not secondary)?
    - Yes → rental loss is zero. B's case strengthens.
  - Neither → A. Without a substitute, one claim makes B's premium savings disappear overnight.

Step 3 — Claim-frequency signal
  - Any at-fault or not-at-fault collision claims in the past 5 years?
    - Yes → expect another within the policy horizon; A is the safer bet.
    - No + low-theft/low-storm ZIP + low annual mileage → B is more defensible.

Step 4 — Vehicle status (separate from the framework, but worth flagging)
  - Financed or leased? Most lenders require collision deductible ≤ $1,000 and many cap at $500. **If financed/leased, B may not even be a legal option — check the lender letter before anything else.** This is not in your stated facts, so I won't weight it, but flag it if applicable.

---

**Concrete verdict thresholds:**

  - **A** if any of: no backup vehicle, no primary credit-card rental, financed/leased, recent claim history, liquid savings < $1,500, or you'd genuinely pay $500–$700 out-of-pocket for a loaner after a claim rather than wait on a friend/partner. (This is the "I value rental coverage enough that $144/yr feels cheap for it" path.)
  - **B** if all of: backup vehicle or primary credit-card rental, paid-off car, $1,500+ in savings, no claims in 5+ years, low weather/theft exposure, AND you'd actively rather self-insure the rental gap for $144/yr than carry coverage you may not use. (This is the "I have alternatives and want to bank the premium" path.)

The cheapest premium is B, but it's only the better deal if Step 2 (rental substitute) and Step 1 (liquidity) both check out. If rental substitutes are weak, the premium math collapses the first time you need a loaner — and that's the part a pure price comparison misses.

The safest sequence is: take a rideshare home now, leave the bike locked in the secured office storage overnight, and retrieve it tomorrow morning. Why, and the bike plan:

Why rideshare beats the other two for this window:

1. Leaving immediately is the worst option. The warning is live now and would cover your whole ride. A 4-mile exposed bike segment is roughly 20-25 minutes in the open — under frequent lightning, possible hail, and strong wind. You'd be elevated, on metal framing, with effectively no insulation (tire rubber doesn't protect from lightning), wet road, and reduced visibility. "Leaving immediately" still means riding into the warning.

2. Waiting it out is safe but costly and not strictly safer. The warning expires at 6:30pm, so about 2 hours 15 minutes indoors. If the office is comfortable and the storm clears on schedule, biking home after 6:30pm is essentially zero lightning risk. The downsides: you burn two-plus hours, and severe-thunderstorm warnings sometimes run long or are extended. It depends on the warning actually clearing at 6:30.

3. Rideshare and collect later is the strictly safest. Zero lightning/hail/wind exposure on the trip home, and the bike sits indoors where hail and wind can't touch it. The only cost is one rideshare fare plus a retrieval trip tomorrow.

- Lock it to the indoor bike rack with whatever lock you normally use. Even in a secured room, lock it — indoor bike theft from office storage happens.
- Remove anything detachable: front light, rear light, computer/GPS, panniers, saddle bag, water bottle. If your saddle is quick-release and the rack is in a shared-access space, take the saddle too.
- Wheels: if the bike has quick-release wheels and the storage room is only loosely controlled, take the front wheel or run a cable through the frame and both wheels to the rack. If the room is badge-controlled with only employees entering, a frame lock to the rack is sufficient.
- Tires: not strictly required, but if either tire is soft, add air before you leave so the bike isn't resting on a flat all night.
- Take a photo of the bike locked in place, with the lock position visible, so you can find it quickly tomorrow and have a record.

  Cushion: slightly firmer — better ground feel and proprioception, which is the conservative call for an ankle that's been sensitive. Softer foam tends to mask late-run form drift; firmer foam gives earlier feedback.
  Weight: -1.2 oz vs B. Small, but favorable (less mass to control per step, lower ankle moment).
  Net change: one minor cushioning shift + a small weight drop. Lowest-variable option.

Option B (10 mm / softer / 10.4 oz)
  Drop: +2 mm — a real biomechanical shift. Protective in theory (small offload of calf/Achilles) but still an adaptation your ankle and posterior chain have to negotiate.
  Cushion: softer — can dull form feedback over 30 min.
  Weight: +1.2 oz vs A — minor.
  Net change: three concurrent changes. Hardest to attribute a symptom to if anything surfaces.

Recommendation: Option A.

Reasoning, tied to your stated goal: drop is the most consequential variable in a shoe swap for a runner with right-ankle history. Keeping it at 8 mm removes the largest adaptation load. "Slightly firmer" (not softer) sits on the conservative end of the cushioning spectrum for your situation. Softer foam at 30 min continuous can let form degrade quietly before your symptom rule catches it. The lighter weight is a small additional point in A's favor.

Honest caveat: Option A is not zero-variable. Midsole foam compound, last shape, stack height, upper fit, and outsole geometry are all new even with the same drop. Treat it as a controlled single-variable intro, not a no-change.

Transition plan — holds duration, frequency, strengthening, and the symptom rule, and does not combine the shoe change with any other progression:

  Week 1, Run 1: current shoes. Baseline, nothing else changes.
  Week 1, Run 2: Option A. Same 30 min, same pace intent, same lake-trail loop.
  Apply the standing rule at three checkpoints: during the run, on the rest day, and the next morning. If any R-ankle signal at any of those three, revert to the old shoe and hold the swap until you've reassessed — do not "push through" to a third shoe run that week.
  Week 2: if Week 1 Run 2 plus the following ~24 h were clean, both runs in Option A.
  Week 3+: Option A as your standing pair, continuing 2×/wk nonconsecutive / 30 min / lake-trail easy.

What this preserves, point by point against your constraints:
  Duration: 30 min on both runs every week. No bump.
  Frequency: 2×/wk nonconsecutive. No third run added.
  Strengthening: ankle + calf routine unchanged.
  Symptom rule: applied to the shoe-intro run and the following day, exactly as written.
  Single variable: shoe change isolated to one session first; not combined with any duration or frequency increase.

Optional low-cost pre-check (does not count as a run, no extra training stress): 5–10 min of walking plus a few easy strides in Option A on a non-run day to confirm heel-lock, toebox width, and tongue pressure. If anything feels off in that window, you've caught it without spending a 30-min session.

The instinct is wrong, and worth pushing back on.

Holds aren't a symptom of the path being unhealthy — they're a different lifecycle state. The shared-state contract being the sole prod decision path means: when release IS decided, the execution is clean. It doesn't mean every customer should auto-release. Holds = pre-decision (system correctly not deciding yet, waiting on confirmation / eligibility window / review). Delivery failures = post-decision (system tried to release/refund and the execution failed). Two different phases, two different root causes, two different metrics.

If we bucket holds as delivery failures we lose three things at once:
  - the real delivery-failure rate gets buried (ops signal disappears into a bigger, noisier number)
  - wrong incentive — pressure to release early just to clear the "failure" count, which is exactly what the governed meanings were designed to prevent
  - hold-reason distribution vanishes, and that distribution is where the actual issues live (customer-confirmation lag, eligibility-window timing, fraud-review backlog)

Better framing for Marcus: "healthy single path = release decisions execute cleanly. Holds = the system correctly NOT deciding yet. Different problem, different metric — and conflating them would mask the signal we just spent the last month getting clean."

If he wants a single headline number for the board, give him release-execution success rate on decided cases, not a holds-as-failures mashup.

Draft reply (concise; reads as internal ops/eng, not customer-facing):

---

Two things to keep separate in the export picture:

- **Evaluated decisions** — the unique final actions the system actually takes on a given workstream (e.g. one support-effort line, one refund-adj cash release). These are what we report on; each one corresponds to a single customer-visible outcome and stands on its own.

- **Intermediate fail-closed checks** — the upstream gates (state readiness, freshness, conflict resolution) that decide *whether* a decision is allowed to be evaluated at all. They are not decisions themselves; they either pass or they hold.

A **hold** is the intended, correct result when any required state is stale, unresolved, or conflicting. It is not an outcome, and it is not a delivery failure — nothing was sent, nothing was blocked from sending. It just means the system declined to evaluate the decision until the prerequisite state is clean.

So when you're reading the export:

- A hold ≠ a support-effort decision and ≠ a refund-adj release. It precedes both.
- A hold ≠ an error. Nothing broke; the gate did its job.
- A hold ≠ a customer-side send. There is no customer-facing artifact, and "the customer didn't receive it" is the wrong frame — there was nothing to receive yet.

Treat holds as the system refusing to commit on bad inputs, not as noise and not as contact.

Here's a tight, content-neutral packing method mom can run by herself. The goal is physical protection and sequence — no inference about what any of the photos shows.

Materials (one trip to a photo/art-supply store):
- 6 individual archival sleeves (polypropylene or polyethylene), sized to each photo — or, if none on hand, 6 clean glassine envelopes, or plain acid-free tissue for interleaving
- 1 rigid box slightly larger than the stack (a clean small cardboard box works; archival clamshell is better)
- A few sheets of acid-free tissue or unbleached muslin for cushioning
- 1 index card + soft pencil
- Optional: 1 silica gel packet (humidity, August travel)

Method:
1. Clean, dry surface. Handle each photo by edges only — no fingerprints on image or back.
2. One sleeve (or one tissue interleaf) per photo. No face-to-face stacking.
3. The one with handwriting on the back: orient it so the ink side rests against a clean tissue sheet, never against another photo's emulsion. Keep it flat — don't bend or flex.
4. Preserve order with a sequence card, not markings on the photos themselves. On the index card, write "1 of 6, 2 of 6, … 6 of 6" in pencil and tape the card inside the box lid. Pack photos in that numbered order; the lid's index tells you which end is "1" if the box gets re-oriented in the cabin.
5. Lay sleeved photos flat in the rigid box. Pack tissue around the sides and top so nothing shifts when the box is moved.
6. If using a desiccant, slip it between tissue and box wall — never in direct contact with photos.
7. Carry-on: box inside a soft tote, placed on top of soft items in the bag. If TSA asks, request hand inspection rather than multiple X-ray cycles.

Don'ts (worth telling mom explicitly):
- No paper clips, rubber bands, tape, sticky notes, or any writing on the photos or their backs.
- No scanning, photographing, or labeling the images before the visit.
- Don't unpack or sort at your end until you're both in the same room.
- Avoid checked luggage — heat, pressure, and handling are the main risks for loose prints, and carry-on sidesteps all three.

That keeps surfaces and the one inked back safe, keeps the six in source order, and leaves every identification call until you're together.

Quick read of the situation

A closed-door outage of about 4 hours with a fridge that has now stabilized at 44°F means the interior crossed the 40°F safety line during the outage. Peak temperature is unknown, "frozen items still feel solid" is reassuring but not definitive, and "no odor or fault" is positive but not a food-safety signal. Apply the conservative USDA-style 4-hour / 40°F rule and assume the perishable fridge food spent meaningful time in the danger zone.

Immediate triage — do these in order

  1. Let the compressor run 30–60 minutes before opening anything. Resist the urge to open and "check." Every open now costs recovery time.

  2. One careful pass through the freezer with the door closed the rest of the time:
     - rock hard with visible ice crystals  -> refreeze (expect quality loss)
     - soft but still icy, crystals in/around the package  -> cook now, do not refreeze raw
     - fully thawed and at fridge temp or warmer  -> treat as a refrigerated perishable below

  3. Fridge pass — decide by category using the lists below. When undecided, discard.

  4. Cool what survives promptly (or bag-and-bin for disposal) before the day ends.

  5. Sanitize after the pass — see end.

Discard (do not taste, do not feed to Kibo)

  - Raw or cooked meat, poultry, fish, shellfish
  - Eggs (raw, cooked, or in shell)
  - Milk, cream, yogurt, cottage cheese, sour cream, soft cheeses (brie, ricotta, cream cheese, fresh mozzarella)
  - Cooked rice, pasta, casseroles, soups, stews, gravies, stocks
  - Cooked vegetables, cut melons, cut leafy greens, cut tomatoes, sprouts, pre-cut produce
  - Deli meats, hot dogs, pâtés, lunch meats
  - Custards, puddings, cream-filled pastries
  - Anything slimy, sticky, or off-smelling — but don't rely on smell alone; if it's on this list, discard regardless
  - Do NOT feed any of the above to Kibo — cooked onions/garlic, grapes/raisins, xylitol-sweetened items, chocolate, macadamia nuts, and most seasoned cooked foods are toxic to dogs

Can be cooled promptly (these held or recover)

  - Whole intact fruits: apples, oranges, lemons, bananas, whole melons — fine at room temp; chill for longevity
  - Whole intact vegetables: potatoes, onions, whole carrots, cabbage, squash, garlic bulbs — fine in a cool spot; chill for longer life
  - Unopened shelf-stable: UHT milk, shelf-stable juice, pickles, vinegar-based hot sauces, soy sauce, ketchup, mustard, jellies, honey, syrups, commercial (xylitol-free) peanut butter
  - Hard aged cheeses: parmesan, romano, aged cheddar, grana padano — fine at room temp a few hours, then chill; not the discard line
  - Salted butter (closed) — fine at room temp short term, then chill
  - Bread, tortillas, dry crackers, dry pasta/rice, canned goods (never went above ambient indoor)
  - Whole uncut onions and potatoes in a dark cool place

Freezer (still cold enough to keep or cook from thawed)

  - Items with ice crystals still visible and package below 40°F internally  -> refreeze or cook now
  - Items thawed but still below 40°F internally  -> cook now, eat within 24 hours, do not refreeze raw
  - Items thawed AND warmer than 40°F  -> cook immediately, eat within 24 hours, or discard
  - A probe thermometer pushed into the center of the thickest package is the only reliable read; "feel" alone cannot distinguish fully frozen from mostly thawed

Where uncertainty should be treated cautiously

  1. 44°F is the post-power reading, not the peak. During a 4-hour closed-door outage a half- to three-quarter-full fridge commonly peaks in the 50s. Without a logger, assume the higher end.
  2. A closed door buys real time, but it does not buy you 4 hours when the outage itself is 4 hours — you are right at the limit, not safely under it.
  3. "Frozen items still feel solid" cannot reliably distinguish fully frozen from mostly thawed. Probe any high-value package (steaks, fish, breastmilk, leftovers you care about).
  4. Smell and look are NOT reliable safety tests. Salmonella, Listeria, E. coli, and Staph often grow without obvious odor or texture change.
  5. Kibo: even if food looks and smells fine to you, do not give any refrigerated-perishable leftovers from this window — dogs get foodborne illness too, and the cooked-onion/garlic/xylitol risk is real.
  6. If a fridge thermometer is your only instrument, treat the next 60–90 minutes as a confidence signal: if the fridge is solidly back below 40°F and holding by ~5:30pm, the fridge has recovered, but anything that already crossed into the danger zone does not get a second chance — discard decisions stand.
  7. Compressor health: the "no electrical odor or equipment fault" reading is good, but if the fridge runs constantly without pulling below 40°F within 2 hours, the seal or coolant may have been stressed by the event — flag it for follow-up; food decisions above stand either way.

Cleanup after the pass

  - Remove everything; wipe interior with hot water + mild dish soap; rinse; then sanitize with 1 tablespoon unscented liquid bleach per gallon of water; wipe dry.
  - Same for the freezer if anything leaked.
  - Reset fridge target to 37°F, freezer to 0°F.
  - Consider a small plug-in temperature logger for next time — about the cost of two takeaways and removes the guesswork that forced this triage.

The convergence you're describing is the classic damp-dry collapse: two adjacent washes at similar dilution settle toward the same middle value as the water equalizes, and the warm side reads as flat because it's lost its relative lift against the wetter, pigment-richer cool side. You're right that adding orange would just push it into a saturated corner and commit you to a focal area you don't want in a study. Here's a controlled sequence.

1. **Target the damp-dry window, not wet, not bone-dry.** Surface sheen gone, paper still cool to the cheek, pigment no longer migrating when you tilt. This is where you can still manipulate without the paper rejecting the brush or the wet edge continuing to bloom. If you act wet, you'll just feed the merging. If you wait for bone-dry, you'll need full rewetting and lose the soft-edge control.

2. **Lift the warm interior edge instead of painting into it.** Clean damp brush, squeezed out so it's moist not loaded. Drag it along the brightest strip of the threshold once or twice, blot on a scrap. This subtracts pigment, deepening the relative value gap between the warm interior and the cooler doorway without touching chroma. The separation comes from the cool side reading darker by comparison, not from the warm side getting hotter.

3. **Reinforce the doorway/street with a thin glaze of the same neutral mix, slightly more concentrated, wet-on-damp.** Same blue-to-brown ratio, just less water. Apply only along the cool side, stopping at the lifted edge. This deepens value on the cool side while keeping the hue unchanged, so saturation stays where it is. One pass, no chasing.

4. **Hard-edge the threshold while the surface is still receptive.** If the interior-to-doorway edge has feathered, a damp brush (damp, not loaded) run along the line will define a clean architectural boundary. This is edge work, not value work, and it locks the separation in before the next drying phase smears it again.

5. **Stop and let it dry fully before deciding whether it needs anything else.** Studies benefit from the drying reveal. A wet pass that looks flat often resolves into acceptable separation once both sides reach true dry state, because the pigment settles into its final value relationship. If after drying the cool side is still reading too close to the warm, you'll know it's a value problem, not a chroma problem, and the fix on a future study is just a slightly heavier first-pass dilution differential.

The data point worth keeping from this swatch is that this particular blue-plus-brown ratio collapses hard at the damp-dry transition - it wants to be either more separated in the first pass (heavier cool, lighter warm) or lifted/reglazed at that window. That's useful information for the next time you reach for it, and it's exactly what a study is for.

A simple decision framework that holds up across most residential utility choices:

1. Anchor on the most likely future, not the past.
   Use your highest-usage month from the recent range as the stress case, not the average. Plans look great against averages and bad against peaks.

2. Build three monthly scenarios for each option, using your actual recent range:
   - Low usage (your lowest recent month)
   - Median usage (typical recent month)
   - High usage (your highest recent month, or last summer's peak)
   The plan with the lowest median is usually the right one; the plan that wins only at the extremes is a bet.

3. Layer in the housing decision separately, not as a tiebreaker.
   The unresolved renewal is a separate risk dimension — don't let it tip a close utility call. Compute the utility decision as if housing is settled either way, then add housing as its own branch.

4. Treat the ETF as a sunk cost, with one exception.
   Default: ignore it emotionally and include it only in a strict payback calculation. Exception: if the new plan's annual savings minus the ETF give you less than ~6 months of cushion, the switch is fragile — one usage change wipes out the gain.

5. Decision rules of thumb:
   - If the variable plan's median is ≤ fixed plan's median by more than the ETF spread over 12 months, switch.
   - If the fixed plan wins on the median and you're within 6 months of a known move, stay fixed (avoid a switch cost during a transition).
   - If variable wins only on the high-usage scenario, you are essentially betting on a hot summer or a behavior change — don't switch on a bet.

6. Sequencing when housing is unresolved:
   - If lease renewal is due within 60 days: lock a short/no-ETF utility option if available, or stay on whatever requires the least commitment. Resolve housing first, then optimize utility.
   - If lease renewal is 3+ months out: optimize utility now on its own merits; housing won't change the answer unless rent swings enough to change your baseline usage budget.

Briefly: both passages are about what attention *does* when it meets another life, and both refuse the idea of neutral observation. Passage A names the failure on the side of *counting* — the observer's ledger turns ordinary life into a sequence of deviations, which is a soft form of control because it makes the observed person legible only as data against a standard. Passage B names the failure on the side of *not counting* — refusing to record is complicit when the default record already erases certain rooms, buses, and requests, so opting out is a way of letting the disappearance stand.

The pairing works because each passage cancels the easy escape from the other. You can't resolve A by saying "well, counting is bad, so we won't count," because B answers that. And you can't resolve B by saying "well, we should document everything," because A answers that. What's left is a question about *position* — who is counting, who is being counted, and who is left out of either operation.

One question for Tuesday, deliberately not steering:

    "The two passages point at the same act from opposite sides — one says
    counting is how an observer turns a life into deviations, the other says
    refusing to count is how an observer lets certain rooms stay flooded.
    If the line between 'useful accounting' and 'controlling ledger' is real,
    what is it drawn around: the person counting, the thing being counted,
    or the people who would otherwise be left out of either category?"

That keeps all three axes open — the counter, the counted, the uncounted — so the group can land wherever their reading takes them, without the question pre-deciding the answer.

Five minutes is a useful working window, but it's the lower bound of what you want — it gives you two of your three goals and pays for them with one bloom.

What 5 minutes earned:
- Wash continuity: yes. The cool plane reads as one field.
- Warm doorway edge: yes. It held against cool bleed.
- Dark interruption: no. A bloom at the entry means the receiving surface was still wet enough to be pushed around by the new pigment.

So 5 min is "damp enough to preserve the wash, wet enough to bloom a drop." The next study targets the bloom by firming the surface up without losing the wash.

Recommended next study — 7 minutes, everything else held:

- Same paper (and same sheet/batch if you've been tracking it).
- Same blue-plus-brown mix at the same ratio and dilution.
- Same brush, same load — and keep whatever method you've been using to make "same" mean same (dip count, dab count, or weight, whichever you started with).
- Same cool wash: same pigment volume, same water-to-pigment, same stroke order, same doorway timing.
- Place the dark rain mark at 7:00 instead of 5:00. That is the only change.

Why 7 and not 8 or 10: a 2-minute increment is the smallest step that reliably moves a damp watercolor surface from "wet" into "damp" at this scale, and it keeps the study inside the "only timing changed" envelope. A bigger jump risks overshooting into hard-edge territory in one move and forcing a third study to walk back.

What to watch at 7:
- If the bloom disappears and the dark mark still softens into the wash (no hard stamped edge), 7 min is your working window. Stop the series, or run one more at 9 to find the upper bound where the mark starts to harden.
- If the mark hardens at 7 — loses its soft rain edge — the window for this paper/load/mix is 5–7 min and the working answer is "aim ~6," not a single minute.
- If the bloom persists at 7, surface dampness isn't the variable anymore; pigment volume or water ratio in the dark mark is, and that's a different study with a different setup.

Two small notes on method, not on the result:
- "5 minutes" is only meaningful if the clock starts the same way each run — end of the cool-wash stroke, not the start of it. Worth pinning down in the margin if you haven't already.
- If the sheet changes between runs, you've added a variable without naming it. Same batch through the whole bracket.

CONSERVATIVE COMMUTE PLAN — Tue 8/26, heat advisory 108°F 3-7pm

1. RIDE IN THIS MORNING — YES, with conditions

The advisory window is afternoon-only. Morning should be 15-25°F cooler on the heat-index scale, but check the actual current reading before you leave:
- If the current heat index is already in the mid-90s+ with high humidity, the same risk calculus that kills the afternoon ride starts to apply — fall back to transit/car for the inbound leg too
- Pre-hydrate 16-20oz water + electrolytes 1-2hrs before you leave
- Ride at conversation pace, no hard efforts — treat it as a commute, not a workout
- Glance at NWS or your weather app right before departure; 10 seconds, worth it

2. DO NOT RIDE HOME 3-7PM

108°F heat index is in the NWS "Danger" range (105-129°F), where sustained exertion carries real heat-stroke risk. Non-negotiable conservative call:
- Leave the bike secured at Helio overnight
- Get home via rideshare (Uber/Lyft), public transit, or a coworker ride
- Retrieve the bike Wednesday morning before work, assuming a normal forecast

3. HYDRATION

- Pre-load: 16-20oz water + electrolytes, 1-2hrs before ride
- During ride: aim for 20-30oz per hour, sip regularly
- Add sodium — salt tab or electrolyte mix (LMNT, Skratch, Nuun). Plain water plus heavy sweat is a hyponatremia risk, not just a comfort issue
- Keep drinking at the office — don't stop hydrating once you arrive
- Skip alcohol and excess caffeine the rest of today
- Eat normally; skipping meals makes heat tolerance worse

4. CLOTHING

- Light-colored, loose-fitting, technical wicking fabric (polyester or merino). Not cotton — it stays wet and hot
- Helmet with good venting (most commuter helmets do)
- UV-protective sunglasses
- SPF 30+ on all exposed skin; reapply if you're sweating heavily
- Light cycling gloves if you have them — keeps hands from swelling and protects from sun
- Avoid dark colors and anything that traps heat against the body

5. RETURN-TRIP PRECAUTIONS (Wednesday, or whenever you retrieve the bike)

- Don't ride just because the advisory window has technically closed if temps are still extreme. Wait until heat index is comfortably safe
- Cool down at the office first — 12-16oz water + electrolytes and a snack before you head out
- Easy pace; cumulative heat exposure lingers even after temps drop
- Watch for heat-illness signs and stop immediately if any appear:
    - Dizziness or unusual headache
    - Nausea or stomach cramps
    - Cessation of sweating (or suddenly heavy sweating)
    - Confusion, slurred speech
    - Muscle cramps
- Phone charged; share your route and ETA with someone
- Bail-out plan: if you start feeling off, stop in the nearest shade/AC and call a rideshare. Don't push through
- If you're on the fence about whether it's safe to ride home, it isn't — take transit

6. OVERNIGHT BIKE STORAGE

- Lock it (your own lock as backup to whatever Helio's secure area uses)
- Bring lights, computer, removable bags inside with you

One additional thought: if Wednesday's forecast is also hot, ride both ways Wednesday morning and leave the bike there again, or take transit both ways until the pattern breaks. There's no rule that says one missed ride home forces you back on the bike the next day.

The minute between bloom and crisp tells you the wash crosses its damp zone somewhere in that window. At five minutes the paper is still wet enough that fresh pigment displaces the wash and feathers into it — that's the bloom. At six the surface has passed into damp-dry, and the mark sits on top, keeps its edge, doesn't move. The transition is sharp, which is useful information on its own.

On the 5.5-minute test — yes, but with a few caveats:

A single 5.5 trial won't show you the shape of the transition. Because five and six produced opposite qualitative results, 5.5 could land closer to either end depending on humidity, room temperature, and how saturated the paper was to begin with. Two or three 5.5-minute runs under matched conditions will tell you more than one — specifically whether the result is repeatable and where it sits on the bloom-to-crisp gradient.

Clock minutes are a fragile control. The actual variable is surface state at the moment of interruption, not elapsed time, and humidity shifts week to week. While you run the 5.5s, also note the tactile cue — sheen just gone, paper cool but not cool-dry — so you start building a "feels like" reference alongside the clock. That model will travel; the five-minute figure won't.

Look at which failure is closer to your goal. The five-minute bloom softens the rain into the wash but disrupts it; the six-minute version preserves the wash and warm edge cleanly and only makes the rain mark too sharp. If the target is preserved wash plus warm edge plus a mark that belongs in the doorway rather than sitting on top of it, the six-minute result is structurally closer. You'd probably want to push slightly earlier from six (say 5.75), not split the difference from five.

So: run the 5.5, but plan it as two or three with surface-state notes, and treat the midpoint as exploration rather than the answer.

Eligibility vs. Exposure — Operating Interpretation

Eligibility = an account meets the gating criteria for a treatment (allowlist, contract, plan, cohort, integration). A precondition, not a delivery event.

Exposure = an account was actually subjected to the treatment (saw the variant, received the message, had the feature live). What runs through the experimental and operational machinery.

Rules

1. Eligible is a denominator, not an achievement. It sizes the population that could be reached; it does not represent reach, response, or value created.

2. Eligible is not pipeline. Pipeline = eligible + exposed + an observed progression signal. Eligibility alone is a gating filter, not a funnel stage.

3. Eligible is not causal evidence. A converted eligible account does not prove the eligibility rule caused the outcome. Causal claims require exposure paired with a comparable control.

4. Eligible is not forecast credit. Revenue, ARR, or retention credit is booked on exposed-and-observed behavior (conversion, expansion, save), not on eligibility. Eligible-base sizing informs forecast floors (population caps), never realized performance.

Litmus: if the account never saw the touch, it earned nothing — no credit, no pipeline credit, no causal credit, no forecast credit.

CHICKEN & EGG FRIED RICE — one skillet, ~25 min, with a portion banked for Sam.

Prep first (mise en place — this is what keeps cleanup low and timing tight):
  - Cut chicken into ~1/2 inch pieces (smaller = warms through faster)
  - Slice scallions, whites and greens in separate piles
  - Roughly chop spinach if leaves are large
  - Halve the lime
  - Break up rice clumps with wet hands or a fork

Timed sequence (large skillet over medium-high):
  0:00   Heat 1–2 tbsp oil until just shimmering
  0:30   Chicken in a single layer; leave it alone 60–90 sec for color
  2:00   Stir chicken — it's already cooked, just crisping and warming
  3:00   Push chicken to the perimeter of the pan
  3:30   Scallion whites + corn into the center, 30 sec
  4:00   Add rice, press flat, let it sit 60 sec to toast, then break up and toss
  6:00   Push rice to one side, clear a well in the center
  6:30   Both eggs into the well; scramble, then fold into the rice
  8:00   Spinach in, toss until just wilted (~60 sec)
  9:00   OFF HEAT. Squeeze half the lime over, salt and pepper to taste
  9:30   Toss in scallion greens; squeeze the other lime half if it needs lift

Portion for Sam:
  - Scoop roughly 1/3 to 1/2 into a container before you eat
  - Cool 5 min on the counter, then fridge (covers and lid off steam = less soggy rice later)

Sam's reheat (covered, splash of water):
  - Microwave 60–90 sec, or
  - Skillet over medium with a lid, 3–4 min

A few things worth knowing:
  - Two eggs across the whole dish is light. If the carton has more, add one.
  - Don't crowd the pan. If your skillet is small, cook the rice in two batches — crowding is what turns fried rice into a wet clump.
  - High heat is the whole game. If the rice is sizzling when you add it, you're doing it right.
  - Soy sauce or fish sauce at the 8:00 mark lifts this noticeably, but neither was in your list, so skip if the pantry's bare.
  - The lime goes in off heat. Citrus over direct flame goes bitter and flat.

VERIFY (independently — don't use anything in the message)
  - Don't tap the link, don't reply, don't call any number in it, don't open attachments.

  - Reach the company through a channel YOU trust: the app already on your phone, a phone number from a recent statement or the back of your card, or a URL you type yourself into a browser.
  - Ask that channel, with no reference to the message: "Did you send this?" If they didn't, it's not from them.
  - Search the exact message wording in quotes — scams get reported and copied widely.

REPORT
  - US phishing email: forward to reportphishing@apwg.org (keeps the headers intact — forward, don't re-type).
  - US fraud/scam: reportfraud.ftc.gov.
  - US text/SMS scam: copy and forward to 7726 (SPAM).
  - If it impersonates a specific company, forward to that company's abuse@ address (most banks and big tech publish one).
  - If any money, credentials, or personal data were already shared, also report to your bank and file at IdentityTheft.gov.
  - Screenshot everything BEFORE you delete — report forms often want the headers, sender, link text, and timestamp.

BLOCK
  - Phone: block the number in your dialer.
  - Email: mark as phishing (this trains the filter better than "spam"), then block the sender.
  - Messaging apps: use the in-app Report → Block flow in that order so the platform sees the report.

DELETE
  - Delete from Inbox, then from Trash/Junk, then empty Trash. On phone, repeat in any secondary mailbox/tab.
  - Don't delete until you've screenshotted and reported — once gone, headers and full senders are hard to recover.

Conservative shutdown, in order:

1. Do not start another cycle. A low hum on restart means the pump motor is receiving power but cannot move the water — most often because the drain path is blocked. Every retry stresses the pump against that blockage; the moment it gives, water can be pushed past the door seal or the pump motor can burn out.

2. Cut power at the breaker for the dishwasher circuit, not just at the control panel. The hum tells you something is still energized. A breaker-off is the cleanest kill.

3. Leave the standing water in the tub. It is contained, it is not an emergency, and it gives the tech useful information (whether it eventually drains on its own).

4. Keep the door latched or fully closed. The water is dirty wash water — food particles, detergent residue, bacteria — and Kibo will be curious. A closed door also keeps anything from being startled or knocked if the unit unexpectedly re-energizes.

Safe basic user checks (hands and a flashlight only):

  - Look under the sink at the dishwasher drain hose. If it is kinked, sharply bent, or pushed hard against the cabinet wall, you can straighten it without moving the appliance.

  - If your sink has a small chrome cylinder on the counter near the faucet (an air gap), unscrew the cap and look inside. A clogged air gap will block drainage. Pull out debris with gloved fingers, rinse the cap under the tap, reinstall.

  - If the dishwasher drains through a garbage disposer: run the disposer for 15 seconds with a strong stream of cold water. A common installer mistake is leaving the plastic knockout plug inside the disposer inlet — that lets the dishwasher fill but not drain. Do not reach into the disposer.

  - The filter at the bottom of the tub (a cylindrical basket that twists out under the lower rack) is explicitly user-serviceable. Twist, lift out, empty into the sink, rinse under the tap, reinstall. This is the single most common cause of standing water. It is fine to do this even with water still in the tub.

Do not disassemble:

  - The kick plate / lower front access panel (the screws along the bottom front). Behind it are the pump, motor, and wiring harness.

  - The door latch, door switch, or interlock.

  - The control board, user interface, or any wiring.

  - The drain pump itself, the inlet valve, or the heating element.

  - Anything that requires pulling the unit out from under the counter.

Submit a maintenance request (non-emergency, do not try another cycle first) when:

  - Standing water remains above the filter after the breaker has been off for an hour, and none of the safe checks above resolved it.

  - The hum returns the moment the breaker is restored, without pressing start.

  - The control panel is unresponsive or shows an error code you cannot identify.

Seek emergency service (skip the maintenance request) when:

  - Any water appears on the floor — near the dishwasher, under the sink, or near an outlet.

  - Any burning smell, smoke, sparks, popping, or the breaker trips again on reset.

  - The hum changes to a louder whine, rattle, or grinding.

  - You smell gas — leave the house and call your gas utility.

When you submit the request, include the four facts you just told me: stopped mid-cycle, standing water above the filter, low hum on a single restart attempt, no leak/no smoke/no breaker trip, breaker now off. That gives the tech a clear starting point.

One last note: once the breaker is off, you do not need to rush the rest of this. The tub water is contained and not getting worse. A standard non-emergency dishwasher ticket is normally handled the next business day without anything deteriorating in the meantime.

Below is a stabilization-only protocol — not a cleaning protocol. The goal is to keep visit_05 (and its current state) intact until a photograph conservator can take it from here.

CORE PRINCIPLE
  Dry, flaking residue is more stable than tacky residue, but it is still the original
  problem (likely a degraded adhesive from an old album page, possibly plasticized).
  Your job from this point is to prevent that residue from doing more harm and to
  keep every other property of the object — image, back, orientation, ID — untouched.

SEQUENCE (do in order, once)

  1. Document before you touch.
     - Photograph visit_05 in current position: front, back, and two close-ups of
       each corner with residue. Use even, raking light for the corners so the
       flakes are visible. Date-stamp the new shots.
     - These are now part of the file's provenance. Save them with the existing
       f+b shots from 8/19.

  2. Prepare a clean workspace.
     - Flat, dry, dust-free surface. No food, drink, pens, lotion nearby.
     - Wash and dry hands thoroughly (no jewelry on hands/wrists; short nails;
       no hand cream for at least 30 minutes). Clean cotton or clean nitrile
       gloves are fine if you prefer — cotton is the more conservative choice
       for photographic material; whichever you use, touch only the edges.

  3. Move and isolate.
     - Lift visit_05 by opposite edges; do not pass fingers over the image side
       or the handwriting.
     - Do not separate the flakes from the photo. Do not press on them.
     - Place it alone, image-side up, into a clean housing (see step 4).
     - Keep it physically separate from visit_01–04 and 06 — residue particles
       can transfer, and you want no accidental contact.

  4. House it.
     - Acceptable: a polyester (Mylar D / Melinex 401) sleeve, or a folded
       sheet of unbuffered, lignin-free archival paper around it like a four-
       flap enclosure.
     - Not acceptable as housing: any plastic you cannot identify as polyester,
       any "magnetic" or self-stick album page, glassine that is not
       conservation-grade, regular paper, paper towels, tissue.
     - Keep the sheet flat. Do not stack weight on top. Do not bend the housing.

  5. Keep the temporary-index slip with the photograph, not on it.
     - Your standing convention: tentative ID lives on a separate paper slip,
       kept together with the photo. Continue that. The current slip should
       travel with visit_05 into storage and onward to a conservator.

  6. Set the storage environment.
     - Cool, dry, dark, stable. Roughly 65–70°F and 30–50% RH. No attic, no
       basement, no exterior wall, no window ledge, no heating vent.
     - Store flat, in a clean archival folder or box, with the other five photos
       in their original order (do not reorder the set).

MATERIALS AND ACTIONS TO AVOID
  - Do not use any tape — including "acid-free," "archival," or photo-corner
    tape — anywhere on or near this object.
  - Do not try to lift, brush, blow off, soften, dissolve, or scrape the flakes.
    No water, no saliva, no eraser, no kneaded eraser, no brush, no swab, no
    cotton ball, no microfiber cloth on the residue.
  - No household cleaners, no alcohol, no acetone, no citrus solvents, no
    oils, no "goo gone" type products, no heat (hair dryer, iron, sunlight
    through a window).
  - No lamination, no plastic wrap, no PVC sleeves, no self-stick album pages.
  - No writing or labeling on the photograph, the residue, or the housing
    where it would touch the photograph. Label the enclosure only.
  - No stacking weight on the photo. No paper clips, binder clips, rubber

What interests me is whether the substitution is purely institutional — a bad-faith claim layered on top — or whether the record's form makes the claim land so easily that the institution barely has to assert it. A record made by an institution describes people in institutional terms: categories, incidents, dispositions, outcomes. That description is answer-shaped enough that "we have answered you" can be said without obvious falsehood, even though the people inside the record have not been addressed in terms their situation required.

If that's right, the danger the passage names is partly structural. The record doesn't just fail to repair; it produces a surface on which "answered" looks true.

Reading: Recording a problem fixes it in a record — the notation preserves the event as something that happened and was seen. Responding goes further: it commits to a stance, an actor, and a change. A problem can sit in a log indefinitely without anyone responding to it; a response, by contrast, presupposes the notation but adds a claim about what should follow from it. The two are easy to confuse because both produce language about the problem, but only one of them takes responsibility for it.

# Lifecycle Systems operating case — Growth leadership, 2025-10-08

Audience: Growth leadership. Format: 10 min case, 10 min Q&A.
Operating case for Priya, owner: Riley. Decision date: 2025-09-24.
Working brief — evidence limits stated, no causal claims.

## 1. The operating problem the shared-state contract solved

Lifecycle Systems had been asked to do two things in one step: decide that a customer touch was routine, and act on that decision without a structured record of why it was safe. The result was that any single missing, stale, or conflicting piece of required state — an expired entitlement, a connector that hadn't re-checked in, a CS rep already mid-thread with the customer — could pass through silently and surface only as a later incident or customer correction.

The shared-state contract treats each routine decision as a join across five required fields. Every field is governed separately; nothing is collapsed. A decision can only resolve to "proceed" when all five fields are present, current, and non-conflicting. Anything else resolves to a field-specific hold with the failing field named, not a generic block.

What this changed operationally:
- Holds stopped being invisible. A hold now has a field name attached, so the operator and the customer-correcting team see the same reason.
- Disagreement between fields (for example, entitlement says active, CS-work status says suppressed) is impossible to paper over: the contract requires each field to be read on its own terms.
- The audit story is per-decision, not per-quarter narrative.

## 2. The five separately governed fields

Each field is governed by a distinct source and a distinct freshness rule. They are deliberately not collapsed into a single composite "is this safe to send" flag, because that composite is exactly what produced the prior incidents.

1. External-system authority — whether the connector's owner-side permission/allowlist readiness is current. This is a connector-side readiness check, not a customer contact permission. Governed by the connector owner's record.
2. Connector authentication — whether the connector itself is currently authenticated to its upstream system for this decision window. Separate from authority.
3. Entitlement — whether the customer holds a currently supported entitlement on the product surface this message targets. Read from the entitlement system of record.
4. Qualifying-human-admin (QHA) status — whether a human admin with standing qualification exists for the customer's account, on the surface in question.
5. Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work — whether CS owns an active adoption or renewal workstream on this account right now. Read from CS-work state, not from CS sentiment.

Failure modes, all fail closed as a named hold:
- Missing — field absent for the account in the join window → hold, field name = the missing field.
- Stale — field present but outside its freshness window → hold, field name = the stale field.
- Unresolved — field present but in an unresolved state (e.g. connector auth pending re-check) → hold, field name = the unresolved field.
- Conflicting — field disagrees with another required field on the same account (e.g. entitlement active vs. CS-work suppressed) → hold, field name = the conflicting field.

- 1,362 unique CS auto-nudge decisions run through the contract.
- 57 field-specific holds surfaced by the contract.

## 4. The 2025-09-24 authority decision and what it changed for handoffs

The 2025-09-24 decision restructured routine CS auto-nudge review work so that the routine path has clear ownership without granting any operator cross-surface authority. The handoff shape:

- Ines — independently closes only routine CS auto-nudge messaging-state reviews (the five-field join on the auto-nudge surface). Owns related routine operator guidance for that scope. Authority is bounded to messaging-state reviews of routine CS auto-nudge decisions. Nothing in this decision gives Ines authority over Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, or lifecycle preflight.
- Owen — retains routine operating explanation (what the fields mean, how holds resolve) and the exception ledger (the running record of field-specific holds and their dispositions). Owen does not close routine decisions.
- Riley (me) — retains disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing decisions, ambiguous cases, exception-heavy matters, and any executive claims. Ines's routine close does not extend to any of these.
- Daniela — retains engineering release and rollback control over the shared-state contract itself. The decision did not change release authority.

What this decision explicitly did not do:
- It did not grant Ines authority over Helio Start reporting.
- It did not grant Ines authority over Expansion Assist selection.
- It did not grant Ines authority over lifecycle preflight.
- It did not change lifecycle-send release authority (still Daniela).
- It did not broaden Lifecycle Systems beyond its four existing consumers. The four-consumer scope is unchanged.

The decision is a handoff redesign on one surface (routine CS auto-nudge messaging-state review), not a re-chartering of Lifecycle Systems.

## 5. Reserved Q&A — anticipated questions and short answers

Q1. "Why are holds framed as controls rather than delivery failures?"
A. A hold is the contract surfacing that one of the five required fields failed its check on this account. That is the control doing its job — it produced a named, auditable reason instead of a silent proceed. The 57 Q3 holds are the controls firing, not a backlog of failed sends. Delivery would be the wrong frame because nothing was sent on a hold; the system stopped at the gate with the reason attached.

Q2. "Why doesn't the 2025-09-24 decision extend across all four Lifecycle Systems consumers?"
A. The decision is scoped to routine CS auto-nudge messaging-state reviews because that is the surface where the five-field join had accumulated enough operating evidence to redesign the handoff without changing release authority. The other three consumers were not part of the 2025-09-24 scope and their authority shape is unchanged. Broadening Lifecycle Systems was explicitly out of scope. Ines's new close authority applies only to routine CS auto-nudge messaging-state reviews; it does not reach Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, or lifecycle preflight.

Q3. "Why isn't a proceed result blanket contact permission?"
A. Proceed means the five required fields were present, current, and non-conflicting for this decision. It does not authorize contact on any other surface, for any other product, or under any other decision type. A different surface (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle preflight, lifecycle-send release) has its own authority and its own governance. Proceed is also bounded by field freshness: a stale field that re-checks to current does not retroactively bless earlier decisions. And proceed does not override customer correction — a correction request stops the relevant decision path regardless of prior proceed state.

ONE-SKILLET BRUNCH HASH WITH EGGS (serves 2)

Timing assumes 10-inch cast iron or nonstick, medium-high to start, then medium-low for the eggs.

00:00  Prep (8 min)
  - 2 medium Yukon gold potatoes, diced 1/2-inch (no peel)
  - 3 scallions, sliced; whites and greens in separate piles
  - 3 oz baby spinach, left whole or torn
  - 4 oz sharp cheddar, grated (pre-shredded is fine)
  - 4 eggs, cracked into a small bowl
  - Olive oil, butter, salt, pepper ready on the counter

00:08  Potatoes (8 min)
  - 2 Tbsp olive oil + 1 Tbsp butter in the skillet over medium-high
  - Potatoes in a single layer, season with 1/2 tsp salt + pepper
  - Press flat, do not stir for 4 min (builds the crust)
  - Flip/toss, add scallion whites, cook 4 more min until tender and browned

00:16  Spinach (2 min)
  - Add spinach, stir just until wilted, ~60 sec
  - Spread the hash evenly, drop heat to medium-low

00:18  Eggs (5-6 min)
  - Make 4 shallow wells with a spoon
  - Slide one egg into each well
  - Scatter most of the cheddar around the eggs (keep it off the yolks)
  - Cover with a lid or rimmed plate, cook 5 min for just-set whites / runny yolks
  - 6 min if you prefer firmer yolks

00:24  Finish + plate (1 min)
  - Off heat, keep covered 60 sec (carry-over finishes the eggs)
  - Top with scallion greens, remaining cheddar, cracked pepper
  - Serve straight from the skillet

00:25  Reset while you eat (5 min)
  - Skillet goes straight to the sink with hot water and a squirt of soap to soak
  - One cutting board, one knife, one spatula, one egg bowl straight into the dishwasher
  - Wipe the counter, done before Sam's out the door

Minimizing cleanup
- Use the egg bowl as your cheese-grating catcher to skip a dish.
- Skip the egg bowl entirely and crack straight into the wells if your skillet is well-seasoned nonstick.
- A rimmed plate works as a lid; no need to dig out a real pan lid.
- Eat from the skillet with a spatula and skip plating two portions.

Timing flex
- In a rush: dice potatoes smaller (3/8-inch) and you can shave 2-3 min off the cook.
- Running ahead: hash base can sit covered on low while you wait for him to head out; eggs go in when you want to eat.

The flatness you're describing is the classic "dark mass as punch-out" reading: when a doorway carries a single value and a clean rectangular contour, the eye registers it as a shape sitting on the warm field rather than as a recess into it. The value-separated warm edge holds up, but it has nothing asymmetric to register against where it meets the dark, so the warm interior loses its third dimension.

One controlled next study: keep paper, pigment family, the large cool wash, and the value-separated warm edge exactly as today. Change only the shape of the dark accent — convert the uniform rectangle into an L-profile that turns 90 degrees at one corner. Place the L's inner corner roughly where the original doorway's lower-inside corner sat, and let one arm run a short distance along the implied floor plane while the other climbs partway up the wall.

Why this is the right single lever:

  The corner of the L becomes the deepest value on the page. That corner is what the eye reads as "going back into space" — it gives the dark mass an internal pocket of recession instead of one flat fill.
  
  The two arms now meet the warm edge at different angles, so the warm edge has something asymmetric to land against rather than wrapping a single continuous rectangle. That is the relationship that was missing today.
  
  Total dark mass stays close to the original footprint, so the composition stays anchored. You are only redistributing silhouette, not adding pigment load or shifting weight across the page.

Pre-study targets to keep the variable clean:

  Same darkest value at the L's inner corner. Let the two arms step down only by roughly a half-value toward their outer ends — that is internal modulation inside the dark accent itself, not a change to the value-separated warm edge.
  
  Total area within about 10 percent of today's rectangle. Same drying sequence: cool wash fully dry, warm edge set, then the L on top, so timing is held constant.
  
  Mix the L from the same pigment family at the same concentration as today's doorway, so the only thing your eye can attribute any change to is contour.

If the L still reads flat after that study, the next controlled move is placement — slide the accent off-center onto the rule-of-thirds vertical — not value, not pigment, and not the warm edge.

Setup before opening the frame

- Clean, dry, flat surface. Wash hands; nitrile or clean cotton gloves for the sheet.
- Tools out: soft brush, bone folder or Teflon folder, plastic-tipped tweezers, scissors, distilled water in a small dish, water-activated gummed linen or methylcellulose tape (never PSA), blotter/cotton rag, soft pencil.
- Photograph the framed piece straight-on and a close-up of the shifted corner. Mark orientation.

Opening back-to-front

1. Lay the frame face-up. Remove hanging hardware if any.
2. From the back, peel the dust cover and note where it was taped.
3. Remove the backer board and any spacers, in order, so they go back the same way.
4. Lift out the mat + sheet as a single package and lay it face-down on the clean surface. Do not separate mat from sheet yet.

Inspect the corner mounts

- Conservation corner mounts are small cotton-rag triangles or strips that fold over each corner of the sheet, hinged to the mat with water-activated gummed tape (methylcellulose or wheat starch paste) — not glued to the sheet itself.
- Confirm no PSA is touching the sheet. If PSA is found anywhere on the sheet, stop and hand the piece to a paper conservator.
- While the package is open, check the other three corners. If any hinge is lifting, address all of them now so you only open the frame once.

Reseat or replace the shifted corner

- If the existing mount is intact and just slipped: lightly re-moisten the hinge with a barely-damp brush (distilled water only), reposition the sheet against the mat window using tweezers on the mat edge — never on the sheet — and re-bond the hinge. Burnish gently through a blotter.
- If the mount or hinge is torn, slack, or won't re-adhere: cut a fresh strip of gummed linen tape, or make a new cotton-rag corner from archival stock. Activate only the hinge; the mount itself must never contact the sheet surface.
- Before re-hinging, re-measure the sheet edge-to-edge and reconcile against the 7 × 9 inch painted-image entry in the inventory. The 2024 porch-watercolor precedent is technique reference only — verify on this sheet.

Reassemble

- Return the mat package in the same orientation, replace spacers and backer, refasten with framer's points or flex-tabs (not PSA), and reseal the dust cover with gummed paper tape.
- Confirm window-to-image alignment before rehanging.

Stop handling the sheet at home and consult a paper conservator if you see any of:

- Tackiness, shine, or discoloration at corners or edges (suggests prior PSA contact).
- Foxing (small brown/red spots), mold, or musty odor.
- Pigment lifting, smudging, or transferring onto a blotter.
- New cockling, warping, or planar distortion.
- Tears, creases, or fiber loss at any corner.
- A hinge that won't release cleanly with moisture, or that pulls fiber when lifted.
- Any moisture reaching the painted image area.

If you hit any of those, set the sheet face-up on clean buffered tissue, loosely cover with interleaving or a clean folder, and take it to a conservator rather than continuing.
