The blue/orange split is your phone's auto white balance averaging the cool wash and then overcompensating on the warm edge in the opposite direction. A neutral reference in the same indirect light is the single fix that matters; everything else is just removing things that were making it worse.

Five-minute setup

1.  Light placement. Face the painting squarely toward the window so the cool wash and the warm interior edge sit in the same diffuse light, not angled past it. If the side opposite the window falls into shadow, prop a white card or piece of foam board there as a soft fill so the warm edge doesn't read darker than it is. If any room lamp is on, turn it off — mixed light defeats every step below.

2.  Backdrop. A sheet of matte gray poster board or gray foam-core behind the painting keeps the surrounding wall from contaminating the color reading. Skip white walls and skip a black background; both push auto WB the wrong way.

3.  Neutral reference. Tuck an 18% gray card, a piece of true-neutral gray paper, or a plain white card without optical brighteners into one corner of the painting's plane — same distance from the window as the painting. A separate reference frame is fine too. This is the one step that makes a phone behave.

4.  Camera alignment. Stack of books or a small tripod, lens centered on the painting and parallel to its surface (no tilt, no shooting down at it). Frame the painting to fill roughly 80% of the frame, not edge-to-edge, so lens distortion doesn't shift the corners. Turn off: flash, HDR, AI scene detection, and any "vivid" or "boost" color mode.

5.  Exposure and white balance.
    -   Pro/Manual mode: ISO 100, WB set to Daylight (or custom-set on the gray card if your phone allows), spot meter on the gray.
    -   No manual mode: long-press on the gray card to lock AE/AF, then shoot without re-tapping.
    -   Capture two frames — one with the gray card visible, one of just the painting.

Minimal post correction

Open the gray-card shot first. Use its gray to set custom white balance (eyedropper on the neutral area in most phone editors). Then, only if it still drifts:

    saturation: down 10–15%
    warm/cool: nudge a few units toward neutral, gauging off the cool wash
    exposure: leave it; the gray card already landed middle gray

Why five minutes is enough: indirect natural light is already consistent (~5500–6500K), the painting isn't moving, and locking the phone off a neutral reference removes the AWB guesswork that exaggerates the blue/orange split. If you want to skip everything except one thing, skip everything except the gray card.

ONE-POT TOMATO-ORZO WITH CHICKPEAS & KALE
Serves 2 dinner + 1 lunch leftover. Active ~25 min. One pot, one spoon.

Quantities:
- 1 cup dry orzo
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained
- 1 can (14-15 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 1.5 cups broth (chicken or veg)
- 1 small bunch kale, stems removed, chopped (~3 cups)
- 3-4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan, plus extra for serving
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- Salt, pepper, pinch red pepper flakes

Timed steps:
0:00  Heat olive oil in a wide pot over medium. Add garlic, stir 60 sec until fragrant — don't brown.
0:02  Add crushed tomatoes, broth, and orzo. Stir, bring to a gentle simmer.
0:05  Simmer uncovered, stirring every couple of minutes, ~9 min until orzo is just al dente and liquid is mostly absorbed.
0:14  Stir in chickpeas and kale. Cook 4-5 min, stirring, until kale wilts and chickpeas are hot through.
0:19  Off heat. Stir in 1/2 cup Parmesan. Cover, rest 3 min.
0:22  Season with salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Loosen with a splash of broth or water if it tightened up.
0:25  Serve. Pass extra Parmesan.

Lunch leftover: once cooled, scoop into one container. Reheat covered in a skillet over medium-low with 1 tbsp water for 3-4 min, or microwave covered 60-90 sec.

Diagnosis first: an equal-value band means the yellow ochre tabletop and the pale focal cup are reading at the same value step, so the cup does not lift off the plane. The cleanest single move with your existing palette is a thin burnt sienna glaze over the tabletop only, leaving the cup untouched. This deepens the warm plane one step while keeping it in the same warm family, so the cup ends up the lightest warm shape sitting on a now-darker warm plane. I would skip ultramarine here — dropped over yellow ochre it goes green-gray and would shift the whole tabletop's temperature and risk muddiness where it crosses the cast shadow.

Practical sequence:

  1. Confirm the sheet is bone dry. Touch the back of the paper; if it feels cool, wait.

  2. Mix burnt sienna to weak-tea strength — roughly four parts water to one part pigment, stirred until no granules remain. Test it on a scrap or the sheet margin. It should look like the paper has been stained, not like pigment sitting on top. If the white of the paper disappears, it is too strong.

  3. Lay the painting flat. With a clean large soft brush (a 10 or 12 round, damp, not dripping), pre-wet only the tabletop area with one even pass. You want a uniform sheen, no puddles, and the pre-wet shape stopping right at the cup's contour and the shadow's edge — not creeping under either.

  4. While the sheen is still there, reload the same brush with the burnt sienna tea and lay it across the tabletop in one confident stroke from one side to the other, keeping a wet edge. Do not go back into any area that has started to lose its shine. If the glaze is drying faster than your hand, stop where you are — a soft drying edge is fine, a reworked edge is not.

  5. Optional, while still wet: drop a tiny additional touch of burnt sienna into the cast shadow where it meets the tabletop, so the two fuse into one shape. Skip this step if you are uncertain.

  6. Set the painting flat to dry. Do not tilt.

Stop condition — this is the part that protects the sheet:

  Stand up, half-close your eyes, and look at the painting from across the room. Stop glazing the moment two things are true at the same time: the cup reads as the lightest warm shape on the tabletop, and the cast shadow is still the darkest mark on the page. If both hold, put the brush down and let it dry. If the cup and tabletop still look like one shape, wait at least twenty minutes for the glaze to fully dry, then do one more thin pass on the tabletop only — same mix, same sequence. If after a second pass the cup still does not separate, stop anyway. A third pass into a limited-palette glaze is how a study gets overworked, and a soft unresolved separation is recoverable in a later session; mud is not.

One last restraint: do not touch the cup, the background, or the window in this pass. Only the tabletop.

Cap arithmetic and what it actually buys us

The "cap" in each shape is whichever limit binds first — it is not a target, a ceiling on cost per admit, or a forecast of where we will land. The two paired numbers (spend and admits) just happen to divide to $300 and $320; those ratios are bookkeeping identities, not expected CAC.

For the recommended six-week shape ($15,000 / 50 admits):
    - spend cap binds first iff true cost-per-admit > $300
    - admit cap binds first iff true cost-per-admit < $300
For the fallback ($8,000 / 25 admits):
    - spend cap binds first iff true cost-per-admit > $320
    - admit cap binds first iff true cost-per-admit < $320

Because we have no paid-source conversion evidence, we cannot predict which side binds. That is the central uncertainty, not a detail. Whichever side binds tells a different story:
    - admit cap binds: paid source filled the funnel faster than we paid
    - spend cap binds: we paid faster than the funnel filled

What the caps let us claim, and what they do not

We can claim:
    - maximum financial exposure is $15K vs $8K (firm)
    - maximum admission exposure is 50 vs 25 (firm)
    - the test cannot exceed either dimension regardless of channel behavior
    - the implicit neutral ratio ($300 or $320) is the breakeven at which both limits bind simultaneously
    - day-7 first integration will be observable for every admit in-window, so it remains the leading operating indicator across both shapes

We cannot claim:
    - expected CAC, expected admit count, or expected total spend
    - that $300 / $320 is a ceiling on acceptable cost per admit
    - that we will "use the budget" or "fill the admit quota"
    - that hitting either cap is success — binding is mechanical, not directional
    - any mature read on paid-active status, refund-adjusted collected cash, or account-level support effort within six weeks; those windows will be incomplete for later-cohort admits and must stay deferred

Comparison of the two shapes against their exposure

Recommended (50 admits / $15K):
    - +$7K incremental financial exposure vs fallback
    - +25 admits of incremental signal, which materially narrows confidence on activation-rate read
    - larger support-load exposure in absolute terms (we should still not assume it scales linearly with admits if effort-per-admit varies by channel)
    - more time for the slower-binding limit to be informative — six weeks is more forgiving when one limit takes longer to bind
    - higher cost of a bad read because more admits will have incomplete post-window data

Fallback (25 admits / $8K):
    - smaller blast radius on both axes
    - admits cap is more likely to bind before spend cap in absolute terms simply because the budget per admit is comparable but the counts are smaller
    - narrower confidence interval on activation rate; read is more sensitive to a small number of outlier admits
    - cheaper to abort or extend; cheaper to learn nothing without burning trust
    - less cushion for the slower-binding limit to actually reveal itself inside six weeks

Net: the recommended shape buys more decision-grade signal at roughly twice the exposure on both axes. The fallback is a strictly safer probe. Neither is a forecast.

Remaining unknowns

    - paid-source conversion rate for the Helio Start audience — currently zero direct evidence
    - true CAC in either direction, and therefore which cap will bind
    - whether paid-acquired admits activate at the same rate as organic admits (selection effect is plausible in either direction)
    - organic-only day-7 first integration baseline through March 31, which is the only comparator we will have on day 1 of any test
    - refund rate and refund-adjusted collected cash beyond the test window for late-cohort admits
    - account-level support effort per admit and whether it differs by acquisition source
    - time-to-binding-limit — six weeks may not be long enough for spend cap to bind even if CAC is unfavorable, which means we could end the window with neither limit decisively hit
    - whether admit quality from paid source matches Helio Start's stated bar, which is a qualitative question the caps cannot answer

Decision questions for Priya

    1. Which binding outcome is the more informative signal for the readout — admit cap binding (we filled faster than we paid) or spend cap binding (we paid faster than we filled)? They are not symmetric.
    2. What is the minimum day-7 first integration lift over the organic-only March baseline that would justify continuing past the first pause point, and at what admit count should the first pause happen?
    3. Do we want volume admits or quality admits from paid source, and is the channel we are proposing aligned with that preference?
    4. If the slower-binding limit does not bind inside six weeks, do we treat that as inconclusive and extend, or as a read in itself?
    5. Which claims should we explicitly defer until paid-active status, refund-adjusted collected cash, and account-level support effort have complete windows, and who owns drafting that deferral note into the read?

Decision questions for the budget owner

    1. Is the $15K / 50-admit ceiling firm, or is partial spend with the admit cap binding at a lower count an acceptable read?
    2. If signal is positive but the windows are not yet mature at six weeks, is extension inside the same budget envelope authorized, or does that require a separate decision?
    3. Should budget release be sequenced after the organic-only March 31 read, or run in parallel with a hold-back?
    4. Are there cross-test budget interactions (other paid tests in flight) that change which limit binding first would mean?
    5. If the spend cap binds first and day-7 first integration is below the organic baseline, what is the stop-loss rule — and is that rule pre-authorized or does it come back for a decision?

Short decision rule for TC-5P8L2 ($50, nontransferable, expires 2026-05-13 11:59pm PT, issuing-airline-only):

Use it ONLY if all three hold:
1. You'd book that specific flight anyway, with or without the credit. The trip is already on your mental list — the credit just lowers its cost. If removing the credit from the picture kills the trip, the credit is manufacturing travel; let it expire.
2. Net fare after the $50 is meaningfully less than your next-best option on a competing airline/carrier. If a $90 fare becomes $40 on this airline while a competitor is $55 round trip, the credit earns its keep. If the competitor is already cheaper post-credit, the credit is just anchoring you to a less-good itinerary.
3. The fare class lets you recover if plans shift. Acceptable: refundable, changeable without fee, or "cancel for airline credit." Not acceptable: basic economy / non-refundable / non-changeable where a same-day plan change strands you with a $X-$50 real loss.

If any of the three fails, let it expire. A $50 credit that locks you into a non-refundable fare you'd only buy because of the credit is worse than the $50 itself.

Two practical corollaries:
- "I'll book a cheap hop just to burn it" is exactly the manufactured-trip pattern you flagged. Skip.

THUMBNAIL PLAN  (three values)

  Light  —  the warm floor strip.  High-key, very lean.  Reads warm.
  Mid    —  the cool wall/floor shadow behind Kibo.  Cool gray, recedes.
  Dark   —  Kibo's coat.  Warm-leaning chromatic dark, not black.  Sits forward.

  Kibo's silhouette is the whole job.  Protect it on the mid pass, don't fight it on the dark pass.

MIXES  (only ultramarine, burnt sienna, yellow ochre)

  Light strip   yellow ochre + a touch of burnt sienna, very dilute.
                No ultramarine here — it will go green/muddy.
  Cool mid      ultramarine + a tiny touch of burnt sienna (or ochre).
                The sienna grays the ultramarine without killing its coolness.
                Lean wash, large area.
  Kibo dark     burnt sienna + ultramarine, slightly more sienna than usual,
                loaded.  A warm-neutral dark — alive where the light grazes
                his back, cool in his shadow side, from one mix.
  Edge lift     burnt sienna + ochre, dilute, glazed on the lit rim of his
                back and head after the body pass dries.  This is what
                separates him from the cool gray wall.

PAINTING ORDER

  1. Light strip.  Flat or graded wash, ochre + sienna.  Dry completely.
     Resist going back in.
  2. Cool mid wash.  Paint the shadow around Kibo, leaving a 1–2 mm
     preserved (lighter) halo along his back and haunch where the warm
     light catches him.  Negative space does the separating work for you.
  3. Kibo, single pass.  Load the sienna + ultramarine mix, one confident
     stroke per body section — back, haunch, head, curled legs.  Don't
     outline; let the preserved halo and the value jump carry the
     silhouette.  Stop and let dry.
  4. Edge lift glaze.  Thin sienna + ochre on the lit rim of his back and
     the top of his head.  Skip the belly and shadow side.

STOPPING POINT

  After step 4, dry.  Done.

  This is a three-value study, not a portrait.  The painting is finished
  when the three values are in place, Kibo's silhouette reads against the
  cool mid without a drawn outline, and the lit edge glows against the
  wall.

  Do not add:
    - a second pass on Kibo's body (this is where coats flatten),
    - eye, nose, or whisker detail (kills the thumbnail quality),
    - a cast shadow under him on the warm strip (tempts more work on
      the body — resist).

  If a passage nags you on review, the fix is almost always to soften
  the Kibo-to-mid edge with a damp brush, not to repaint Kibo.

PAN-SEARED GNOCCHI WITH TOMATOES, SPINACH & PARMESAN

Approximate amounts (2 servings, generous; use ~12 oz of the gnocchi if you want lighter portions or to save half for tomorrow):
  All the gnocchi — or about 12 oz
  Whole pint cherry tomatoes, halved if large
  All 5 oz baby spinach
  3–4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  3 tbsp olive oil
  1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving
  1/4 cup water
  Salt, black pepper, optional red pepper flakes
  Squeeze of lemon at the end (optional but good)

Sequence (~22–25 min, one large skillet):
  1. Prep: halve tomatoes, slice garlic, grate parmesan. (3 min)
  2. Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Add the gnocchi straight from the package in a single layer — do not boil first. Let sit 2 min to get a golden crust, then stir and cook 4–5 min more until most pieces are browned and crispy. (7 min)
  3. Push gnocchi to one side. Add remaining 1 tbsp oil, tomatoes, and garlic to the cleared space. Cook 2–3 min, pressing a few tomatoes to burst, until juices start to release. (3 min)
  4. Add spinach and 1/4 cup water. Toss everything together, cover, and steam 2 min until spinach wilts and gnocchi are tender through. (2 min)
  5. Off heat: stir in parmesan. Season with salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Finish with lemon if using. Serve right from the skillet. (1 min)

Notes:
  Shelf-stable gnocchi (the vacuum-packed kind) browns beautifully when pan-fried from the package — no boiling needed, and that single crusty step is what makes the dish.
  If your tomatoes are very juicy, let them reduce a minute longer before adding spinach so the sauce doesn't water out.
  Cleanup = one skillet, one cutting board, one knife.

Marcus's two concerns are both real. "Hardest thing you have overcome" nudges students toward adversity-as-identity openings, which admissions officers are tired of and which often aren't the student's strongest material anyway. "Interesting" as a feedback prompt is famously useless — it gives the writer no actionable signal, so partners default to "I liked it."

Revised outline:

  5 min  Write a single concrete moment. Pick a place you were physically in and write one paragraph that drops the reader into that scene with sensory detail. No topic statement, no moral, no hardship. Just a moment that felt real to you.

  10 min  Trade openings. For your partner's opening, write two short answers:
            (a) one concrete thing you now know about this person
            (b) one question this opening made you want to ask them next

  15 min  Rewrite your opening. Find a moment, image, or detail from later in your essay and make it the new opening — grounded in a specific place and moment, not a topic.

  5 min   Two volunteers read their new opening aloud.

How it addresses each concern:

  - The first prompt asks for a scene, not a struggle. Students who genuinely want to write about a hard moment still can, on their own terms; students who don't aren't pressured into disclosure.
  - "Interesting" is replaced with two prompts that force specific feedback. "What did you learn about this person" rewards openings that reveal the writer; "what are you curious about" rewards openings that earn the reader's attention.

Two notes Marcus might want to consider before sending this back:

  1. If the hardship prompt was originally meant as brainstorming for the body of the essay (not the opening), it could stay as a separate later exercise — just not as the first prompt, where it sets the tone of the whole session.

SAFE HOME FLATTENING — 140-LB COLD-PRESS, EDGE BUCKLE, PAINT INTACT
Goal is storage-flat, not display-flat, so one gentle pass should do it.

MATERIALS
- Distilled water in a clean fine-mist spray bottle
- 2-3 clean blotters or sheets of unprinted newsprint (acid-free if you have it)
- A rigid flat board larger than the sheet (glass, melamine, or smooth plywood)
- Even weight, 15-25 lbs total (books or wrapped bricks)
- Soft brush, optional, for controlled back-side dampening

SEQUENCE
1. Confirm paint is fully cured and the surface is bone-dry and non-tacky. Lay the sheet face-up on the rigid board.
2. Humidify the BACK ONLY. Hold the mister 12-18 in away and pass over the back 2-3 times so it is evenly damp, not wet. Edges can take one extra pass since that's where the buckle sits. Stop the moment the back looks evenly darkened with moisture — that's plenty.
3. Cover with a clean blotter, then the rigid board, then weight. The board on top spreads the books evenly; books must not touch the painting directly.
4. Leave 36-48 hours in a dry, room-temp spot. Do not peek — opening early lets moisture escape unevenly and can re-cockle the sheet.
5. Lift, remove blotter, inspect. If the edge is flat: rest face-up on the board another 6-12 hrs uncovered to equalize, then sleeve and file.
6. If a faint buckle remains, repeat steps 2-5 once. Do not exceed two passes.

WHAT YOU ARE DELIBERATELY NOT DOING
- No iron, hair dryer, warm shelf, sunlight, or oven
- No mist, damp blotter, or sponge on the painted side
- No tape, glue, or mounting tissue

STOP — TAKE IT TO A CONSERVATOR IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
- Any pigment lift, flaking, cracking, bleed, or tackiness at any point
- A tide line, staining, or color shift after the damp cycle
- The buckle is severe (lift > ~1/4 in) or the cockle spans the whole sheet, not just edges
- Two gentle passes leave the sheet still buckled — a third home pass risks fiber distortion
- The painting's sentimental or monetary value exceeds the cost of a pro flatten (typical $50-150 for a single sheet)

NOTES
- 140-lb cold-press has enough bulk and tooth to tolerate one careful back-side humidity pass; it's the lightest method that actually works on heavy paper.
- If you'd rather avoid moisture entirely, press dry under weight for 5-7 days; this often partially relaxes edge buckles on its own but won't fully flatten a stubborn one.
- Room humidity matters: if the corner is below ~35% RH, doing the press inside a closed cabinet holds moisture in the sheet longer and gives a flatter result.

This reads as a Common App or college application essay draft — a focused leadership moment anchored in a theater-tech emergency. Honest editorial notes below, working from the text alone.

WHAT'S WORKING

The opening is exceptional. "The first time the stage went dark, 312 people inhaled at once" is the kind of first sentence that makes an admissions officer stop scrolling. It establishes scale, tension, and a specific point of view in a single beat. The detail work throughout is strong — 312 people, forty-three seconds, one universe of lights, the crooked pool of amber, the palm. Specificity is what makes this feel real rather than performative.

The pivot in the second paragraph is well-earned and disarming. The reveal that you weren't calm — "My hands shook so badly that I dropped the headset" — is the most honest moment in the essay and the one most likely to land with a reader. Anyone who has been in a high-stakes moment knows that feeling, and admissions readers see a lot of polished calm; yours being undercut by a real human reaction is a strength.

The audience applauding because they thought the darkness was part of the show is a wonderful line. It does double work: it tells the reader the failure was invisible from outside, and it gives you permission to make the lesson about the sequence rather than about heroism.

The thesis — "What mattered was not calmness but having a sequence to follow when calmness disappeared" — is quotable and actually true to your experience. Many applicants land on platitudes here; you land on something specific and earned. The "leave enough room for someone else to take over" line is the most quietly mature thing in the essay. It signals that you don't need to be the hero of every room, which is uncommon and good.

WHAT COULD BE STRONGER

The middle — the actual problem-solving — is the most compressed part. The opening is sensory-rich (green glow, frozen actors, board lights); the middle is more procedural (traced the failure, moved cues, wrote on palm). For a 43-second window, the reader could use one more beat of what it felt like from inside — the breath, the sound of the house, what your eyes were doing on the board. One or two lines would balance the section without slowing the pacing.

The dynamic with your teacher is interesting and currently underused. She reached for the master switch; you asked her to wait. That is a small act of authority being redirected by a student in the moment, and it's doing a lot of structural work. Even one line clarifying what you saw — that flipping master would have lost more, that the board's power light gave you a different read — would deepen the moment and make your intervention feel less like instinct and more like judgment.

The closing is functional but slightly predictable in shape: "In college, I hope to bring that leadership to engineering teams, student theater, and any community that needs someone willing to solve problems under pressure." The list-of-future-activities structure is a common landing spot for these essays and is exactly what admissions officers are trained to skim past. Consider letting the closing pivot on the lesson itself — the sequence, the room for someone else to take over — rather than on a forecast of where you'll join. The reader can extrapolate, and they will trust you more if you don't spell out the future for them.

LENGTH

You're at roughly 280 words; Common App allows 650. You have substantial room if you want to expand the middle beat or develop the "since then" work into something more textured. Alternatively, the tight version may be the strongest version — the punchiness is part of why the opening hits. This is a real choice, not a defect.

OVERALL

The bones here are very good. You have a specific story, a memorable opening, an earned insight, and a voice that reads as adult rather than precocious. The work ahead is mostly in the middle — giving the reader one more sensory anchor during the problem-solving, and possibly clarifying the teacher moment. The closing could also be retuned to land on the lesson rather than the list.

Smoky Chickpea & Cabbage Tacos with Lime-Yogurt Crema — 2 servings (1 dinner, 1 lunch).

Active ~20 min. Yields 2 tacos per portion.

PREP (0:00)
- Drain/rinse 1 can chickpeas; pat dry.
- Thinly slice ~half the cabbage (~2 cups). Slice 2 scallions (whites and greens separate). Mince 2 garlic cloves. Halve the lime.

CABBAGE SLAW (2:00)
- Cabbage + scallion whites + half the lime juice + pinch salt + 1 Tbsp yogurt. Toss, set aside.

CREMA (3:00)
- Remaining yogurt (~3-4 Tbsp) + remaining lime juice + pinch salt. Stir; thin with water if needed.

CHICKPEAS (5:00)
- 1 Tbsp oil in skillet over medium-high. Garlic, 30 sec.
- Add chickpeas; gently smash about a third with a fork or potato masher so they form rough patties. Add 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1/4 tsp salt, black pepper.
- Cook 6-8 min, undisturbed 2-3 min to crisp, then stir occasionally until edges are golden and slightly crunchy. Off heat: taste for salt and acid.

WARM TORTILLAS (13:00)
- Dry skillet, 20-30 sec/side, or directly over gas flame. Stack and cover to stay pliable.

ASSEMBLE DINNER (15:00)
- 2 tortillas: chickpeas, slaw, crema, scallion greens. Eat.

PACK THE LUNCH PORTION (18:00)
- Keep these SEPARATE for best texture at lunch:
  · Chickpeas — small container
  · Slaw — small container
  · Crema — small jar
  · Tortillas — foil-wrapped stack
- Pack lime wedge if you have a spare; skip otherwise.

REHEAT AT LUNCH (3-4 min)
- Chickpeas: skillet over medium with 1 tsp oil, 3-4 min, stir once, until hot and re-crisped at edges.
- Tortillas: dry skillet, 20-30 sec/side.
- Slaw: serve cold, give it a stir; it'll have softened, which is fine.
- Crema: stir; add a few drops of water if it tightened up in the fridge.
- Assemble the same way.

NOTES
- No fresh cilantro or cheese in the pantry — the lime-yogurt crema carries the brightness; the smoked paprika carries the savory depth. If you do add cheese later, a little crumbled feta or cotija on top works.
- Save the leftover cabbage half wrapped in the fridge for the next round.

75-MINUTE LIMITED-PALETTE STUDY — Kibo, cool shadow / warm reflected edge

PALETTE (3 pigments, no others)
  Ultramarine Blue
  Burnt Sienna
  Yellow Ochre (Raw Sienna works too)

THREE-VALUE PLAN
  Value 1 (lightest)  Warm reflected edge on the coat
                     — dilute YO + a *pinch* of BS, desaturated, NOT orange.
                     Reads as lift in value, not as color.
  Value 2 (middle)    Cool window shadow on floor + Kibo's mid-coat
                     — UM + BS mixed gray. This is your workhorse mix.
  Value 3 (darkest)   Kibo's tucked mass (belly contact, between limbs,
                     head-shadow side, ear interior)
                     — heavier UM + BS, slight UM bias for cool depth.

MIXING ORDER (do this before touching paper)
  1. Mix a "mother gray" pool: 2 UM : 1 BS, mid concentration.
  2. From mother gray, dilute a side pool → Value 2 lighter.
  3. From mother gray, add a small dollop of concentrated UM+BS → Value 3.
  4. In a *separate* zone of the palette, mix Value 1 (YO + tiny BS).
     Keep this away from the mother-gray pools — adding it would muddy.

EDGE STRATEGY
  Floor wash:        ONE wet pass, cool-to-warm gradient (wet-into-wet).
                     The warm edge *is* the wash ending softly.
  Kibo silhouette:   Hard edge — dry brush on dry paper, confident stroke.
  Within the body:   Soft edges only (damp brush, or glaze into dry).
                     Shape comes from value shifts, not lines.
  Cast shadow:       Hard outer edge, soft inner edge against the floor.
  Cast vs. Kibo:     Preserve 1–2 mm rim of bare paper between fur and
                     shadow. This is the rim-of-light margin — non-negotiable.

TIMED SEQUENCE
  0–10   Setup, pencil drawing (silhouette + cast-shadow placement only,
         no face detail), mix the four pools, run a test strip on scrap.
 10–25   Floor + rug wash as one continuous gradient:
           wet area → drop cool UM+BS on shadow side, YO+BS on reflected
           side, let them meet wet-into-wet at the value-2 transition.
         Leave Kibo's shape dry paper.
 25–35   Cast shadow (tea strength) — darkest adjacent to Kibo's body
         where it meets the floor, tapering as it recedes. Offset 1–2 mm
         from the fur. Let dry fully.
 35–55   Kibo, first glaze pass — Value 2 across the whole body, soft
         internal edges, hard silhouette. Stop shy of the warm edge zone.
         Let dry fully.
 55–68   Kibo, second glaze pass — Value 3 only in the tucked/recessed
         areas (belly contact, between front and back legs, head shadow
         side, ear interior). Glaze, don't re-wet.
         THEN — still wet edge of the second pass — drop Value 1 along
         the reflected-light side of the coat to lift it. This is the
         "warm edge as value, not color" move.
         Let dry fully.
 68–74   Face priority marks — in this order, stop after each if it reads:
           a. Eye — single dark mark with one tiny unpainted highlight dot.
           b. Nose — simple shape, one value, no texture.
           c. Muzzle value break — a thin lighter line where reflected
              light lifts the chin/cheek. *This* is the face; almost
              nothing else matters.
 74–75   Step back. Read. Stop.

FACE-DETAIL PRIORITY (in order — only the first three)
  1. Eye
  2. Nose
  3. Muzzle value break
  Skip: whiskers, lip line, ear fringe, individual hairs.

STOP CONDITION (all four must hold, otherwise fix and stop)
  □ Kibo reads instantly from 8 feet away.
  □ Warm edge reads as a *lift in value*, not as orange.
  □ Cast shadow has visible rim-of-light margin against the fur.
  □ You have not touched the face in the last 8 minutes.
  Hard cap: 75 minutes, regardless of state. A stopped study is
  a finished study; a finished study is a Sunday watercolor block
  preserved.

## Summary

This year my work centered on Lifecycle Systems — specifically, the integrity of the operating evidence that goes to the board, the slow hand-off of routine source-completeness work to Owen, and the discipline of keeping paid, organic, forecast, and exception channels visibly separate in every claim. Three contributions stand out on the evidence: the Q1 and Q2 board operating-evidence intakes (Helio Start excluded from Q1, retained only for traceability), the capped paid-acquisition working draft for Helio Start, and the first organic Helio Start authority-checklist operating cut (2026-09-15 through 2026-09-28). The boundary I defended under pressure was the decision not to grant Helio Start a second paid batch in Q3 or Q4, and not to extend forecast treatment or pipeline credit to the closed paid cohort. The two development priorities for H2 are concrete behavior changes — one in how I write, one in how I review — and neither implies I have already stepped back from routine monthly preparation or source-closure work.

## Primary work lanes

**Helio Start evidence integrity.** Across the year I kept the paid and organic channels separate in every claim, refused to extend forecast or pipeline treatment to the closed paid cohort, and built the working draft for the capped paid-acquisition shape on the rule that budget authorization does not grant pipeline credit, forecast credit, or a payback commitment. With Owen and Customer Success, I ran the first organic Helio Start authority pre-setup checklist operating cut (2026-09-15 through 2026-09-28). 44 newly admitted organic workspaces; no unsupported admission; no eligibility-route mismatch. The checklist preserved the existing meanings of its governed states and did not extend authority; eligibility requires the current entitlement state to be known, and that requirement was unchanged by the release.

**Q1 and Q2 board operating-evidence intake.** I was the final claim owner for the pricing-page path-quality row across Q1 and Q2, and the lane work ran on the rule that source owner and final claim owner are separate fields so source-of-data responsibility does not collapse into final-narrative responsibility. On 2026-03-24 Tomás Vega approved the Q1 operating-evidence section (Expansion Assist, pricing-page path quality, CS auto-nudge) without a Helio Start forecast claim; Helio Start was excluded from the section and retained only for traceability. In Q2 the pricing-page path-quality preparation was source-complete in the June 12 packet, and Owen completed his owner input on 2026-05-29.

**Pricing-page path-quality ownership.** Pricing-page path quality reached `board-ready` on 2026-03-16. I held the final claim through Q1 and Q2, with Owen as source owner. The row carried denominator or exact coverage dates, measurement limits, exclusions, source owner, source or release-reliability evidence, revenue and forecast treatment, and final claim owner through both intakes.

## Boundary defended under pressure: no second paid Helio Start batch, no forecast treatment

The clearest pressure point of the year was the request — internal, repeated, well-intentioned — to grant Helio Start a second paid batch in Q3 or Q4, and to extend forecast treatment or pipeline credit to the closed paid cohort. The decision was no on both counts, and the reasoning is the boundary I want to defend in this review.

The closed paid Helio Start cohort is fixed at 50 workspaces, drawn from admissions between 2025-10-01 and 2025-10-28. Budget authorization for the paid-search shape does not grant pipeline credit, forecast credit, or a payback commitment; granting any of those now would silently re-open the cohort and overwrite the preserved rules that governed it (paid acquisition before 2026-04-01 remains out of scope, mature cohorts are not treated as a forecast, and the Helio Start draft excludes pipeline and forecast credit, payback claims, and changes to preserved rules). I held the line on three things specifically: no new paid batch in Q3, no new paid batch in Q4, and no Q4 forecast or pipeline credit for the cohort. The closed-pilot record has not been reopened, and that is the position as of the 2026-10-07 staff review.

The October 14 Helio Start authority-checklist review is a descriptive read-through of the organic release, not an authorization decision. Eligibility is unchanged by it. Holding the line here is what lets the checklist release stay a release and not become a quiet extension of authority.

## Leadership through delegation: what Owen owns, what I retain

The most concrete example of leadership through delegation this year is Owen's transition into routine Lifecycle Systems preparation and source-closure review, and the discipline of keeping that delegation bounded against my own retained authority on claims and exceptions.

**Delegated — Owen runs, I receive.** Routine monthly Lifecycle Systems preparation and routine source-completeness closure across the four board-evidence lanes (Helio Start, Expansion Assist, pricing-page path-quality, and CS auto-nudge controls) run through Owen. He owns exception triage, classification, and suppression-rule authoring; he owns the inventory of exception views; he is the source owner on the rows I claim. Standing continuity requirements for CS auto-nudge checkpoints — preserving the denominator, the field-reason breakdown, fresh-check final dispositions, cross-view itemization, customer-correction reporting, and operational-freshness evidence — are his to maintain.

**Retained — I own the claim and the exception.** I am the final claim owner on every row I sign. Source owner and final claim owner stay as separate fields so the source-of-data responsibility does not collapse into the final-narrative responsibility. I retain authority on cohort claims (closed-pilot record; cohort fixed at 50) and on board-readiness calls. I join a Lifecycle Systems exception when it reveals a disputed source owner; that is the trigger, not a routine handoff. The Q4 case-review gate (full rules in doc_1789855549773) holds: Owen's 2026-09-24 source-completeness closure is the working perimeter — seven high-supervision workstreams, cohort of 50 — and any widening of that perimeter re-enters the gate at stage S1. Daniela's pre-read for the 10-7 staff review (doc_1789872895649) is descriptive; it did not authorize anything.

**Why this matters for the leadership-through-delegation read.** The hand-off is real and it is bounded. Owen now runs the operating cut that produced the 44 organic admissions and the no-unsupported-admission / no-eligibility-route-mismatch findings. I am not running that work; I am receiving it and deciding what it means for the claim. Holding the line on the no-second-paid-batch and no-forecast-credit decisions, and on the case-review gate, is what the delegation actually buys — it lets me spend my own attention on the claim and the exception rather than on the routine operating readout.

## Development priorities (H2 2026)

**Priority 1 — Lead with my own behavior, not the tooling.** When I write a post-mortem or an evidence write-up this half, I will describe my own leadership behavior — the call I made, the call I declined, the pressure I absorbed or didn't — as the primary cause, with tooling and process described as the conditions that shaped the call. The instinct to frame the work as a tooling or system story is real and it is what I am building the reflex against. To make this stick, I have asked Owen and Ines to flag any draft I produce that reverts to tooling-first framing.

**Priority 2 — Stop line-editing routine operating readouts after the checks pass.** Once a routine operating readout has cleared source-completeness, refusal-boundary, lifecycle-overlap, and owner-signoff checks, I will stop line-editing it. The boundary is the four-check sign-off, not the calendar. This is a behavior change in how I review, not a step back from the reviews themselves — I am still in routine monthly Lifecycle Systems preparation and in source-closure review; what changes is that I stop second-guessing the prose after the checks have passed.

Neither priority is a handoff. I am still the final claim owner; I am still in the routine preparation and the source-closure reviews; the case-review gate still holds.

Quick read on the situation: one tire 6 psi low while the other three are at placard is asymmetric. Weather drops hit all four roughly equally, so this is more likely a slow leak (or a one-time cold-soak effect, but that's the less probable explanation given the gap). Treat it as a suspected slow leak until a recheck proves otherwise.

IMMEDIATE INFLATION SEQUENCE

1. Confirm cold. You said the gauge check was cold — good. If the car has sat 3+ hours or was driven under a mile, the 29 psi reading is real.
2. Inflate the front-right to 35 psi (the placard number), not to "match" the others. Don't over-inflate as a hedge — a distorted baseline hides the leak signal on the next reading.
3. Use a gauge you trust. Gas-station gauges drift; a personal gauge or a second gauge cross-check is better. If you only have the one gauge, inflate a few psi past 35, deflate back to 35, and recheck — this can shake off a sticky valve core and gives a more accurate final reading.
4. Do a short low-speed loop (a mile or two). Confirm no pull, no vibration, no warning light change.
5. Note the position (front-right) and the date. Mental log is fine; chalk on the sidewall also works.

SAME-DAY AND COLD RECHECK PROTOCOL

- Same-day, after the car has been parked 1–2 hours: recheck the front-right. This is a "warm-soak" reading, not directly comparable to cold, but it gives you a baseline to track fall-off overnight.
- Next morning, before driving, cold recheck the front-right. This is the decision point:
   - Holds at ~33–35 psi → likely a one-time cold-soak or a very slow leak; recheck again the following morning.
   - Drops back to ~29 psi or lower → confirmed slow leak. Do not rely on this tire for the airport run until a shop has looked at it.
- For the other three tires: recheck them too at the same time. If they've all dropped 1–2 psi in 24 hours, that's weather; if only the front-right keeps falling, that's the tire.

LOCAL-DRIVING LIMITS WHILE UNDIAGNOSED

- Treat the front-right as conditionally usable, not trusted.
- Stay local, stay under ~45 mph, avoid highways.
- Keep the load light on that corner (no passenger / no cargo up front if you can help it).
- No long drives. Round trips should be short and planned around a shop visit.
- Recheck pressure before every drive until the pattern is clear.

STOP-DRIVING / GO DIRECTLY TO A TIRE SHOP

Do not drive, or drive only directly to a shop (very low speed, shortest route), if any of the following appears:

- Cold pressure at or below 25 psi on the front-right (well into the underinflated-danger zone, especially for a driven wheel).
- Visible sidewall bulge, blister, crack, or a nail/screw you missed on first inspection.
- Audible hiss at the valve or from anywhere on the tire.
- TPMS light flashing at startup (steady-on is low pressure; flashing is a sensor/system fault — different problem, still needs diagnosis).
- Any pull, vibration, or handling change that wasn't there on the drive home.
- Pressure falling more than ~1 psi per day even after reinflating to 35 — that's a real leak rate and the tire cannot be trusted for an airport trip on a deadline.
- Tire visually looks low when you approach the car (squatting more than the others).

PRE-TRIP CHECK BEFORE MOM'S AIRPORT PICKUP

Before you commit the car to that run:

- Two consecutive cold mornings at 33–35 psi on the front-right, with no other tire drifting.
- No TPMS light.
- Ideally a tire shop has at minimum inspected and confirmed no active leak, even if they don't repair it that day. A visual + soap-bubble check at the valve and over the tread takes five minutes and most shops will do it on a walk-in.

If you can't get those two clean cold readings before the pickup day, the conservative move is to inflate to 35 the morning of, recheck at the airport, and have a backup plan (rideshare, ask Sam, rent a car for the day) rather than discover a flat on the cell-phone lot.

One more thing worth flagging since you mentioned the airport: a tire that has been running 17% low can have uneven wear or a developing issue at the bead that a shop can spot before it strands you. If you can spare 20 minutes this weekend, a walk-in inspection is cheap insurance against the trip.

The Rx side can flip the comparison in either direction for users with steady monthly meds, and none of these have been verified yet:

  1. Formulary tier (1–5) under each plan for each current medication. List each drug + dose + frequency; check PPO formulary and HDHP formulary separately. A drug that's tier-2 copay under the PPO can be tier-4 (and subject to deductible + coinsurance) under the HDHP — or vice versa.
  2. Whether each plan has a separate Rx deductible, or whether Rx spending applies to the medical deductible. PPO summary pages often show "Rx deductible: $X" as its own line; HDHPs almost always fold Rx into the medical deductible. This decides whether your January refill is $10 or $2,000.
  3. Coinsurance vs flat copay for non-generic drugs after the deductible is met. HDHPs commonly charge coinsurance (e.g., 10% of allowed amount) post-deductible, so a $400 brand-name fill becomes $40. PPOs commonly charge flat copays (e.g., $40 flat) for tiers 2–3. Model your specific drugs under each rule.
  4. Preventive-drug list under each plan. Some PPOs waive the deductible for a defined preventive-Rx list (statins, ACE inhibitors, certain asthma controllers). If your meds are on that list, the PPO's effective Rx cost drops. HDHPs after the ACA also cover certain preventive Rx at $0 pre-deductible under IRS Notice 2004-2 / preventive-care safe harbor, but the carrier-specific list varies.
  5. Mail-order vs 90-day retail pricing differential for each med under each plan. A 90-day mail-order fill is often 2–3× cheaper than three 30-day retail fills for the same drug, and the savings rate differs between PPO and HDHP.

  Copy 1: laptop scan folder (already exists; treat as canonical)

Rule of thumb: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite. Don't rename, don't re-folder, don't run anything that touches EXIF or other metadata.

 1. Freeze the source.
    Close any viewer/editor on the laptop folder. List it and confirm all 26 scans are present, with the front/back structure you already use (paired filenames or per-photo subfolders) untouched.

 2. Build a baseline checksum list on the laptop.
    `find /path/to/scan-folder -type f | sort | xargs sha256sum > /path/to/scan-folder/.checksums.txt`
    Travel this file with the archive — it's part of provenance.

 3. Mirror to the SSD.
    `rsync -av --delete /path/to/scan-folder/ /mnt/ssd/scan-folder/`
    Then, from the SSD: `sha256sum -c /mnt/ssd/scan-folder/.checksums.txt`
    Every line must say OK. Spot-open one front/back pair from the SSD to confirm files are actually readable, not just bit-identical.

 4. Mirror to the cloud.
    Use your normal sync tool (rclone sync, provider client, mounted folder). Mirror the same tree, no renaming, no metadata rewrites.
    Verify after the tool reports done — re-download at least a few files (or pull a directory listing with hashes if the tool exposes them) and check against the baseline. Don't trust "sync complete" on its own.

 5. Confirm the card is a subset, not a superset.
    Mount the card read-only. Hash its files and diff against the laptop list. Every card file should already exist in laptop/SSD/cloud. If anything is on the card but not in any backup, pull it into the laptop folder and redo from step 2.

 6. Clear the card only if 3–5 all pass.
    Delete files (or reformat). Re-list the card to confirm it's empty.

 7. Update the provenance note.
    Date copies were made, SSD label, cloud path, that no metadata was edited, that verification was hash-based. Keep `.checksums.txt` with the archive.

If any verification step fails, stop — don't clear the card, don't touch the laptop folder. Diagnose the mismatch first.

Symptoms & function
  □ Does the end-of-day blur actually interfere with work, driving, or evening reading — or just mildly annoy?

  1. Squint test at arm's length — value masses still readable? If everything flattens to one tone, the lamp is washing things out; drop brightness one step.

Three options for the monthly hands-on audit, assessed against the four dimensions, then a recommendation and what to carry into the proposal. No doc or calendar changes — this stays at proposal stage.

ASSESSMENT

Option A — Rotating deep recheck of one evidence lane after closure
  Direct evidence-system contact: HIGH. Re-derives a lane's headline from raw rows.
  Duplicates Owen's source-completeness: LOW only if scoped to derivation. Owen verifies inputs are complete; this verifies outputs are reproducible. Without a scope guard, duplication is real.
  Owner-role ambiguity: LOW if Riley signs. The audit becomes a Riley attestation, not a co-approval.
  Second approval queue risk: LOW if timing is strictly AFTER closure. The lane is already final; the audit surfaces discrepancies, it does not gate the closure.

Option B — Targeted sample drawn from that month's exceptions
  Direct evidence-system contact: MODERATE. Exceptions often have partial or bridged data.
  Duplicates Owen's source-completeness: LOW. Exceptions sit outside the standard pipeline Owen audits.
  Owner-role ambiguity: MEDIUM. Exceptions usually have an interim handler; an audit sits between that handler and Riley.
  Second approval queue risk: HIGH. Exceptions are decision-adjacent; a sample that touches them becomes a parallel review where exceptions cannot close until the audit clears. This is the option most likely to quietly grow into a second queue.

Option C — Small cross-lane trace of governed fields and claim treatment
  Direct evidence-system contact: MODERATE. Touches multiple lanes but does not deeply re-derive any single one.
  Duplicates Owen's source-completeness: LOW. Cross-lane coherence is a different concern.
  Owner-role ambiguity: MEDIUM-HIGH. Cross-lane fields often lack a single named owner, and "claim treatment" reads differently across lanes.
  Second approval queue risk: LOW. A coherence check is less likely to gate a single decision.

RECOMMENDATION

Primary: Option A as the standing monthly audit, with explicit scope guards. The current proposal's "one random source row per month, re-pulled, re-checked, re-derived, Riley signature" is too narrow — a single row does not validate a lane, and a rotating lane-level re-derivation is what actually preserves your authorities.

Carry-forward conditions:
  1. Name it "lane re-derivation audit" and write that into the proposal. It re-derives a lane's downstream artifact from raw source rows. It does NOT redo source-completeness verification; that remains Owen's lane. This is the scope guard that removes duplication with Owen.
  2. Timing is strictly AFTER closure. Discrepancies found in the audit do not gate the lane; they route through existing escalation triggers. If a re-derivation lands inside an open trigger window, the audit pauses on that lane until the trigger resolves — the audit never competes with an active escalation.
  3. Riley signs the re-derivation. Not a delegated sign-off. This is the single line that keeps final-claim authority on Riley.
  4. Rotation across all governed lanes on a defined, itself-auditable order. One lane per month; low fatigue.
  5. Option B stays out of the standing audit. Exceptions already have a path through triggers; folding them into the monthly cadence is what creates the second-queue risk that Option B carries. If exception volume warrants it, exceptions are a triggered supplement, not a default.
  6. Option C becomes a quarterly check, not monthly. Lanes move on different cadences; cross-lane work monthly inflates fatigue without improving signal. Quarterly keeps coherence coverage without competing with the monthly audit.

WHAT THIS PRESERVES

  Causal authority — re-derivation from source confirms the causal chain that produced the lane's headline.
  Revenue authority — same logic; re-derivation is the strongest single check on revenue treatment.
  Forecast authority — forecast lanes get rotation slots; the re-derivation feeds the next forecast.
  Board-readiness authority — a signed Riley re-derivation is the exact artifact a board needs to see the headline is reproducible.
  Final-claim authority — Riley signature, no delegation.
  Existing escalation triggers — the audit does not replace, modify, or compete with any trigger.

EDGE CASES TO PRE-SPECIFY IN THE PROPOSAL

  Re-derivation discrepancy that changes a closed headline → existing post-admission scope-change path; not a re-open triggered by the audit.
  Re-derivation discrepancy that does not change the headline → audit metadata only; no re-open.
  Mid-cycle incidents or active triggers → audit pauses on the affected lane until the trigger resolves.
  Source-completeness finding uncovered during re-derivation → routes to Owen; not absorbed into the audit.

WHAT THIS EXCLUDES FROM AUDIT SCOPE

  Source-completeness re-verification (Owen).
  Per-exception reviews (triggers).
  Cross-lane field-level coherence (quarterly, separate cadence).
  Executive-language review, mid-packet change review, role-drift monitoring — these are proposal implementation risks, not audit scope. Keeping them out prevents the audit from quietly absorbing governance work that already lives elsewhere.

Short sequence:

1. Lamp first. High and off-axis — roughly 45° above the still life, 30–45° to one side. Aim at the top-front of the cup, not directly at the dark side. The primary cast shadow should fall onto the surface beside or behind the cup, away from your brush hand.

2. Reflector opposite the lamp, but FARTHER from the cup than the lamp is, and tilted to bounce light into the shadow side of the cup — not back at the lamp. Start at arm's length.

3. The second-edge problem has a geometric cause: the foam board has an edge, the cup is curved, and any point on the cup's shadow side either "sees" the reflector or it doesn't. The boundary is the second edge — a visible terminator inside the dark side. Two fixes, use whichever fits the setup:
   - Slide the reflector until its near edge is hidden behind the cup's silhouette from the lamp's viewpoint. The lamp then fully lights the reflector and the cup masks its edge.
   - Or pull the reflector back far enough that its angular size from the cup's surface shrinks below the curvature — the edge falls outside the cup's "horizon" and disappears from view on the form.
   Either way the reflector becomes a uniform fill with no visible terminator on the cup.

4. The flattening problem: the reflected side still needs to show a gradient — a core shadow band (darkest strip just past the primary terminator) easing into reflected light near the cup's bottom or front edge that faces the reflector. If it reads flat, the reflector is too close or aimed too directly. Pull it back, or rotate it slightly away from the cup so the bounced light is weaker. The form comes back when the gradient returns.

5. Value check without wet-wash glare. Squint always works. For a sharper read, use a value-finder — a small gray card with a punched hole, or cup one hand around an eye to kill peripheral glare. On wet paper the specular reflection overstates value (everything looks lighter than it is). Two clean fixes: step back until the glare falls below your line of sight, or tilt the board so the reflection slides off toward your palette side. Cleanest of all: do the value calibration on dry paper or a test swatch first, mix the puddle to match, then paint.

6. Stop condition. Paint ONE primary shadow system: the terminator on the cup's form, plus its gradient (core shadow band and soft reflected light) — all one shadow. If a second hard edge starts to appear inside the dark side, STOP. That edge is the reflector's artifact, not the still life. Lift the wash, re-read from the corrected lighting, then re-paint. Signal to hold to: two hard edges on the form = wrong setup or wrong reading; one hard edge with a smooth gradient below it = right. Don't alter the painting to chase the second edge — change the light, then read again.

One framing rule worth keeping: the painting records what you see, not what the lighting is doing. When the lighting creates an artifact, fix the lighting, not the brushwork.

Cadence comparison — hands-on evidence audit (decision input; no role change proposed)

Three options on the table:
  A. Monthly rotating one-lane
  B. Quarterly rotating one-lane
  C. Exception-triggered only

Dimension 1 — Direct system contact
  A. ~12 system touches/year; full lane pass every quarter (3 lanes) or 4 months (4 lanes). Continuous signal, low decay.
  B. ~4 touches/year; full pass in 3–4 quarters. 60–90 day freshness gap between same-lane contacts.
  C. Touch volume equals anomaly rate; can be zero between events on stable lanes, clustered on noisy ones.

Dimension 2 — Duplicate work
  A. Highest re-pull risk; lane state often unchanged between reviews. Needs a delta-only protocol to keep this honest.
  B. Lower re-pull risk because the quarter is a natural evidence-cycle boundary; aligns to the 11/1–12/31 window and the next 60-day windows.
  C. Re-pull is by definition targeted; no scheduled duplication.

Dimension 3 — Owner-role ambiguity
  A + B. Clean split as long as audit findings don't quietly turn into re-work requests on the audit lane: Riley reads system state, the named lane owner (Priya / Daniela / Marcus Vail–Tomás) maintains it. Audit lane and owner lanes are different lanes, so the self-audit concern doesn't apply. The real ambiguity is the time-to-acknowledgment SLA when a finding lands on an owner's desk.
  C. Ambiguous trigger ownership. If "exception" is defined by the lane owner, the auditee effectively controls cadence. If by Riley, the auditor does. Without an explicit trigger owner this drifts.

Dimension 4 — Second-approval-queue risk
  A. Highest steady-state queue pressure; ~monthly findings unless audit findings explicitly don't enter the approval queue by default.
  B. Queue pressure batches with existing decision windows (12/10 board segment, quarterly close); easier to absorb.
  C. Bursty — light between events, spikes when one fires. Hard to staff steady-state.

Frame for the choice
  - Monthly wins on freshness and early drift detection; the queue is the cost to manage.
  - Quarterly wins on alignment with the 60-day evidence window and the quarterly board rhythm, with the cleanest role split.
  - Exception-triggered is the lowest-cost option only if a trigger owner and a burst-handling protocol are already in place; without those it is the highest-risk option despite the lowest volume.

Lean: quarterly rotating for the 12/10 window, with monthly as the upgrade path if a same-window drift surfaces; exception-triggered as the floor, gated on a named trigger owner.

I don't have the pack details or your Jan–April usage rate anywhere I can pull from, so I can't run the actual numbers yet. Rather than guess and give you a made-up comparison, here's the framework — once you drop in the three inputs, the answer is quick.

What I need from you:
  - Pack A (smaller): sheet count + total price
  - Pack B (larger): sheet count + total price
  - Your Jan 1 – Apr 30 usage: sheets per week, or sessions/week × sheets/session

The framework I'll apply once you have those:

  1. Per-sheet cost = pack price ÷ sheet count
       The larger pack will almost always win this. The point is to ignore it as a tiebreaker.

  2. Total sheets supplied = existing 3 + pack count
       Coverage = total ÷ weekly use = weeks the supply lasts.

  3. Compare coverage against the Jan 1 – Apr 30 window (~17 weeks).
       - Option "wins" if it covers the full 4 months without leaving a big surplus, OR covers them and the leftover is small enough that it doesn't go to waste (paper yellows / warps if it sits too long).
       - Option "loses" if it forces a second purchase mid-window (extra shipping, extra decision), or if it leaves a large leftover that won't get used before it degrades.

  4. Lower-waste fit = the one whose supply lands closest to (but not under) 17 weeks of use. The larger pack's lower unit cost only matters if it also lands near that target — otherwise the savings per sheet are paid for in unused sheets.

SILVER RIBBON ON KRAFT — 60-MINUTE SEQUENCE
==============================================

0:00–0:10   VALUE MAP (10 min)
- Pre-mix on the palette, in this order:
  1. Light warm gray  — raw umber, ~4:1 water to pigment
  2. Cool neutral mid — ultramarine + burnt umber, ~1:2 ratio
  3. Cool neutral dark — same pair, double pigment, less water
- Squint at the subject. Force yourself into 3 value zones only:
  · light  (kraft + lit ribbon faces)
  · mid    (most of the ribbon mass)
  · dark   (deepest folds + one cast shadow)
- Pick 4–5 STRUCTURAL folds. Everything else is invisible chrome you will not paint.

0:10–0:25   RESERVE HIGHLIGHTS (15 min)
- For the 5–8 pinpoint specks: dampen with clean water, lift immediately with a thirsty brush or tissue. Stop while the lift is still bright.
- For the 2–3 hardest sparks: either mask now or paint bone-dry around them later. No half-measures.
- Let the lifted spots dry fully before the next wash — a damp halo will grey them for you without permission.

0:25–0:40   COOL-NEUTRAL FIRST PASS (15 min)
- Mixing order on paper, not palette: start warm, end cool.
- Step 1: light warm gray, swept broadly across the kraft + lit ribbon faces. One pass. Soft edges everywhere.
- Step 2: while that wash is just-damp (not wet), drop the cool neutral mid into the ribbon's body — into the shadow pattern BETWEEN the highlights, not over them.
- Step 3: a single touch of the dark cool-neutral into the 2 deepest creases only.
- Rule: every stroke pre-loaded from the palette. No mixing on paper. No retouching.

0:40–0:50   SELECTIVE EDGES (10 min)
- Hard edges — paint exactly 4–5 of them, and only where a lit facet snaps into a deep fold. One stroke each. Damp brush, dark mix, then leave it.
- Lost edges — everything else. Let the cool-neutral mid bleed into the kraft where the ribbon lies flat. That bleed IS the silver.
- One soft cast shadow under the deepest fold onto the kraft: cool gray, well diluted, fading at both ends.

0:50–0:58   STOP CONDITION (8 min)
- Squint. Four questions, all must pass:
  · Can I still see kraft-paper texture between the folds?           (yes → pass)
  · Are the reserved highlights still paper-white, not pale gray?   (yes → pass)
  · Can I count the visible strokes and is it under ~15?             (yes → pass)
  · If I add one more stroke, does it cross into a muddier value?   (no → pass)
- Any failure = ONE corrective stroke, then stop. Do not re-evaluate.
- Sign the corner while it's dry. Walk away before you "improve" it.

0:58–1:00   CLOSE (2 min)
- Tape the sheet. Don't critique until tomorrow — silver reads differently after the wash dries overnight.

RESTRAINTS TO HOLD THE LINE
- Two pigments do 90% of the work: burnt umber + ultramarine.
- Three reserved whites, max — silver is mostly mid-value.
- One cast shadow. One dark mix. One first pass.
- The moment you want to add a 6th stroke in any single fold, you are already overworked.

Have a good block — the brown kraft is doing half the work for you, so let it.

2027 IRS HSA cap, self-only HDHP: **$4,500** (Rev. Proc. 2026-24). Set by IRC §223(b)(2)(A) and inflation-adjusted; Helio's portal doesn't show it, but it's the binding constraint.

Helio's employer contribution: **$225 × 4 = $900/year**, deposited quarterly, contingent on HSA eligibility at each deposit. So your employee-side room is **$4,500 − $900 = $3,600/year**.

Per paycheck (24 pay periods):

| Per paycheck | Annual employee | Annual total (you + Helio) | Headroom vs $4,500 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $75 | $1,800 | $2,700 | $1,800 |
| $100 | $2,400 | $3,300 | $1,200 |
| $125 | $3,000 | $3,900 | $600 |
| **$150** (max) | **$3,600** | **$4,500** | **$0** |
| Custom > $150 | > $3,600 | > $4,500 | exceeds cap |

The custom option has an upper bound: per-paycheck × 24 must be ≤ $3,600, i.e. **≤ $150/paycheck**. Anything above that, combined with Helio's $900, will exceed the IRS limit and trigger excess-contribution excise tax (6% per year until corrected).

Three things worth keeping in view when you choose:

1. **Election deadline is Jan 4, 2027** — same day as the operating-model transition in your other workstream. Don't let the two collide; the election window will close.
2. **Helio's $225/quarter is contingent on eligibility at each deposit**, not on annual elections. If HDHP eligibility lapses during a quarter (e.g., briefly enrolled in non-HDHP coverage, Medicare enrollment, etc.), that quarter's $225 simply doesn't deposit. The IRS cap is unchanged, but your actual employer-side total can be less than $900, which means more employee-side room is available — but only within the same calendar year (you can't retroactively exceed the cap, but you also can't deposit Helio's missed quarter later).
3. **Age-55+ catch-up** is $1,000 (statutorily fixed, doesn't change for 2027), on top of the $4,500. If you're 55 or older at end of 2027, the catch-up is typically contributed directly to the HSA custodian, not via Helio's payroll election — and it doesn't change your per-paycheck ceiling above.

Hoppin' John with Braised Collards — perfect for New Year's Day

You've essentially got the Southern New Year's plate already: black-eyed peas (coins), greens (paper money), rice. Serendipitous timing. Serves 2 generously, with leftovers.

About 10 min prep, 25 min cook.

Prep the collards. Strip the leaves off the center stems — discard the stems (or save for stock). Stack the leaves, roll them like a cigar, and slice into roughly 1/2-inch ribbons. Rinse but don't dry; the water clinging to the leaves helps them wilt down.

While you're at it: drain both cans of black-eyed peas. Zest the whole lemon, then juice it.

Build the dish.

1. Warm about 3 tablespoons olive oil in a wide pot or deep skillet over medium heat. Add 4 to 5 cloves of garlic, sliced thin. Cook 60 to 90 seconds — fragrant, just barely turning gold. Don't let it brown.

2. Add the collards in a few handfuls, stirring, until everything wilts down (3 to 4 minutes). Season with about 1 teaspoon salt and several grinds of black pepper.

3. Pour in roughly 3/4 cup of the vegetable broth. Cover, drop the heat to low, and braise 15 to 18 minutes — until the collards are silky and a fork goes through with no resistance. Stir once or twice.

4. Uncover. Add the drained peas and about 1 teaspoon smoked paprika (more if Sam likes it). Stir gently and simmer uncovered 4 to 5 minutes, just to heat the peas through and let the liquid gloss up.

5. Off the heat: stir in the lemon zest and 1 to 2 tablespoons of the lemon juice. Taste. Adjust salt and acid.

Serve over the rice — warm it with a splash of water in a covered bowl in the microwave (about 90 seconds), or loosen it in a small pot with a splash of broth. Pass the remaining lemon wedges.

A few notes for the occasion:
- This is gentle and restorative — exactly right after a late shift. The lemon at the end brightens it; the smoked paprika gives warmth without heat. If you happen to have a hot sauce on the door of the fridge, it's traditional alongside, but not needed.
- Leftovers hold 3 days easily. The peas and rice thicken as they sit — loosen with broth or water when you reheat.
- If the bunch of collards is on the large side and the greens still feel fibrous after 18 minutes, give them another 5; they should yield to a fork.

ONE-POT LEMON ORZO WITH CHICKEN SAUSAGE & SPINACH

Serves 3 (2 now, 1 leftover). One large pot or deep skillet, lid-off cooking, ~30 min.

INGREDIENTS (approximate)
- 1 lb Italian chicken sausage, sliced into 1/2" coins
- 1 cup dry orzo
- 3 cups chicken broth
- 3 oz baby spinach (~3 cups)
- 1/3 cup grated parmesan
- 1 lemon: zest + 2 Tbsp juice
- 1/3 cup sun-dried tomatoes, chopped (optional)
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 Tbsp olive oil
- Salt, pepper, red pepper flakes

30-MINUTE SEQUENCE
- 0:00  Heat oil in pot over medium-high.
- 0:02  Add sausage coins; brown 5 min, stirring once or twice.
- 0:07  Add garlic + sun-dried tomatoes; cook 30-60 sec.
- 0:08  Stir in orzo; toast 1-2 min so it drinks up the oil.
- 0:10  Pour in broth + lemon zest + pinch of salt + pepper flakes; bring to a simmer.
- 0:13  Reduce to medium-low; simmer uncovered 10-12 min, stirring every couple minutes, until orzo is tender and most liquid is absorbed (should look creamy, not soupy).
- 0:24  Stir in spinach until wilted, ~1-2 min.
- 0:26  Kill heat. Stir in parmesan and lemon juice. Taste for salt/pepper.
- 0:28  Plate two portions; keep the third in the pot for cooling.

CLEANUP: One pot, one cutting board, one knife. Done.

COOLING THE LEFTOVER SAFELY
- Move the leftover to a shallow metal or glass container (thin layer cools faster than a deep mound). Aim for ~2" max depth.
- Set the container on a cool surface — a metal baking sheet, a wire rack, or briefly in an ice bath (pot nested in a larger bowl of ice water for 5-10 min, stir once). Don't cover tightly until the steam stops.
- Goal: 140 → 70°F within 2 hours, then 70 → 40°F within the next 4 hours. The ice-bath path gets you to fridge-temp in ~20-30 min.
- Once cooled, cover and refrigerate. Use within 3-4 days.

REHEAT (when you want it)
- Skillet, covered, medium-low: 2-3 Tbsp water or broth, lid on, 4-5 min, stir once. This restores the creamy texture best.
- Microwave, covered with a damp paper towel: 2-3 min on high, stir halfway. Backup option.

The main risk on an untested-colorfast cotton jacket isn't really the coffee — black coffee with no milk or sugar is mostly tannin and lifts easily with cold water. The bigger risk is the dye in the fabric bleeding or the spot fading unevenly under any wet treatment, so the order of steps matters.

1. Blot now. Press a clean damp cloth or paper towel against the spill, working from the outside of the stain inward, no rubbing. Lift, rotate to a clean section, repeat. This pulls most of the liquid out before it spreads or starts to set.

2. Spot-test for colorfastness before going further. Pick a hidden spot — inside the cuff facing, inside a hem, under a pocket flap. Press a cotton swab dampened with cold water against it for about 30 seconds, then blot onto a white paper towel. If any dye transfers to the towel, the jacket is not colorfast and you should stop with cold water only: skip the detergent pre-treat and just rinse and wash cold, alone. If the swab stays clean, you're clear to use a mild soap on the stain.

3. Cold-water flush from the back. Hold the cuff under a cold running tap with the stained side facing down, so the water pushes the coffee out of the fibers rather than deeper through them. A minute or two of gentle flushing is enough for a small fresh spill.

4. Pre-treat only if colorfast. Work a tiny amount of clear liquid dish soap or mild liquid laundry detergent into the stain with your fingertip. Let it sit 5 minutes. Don't scrub — friction can rough up the cotton surface and leave a lighter "cleaned" patch that's visibly different from the surrounding fabric.

5. Wash cold, alone. Machine wash cold on a gentle cycle by itself, or with similarly colored items you wouldn't mind if a little dye bled. Do not add the regular load.

6. Inspect damp, then air dry. This is the step most people miss: the label says no tumble dry, and heat will permanently set any tannin that's still in the fibers. Check the cuff while it's still wet. If you can still see a tan or brown ghost, repeat the pre-treat and rewash before letting it dry. Once the stain is clearly gone, lay flat or hang to air dry.

The two "don'ts" that matter most here: don't use hot water (sets tannin and encourages dye bleed), and don't let it go through a dryer even once if any stain is still visible — heat locks tannin into cotton permanently.

I don't have the actual care label text, so treat this as the conservative default and skip any step the label prohibits (e.g., "no solvents," "dry-clean only," "do not wet"):

1. **Spot-test, hidden area first.** Cotton swab + the cleaning agent you plan to use, 60 seconds, blot dry. If the finish softens, dulls, or the swab picks up pigment/color you didn't put there, stop and step down to plain water only.

2. **Blot first, no rubbing.** Press a clean dry microfiber or paper towel straight down on the stain, lift straight up. Wiping sideways is what carries pigment into clean finish and into grain.

3. **Pre-dampen a ring just outside the stain.** Plain water on a barely-damp cloth, wiped around the perimeter only. This creates a barrier so the wash step doesn't drag pigment outward.

4. **Wash outside-in.** Barely-damp microfiber + a few drops of plain dish soap diluted in water. Start at the outer edge of the stain and work toward the center (center-out pushes pigment into clean finish). Brief blotting contact, 5–10 seconds per pass. Hard cap: 2–3 passes, then re-evaluate.

5. **Rinse.** Fresh barely-damp microfiber, plain water, same outside-in direction. Lift the soap film so residue doesn't haze the finish as it dries.

6. **Air-dry.** Pat with a clean dry cloth, then leave at room temperature. No hairdryer, no heater register, no sun — heat can flash-set anything you didn't lift.

Stop condition: if it's visibly lighter after the 2–3 pass cap, stop and let it dry. Damp pigment always reads darker than dry, so the real verdict is after it air-dries. Re-inspect, then decide whether another round is warranted.

Escalation only if the spot-test passed and water/soap didn't move it: isopropyl alcohol on a lightly dampened cotton swab, outside-in, 5–10 seconds per pass, blot dry, same 2–3 pass cap.

SHEET-PAN CHICKPEA, SWEET POTATO & BROCCOLI
with COUSCOUS and LEMON-TAHINI

Serves: dinner tonight + 1 lunch portion
Active time: ~15 min   Oven: ~25 min   Oven trips: 2

PREHEAT 425°F. Line a rimmed sheet pan with parchment (no scrubbing later).

PREP (all at the counter, seated is fine):
- Sweet potato: peeled, 1/2 to 3/4 inch cubes
- Broccoli: bite-size florets
- Chickpeas: drained, rinsed, patted dry

TOSS on the sheet pan:
- Sweet potato + chickpeas + broccoli
- 2 Tbsp olive oil
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 3/4 tsp salt, several grinds pepper
- Spread in a single layer (crowding = steaming, not roasting)

ROAST at 425°F:
- In at minute 0
- Pull rack out at minute 12, toss once with a spatula, push back in
- Pull at minute 22 to 25 — sweet potato edges caramelized, broccoli just tender

WHILE IT ROASTS (one stove trip):
- Bring 1 cup water + pinch salt to a boil
- Pour over 3/4 cup dry couscous in a heatproof bowl, cover (plate on top), rest 5 min, fluff with a fork

LEMON-TAHINI SAUCE (whisk in a jar or bowl, use the same bowl for serving):
- 3 Tbsp tahini
- Juice of 1/2 lemon (start with 1 Tbsp; add more if you like it sharp)
- 1 small garlic clove, grated or very finely minced
- 2 to 3 Tbsp warm water, added a splash at a time, until it drizzles
- Pinch salt

SERVE: couscous on the plate, veggies and chickpeas on top, sauce drizzled over. Save the other lemon half for tomorrow's lunch.

LEFTOVER PORTION — SAFE COOLING
- Spread the lunch portion in a SHALLOW container (rim of the sheet pan with foil, or a wide tupperware). Thin layers cool fast; deep piles do not.
- Leave the lid OFF or loosely vented while it steams — never seal hot food.
- Aim to drop from hot to room temp within ~90 minutes. Quick-chill trick: set the container on a cool metal tray, or float it in a cold-water bath in the sink for 5 to 10 minutes before fridging.
- Into the fridge (≤40°F) within 2 hours of cooking, 1 hour if the kitchen is warm. Use within 3 to 4 days.
- REHEAT to steaming, 165°F — microwave covered with a splash of water, or covered skillet over medium-low 4 to 5 minutes. Reheat the sauce separately or add a fresh squeeze of lemon after warming.

DISHES TO WASH: sheet pan (parchment lifts out), cutting board, knife, one bowl (sauce/couscous), spoon.

Short answer: put the warm reflection down early as a thin low-chroma glaze; deepen the cool shadow in stages beside it; leave the lit side as paper. Don't try to keep the whole mug "mostly white until the end" — it concentrates too much decision into the final commit and is where overworking usually starts.

Why this works:
  - The mug is really three zones (lit, warm bounce, cool shadow), not one block. Treating it as one is what makes "save it for the end" sound right but actually backfires.
  - The warm bounce is a low-chroma note, so committing to it early is low-risk — paint it with a dilute version of the orange's hue, not the orange itself at full strength.
  - The cool shadow is where the deepest value lives, so it benefits from two thin passes (first wash, dry, second pass only where it needs it) rather than one heavy late commit.
  - Warm down first means the shadow glazes beside a dry edge instead of into wet pigment, so both notes stay readable instead of muddying into each other.

Order for the 75 minutes:
  1. Orange first. It has to read as a clear warm source on the page, or the bounce on the mug will just look like local color.
  2. While the orange is fresh in your eye, lay the thin warm glaze on the bounce side of the mug. Dry completely.
  3. Cool shadow in two staged passes (e.g. ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna, or Payne's gray) starting thin, drying between passes. Keep it adjacent to the dried warm edge, not over it.
  4. Lit side stays as paper — or at most one very thin cool atmospheric wash if the surrounding context needs it.

One thing to watch: the warm glaze wants to be on the mug's shadow side (opposite the window), not on the lit side. If you find yourself wanting to put warmth on the sunlit cheek, that's a tell that the orange needs to come forward more in chroma, not that the mug needs warming.
